title: ‘There’s a lot of silence’: have we created a new ‘Lonely Generation’? | Loneliness | The Guardian
description: Learning to be one human among many has always been a little lonely and discombobulating. But young people around the world are lonelier than ever. Why?
Author: Celina Ribeiro
Headline: Learning to be one human among many has always been a little lonely and discombobulating. But young people around the world are lonelier than ever. Why?
Content: Illustration: Yutthana Gaetgeaw/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenIllustration: Yutthana Gaetgeaw/Getty ImagesLoneliness‘There’s a lot of silence’: have we created a new ‘Lonely Generation’?Learning to be one human among many has always been a little lonely and discombobulating. But young people around the world are lonelier than ever. Why?Celina RibeiroSat 3 Oct 2026 15.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 3 Oct 2026 19.14 EDTShareIn September, a Reddit user identifying themselves as a 25-year-old man turned to the r/ForeverAlone subreddit witha question: How do you deal with touch starvation? “It’s becoming obvious to me that I’ll probably be alone forever,” he wrote. He used to be worried about missing out on sex, but now he just misses hugs. Cuddles.“I don’t have many friends and none with that kind of physical relationship. I don’t really hug family either anymore. Some days, I feel so desperate for a hug with someone I love.”On another thread, a user identifying as a 20-year-old woman took to the platform to ask if anyone else hadexperienced universityas one of the loneliest times in their lives. “I eat lunch alone, go to class, drive home, study, and repeat,” the user wrote. “Evenings and weekends are the hardest because I crave social connection, but there’s no one to go out with or even talk to.”Another user, onanother subreddit thread, expressed that they had tried to ease their unwanted solitude, but failed. “The loneliness is unbearable,” they wrote. “Is anyone else experiencing this” No question mark. No full stop.The answer is yes.Around the world, young people, according to the2025 World Health Organization Social Connection Commissionreport, “feel the loneliest”. Between 17 and 21% of 13-to-29-year-olds report feeling lonely, a greater proportion than any other age group, the report found. Anotherstudy, based on a survey of more than 1 million young people from 38 countries, found that youth loneliness had increased in many regions between 2002 and 2022. FromGermanytoAustraliatothe UK, studies are showing an uptick in loneliness and social isolation among teenagers and young adults.That much of the world has produced a generation in which so many regularly feel unable to meet their needs for social connection is a curiosity which has propelled years of work for Dr Michelle Lim.I’m nearly 30, a virgin and feel lonely. The manosphere is trying to draw me in – where else can I seek assurance? | Leading questionsRead moreThe act of learning to be one human among many has always been a lonely, discombobulating exercise in parts, she says. But in her new book, The Lonely Generation, the loneliness researcher and clinical psychologist examines exactly what has happened over this century to make many young people even lonelier.In short, she writes, “It must be said that the nature of childhood has changed dramatically over the past few decades.”The list of aggravating factors Lim identifies is long: our hyper-competitive education culture, digital technology, the long tail of Covid (“they’re grieving”), the shift towards smaller families, thedecline of third spaces, the high cost of living, hybrid working, hybrid learning, the decline of religion, and the rise of automation which means a trip to the supermarket can be conducted entirely without speaking to another human. Young people, she argues, are being offered fewer and fewer opportunities to form meaningful connections.“What I fear is social atrophy,” she writes. “People are getting used to being alone.”‘Being very busy didn’t protect me’Lim is one of the world’s pre-eminent loneliness scholars. Alongside her work as a psychologist and researcher, she leads the University of Sydney’s School of Public Health’s Social Health and Wellbeing Group, is CEO of the Australian EndingLonelinessTogether campaign, is on a loneliness advisory panel to the World Health Organization and in 2020 cofounded and led the Global Initiative on Loneliness and Connection, which has since expanded to six continents.In The Lonely Generation, she seeks to dispel myths around loneliness and expound on its many individual and societal consequences. But it is in diagnosing the cause of the “crisis” levels of youth loneliness that she spends the most time. And the first among the culprits she identifies is education.“The current education systems are built to prioritise academic excellence from children and adolescents,” she writes. And this focus entails “hidden costs”.After-school tutoring, high-stakes testing and well-intentioned enrolments in extensive extracurricular activities are the hallmarks of a 21st-century education. Lim says that parents tell her: “If I stop, then [my child] will fall behind and I’m not doing the best job I can.”double quotation markSocial media has not been an entirely negative developmentDr Michelle LimHowever, children need rest, free play and empty time in order to practise organic social interactions, says Lim – interactions which are essential to developing their fledgling social skills and a sense of identity outside their family.“The more time you spend studying, it will come at the expense of [other] important skills,” she says. “We run the risk of raising them to be academically strong, but not socially well-equipped to manage the challenges of adulthood.”The idea resonates with Usha Makkena, a 22-year-old student at university in Sydney.“I think when you’re growing up with school, extracurricular activities and then later study and work, a lot of your time can become very structured and goal-oriented,” she says. “Something I realise as I’ve gotten older is that meaningful connection often develops in quite unstructured and almost unproductive times.“And for me, being very busy certainly didn’t protect me from loneliness.”Makkena, who is now a national reference group member for Australian youth mental health charity headspace, first started experiencing loneliness in her late teens, around her last year of high school. She did a lot of extracurricular activities and had an active social life, but she had a persistent feeling of disconnection. “What I was missing wasn’t necessarily having more people around me, but that deeper sense of feeling understood and genuinely connected to people.”Her life did not have the contours of a lonely life. “And I think that can make it harder to recognise,” she says. “When you look at your life and you see all this happening, sometimes it makes you think ‘I shouldn’t be lonely.’”Awkward anywayAt the high-rise campus of the University of Technology Sydney, in the centre of the city, students wander through chatting in pairs, threes. Some, solo, walk or sit with earbuds in and eyes fixed on their phones. Across the flight of stairs in the foyer of the main building are cast the words “MAKE NEW CONNECTIONS”.Nenyasha Dongo has struggled to do as the stairs advise.The Zimbabwean 18-year-old was excited to move to Sydney for her studies. She is a friendly person. She doesn’t want for a huge group of friends, or for parties. Three good friends would do it. But at the end of a day of classes where she didn’t really establish relationships with peers, she would return home to where every one of her five housemates were either out or had retreated to their bedrooms. “There’s a lot of silence,” she says.“When I do get home, the loneliness,” she shakes her head. She would watch movies and TikTok to fill time until she could call family or friends back home. She carried on like this for six months. “You just have to get used to it.”Lonely planet: why are we addicted to the social media scroll when it is so clearly harming us? | Paul DaleyRead moreDongo sits with Mihindi Pathinyake at a table in the sun outside a campus cafe. Around them, students and staff mill in and out. Often what the pair describe might have been a situation transplanted from university halls decades ago; the trepidatious step into a lecture hall, scanning to see who might be open to a greeting by a stranger, watching the one big group of old high school friends chat together in the front row, wondering whether the person you just spoke to might like you, might be interested in hanging out one day.“Just to be clear, young people are just generally awkward,” laughs Lim. “They’re really awkward.”And the transition from school to university, vocational training or work has always been an inflection point for loneliness, Lim says. Individual young people leave their highly structured environment of high school, with a set cast of characters with whom they are familiar and enter a new world populated by new – and often a vastly greater mass of – people. It is also a time when, often, the desire for a great deal of social interaction and a volume of connection is at its highest. Add to this their prefrontal cortex is still developing and adolescence has yet more years to run its course, the period can be one of flux, confusion, self-questioning and, of course, loneliness.But this awkward rite of passage is now charged in a new way, says Lim. “Our young people in this generation are living in a world that is very different.”‘Digital is not the enemy’“You meet new people every day,” says Pathinayake, an exceedingly bright-eyed 20-year-old student from Sri Lanka. But she describes a new social script to developing friendships in 21st century adolescence and young adulthood.“They take your Instagram and then you never talk to them again.”Due to the hybrid online-real life attendance structure to many tutorials and lectures which has proliferated since Covid, it can be difficult to be sure that you may run into the same people with the frequency needed to establish organic connection.“Sometimes following someone or reacting to something that they post can almost be a substitute for reaching out, even though those interactions don’t meet the same need,” says Makkena over a video call in late September. “And then there’s also that element of comparison.“For me, when I was already feeling lonely, constantly seeing other people’s friendship groups or social lives could sometimes create the impression that everybody else had found their people and I somehow hadn’t.”She is, however, wary of narratives which pit technology as the silent assassin of social connection. “It also helped me maintain relationships.”“Social media has not been an entirely negative development”, writes Lim. While the professor is concerned about the dopamine hit from social media blunting the rewards we feel from other interactions and that, for people who are already lonely, it can embed an aversion to real-life connection, her own research has shown it can fortify young people living in communities that don’t accept them, or help others to learn about the world. “Digital use is not the enemy.”View image in fullscreenHowever, she openly imagines (not happily) a future in which her own daughter might tell her that her best friend is an AI avatar. It does not feel like a big leap from what she already sees in her clinical practice, where she might be helping a young person navigate problems in their romantic relationship only to realise they have never met their boyfriend or girlfriend in real life. “It’s really common,” she says.These virtual relationships, whether remote between human beings on separate continents or between human and AI avatar, are lower in the friction typical of in-person relationships, and entirely absent of touch.“Humans are hard,” says Lim. “But that’s actually the beauty of relationships as well. We are being challenged, we are being pushed. Our ability to think more diversely, be empathetic are challenged by other humans.”“Do we run the risk of getting de-socialised with real humans?”The ‘loneliness loop’Anxieties about the decline of social fabric and interaction – particularly for young people – have abounded for decades. Telephones and televisions were derided for their antisocial powers long before the term the “antisocial century” was coined by US writer Derek Thompson.“But there is a sense of feeling unsafe right now, generally, whether it’s political safety around the world, or the lack of community,” says Lim. “It affects the way we see our relationships, the way we relate to people, what we choose to do.”Lim writes about the “loneliness loop” – a particularly nasty trap for young people – by which experiencing loneliness causes the lonely person to perceive social interaction as more threatening, and so they retreat, reduce their social interaction and in doing so become more lonely.But there is a bigger, community-wide loop too. We have settled, she writes, into a social disconnection crisis.Bed rot, doomscrolling and a single goldfish: the Melbourne art show blowing loneliness openRead moreIn The Lonely Generation, Lim imagines a world where social interaction becomes something like exercise has become today: something we once did as part of daily life, but which now we need to make a concerted effort to schedule in our diaries.“We already see this,” says Lim. Paid-for services coming on to the market as apps or activities in order to facilitate human interaction and combat loneliness. Lim herself receives “so many” requests to endorse different offerings.“People are capitalising on that,” she says. “This is not to say that they are not a good thing, but I think that it’s really reflective of the erosion of other kinds of social life that we once had.”Loneliness, particularly youth loneliness, writes Lim, is a signal. A sign that we need to reassess our social world. “There is an ‘us’ problem here.“People just go, ‘well, it’s not my responsibility’. But the problem is, actually everyone’s responsible,” she says.“If everyone says that, then we are going to be living in a world, and raising kids in a world, where healthy social connection is ‘a nice to have’.”

title: The hill I will die on: not everything is a ‘girl’ thing – stop gendering and infantilising it all | Elle Hunt | The Guardian
description: No, I don’t want to go for a girl walk before my girl dinner with my girl mates: I am a grown woman who walks and eats and votes – and, patriarchy, I am on to you, says freelance journalist Elle Hunt
Author: Elle Hunt
Headline: No, I don’t want to go for a girl walk before my girl dinner with my girl mates: I am a grown woman who walks and eats and votes – and, patriarchy, I am on to you, says freelance journalist Elle Hunt
Content: Photograph: Guardian design/AlamyView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Guardian design/AlamyThe hill I will die onWomenThe hill I will die on: not everything is a ‘girl’ thing – stop gendering and infantilising it allElle HuntNo, I don’t want to go for a girl walk before my girl dinner with my girl mates: I am a grown woman who walks and eats and votes – and, patriarchy, I am on to youSat 3 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 3 Oct 2026 13.28 EDTShareThis morning, after waking up with my girl cats, I made myself a cup of girl coffee then got stuck into some girl work. I took a break to lift some girl weights, then sent some more girl emails. Finally, after my girl dinner, it was time to get some sleep ahead of another long, hard day of being a girl.I know what you’re thinking: why is this woman so insistent on gendering her unremarkable activities, and infantilising herself when she is clearly an adult? It’s a fair question. Since the pandemic, when “hot girl walks” followed Megan Thee Stallion’s2019 song Hot Girl Summerto become one of the first big TikTok trends, this framing has become dismayingly ubiquitous, in person and online.Today you might be a “clean girl” (wearing natural-looking makeup) or a “cool girl” (projecting an unbothered image) or a “tomato girl” (pass). To insist that you are an adult woman, however, marks you as a killjoy. This trend infuriates me, to a humourless and even antisocial degree.My self-restraint ran out while on holiday in Paris with my poor sister, whose unwitting proposal of a lighter evening meal sparked a minutes-long tirade from me, stemmed only by the arrival of our charcuterie board. It transpired then that I was just hangry, and I apologised for ranting. On the upside: my sister hasn’t referred to “girl dinner” around me since.I know my response is disproportionate – that it’s only fun, a lighthearted attempt to wring levity from daily mundanity. One could argue that the “girl” trend is an effort to elevate young women, a powerful cultural force that has historically been dismissed (see: pop music). With girls often socialised into taking care of others, some women may be trying to conjure up the playfulness and freedom they felt denied as children.You might also reasonably say: it’s just not that deep. I’d argue, however, that the “girl” trend is far from harmless. For one, it is frequently a Trojan horse for consumerism, with beauty products and fashions prescribed with each new iteration. More importantly, the trend is self-infantilising and insidious, all the more so for seeming so innocuous. In an equal world, sure, grown women could feel free to joke about being just girls, blissfully free from responsibilities such as voting; but at a time when so many are actively working to disenfranchise us, it feels a bit like cooperating.With women’s rights “regressing worldwide”,per the UN, we can’t risk giving ammunition to those who want to take them away; we should be standing firm in our political power and taking every opportunity to express it. Today’s girls are counting on us.Meanwhile, whenever I hear grown women talking about their hot girl walks or clean girl makeup or messy girl desks, I’m reminded of Malibu Stacy, the Barbie-parodying doll from The Simpsons, vacuously trilling “Don’t ask me – I’m just a girl!”. Lisa Simpson, an actual child, didn’t play along, and I shan’t either.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionElle Hunt is a freelance journalistExplore more on these topicsWomenThe hill I will die onGenderMegan Thee StallioncommentShareReuse this content

title: ‘One person turned up at my house’: Russell T Davies on fierce fandom, finding love after grief - and the fear that drives him to keep a knife by the door | Russell T Davies | The Guardian
description: He’s the titan of TV who revived a flatlined Doctor Who and turned British queer life into jaw-dropping drama. But the screenwriter’s groundbreaking writing has sometimes made him a target of hate – from homophobes and Whovians alike
Author: Joe Stone
Headline: He’s the titan of TV who revived a flatlined Doctor Who and turned British queer life into jaw-dropping drama. But the screenwriter’s groundbreaking writing has sometimes made him a target of hate – from homophobes and Whovians alike
Content: Russell T Davies, photographed last month.Photograph: Harry Borden/The GuardianView image in fullscreenRussell T Davies, photographed last month.Photograph: Harry Borden/The GuardianRussell T DaviesInterview‘One person turned up at my house’: Russell T Davies on fierce fandom, finding love after grief - and the fear that drives him to keep a knife by the doorJoe StoneHe’s the titan of TV who revived a flatlined Doctor Who and turned British queer life into jaw-dropping drama. But the screenwriter’s groundbreaking writing has sometimes made him a target of hate – from homophobes and Whovians alike‘Goodbye Whoniverse. God, that was fun!’:Read an exclusive extractfrom Davies’s memoirSat 3 Oct 2026 06.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRussell T Davies is a man who prefers to look on the bright side. That time he was gay-bashed by a gang of bus conductors? “People have been beaten up far worse than me, that was just a bit of a thumping in the street.” When the production schedule of his dystopian dramaYears and Yearsforced him back to work within days of his husband’s death? “Writing was a nice escape.” Even a story about his “tough” father branding him “yesterday’s man” after his initial departure as showrunner on Doctor Who concludes with a cheerful: “I knew I wasn’t.” It’s easy to see how he’s earned a reputation as the most affable man in TV, if not the world. So why has he taken to keeping a kitchen knife by his front door, “ready to use”?“I’m called a paedophile and a groomer online by people like [Father Ted creator and anti-trans activist] Graham Linehan, and now people believe what they read. People believe it when they’re told the Earth is flat,” he says. His support for trans rights has resulted in years of death threats and “groomer” smears, which he used to brush off. “But the online world is becoming the real world. People have worked out my address, and one person turned up at my house. If you believe a paedophile lives here, it’s not the maddest thing in the world to come and get me. I’ve been saying for years that our rights are paper-thin, and here we are. What scares me is that I can’t see an end to it. Nothing is going to unseat these tech barons – it will require some sort of revolution to stop them. So for the first time in history, hatred is being monetised by an algorithm.”Davies, 63, is the great chronicler of queer British life, having made his name with the groundbreaking (and jaw-dropping) Queer As Folk in 1999. The show followed the lives of three gay men in Manchester, and was a surprise hit, but not without its provocations. The Daily Mail wrote that, “Any nation which allows this … [is] hell-bent on destruction.” Among the controversies was its depiction of a one-night stand between Stuart, 29, and Nathan, 15. In today’s climate, where accusations of grooming are regularly levelled at gay men, would he still write such an inflammatory storyline? “I would,” he says. “Although it’s slightly different these days – because in 1999 Nathan would’ve been in school undersection 28[a law banning the ‘promotion’ of homosexuality], meaning that he had no one to talk to. I was trying to say, ‘This is what’s going to happen.’ Of course, Nathan wants to get fucked, and he’s got no one to talk to about it. People say: ‘Oh my God, he was 15, that’s illegal.’ It’s a drama!”View image in fullscreenAidan Gillen and Craig Kelly in an episode of Queer as Folk, 1999.Photograph: Channel 4View image in fullscreenThe Queer as Folk cast and crew, Canal Street, Manchester,  1998.Photograph: Courtesy of Russell T DaviesWe’re meeting to discuss The Queerest of Folk, a galloping memoir of Davies’s life as Britain’s most celebrated showrunner. He’s previouslycriticised the new generation of TV writersfor prioritising positive representation over good storytelling – his own interest lies in the nuances. His most recent drama,Tip Toe, about a simmering feud between neighbours on opposite ends of the political divide that boils into a horrific act of violence, upset some viewers by including a gender-critical character, Stephanie. What inspired her? “I think it’s important to hear all voices. Years and Years and It’s a Sin both had lead gay characters who were Tory voters – if you watch most dramas you’d think those people don’t exist. I know people who are gender critical. The whole argument is so polarised that to some people the fact that she’s gender critical means she might as well be a murderer, which is just nonsense. There are people with genuine concerns, and they need to be discussed. Where is the debate?”Another character, Melba, delivers a powerful monologue about the state of LGBTQ+ rights, with a fleeting reference to ‘‘women who are furious, and with good reason”. What did he mean? “He’s saying maybe on the issue of women’s sports he agrees [with a gender-critical perspective]. We left it vague, but why’s there an assumption that no camp gay man would ever say that? Why’s it a surprise? I could absolutely go out on Canal Street and find you a rightwing drag queen. It’s important to show that. It’s kind of my job to show those complexities.”Davies is a titan of television – and in real life. His 6ft 6in frame fills the doorway of his Swansea home, where he greets me with literal open arms. Inside, I’m gratified to discover that the TV is on; he famously never turns it off, even when he goes out (“My new one turns itself off automatically. I really resent that.”).It continues humming away in the living room while we chat at his dining room table, which features a ceramic Tardis and is overlooked by an original Peanuts cartoon illustration – a rare splurge that cost him £2,000. His parents, both classics teachers, were the same, leaving the TV on even when they had guests.double quotation markDavies was three when he watched William Hartnell  regenerate as the Doctor. ‘That episode is missing from the BBC archives, but it’s burned into my head’View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Harry Borden/The GuardianDespite their “awe” at television, Davies could never quite bring himself to admit to his father that he wrote for it full-time. “My mum said never to tell him that I didn’t have a normal nine-to-five job, because he would just nag me about it, he’d never understand. So until his death he never knew.” In 1991, when Davies quit his job as a children’s TV producer to pursue writing, he omitted to tell his dad, Vivian. “When I’d have dramas on television that I’d written, he’d ask: ‘When did you do that, then?’ And I’d say: ‘In my spare time.’” Vivian was blind for the last 25 years of his life, which could make him quite “angry and result in moments of nastiness which didn’t become him” (hence the “yesterday’s man” comment). One consequence of his blindness was that Davies’s mum had to narrate the action of Queer As Folk to him. Davies prefers not to dwell on this. “Can you imagine her having to describe rimming? I think I gave it to them on Christmas Eve.”His first memory is at three and a half watching the originalDoctor Who, William Hartnell, regenerate. “Someone told me the other day that you don’t have strong memories before the age of six, but that’s not true. That episode is missing from the BBC archives, but it’s burned into my head.” It was an origin story in more ways than one; his biggest triumph came when he successfully lobbied the BBC to relaunch Doctor Who after a 16-year hiatus (today, I notice that even his shower is home to a toy Dalek). During his initial tenure as showrunner, from 2005 to 2010, it became the No 1 show on British television. In June 2009, he decided to leave on a high, moving to Los Angeles where he was commissioned to write Cucumber (about a middle-aged man confronting his gay shame) for Showtime, but declined roles rewriting Skyfall and working on a George Lucas Star Wars project. He later turned down another role writing on a little show called Succession.Then in 2011, Davies’s partner of 12 years, Andrew Smith, started having “hallucinations of an Edwardian lady smiling at him sarcastically”. These turned out to be symptoms of a stage four brain tumour, and Smith was initially given just 18 months to live. In a2007 interview, Davies had said his focus was on his work adding: “If I’m writing, I would walk over [Andrew’s] body if he had a heart attack.” But when Smith fell ill, the opposite turned out to be true. The pair moved back to the UK, and Davies quit work to become Smith’s carer. “I surprised myself. Before that, I’d have thought I wouldn’t be able to do it; I’d hire nurses and get people in and outsource it. But when it comes to it, you realise you don’t want a stranger looking after him.”View image in fullscreenDavies with his late partner, Andrew Smith.Photograph: Courtesy of Russell T DaviesDespite his initial prognosis, Smith lived until 2018. Davies resumed working from their home in Manchester – relocating Cucumber from Seattle to Canal Street and winning best writer at the Bafta Cymru awards for A Very English Scandal, among other projects – but rarely left Smith’s side. “We were together for 20 years, but when I think of him now, I think of the last eight years,” he says, his Welsh boom softening.“Up until that time, we’d never really lived together. From 2011 onwards, the memories are vivid. I remember every day, almost. It’s weird, because there’s intimacy in a life-or-death situation. There was honesty. He lived much longer than expected, and so every year after that became a joy.” After his death, Davies writes that he spent eight years sitting at home. In practice, this meant completing Years and Years, a surprise return as showrunner on Doctor Who, and writing the RoyalTelevisionSociety award-winning It’s a Sin (about the Aids crisis), the Helena Bonham Carter-starring biographical miniseries Nolly (about another of his early obsessions, the Crossroads star Noele Gordon) and Tip Toe, alongside other ventures. Aside from these professional highs, Davies concedes that, “It was a little bit monastic.” Then, once again, his optimism rallies. “But I’m happy watching the telly. It was quiet, but that was fine.”Last year, this relative quiet was broken when Davies met Oliver Cole, a 27-year-old model on Instagram. “I normally ignore DMs, but I looked at his photos and thought, ‘Oh, hello!’” he hoots. “We DMd each other for about three months. Not sexting. I didn’t think it was anything like that, because of his age. But he was such a nice man that I thought I’d have dinner with him. It turned out it was far more than that. He’s lovely.” Cole has since become Davies’s third ever boyfriend. “Isn’t that mad?”I’m curious to know how Davies’s friends reacted to their 36-year age difference. “They were all very polite. I’m absolutely certain behind my back some of them were saying: ‘What the hell?’ But then they met him. He’s quite extraordinary. He’s Australian, and they tend to be quite tough and ahead of the game and know what they think. I was dreading what [Davies’s long-term producer] Nicola Shindler might think. Then she met him and said: ‘Oh! I get it, he’s lovely.’” Did Smith encourage Davies to meet someone else after his death? “He’d be really happy. His doctor was at another hospital when the final scan results came in saying he was going to die. She phoned me and said: ‘I can come to the hospital tomorrow and tell him, or you can.’ Actually, I was honoured to tell him. I thought it was better coming from me than anyone else. And this describes how lovely he was – when I told him, the first thing he said was: ‘I feel sorry for you.’ I found that extraordinary. Nobody knew me better than Andrew, and I think he’d be sad to think of me on my own.”Davies divides his time between houses in Manchester and Swansea, replicas of each other, with the same crockery and Pantone colour mugs (today’s choice is yellow). He’s “saved like a miser”, since the early 90s, when he was told it was impossible for writers to make money. This nest egg allowed him to care for Smith during the years when he didn’t work, but even today he struggles to spend. “I’m still miserly. If I like a shirt that costs £20, a voice says: ‘Can I afford that?’ I get paid a nice wage, but I’ll see something online I like for £30 and think: ‘That’s too much!’” In the late 90s, he went out on Canal Street every night of the week – he met Smith in Cruz 101 nightclub 10 minutes before closing – but these days he’s happiest writing, or in front of the TV, and has a dread of parties. Kate Bush invited him for dinner during his first stint on Doctor Who, but he’s yet to fix a date.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenDavies with his partner, Oliver Cole.Photograph: Dave Benett/Jed Cullen/Getty Images for The National TheatreIn January, Cole persuaded Davies to take his first holiday in 14 years, to New York. “It was lovely,” he smiles. “Although I’m not a natural traveller, I can’t bear airports, they’re horrible.”Last November, Cole posted a video of himself in the Tardis. Is he a Doctor Who fan? “He is, but that takes about five minutes of conversation; it’s not like we sit there discussing [show antagonist] the Rani. When it became a relationship, I reported it to the bosses at Doctor Who, in case anyone tried to say I was abusing my position by going out with a fan.” At its height, the show was drawing a record 13 million viewers, which I suggest represents quite a wide dating pool of fans. “And there’s not many you’d go out with,” he laughs. “You know that’s true!”View image in fullscreenDavies with the cast of It’s a Sin.Photograph: Courtesy of Russell T DaviesIf Davies is ribbingly dismissive of some of the show’s more rabid fandom, then the feeling has become mutual. Twenty-one years after he rocketed Doctor Who to unprecedented heights, his most recent time as showrunner was polarising, with some fans criticising convoluted story arcs and anti-climactic plot resolutions. In June, his exit left the show at a perilous juncture. A Disney+ partnership with the BBC ended after two seasons of disappointing ratings, and the show is now off air while production of future series is put out to competitive tender.Was he wounded by the reaction? “I’m not personally wounded by that,” he says. “I thought it was a shame. And maybe I wonder if I should have done something different. Except I fucking love what I did!” He erupts into guffaws. “I work really hard on my shows, and I genuinely love them. I think there are waves of hatred, and maybe in a few years it’ll be more appreciated. But it’s appreciated by ME!” What does he think it would take to save the show? “Part of the problem is that there seem to be spasms and ruptures and cuts at the BBC. My worry is that there’s nobody there to champion it. You need a producer saying: ‘What about Doctor Who? What about Doctor Who? What about Doctor Who?’ every single day. That’s gone. In 2005, I made it exactly like a 9pm ITV drama, with a lot of the rhythms of everyday life. That concept has gone now, so maybe it’ll end up as a vertical drama [clip shows designed to be watched on a smartphone] with a cliffhanger every two minutes? When it returns, it should be part of whatever the rest of telly is doing.” He won’t be drawn on who he should be the next Doctor. “I’ve made the mistake of saying so-and-so would be good, and the next thing you know, journalists are at their door.”double quotation markHe spoke to Harvey Weinstein about financing. ‘He could’ve solved all our problems, but I couldn’t even bear a phone call with the man. He gave me the shivers’View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Harry Borden/The GuardianFor now, Davies remains a free agent, and you’d be naive to try to predict his next move. After the success of Queer As Folk he immediately alienated a sub-sector of his gay audience by making a romcom, Bob and Rose, in which a gay man falls in love with a woman; when It’s a Sin broke streaming records, he followed it with the not-exactly-timely miniseries about Noele Gordon’s sacking from Crossroads in 1981. In 2015, when the head of BBC drama commissioning paid him a home visit following the ratings hit of his first four series of Doctor Who, Davies leveraged their interest to make his version of A Midsummer Night’s Dream, starring Elaine Paige. He spoke to Harvey Weinstein about providing extra financing, but got the creeps. “I should have been running after the money, he could’ve solved all our problems, but I couldn’t even bear a phone call with the man. He was just baleful, he gave me the shivers. My producer Faith Penhale, who was on the call, might as well not have been. She had the schedules, the budgets – and he just dismissed her.”While his pedigree now affords him a degree of creative freedom, Christmas 2017 found Davies in a position where the BBC had initially turned down Years and Years, while It’s a Sin had originally been rejected by the BBC, ITV and Channel 4 (one executive asked if Davies knew Elton John and suggested that he might be able to turn it into a musical). He says he’s fond of a Tolstoy quote: “The revolutions have to keep on happening.” Only, “I looked it up the other day and there’s no record of him saying that, so maybe I made it up!” Does he feel that he kicks doors open, only  to watch them close again? “You know those slow pneumatic hinges that close automatically? I think that’s what happens. They ‘hisss’ closed slowly.”His ideas gestate for years – decades even – before they’re committed to the page in a flurry (he first had the idea for It’s a Sin more than 30 years ago; one Doctor Who script was written in the course of a weekend). Unusually, his first draft is often his final draft. Bonham Carter has said of Nolly that: “It’s the only time I’ve ever been involved in something that the script that I read ended up immaculately on the screen. There was not one thing cut, not one thing re-ordered.” Davies recently struck upon a fresh idea, and sent the first script to his producer, only for her to remind him that he’d already pitched it to her back in 2018. After the operatic trauma of Tip Toe, he’s hoping to give this one a happy ending. “I’m very excited. These are strange days for telly, so I  hope it gets made.” And if not? “I’ll write something else.” The revolutions will keep happening.The Queerest of Folk: A Life in Television by Russell T Davies, published on 8 October by Transworld at £25. title: ‘Sadness, cynicism and deep disappointment’: the Cornell gang-rape case and the failure of #MeToo | Rape and sexual assault | The Guardian
description: As the university and local police defend their treatment of the alleged perpetrators, women decry a familiar story
Author: Alaina Demopoulos
Headline: As the university and local police defend their treatment of the alleged perpetrators, women decry a familiar story
Content: Local elected leaders, sexual assault survivors and advocates outside the Bronx county courthouse in New York City on Thursday.Photograph: Melissa Bender/NurPhoto/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenLocal elected leaders, sexual assault survivors and advocates outside the Bronx county courthouse in New York City on Thursday.Photograph: Melissa Bender/NurPhoto/ShutterstockRape and sexual assault‘Sadness, cynicism and deep disappointment’: the Cornell gang-rape case and the failure of #MeTooAs the university and local police defend their treatment of the alleged perpetrators, women decry a familiar storyAlaina DemopoulosSat 3 Oct 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 3 Oct 2026 09.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleStudent safety advocates in the US call the start of the fall semester at universities “the red zone”. Fraternities, sororities and off-campus bars throw parties welcoming students back to school. It’s supposed to be fun, but it can also be dangerous: more than 50% of sexual assaults that occur at colleges happen during that six- to 10-week period.It was mid-October of 2024, during the red zone and just before a deluge of Halloween celebrations, when, a former Cornell University student says, she was gang-raped by a group of fraternity brothers. Recent attention on these allegations sparked widespread outrage this week, reviving a contentious national debate about how authorities respond to allegations of sexual assault on US college campuses.The anonymous young woman at the center of the story – known as Jane Doe in court documents – filed a civil lawsuit last month, accusing seven men of plying her with drugs and alcohol and assaulting her over the course of seven hours at their fraternity house. The woman originally went to the house to visit a friend; she claims she arrived intoxicated and willingly took the party drug ketamine with the men. Later, she says, she became incapacitated by the drug, which is a dissociative anesthetic, while the men “commanded” her to keep snorting it.Jane Doe also alleges that the Ivy League university’s ensuing internal investigation was too lenient toward the men. None have ever been charged with a crime. Two were expelled for their misconduct, while five were given lighter punishments: writing an essay, attending a workshop or serving a suspension. Some still attend the school. All seven men denied wrongdoing during Cornell’s investigation.Public outcry over the case reached a breaking point on Thursday, when the New York governor Kathy Hochul stepped in to appoint a new special prosecutor to investigate the incident, which the original district attorney declined to prosecute. Now, state attorney generalLeticia James will decidewhether or not to take the case to a grand jury, which would decide whether there was enough evidence to charge the men with a crime.View image in fullscreenKathy Hochul, the New York governor, during a news conference with state attorney general Letitia James, on Friday in New York City.Photograph: Yuki Iwamura/APIn a statement, Cornell University defended its investigation of the incident. It closed the fraternity chapter involved and barred the group from campus. “We will continue to examine and strengthen our policies to ensure we are doing all we can to foster a culture where sexual misconduct is never tolerated, those who come forward are supported, and individuals found responsible through our processes are held accountable,” the statementread. (Cornell directed the Guardian to this statement when reached for comment.) After intense public pressure, the university agreed to hire external, independent lawyers to investigate whether its handling of the allegations was appropriate.Matthew Van Houten, the Tompkins county district attorney, has said that he did not pursue the case two years ago because the woman’s first account to police did not say that she was drugged, incapacitated or forced into sex. He later said he did not read her full interview, only a shorter statement written by campus police and signed by Jane Doe. Her full statement included the sentence: “I can say with 100 percent confidence that I was raped,” but this did not make it into the final statement sent to Van Houten.In the immediate aftermath of the incident, the womanexchangedfriendly messages with some of the men, expressing concern about rumors that were spreading on campus about the event. She also maintains that the alleged assault began as a consensual encounter. It is common for sexual assault survivors todownplaytheir experiences as a coping mechanism. False rape accusations are incredibly rare.One of the most damning pieces of evidence in the lawsuit involves screenshots of Snapchat messages sent in a fraternity group chat; at one point, an alleged participant named Jonathan Newell referred to Jane Doe as “free pussy”, advertising the alleged assault as it unfolded.What upsets many women most about this case is how normalized such actions seem. About one in four undergraduate women experience sexual violence during college; 60% of rapes involving university studentsinvolveperpetrators who are known to the victims. Last year, a survey of female undergrads at Cornell found that 35% of respondentsexperienced“nonconsensual sexual contact involving physical force, threats of force or incapacitation”. That figure was up from 23% in 2023.“There are so many people in America who find this so familiar,” said Lisa Wade, an associate professor at Tulane and author of American Hookup: The New Culture of Sex on Campus. “Not just the incident itself, but also the response by Cornell.”View image in fullscreenThe Cornell University campus in Ithaca, New York, on Thursday.Photograph: Lauren Petracca/ReutersAs the case plays out in the courts, the so-called “Cornell 7” have become the literal faces of the enduring prevalence of sexual assault on campus, and the institutional failure that allows that behavior to flourish. Their names and images are plastered on social media posts calling for accountability. The Cornell Daily Sun, a student newspaper that has doggedly covered the lawsuit, led the way with an op-ed columntitled“Cornell Won’t, We Will”. The piece began by listing the alleged assailants’ names. “We know who you are and we refuse to let you benefit from this University’s concealment,” wrote the editorial board.A former South Park writer named Toby Mortonlauncheda website detailing the specifics of what Jane Doe alleges each man did to her. Morton wrote on Instagram that he plans to sponsor billboards about the case. The actor Florence Pugh weighed in, pleading on social media for men to be “as horrified and as sickened as us [women]”. Sheaddedthat “college/schools/universities repeatedly fail women around the world [building] men [who] get taught through time and time again that they can do extreme harm and won’t be harmed in return”.When content creator and commentator Michael Tracey threatened to release the name and personal details of Jane Doe – going against decades of established journalistic norms for reporting on alleged rape victims – women flooded TikTok in her defense. The Spartacus-style rallying cry of “I’m Jane Doe” hit feeds, with userssharingstories of their own experiences with sexual assault. “All of us women are jane doe, and we will all continue to ban [sic] together for her,” reads the caption of one clip liked more than 267,000 times.College admissions adviserstoldthe New York Post that some of their high school clients pulled their early decision applications to Cornell because they would not feel safe in the community.This outpouring recalls the early days of #MeToo, a global hashtag campaign against sexual abuse ignited in the wake of initial allegations against convicted rapist and former film producerHarvey Weinstein. But Wade, the Tulane professor, said she sees this case as “metabolizing the failure of #MeToo”, which promised a so-called reckoning in 2017. Ten years later, manosphere influencers teach their followers to see women as sex objects, and Americans re-elected a man who infamously bragged about grabbing women “by the pussy”.Sexual assault survivors have long faced victim-shaming. Jane Doe’s narrative is complicated, and the New York Timesreportedthat the alleged victim did not realize she had been raped until she read someone else describe the event as such on a social media forum; she had texted one of the accused that: “At the end of the day non of the sexual stuff was illegal and honestly i really liked being w u and matt.” This is not an unusual trauma response: it iscommonfor victims to continue relationships with their abusers, as it provides some semblance of control over the situation.But the messy timeline emboldens bad actors and conservative commentators who seek to advance an anti-woman agenda. These young men have not been convicted of a crime, and it would be difficult for prosecutors to convict them of rape due to a New York state legal loophole that does not consider a victim to be incapacitated if she willingly contributes to her own intoxication. (Jane Doe stated she arrived at the fraternity house drunk and willingly took substances with the men, though she also says they coerced her into snorting ketamine.)The Free Press, a vocally “anti-woke” publicationrunby Bari Weiss, chastised the “court of public opinion” for “already puni[shing]” the Cornell 7. Dasha Nekrasova, one of the edgelord hosts of the Red Scare podcast, spent much of this week trying to shame Jane Doe andcallingwomen who are upset over the lack of accountability in this case “deranged”.“There’s a sadness, cynicism and deep disappointment that is also driving the response to this,” Wade said. “#MeToo happened, and nobody cared. Here it is again.”View image in fullscreenA poster at Cornell University on Thursday.Photograph: Lauren Petracca/ReutersElizabeth Armstrong, a professor at the University of Michigan who studies gender inequities in universities, says that there have been “big waves of outrage” over sexual assault on campuses since the 1980s, when Mary Koss first coined the term “date rape”. The last national dialogue took place around 2015, when a Columbia University student carried a mattress around campus for a performance art piece based on her sexual assault.More than a decade later, the issue has only gotten worse. The Trump administration has gutted Title IX protections, which prohibit sex-based discrimination in universities that receive federal funding, and limited the definition of what constitutes sexual harassment under it. Just this week, Trump announced that universities no longer have to investigate assaults on students that take place off-campus. (The Cornell case occurred at a frat house.) “We have an administration that is actively rolling back protections for student survivors,” said Amanda Walsh, deputy director for external affairs at the Victim Rights Law Center.But Walsh, who works closely with survivors, says that gen Z women have much less internalized shame over their assaults than previous generations, who were often taught that women invite sexual assault through their actions. “It feels like the focus has shifted away from talking about what the woman did, and more appropriately to exploring the behavior of the men involved,” she said. “I always admire how much they focus on the behavior of the person who harmed them, rather than asking: ‘What could I have done differently? Why did this happen to me? I see college students really pushing back against that.”The Cornell case has revived discussions on abolishing Greek life, the student social club system that is behind fraternities and sororities in the US. This week, a Vogue article called for universities to “ban frats once and for all”. It’s not unprecedented: the Pennsylvania liberal arts collegeSwarthmoredid so in 2019, after campus publications leaked racist, sexist and homophobic documents written by fraternities. “That would be a really real change, but I doubt that will happen,” said Armstrong.Elizabeth Allan, who leads the Hazing Prevention Research Lab at the University of Maine, added: “It’s important for everyone [in Greek life] to think how these groups might reflect larger societal norms and expectations and the ways in which [bad] behavior is reinforced.”Most of all, Walsh worries how all the attention on this case will affect Jane Doe, and the countless other anonymous victims who are sure to come after her. “I’ve been in this field long enough to know that however much support she receives is exactly how much negativity she’ll get on the other side,” Walsh said. “At this point, with the political moment and online response, it almost feels like supporting a survivor of sexual violence feels political or partisan, which is wild.”Explore more on these topicsRape and sexual assaultUS universitiesUS justice systemLaw (US)featuresShareReuse this content

title: What is Zionism and why do some critics describe it as racist? | Israel | The Guardian
description: Green party debate over the motion ‘Zionism is racism’ comes amid renewed arguments over the meaning and history of a contested term
Author: Peter Beaumont
Headline: Green party debate over the motion ‘Zionism is racism’ comes amid renewed arguments over the meaning and history of a contested term
Content: Zack Polanski has described himself as an anti-Zionist as his party prepares to debate the motion at its conference.Photograph: Sean Smith/The GuardianView image in fullscreenZack Polanski has described himself as an anti-Zionist as his party prepares to debate the motion at its conference.Photograph: Sean Smith/The GuardianIsraelExplainerWhat is Zionism and why do some critics describe it as racist?Green party debate over the motion ‘Zionism is racism’ comes amid renewed arguments over the meaning and history of a contested termPeter BeaumontSat 3 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleZack Polanski, the leader of the Green party, has said he is ananti-Zionist. As his party conference prepares to debate a motion that “Zionism is racism”, what precisely is Zionism and what is the history of the claim that it is racist?What is Zionism?Modern Zionism developed in the late 1800s out of several strands of thinking on the future of Jewish collective and cultural identity, emerging from a millennia-old religious yearning to return to Zion, which runs through Jewish holy texts. The term came, however, to be most associated with Theodor Herzl’s brand of political Zionism, the movement for Jewish self-determination and statehood in the context of rising European antisemitism.Although Zionism tends to be seen by critics as a monolithic political idea, its history has encompassed multiple, often contradictory, intellectual strands including the notion – proposed by the philosopher Martin Buber before the foundation of Israel – of a binational Arab-Jewish state in Palestine.Since the foundation of the state of Israel in 1948, the debate over Zionism inside the country has largely centred on liberal and rightwing, or “revisionist”, camps – the latter represented by Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party. Issues such as settlement, occupation and whether Israel should be defined as an ethno-nationalist Jewish state moved to the core of political contest.However, as Dov Waxman, a professor of Israel studies at the University of California,wrote in the Conversation last month, the issue is further complicated by the fact that, despite contested definitions, the idea of Zionism for many Jews represents something more amorphous: “Jewish liberation and sovereignty, a safe haven from persecution, a revival of the Hebrew language, and a renewed sense of collective pride, especially after the Holocaust.”What is the criticism of Zionism?One critique of Zionism – used as a shorthand for the state of Israel – is that it is a “colonial” project.Those critics, in parts of the left, in the wider Arab world and among some anti-Zionist Jews such as Polanski, would point to three pieces of evidence. First, the violent displacement of Palestinians during the Nakba, or “catastrophe” for Palestinians, that accompanied the founding of the Jewish state.Second, they argue Israel has created an apartheid system of unequal rights in the occupied territories that denies Palestinian ambitions to statehood and their own self-determination and, third, that within Israel those of Palestinian origin are discriminated against.Before the establishment of Israel in 1948, Palestinians had a vibrant society across British Mandatory Palestine, but their connection to historical Palestine has often been dismissed or diminished by significant strands of Zionist thinking.At the heart of academic debate is how widespread the use by some early Zionists was of the notion of a “land without people” for a “people without land”, which critics have used as evidence that Zionism was a colonial enterprise at its very beginning.In contrast, Zionists point to the evidence of a historical presence of Jews in the Holy Land, as well as for many a promised biblical patrimony in a homeland from which Jews were displaced and that many hold up as a refuge in a hostile world.What is the history of the claim that ‘Zionism is racism’?The argument that Zionism is racism, while controversial, is not new. The phrase came to particular prominence during the cold war, when the UN passed resolution 3379 in 1975. The so-called“Zionism as racism” resolutioncompared “the racist regime in occupied Palestine” to apartheid South Africa. Sponsored’ by the Arab League and promoted by the Soviet Union, it passed with support from countries in the developing world but was later revoked in 1991 under pressure from the then US president, George HW Bush.Proponents of the argument say Zionism privileges the rights of Jews in Israel over non-Jews via a discriminatory system. Opponents of the framing describe it as antisemitic as it singles out Jews as a group to deny them alone the right to self-determination. They argue that, by delegitimising the basis for Israel’s founding as a Jewish homeland, it acts as a cover for antisemitism.The war in Gaza has intensified arguments about the nature of Zionism, in part driven by the overtly racist framing of senior Israeli political figures towards Palestinian society after the 7 October deadly Hamas attack on southern Israel in 2023.What does British law say about the argument that Zionism is racist?An employment tribunal two years agofound that the views of David Miller, a former professor of political sociology who was sacked by the University of Bristol in 2021, that “Zionism is and always has been a racist, violent, imperialist ideology premised on ethnic cleansing” amounted to a protected philosophical belief under the 2010 Equality Act, a case upheld on appeal.A highly controversial figure, Miller has also argued in social media posts that Zionists have worked as “infiltrators and subversives”, gained access to not just all UK political parties but also “the media, entertainment industries, the law, financial institutions, sports and all sorts of apparently obscure parts of the UK”.Miller is a key figure in the anti-Zionist Movement and has links to Greens for Palestine, which is proposing the Green party motion on Zionism is racism.Explore more on these topicsIsraelGreen partyZack PolanskiPalestineAntisemitismMiddle East and north AfricaexplainersShareReuse this content

title: ‘People are deserting it’: why are London mansions struggling to sell? | Property | The Guardian
description: For decades, the capital’s house prices raced ahead of the national average – but now they are falling in prime areas
Author: Lauren Almeida
Headline: For decades, the capital’s house prices raced ahead of the national average – but now they are falling in prime areas
Content: Egerton Crescent was named Britain’s most expensive street in the 2010s.Photograph: Diego Garcia/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenEgerton Crescent was named Britain’s most expensive street in the 2010s.Photograph: Diego Garcia/Getty ImagesProperty‘People are deserting it’: why are London mansions struggling to sell?For decades, the capital’s house prices raced ahead of the national average – but now they are falling in prime areasLauren AlmeidaSat 3 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 3 Oct 2026 02.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAn elegant Georgian facade, a full-width balcony and an exclusive address in South Kensington just steps from the Natural History Museum and the V&A. Yet the listing price of thiswest London flatat Queen’s Gate Gardens has dropped by nearly £1m since last year, to £4.4m.It is far from an isolated case. A nearby house originally listed at £20m was slashed to £14m this year, says a local estate agent. In neighbouring Notting Hill, a stucco-fronted property that came to market two years ago at £16m is now being offered for less than £14m, they said.London’s premium property market is stuck in a rut. While borrowing costs and stretched affordabilityweigh on everyday buyers, the city’s richest residents are also making deep cuts to the prices of their multimillion-pound homes.This market is a world away from the rest of the UK property market – where the average house price wasjust under £275,000 in September, according to Nationwide. The well-heeled neighbourhoods also present a stark contrast with much of the capital, where Londoners struggle to get on to the housing ladder, facerising rentsand a lack of affordable housing, and estate agents report themarket for flats is now “dead”.But neighbourhoods such as Knightsbridge, bordering Hyde Park and home to Harrods, are also feeling the pinch, said Harry Dawes, a buying agent based in Belgravia.“There is a flat on Pont Street, a five-minute walk from Harrods, which sold at £4.4m in 2014, then sold at £3.5m. It can now be bought at £2.5m.”View image in fullscreenWilton Crescent in Belgravia. The area has experienced a pronounced drop in prices.Photograph: Mike Kemp/In Pictures/Getty ImagesDeflating the bubbleFor decades, London’s property prices raced ahead of the national average. But that gap has been slowly narrowing: while the average price of a UK home rose by about 2% in the year ended in June, prices in innerLondonboroughs fell by 8.3%, according to the Office for National Statistics.That drop has been particularly pronounced in Westminster – which includes areas such as Marylebone, Belgravia and Mayfair – with prices down 25.4% year on year. In the City, prices slumped by 20.4%, and in Kensington and Chelsea, prices fell 14.7%.Graph of residential greater London and prime central London pricesProperties in the capital became overvalued in the mid-2010s after a period of rapid price growth, said Anthony Payne, the chief executive of the data analyst LonRes. London was then hit hard by Brexit, the Covid pandemic, higher property taxes and a surge in borrowing costs.Now, owners who bought at the peak now face losses of as much as 25% if they choose to sell, according to estimates from the estate agent Savills.“London benefited dramatically from international investment and buyers wanting property here as a store of wealth and a way of making money,” Payne said. “These are the people that inflated the market, but now more and more of them are deserting it.”Jeremy Gee, the managing director at the super-prime estate agent Beauchamp Estates – whose portfolio includes a £42m sub-penthouse overlooking Hyde Park – said the decline had also been driven partly by the exit of super-wealthy groups from the UK, especially after the abolition of the non-dom tax regime.“There is a section of society who have left the UK recently for lots of reasons, but mainly because of tax,” he said.View image in fullscreenPrices have also taken a hit in areas such as Notting Hill.Photograph: Christian Sinibaldi/The Guardian“When there are not that many buyers and lots of properties, the prices are going to be softer. Many of our sellers have decided that enough is enough – let’s just sell the property and move on.”Tax changes have put sellers on edge, too, he added. Last year, the former chancellor Rachel Reeves announced plans for a“mansion tax” on homes worth more than £2m.This nervousness has triggered a slowdown across the higher tiers of London’s market. Prime properties spent an average of 186 days on the market in the first half of 2026, up from 178 days in the first half of 2025, according to LonRes. Over the same period, the average discount to asking price widened from 8.3% to 10.4% – sellers have grown more likely to accept lowball offers.Sellers, who normally own these properties for at least a decade, “don’t like it but have to accept it,” said Dawes.“If they are older, they have to take a lifetime view on their property and accept that from a profit and loss perspective, this last trade might not look good.“We bought three flats for a client’s kids last year – two in Chelsea and one in Notting Hill – and every seller was selling at a loss.”Chart of prime London property values for 2025 compared with previous peaksA divided marketEven with multimillion pound discounts propping up on the market, Stuart Bailey, the head of super-prime London sales at the estate agent Knight Frank, said there were still buyers willing to pay above the asking price for “the very best in class” properties.“A fabulous address, lovely views, immaculate style and newly refurbished,” he said. “It is a matter of premium or discount, retail or trade, brand new or not, and there is nowhere in between. It’s the discounted properties dragging the market down.“Sellers are more and more realistic about moving on,” he added. “They do not see material price growth on the horizon.”“With a Labour government the concern is always that there’s going to be some kind of wealth tax somewhere,” he said.View image in fullscreenProperties near Hyde Park are reported to have been sold at a loss.Photograph: Andrew Michael/Alamy“But many wealthy people also just accept the cost of taxation and that London is simply an expensive city to live in.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionCamilla Dell, a buying agent, said demand is still strong from a wide base of international buyers, including Americans, Singaporeans and Nigerians. Politics, she said, rarely comes up in conversation.“Most people accept that the UK does not have the best political stability but they want to live here,” she said. “And actually, it helped that Andy Burnham ruled out an overhaul of property taxes in the next budget.”Chart of prime residential capital value growth in first half of 2026Sluggish prices in London are in stark contrast with the likes of San Francisco and Lisbon (a hub for Europe’s digital nomads). Both cities have benefited from booming wealth in the tech sector, with prices rising by 4.8% and 3.3%, respectively, in the first half of this year. Tokyo has been the global standout, with prices up 7% as international buyers have swooped on a weak yen and snapped up luxury properties already in low supply.Berlin’s prime market, which was the worst performer in Europe, has suffered under the weight of rising borrowing costs and meagre economic growth.London’s trophy homesWhile the multimillionaires’ tier of the property market is being squeezed, the billionaire “super-prime” end of the market is buzzing with activity.This year, billionaire Reform donorNick Candysold his Chelsea home for more than £270m, which is believed to the UK property market’s biggest single house sale in history. Meanwhile, the Holme, the 40-bedroom mansion inside Regent’s Park, is reportedly nearing a £190m sale, less than two years after it was sold for £139m in 2024.View image in fullscreenThe Holme, a 40-bedroom mansion inside Regent’s Park, is reportedly nearing a £190m sale.Photograph: Greg Balfour Evans/Alamy“There have been some very big transactions in super-prime – those are people buying long-term family homes and trophy assets,” Dawes said.For agents, their cut on these deals – typically about 2% – canrun into the millions, and business is thriving. The sale of homes priced at £10m or more climbed 50% in the three months ended in June, compared with the same quarter in 2025, according to the property developer JLL. Meanwhile, Savills found that transactions in the £15m to £20m bracket rose by almost 40%, also in the second quarter of this year compared with last.The rise of newly minted multimillionaires from the world of tech and social media is driving new renovation trends, too – with more calls for home cinemas, steam rooms, saunas and dedicated yoga and meditation spaces, according to the interior designer Nu Projects.Still, many of the wealthy are waiting on the sidelines. Beauchamp says that seven out of 10 of its ultra-prime clients are now choosing to rent rather than buy, because they want to save on maintenance, stamp duty, service charges and property taxes – as well as anxiety over whether the government will introduce higher taxes on property, wealth and pensions.It is pushing prime rental stock into scarce supply. Prices in this market rose 1.6% in the year ended in June, according to Savills. Super-expensive tenancies, where tenants hand over at least £5,000 a week – were up 17% last year, according to Knight Frank.View image in fullscreenHouses and mansion blocks in Hill Street, Mayfair. Some wealthy people are choosing to rent rather than buy in an uncertain market.Photograph: Steve Vidler/AlamyA buyers’ marketSuch intense competition for “best in class” properties mean that even in a fragile market, the most discerning buyers can still face stiff competition, advisers said.“There’s still demand from overseas buyers who want to buy best-in-class trophy assets,” Gee says. “American and Middle Eastern buyers are underpinning that market.“But then there is everything beneath that. Anything secondhand, needing a bit of work, where you might normally find a domestic buyer, that is where it is a bit stickier.”The outlook for the broader prime market remains less rosy. The estate agent Strutt & Parker has downgraded its forecast for prime central London price growth to 4.4% by 2030, compared with an estimate of 9% to 12% at the start of the year.For now, the balance of power remains with buyers in London, Payne said.“I look at some of the stuff that’s coming on the market and you just think to yourself, ‘My God, this is such unbelievably good value’,” he added.“Hand on my heart, I do not think we are at the bottom of the market yet.”Explore more on these topicsPropertyHouse pricesReal estateLondonHousing marketThe super-richTax and spendingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Ministers drop plans to cut jury trials in England and Wales after outcry  | UK criminal justice | The Guardian
description: Critics say scrapping of plans, which aimed to increase judge-alone trials to deliver swifter justice, leaves court system and victims vulnerable
Author: Haroon Siddique
Headline: Critics say scrapping of plans, which aimed to increase judge-alone trials to deliver swifter justice, leaves court system and victims vulnerable
Content: The justice secretary Alex Norris, pictured at Westminster Abbey’s annual judges’ service, said he had changed course after hearing ‘the strength of feeling on the proposals’.Photograph: Jordan Pettitt/PAView image in fullscreenThe justice secretary Alex Norris, pictured at Westminster Abbey’s annual judges’ service, said he had changed course after hearing ‘the strength of feeling on the proposals’.Photograph: Jordan Pettitt/PAUK criminal justiceMinisters drop plans to cut jury trials in England and Wales after outcryCritics say scrapping of plans, which aimed to increase judge-alone trials to deliver swifter justice, leaves court system and victims vulnerableHaroon SiddiqueLegal affairs correspondentSat 3 Oct 2026 19.01 EDTLast modified on Sat 3 Oct 2026 19.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMinisters have scrapped plans that would have slashed the number of jury trials inEnglandand Wales and replaced them with a judge sitting alone.The proposals had sparkeda fierce backlash from lawyers, who have welcomed the U-turn. But the victims’ commissioner expressed concern about the abandonment of measures drawn up by the then justice secretary, David Lammy, under Keir Starmer’s government, to tackle the record backlog in the courts.There are almost 81,000 cases in the crown courts – with the number projected to hit 100,000 without the now-ditched changes – leaving victims and defendants waiting years for justice. The Ministry of Justice is selling the U-turn as a quicker way to address the problem, by saving the time it would take to set up a new judge-only crown court bench division.Jury-free trials proposed to save criminal justice system from collapseRead moreThe justice secretary,Alex Norris, said: “This government inherited criminal courts on the brink of collapse, with victims waiting years for their day in court. I remain committed to bringing down the backlog and delivering swifter justice for those who so desperately need it. But I have heard the strength of feeling on the proposals for increasing the number of judge-alone trials in the crown court and have made the decision to change course.“This allows us to start that work far earlier, ensuring that under this government we do not have victims waiting endlessly for justice.“Justice delayed is justice denied, and I am committed to maximising efficiencies in our system alongside record investment.”View image in fullscreenSir Brian Leveson proposed jury-free trials to save the criminal justice system from collapse.Photograph: Karl Black/AlamyLammy’s proposals came after a government-commissioned review by the former judge, Sir Brian Leveson, whorecommendedtaking away the right to jury trial from thousands of defendants to prevent the criminal justice system from collapsing.But critics, includingGeoffrey Robertson, founding head of Doughty Street Chambers, where Starmer, Lammy and the attorney general, Richard Hermer KC, spent part of their professional careers, accused Labour of abandoning a centuries-old right and claiming that itwould not reduce the backlogsubstantively. Some Labour MPs alsoopposed the move.Founder of Starmer’s legal chambers condemns Labour plans to cut jury trialsRead moreLegislation would have removed jury trials for defendants who were likely to receive a sentence of up to three years.Ministers have not abandoned judge-only trials altogether, but they will only be for a small number of especially lengthy and technical fraud cases where the judge decides a jury trial is not appropriate.The government will also retain Lammy’s plans to take away the right of a defendant charged with an “either way” offence to decide whether they will be tried by a jury in the crown court or magistrates. Instead those decisions will be in the hands of magistrates.And the planned increase in magistrates’ sentencing powers – from the current 12 months maximum to 18 months, with an option to extend to two years – will still go ahead.Kirsty Brimelow, chair of the Bar Council of England andWales, welcomed the new government’s “swift action” but said: “We underline that it is a dangerous experiment to increase sentencing powers of magistrates and remove the right to elect from defendants at a time when prisons are at capacity and the backlog of cases is accelerating in the magistrates courts.She added: “We know that women, black people, mixed race people and older people elect jury trials more often than other groups and this proposal risks deepening existing disparities and exacerbating distrust in the justice system from minoritised communities.”The Law Society of England and Wales and the Criminal Bar Association also welcomed the change of heart while expressing concern about pushing more cases to magistrates. The former additionally called for more investment, including in legal aid.View image in fullscreen‘Victims need hope,’ said Claire Waxman, the victims’ commissioner.Photograph: Linda Nylind/The GuardianThe victims’ commissioner, Claire Waxman, said: “Victims are entitled to ask whether what remains will be enough to meet the challenge [of delivering swifter justice]. “Indeed, they are being asked to place their faith in a plan that ministers themselves previously argued would not be.“The lessons from the prisons crisis should be clear: postponing difficult decisions rarely solves problems. More often, it simply stores them up for the future.“Victims need hope. They need to know this is genuine reform that matches the scale of the challenge: reform that will alleviate their prolonged suffering, rather than an easy compromise that delivers only marginal improvements today while leaving both the justice system, and the victims who rely on it, vulnerable tomorrow.”The courts minister, Sarah Sackman KC, said other steps to tackle the backlog could include using AI to help list cases, more virtual hearings and ensuring defendants arrive to court on time.Explore more on these topicsUK criminal justiceEnglandWalesLabourAlex NorrisDavid LammyRichard HermernewsShareReuse this content

title: Tories plan to extend cuts beyond £47bn previously pledged, leak reveals | Conservatives | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith told party members last year he had discussed making further savings if they win next election
Author: Kiran Stacey
Headline: Exclusive: Shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith told party members last year he had discussed making further savings if they win next election
Content: Andrew Griffith’s comments suggest the Conservatives are planning to make cuts similar in scale to those made during the austerity years.Photograph: Leon Neal/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAndrew Griffith’s comments suggest the Conservatives are planning to make cuts similar in scale to those made during the austerity years.Photograph: Leon Neal/Getty ImagesConservativesTories plan to extend cuts beyond £47bn previously pledged, leak revealsExclusive: Shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith told party members last year he had discussed making further savings if they win next electionKiran StaceyPolicy editorSat 3 Oct 2026 11.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Conservatives are planning to make sweeping cuts beyond the£47bn announced last yearif they win the next election, according to leaked comments by the shadow chancellor.Speaking last year when he was shadow business secretary, Andrew Griffith told Conservative members he and fellow shadow cabinet ministers had discussed making further cuts in “every part of government”.The comments, which have emerged on the eve of the Tory party conference in Birmingham, suggested that theConservativesare planning to make cuts similar in scale to those made during the austerity years should they take power.More than a fifth of UK’s ‘austerity children’ scarred by poverty, study saysRead moreLast October, Griffith said: “There are decisions made and signed up to by everybody to deliver that £47bn. Last week at the shadow cabinet, we talked about [how] we will need to go further.“The rate at which the economy is deteriorating, as well as our ambition to cut more taxes, means that we will have to find further savings, and I’m up for that in my department. I know there are areas that we can make savings, and that’s true of every every part of government.”He added: “There is a moral mission to get our economy growing, give people opportunity, as well as let people keep more of what they earn. It’s pretty simple.
