We’re Conservative, this is what we stand for.”A Tory spokesperson acknowledged the party was seeking to make cuts beyond what it had already announced.“Under Kemi Badenoch’s leadership, the Conservatives have consistently advocated for a smaller state and a government that does fewer things but better,” the spokesperson said.“InBirmingham, we will go further, setting out further savings to Labour’s bloated welfare bill and cracking down on wasteful spending as part of our plans to build a stronger economy and a stronger country.”Kemi Badenoch has previously outlined how the government wouldcut government spendingby £47bn, mainly by cutting welfare spending for all non-British or EU citizens.The plans would also save £8bn by cutting 132,000 civil service jobs, another £1.6bn by scrapping almost all of Labour’s clean energy scheme and more than £7bn by cutting international aid.In August she promoted Griffith, who previously worked as chief operating officer for Sky, from his role as shadow business secretary.In government, Griffith worked in the Treasury under Kwasi Kwarteng and was one of the ministers tasked with defending the mini-budget even as the markets tanked in response.On Friday Badenoch promised another £4bn of spending reductions, including taking another £2.5bn out of the aid budget – leaving it with just £1bn as year – as well as reducing the budget of the Department for Culture, Media and Sport by £1bn.The Tory leader said she would use half of those savings to pay for an additional 50,000 prison places. She has previously promised to use half of any cuts she makes to reduce the deficit.Griffiths’ leaked comments come as the Tories prepare to gather in Birmingham for their annual conference, with Badenoch seeking to make a virtue of the growing distance between Labour’s plans for government and her own.The prime minister, Andy Burnham, has promised a series of potentially expensive interventions, including a new national care service and public control over utility companies, as he seeks to end what he calls “40 years of neoliberalism”.However, Badenoch, who has calledMargaret Thatcherher hero, is attempting to gain an electoral advantage with her vision of lower taxes and a significantly smaller state.“[Thatcher] is somebody who brought a lot of wealth and prosperity to this country,” the Tory leader told ITV Meridian on Friday.“Privatisation was a success … I don’t think that Andy Burnham running the water companies is the answer to those problems.”The Tories remain in third place in the polls, behind Labour and Reform UK, although Badenoch’s personal ratings have rallied over the last 12 months.Explore more on these topicsConservativesConservative conferenceAusterityPublic sector cutsLabourMargaret ThatcherBirminghamnewsShareReuse this content

title: OpenAI safety leader quits, warning AI company’s culture is ‘broken’ | OpenAI | The Guardian
description: David Robinson joins other insiders in urging industry to take more care over rapidly developing technology
Author: Dan Milmo
Headline: David Robinson joins other insiders in urging industry to take more care over rapidly developing technology
Content: David Robinson said AI firms were not ‘being nearly careful enough’ about developing the technology.Photograph: Dado Ruvić/ReutersView image in fullscreenDavid Robinson said AI firms were not ‘being nearly careful enough’ about developing the technology.Photograph: Dado Ruvić/ReutersOpenAIOpenAI safety leader quits, warning AI company’s culture is ‘broken’David Robinson joins other insiders in urging industry to take more care over rapidly developing technologyDan MilmoSat 3 Oct 2026 15.41 EDTLast modified on Sat 3 Oct 2026 16.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA safety leader atOpenAIhas quit the company, warning that its culture was broken and that AI firms were not “being nearly careful enough” about developing the technology.David Robinson, who led the writing of safety reports that accompanied the ChatGPT developer’s product releases, explained his resignation in an essay headlined, “I quit OpenAI because its culture is broken”.Robinson wrote that a cultural overhaul was needed at cutting-edge AI firms and incidents such as a “swarm” of OpenAI agents – AI programmes operating autonomously without human oversight –attacking the AI startup Hugging Facewere “typical of the industry, given the speed and flexibility with which people operate”.Writing inThe Atlantic magazine, Robinson wrote: “I agree with other recently departed staff that the companies building this technology aren’t being nearly careful enough. But I believe that we need to look deeper than specific rules or new laws. We need to talk about culture.”Referring to OpenAI’s pace of development, he wrote: “As the company sprints from one launch to the next, it is failing to achieve the level of care that I believe is needed.”OpenAI has, however, shown signs of caution in recent weeks following the Hugging Face incident and the revelation that it has notified more than 100 organisations about rogue agent activity. This week it announced it wasscrapping the release of a next-generation ⁠AI modelafter researchers raised safety concerns ⁠during internal testing. OpenAI hasalso paused trainingof its most advanced models.Geoffrey Irving, who worked at OpenAI and DeepMind before becoming chief scientist of Resolution, also joined the warnings on AI on Saturday.Writing in Time, he said: “Recent warnings about the potential destructive power of AI are understating the severity of the situation.“I believe there’s about a 50% chance we all die because of the development of smarter-than-human AI systems, and that our actions over the next two to 10 years will determine the outcome.”Robinson’s essay also follows the resignation of Jacob Coxon, a researcher at OpenAI rival Anthropic, who quit the Claude chatbot developer last month. He warned AI “could kill us all by the end of the decade” – and wasfollowed by Anthropic warningthere was a more than 10% chance AI would wipe out humanity within the next decade. Critics of such warnings have cautioned, however, that they areunscientificbecause they cannot be verified or falsified.Robinson wrote Silicon Valley lacked an awareness of “how to handle dangerous technology” and “what it means to care for people”. Warning that OpenAI had “unimpeded optimism” about solving problems as they arose, he wrote that this internal culture meant safety failures would only grow as systems become more capable.“Imagine ‘rogue’ agents that work like teams of hackers (for example, holding hospital computer systems for ransom) but never need to sleep,” wrote Robinson.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionRobinson called for two safety changes: that AI firms rely on safety expertise in other fields such as nuclear and aviation and develop “new science” that ensures powerful systems in the future are capable of being reined in when they are operating autonomously.“Given today’s risks, frontier labs need to run like nuclear-power plants or busy airports, with layers of redundancy and careful, time-consuming planning, so that the occasional and inevitable human error does not open a door to disaster,” he wrote.An OpenAI spokesperson said the company was continuing to “strengthen our safety and security practices to address the risks we see today”, while working on dealing with the risks that might be created by future AI breakthroughs.“We’re making sure our models don’t become more capable than we can safely manage and secure, and we pause training or hold back models when we need to slow down,” said the spokesperson.Explore more on these topicsOpenAIAI (artificial intelligence)ComputingData and computer securityEthicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘He feels more relatable’: Burnham’s conference speech wins praise from drifting Labour voters | Andy Burnham | The Guardian
description: The UK prime minister has earned his party a rehearing but the battle of public opinion is not yet won
Author: Luke Tryl
Headline: The UK prime minister has earned his party a rehearing but the battle of public opinion is not yet won
Content: The UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, spoke emotionally at the conference about the death of his father.Photograph: Michael Bowles/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenThe UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, spoke emotionally at the conference about the death of his father.Photograph: Michael Bowles/ShutterstockAndy Burnham‘He feels more relatable’: Burnham’s conference speech wins praise from drifting Labour votersThe UK prime minister has earned his party a rehearing but the battle of public opinion is not yet wonLuke TrylSat 3 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 3 Oct 2026 08.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“He’s offering what no other politician has offered for a long, long time. He actually feels like he’s one of us,” was how Neil, a geography teacher, describedAndy Burnhamin our focus group on Thursday night.Neil wasn’t alone in his praise: this group ofLabour2024 voters – some of whom had drifted to Reform, the Tories and Greens during the Starmer era – provided the most positive reception for a politician since Boris Johnson at the height of his Covid-vaccine bounce.Talent manager Megan said: “He feels more relatable to people from a working–class background.” Simran, another teacher, added: “He’s obviously better than the others in the short timeframe that he’s been in his position.” Linda, who works in banking, went further, saying: “He actually sounds like a person that’s there, not just for himself, but for all of us, which none of the others prior to him came across that way.”That praise for Burnham stood in stark contrast to his predecessor Keir Starmer who was, as contracts manager Craig put it, “just a shambles from the moment they won the election up until he left”. None of the group felt it would have been better to keep the former PM in place.Labour’s conference also seemed to have cut through the noise of the attention economy. Most had picked up at least something from the prime minister’s speech and liked what they had heard. After seeing the clip where Burnham spoke emotionally about the death of his father, the group, in contrast to some online criticism, appreciated a politician willing to show his human side.But what about two of the substantive proposals in the speech?On Burnham’s pledge to revisit the UK’s relationship with the EU there was an overwhelming feelingBrexithad been a disaster. Most in this group had voted to remain, but even those like Darren, a field manager at a utility company who had voted Leave, felt cheated: “The amount we got told we were putting into the EU, I thought we could stand on our own two feet … we got told quite a few things, and it didn’t quite happen.”Interestingly, for most of the group it was less the economic impact of Brexit that worried them but instead the sense of isolation in an increasingly dangerous world and a less reliable US.But, and here is the caveat, once it came to the specifics of what rejoining may involve the group were far more cautious. Many felt if Britain could rejoin on its old terms it would be a “no brainer”. But the participants now worried that Britain would end up with a worse deal as punishment.Neil said: “I voted remain, but we’ll get utterly shafted if we rejoin … what do they gain?” Others described feeling 50/50 and nervous about where we’d end up. If this group is anything to go by, Burnham’s biggest fight won’t be in the principle but the details.What about Burnham’s other, more controversial, pledge that the triple lock would be reformed to pay for social care? The discussion here revealed two things. First the rise in wages is less salient to people than other bits of the lock; most of the group felt as if their wages had not kept up with inflation for a long time anyway, so pensioners would not really lose out. As Linda put it: “My salary has not been increasing that greatly.”Second, reforming care is a real priority. For Tariq, who works in the pharmaceutical industry, this was an example that “sometimes you need to take hard decisions”.But the mood definitely shifted when the group were played a clip from Unite leader, Sharon Graham, opposing the move. Suddenly some participants worried this was “taking off pensioners” while others asked “couldn’t the highest earners fund it instead”.And the group were even more negative when they read former Institute for Fiscal Studies chief Paul Johnson’s analysis that triple lock reform wouldn’t pay for a national care service in the near term and so taxes would have to rise.None of the group were willing to pay more taxes, personally, for care. Simran said: “If the income tax increases any more, you’re going to find people are going to migrate.” Joanne, who works in dentistry, added: “I feel rather selfish about it because I don’t want to pay any more tax ... people just can’t afford to live a decent life at the moment.”This led to a wider discussion about the budget and people’s worries that, while Burnham had done some “small things”, was it just going to be, as Linda put it, “robbing Peter and paying Paul”.If this group is anything to go by, Burnham is impressing the voters who put Labour into office in 2024, and has earned his party a rehearing that Starmer simply could not. But beyond the top line, big questions remain on the details. The Labour leader can be happy with the reception for Tuesday’s speech but definitely cannot afford to rest on a post-conference glow in the battle for public opinion on his plans.(Participants’ names have been changed)Luke Tryl is the UK director of the research group More in CommonExplore more on these topicsAndy BurnhamLabour conferenceLabourLabour conference 2026Labour party leadershipBrexitSocial carenewsShareReuse this content

title: Man shot dead at London memorial service in ‘senseless act of violence’ | London | The Guardian
description: Forty-year-old victim declared dead at the scene in East Acton in a ‘senseless act of violence’
Author: Nadeem Badshah
Headline: Forty-year-old victim declared dead at the scene in East Acton in a ‘senseless act of violence’
Content: Police were called on Friday at 7.47pm after multiple shots were heard by members of the public in East Acton.Photograph: Peter Byrne/PAView image in fullscreenPolice were called on Friday at 7.47pm after multiple shots were heard by members of the public in East Acton.Photograph: Peter Byrne/PALondonMan shot dead at London memorial service in ‘senseless act of violence’Forty-year-old victim declared dead at the scene in East Acton in a ‘senseless act of violence’Nadeem BadshahSat 3 Oct 2026 18.04 EDTLast modified on Sat 3 Oct 2026 18.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA murder investigation has been launched after a 40-year-old man was shot dead in a “senseless act of violence” during a memorial service in westLondon, police have said.Police were called on Friday at 7.47pm after multiple shots were heard in East Acton.Officers attended alongside the London ambulance service. The victim was treated at the scene on the junction of Braybrook Street and Erconwald Street, however, he was pronounced dead.The Metropolitan police said about 40 to 50 people were at the scene, including children. The man’s family have been informed and are being supported by specialist officers.A postmortem examination is scheduled to establish the cause of death, but the victim is believed to have sustained a gunshot wound, the force added.No arrests have been made.DCI Brian Howie, who is leading the investigation, said: “Our thoughts are with the family and friends of a man whose life was taken in a senseless act of violence.“We understand a large number of people had gathered for a memorial service and what should have been a time to come together in remembrance has instead left a family devastated.“We believe between 40 and 50 people, including children, were present when this incident occurred. Someone knows what happened and we need them to come forward.“If you were around Erconwald Street, Braybrook Street, the surrounding roads or Wormwood Scrubs playground between 6pm and 8pm, please think carefully about what you saw. Did you see anyone carrying or concealing weapons, people on bicycles acting suspiciously or vehicles being driven at speed?“We also want to hear from anyone with photographs, video, dashcam, doorbell or mobile phone footage or who has seen anything relevant on social media.”Explore more on these topicsLondonCrimePoliceGun crimenewsShareReuse this content

title: Paw patrol: Mexico debuts tiniest national guard recruit | Mexico | The Guardian
description: Chihuahua Comando is being trained for search-and-rescue work, and helping bring a warm connection with the public
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Chihuahua Comando is being trained for search-and-rescue work, and helping bring a warm connection with the public
Content: Comando, the newest member of Mexico's national guard, in Lomas de Sotelo, Naucalpan, Mexico, on Thursday.Photograph: Gerardo Vieyra/NurPhoto/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenComando, the newest member of Mexico's national guard, in Lomas de Sotelo, Naucalpan, Mexico, on Thursday.Photograph: Gerardo Vieyra/NurPhoto/ShutterstockMexicoPaw patrol: Mexico debuts tiniest national guard recruitChihuahua Comando is being trained for search-and-rescue work, and helping bring a warm connection with the publicReutersSat 3 Oct 2026 17.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleComando may be tiny, but Mexico’s national guard is giving him ⁠a very big role.Outfitted with miniature goggles, a fitted tactical vest, a helmet and even a petite head-mounted camera, ⁠the 7lb (15lb) chihuahua ⁠has become ​the most unusual – and smallest – canine member of the force.Officers said the 13-month-old pup is being trained not ⁠just as a crowd-pleasing mascot but for search-and-rescue work as well.View image in fullscreenMembers of the national guard prepare to guide Comando through an obstacle course.Photograph: Toya Sarno Jordan/ReutersView image in fullscreenA national guard member puts Comando through his paces.Photograph: Gerardo Vieyra/NurPhoto/ShutterstockDiminutive Comando, who stands 21cm (8in) tall, looks nothing like the ⁠powerful dogs usually associated with military or police units.Duringa training sessionin ​Mexico City last week, the little dog ‌scampered up stairs and ‌over obstacles while a much larger, fully trained canine named Roko looked on.Lt ‌Debora Hernandez said Comando challenges two stereotypes: that only big dogs can serve in the national guard, and that a military-style force cannot build a warmer connection with the public. His presence, she said, reminds people that “beneath the uniform, we are human beings”.The force adopted Comando about six months ‌ago in the northern state of Chihuahua, which inspired the breed’s name, after his elderly owners became unable to care for him. ​Comando now appears at civic ceremonies, school events and community outreach programs.View image in fullscreenComando gets a break from training.Photograph: Gerardo Vieyra/NurPhoto/ShutterstockComando is an outlier in a national guard canine force of about 350 dogs, most of them traditional working breeds such as German shepherds and labrador retrievers.Chihuahuas, known for their ⁠large, upright ears, big personalities and expressive eyes, may be alert ​and energetic, but they are ​rarely seen as candidates ​for serious operational work.Comando has already appeared in Mexico’s Independence Day parade ​and has inspired ‌his own animated ​likeness and ​a growing crop of memes on social media.Explore more on these topicsMexicoAmericasDogsShareReuse this content

title: Kane and Saka double up as England school Croatia in historic Nations League rout | Nations League | The Guardian
description: Harry Kane and Bukayo Saka scored twice with Jude Bellingham, Anthony Gordon and Morgan Rogers also on target as England ran riot in Rijeka
Author: Jacob Steinberg
Headline: Harry Kane and Bukayo Saka scored twice with Jude Bellingham, Anthony Gordon and Morgan Rogers also on target as England ran riot in Rijeka
Content: Bukayo Saka celebrates scoring England’s sixth goal with Harry Kane as Thomas Tuchel’s side floored Croatia.Photograph: Paul Childs/Action Images/ReutersView image in fullscreenBukayo Saka celebrates scoring England’s sixth goal with Harry Kane as Thomas Tuchel’s side floored Croatia.Photograph: Paul Childs/Action Images/ReutersNations LeagueKane and Saka double up as England school Croatia in historic Nations League routJacob Steinbergat Stadion HNK RijekaSat 3 Oct 2026 14.04 EDTLast modified on Sat 3 Oct 2026 17.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt had all the edge of a pop concert in the stands but England looked ready to steal candy from a baby. The 6,200 Croatian under-14s allowed inside Stadion HNK Rijeka were invited free of charge and this was a priceless footballing experience. England ripped Croatia to shreds to take a firm grip on second place in their Nations League group, boosting their hopes of reaching next year’s quarter-finals, and anyone supporting the home team could at least find consolation in watching Harry Kane andJude Bellinghamcombine to devastating effect.Perhaps the ticket should have come with an adult age rating. This was grisly viewing for the locals but Thomas Tuchel delighted in England’s most complete performance since surging to a 4-2 win over Croatia at the World Cup. Kane marked his 124th cap with his 88th and 89th international strikes and had plenty of help. Three assists and a goal decorated a scintillating display from Bellingham and Tuchel found satisfaction in the other members of his ruthless front four getting on the scoresheet.Tuchel convinced England have buried World Cup woes with Croatia thrashingRead moreEverything clicked. England could have had double figures against opponents ranked 13th in the world but they settled for seven. Anthony Gordon and Bukayo Saka were in lightning, goalscoring form on the flanks and another story was an exceptional full debut from Alex Scott. The 23-year-old proved that he belongs, impressing with his tenacity and quality on and off the ball, and made it hard to shake off the sense that Tuchel missed a trick by not taking him to the World Cup.One gorgeous, defence-splitting ball from Scott to release Gordon emphasised that this is a player with a big England future. This was the Bournemouth youngster’s second cap and it said much about Tuchel’s belief in Scott that he deployed him against Luka Modric, even if the greatCroatiamidfielder has seen better days.The occasion was nowhere near as surreal as when England played here with no supporters present in 2018. It was meant to be behind closed doors again – Uefa had punished Croatia after discriminatory and racist fan behaviour during last year’sNations Leaguequarter-finals – but the rules allow tickets to go to local children and the constant high-pitched cheers were a reminder that much of the crowd were not alive when Modric first faced England 20 years ago.Tuchel knew youth was on his team’s side. Modric is 41 and, given that he was accompanied by another old timer in Mateo Kovacic, it not a surprise that Scott and Elliot Anderson, resuming their partnership when England won the Under-21 European Championship last year, dominated.Anderson, Scott and Bellingham were superb. Bellingham, back in the side after being rested during Tuesday’s 2-0 win over Czechia, was still going near the end, sending the England substitute Morgan Rogers through to make it 7-0.View image in fullscreenEngland’s Anthony Gordon scores their third goal past Croatia’s Dominik Livakovic.Photograph: Paul Childs/Action Images/ReutersThe mind went back to when these sides met in their opening game at the World Cup. Anthony Barry gave an impassioned half-time interview and, having struggled in defence during the first half, England emerged triumphant after producing one of their best spells of attacking football under Tuchel.Replicating those levels has been hard since then, but this was like Dallas. There was a moment when Bellingham went shoulder to shoulder with Modric and just eased his former Real Madrid teammate aside. England were quicker and stronger. The press was aggressive and Croatia were in damage limitation mode by the time Bellingham made it 2-0 in the 21st minute, stabbing past Dominik Livakovic from close range after Gordon plucked Saka’s cross out of the sky before cracking a low ball into the six-yard box.Slaven Bilic, back in charge of Croatia for a second spell, was powerless to respond. England led after eight minutes, moving in a blur when Marc Guéhi cut out a loose pass from Josko Gvardiol. Bellingham scanned, turned and chose the logical option. He shovelled the ball through a gap; Kane, free of Gvardiol and Luka Vuskovic, set himself and rammed a shot past Livakovic.The kids booed and gave a collective thumbs down as England’s captain celebrated, but they were watching greatness. Funny, of course, to think there was a time when Kane and Bellingham barely passed to each other. There is no problem with their relationship these days.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionGordon, again linking well with Lewis Hall, was a constant outlet on the left. He kept bursting beyond Josip Stanisic and now has a goal or assist in each of his last seven England games. It was 3-0 when Jarell Quansah, in for Trent Alexander-Arnold on the right, hit back at criticism of his crossing ability by whipping in a ball for Gordon to head past Livakovic.Quansah was one of five changes by Tuchel, who also restored Jordan Pickford in goal. Pickford remains the No 1 and made a key intervention at 1-0, rushing out to smother as Ivan Perisic threatened.View image in fullscreenBukayo Saka scores from close range as England dominate the first half.Photograph: Darko Bandic/APEngland dozed off after Gordon’s goal. A rare misstep from Anderson led to an opening for Kovacic, who somehow shot wide after rounding Pickford. England responded on the stroke of half-time. Kane dropped back to help out and start a counterattack which ended with Bellingham toying with Croatia before crossing for Saka to score.The 100 England fans given tickets enjoyed their evening. There was no let-up after the break. Anderson zipped down the right and crossed for a stretching Kane to score.It was not long before Croatia, who suffered their biggest ever defeat, removed Modric. The night belonged to England’s stars. Kane, who set up Saka to make it 6-0 in the 68th minute will equal Peter Shilton’s appearance record when England host Czechia on Tuesday. The 33-year-old is not slowing down.Explore more on these topicsNations LeagueCroatiaEnglandHarry KaneJude Bellinghammatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: ‘It’s been hard’: families await the return of the USS Abraham Lincoln | US military | The Guardian
description: After reports of suicide attempts and food shortages, the aircraft carrier is expected to dock in San Diego this week following a record-breaking 250-plus days at sea
Author: Anna Betts
Headline: After reports of suicide attempts and food shortages, the aircraft carrier is expected to dock in San Diego this week following a record-breaking 250-plus days at sea
Content: Illustration: Guardian DesignView image in fullscreenIllustration: Guardian DesignUS military‘It’s been hard’: families await the return of the USS Abraham LincolnAfter reports of suicide attempts and food shortages, the aircraft carrier is expected to dock in San Diego this week following a record-breaking 250-plus days at seaAnna BettsSat 3 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 3 Oct 2026 12.01 EDTShareA mother inSan Diegois counting down the days until her son comes home.“I had a big sign made, welcoming him back,” she said. “I can’t wait to see him.”Her son is one of roughly 5,000 sailors and marines onboard the USS Abraham Lincoln, the US aircraft carrier that has been deployed for nearly a year, and since late February was supportingUS military operationsagainst Iran.What began as a deployment bound forthe Pacific,anticipatedtoreturnin the spring, became something entirely different after the United Stateslaunched its war with Iran. The Lincoln was diverted to the Middle East, and the deployment became what one military official described as “one of the most operationally intense and consequential of the modern era”.The months that followed weremarkedby combat operations, deployment extensions, a record-breaking stretch at sea, and reports of shortages of food and basic supplies and deteriorating mental health among some crew members, includingreportsthat several crew members had attempted to jump overboard.Senior Trump administration officialspushed back againstaccounts of poor conditions, but some families and veterans warned that the length and intensity of the deployment were taking a toll on both those serving onboard and their loved ones.As reports of conditions leaked out, the Lincoln soon became a flashpoint in theincreasingly contentiousdebate over the war and, for some, a symbol of the strains and pressures the conflict has placed on the US military and the people serving in it.Now, after months at sea, the Lincoln is in the final stretch of itsjourney back to San Diego, where it is expected in the coming days.But as the carrier heads home, the toll of the deployment has come into sharper focus. In late September, the navy disclosed that during the deployment,eight service membersfrom the Lincoln and its accompanying strike group had attempted to take their own lives.View image in fullscreenA crew member walks next to aircraft on the flight deck of the USS Abraham Lincoln as it departs the port of Laem Chabang, near Pattaya, Thailand, on 6 September 2026.Photograph: Chanakarn Laosarakham/AFP/Getty ImagesWhen the Lincoln left San Diego last November, its deployment was expected to be relatively routine. The carrier was scheduled to spend several months in the Pacific region before returning home toCaliforniain the spring.Instead, as the US and Israel launched their war against Iran, the carrier was redirected to the Middle East.The Lincoln and its strike group, carrying approximately6,000 to 7,000sailors across roughly a half-dozen ships, were soon pulled into combat operations, which would see them shoot down “more than 200 Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps drones threatening international shipping and US forces”,according toAdm Brad Cooper, who heads US Central Command. The group’s guided-missile destroyers, he said, engaged in “arguably the most intense combat at sea the navy has seen” since the second world war while the carrier’s air wing carried out hundreds of “decisive strikes on IRGC targets”.The crew worked long hours as the carrier remained at sea for months without a port visit. The war disrupted regional resupply routes and traditional hubs, making it harder to replenish the ship and rotate personnel, especially after Irandamageda US navy base in Bahrain.By August, the Lincoln had spent more than250 consecutive daysat sea.Armen Kurdian, a retired US navy captain who served on the Lincoln in 2005,describedthe carrier as a “giant floating city” where sailors live in close quarters, and “you’ve got aircraft smacking down on decks repeatedly, hundreds of times per day, and that rattles the ship”.The strain of this deployment was compounded by uncertainty over when the sailors would come home. Some familiessaid they went weeks without hearing from their loved ones, and for stretches of time, they said, those onboard did not receive letters and care packages from home.Then reports began to emerge aboutconditions on the ship.In April, photographspurporting to show poor-qualitymeals on the Lincoln circulated widely online. The US navydeniedreports of food shortages, calling such claims“false”.But by August, some families begandescribing a more troubling pictureof what their loved ones onboard had told them about the conditions: shortages of food and basic supplies, plumbing problems, and exhaustion and deteriorating mental health among the crew. Two leading military newspapers also reported that there had beentwo attemptsby sailors to jump overboard, causingconcernamong families and military health experts.That month, it was reported that more than 200 family membersattended a virtual town hallwith navy leaders to discuss their concerns. One spouse reportedly said her husband, a sailor onboard, had texted her that day, saying: “He hopes he doesn’t wake up tomorrow.”One mother whose 19-year-old son is onboard the carrier said this week that there were periods when she went a month without hearing from him. When they did communicate, she said, he sometimes sent photographs of the food, which she said looked “horrible”.At one point, he told her about a power outage on the ship, but assured her that he was doing OK. He would tell her how other sailors had begun “to not be themselves” and were “losing themselves”.“It’s been hard knowing the conditions and the type of food they’re being fed, and just not having any contact for long periods of time, and them being gone so long,” the woman, who requested anonymity, said. “It’s just been difficult.”The reports of supply shortages and declining morale and mental health promptedoutrage from Democrats, and swift pushback from senior officials in the Trump administration.View image in fullscreenThe US defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, at Norfolk, Virginia, on 5 October 2025. He said reports of poor conditions on the USS Abraham Lincoln were ‘completely misrepresented’.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesPete Hegseth, the US defense secretary who has pledged to restore the “warrior ethos” to the US military, said the conditions on the Lincoln had been“completely misrepresented”. Navy officialsacknowledgedthat the war had disrupted traditional supply networks, but maintained that the carrier had adequate food, medical care and supplies.When reporters asked Donald Trump whether the families were concerned about the reported conditions on the vessel, heclaimed, “No, they’re not,” and when asked if he thought the deployment had gone on too long, heresponded: “Not nearly long enough.”For some naval families, that commentwas difficult to hear.One mother whose son was onboard the Lincoln said she became angry when she heard Trump’s comments.“I thought, you know, this guy has never served a day in his life,” she said. “Neither has his family, none of his children have – how would he feel if it was his kid on that ship?”She said she understood that the sailors were at war, but what troubled her was how long the deployment had lasted, with no opportunity to leave the ship and little sense of when the crew would return.“For a long time I didn’t hear from him because he didn’t have internet or whatever,” she said. “So it was hard not knowing what’s going on, and then listening to news reports about all this stuff that’s going on, I was very worried.”When she was finally spoke with her son after the reports of the suicide attempts and poor living conditions emerged, she asked whether he was eating, and if he was OK. She said he told her he was eating three meals a day, and sounded well. But from thousands of miles away, it was impossible to know for sure.View image in fullscreenDonald Trump, when asked about the length of the deployment of the USS Abraham Lincoln, said it was ‘not nearly long enough’.Photograph: Andrew Caballero-Reynolds/AFP/Getty ImagesThe picture emerging from the Lincoln was complicated, and worried families scrambled to try to piece together what was happening through brief phone calls and text messages, as well as news reports relaying what other relatives had heard.Some families weren’t surprised by the reports, saying that their relative onboard had described similar conditions. Others, however, said their relative had described nothing of the sort, which led them to believe that some of the accounts circulating online had been overblown or just the experience of a handful of sailors.One mother, herself a navy veteran, said she believed some reports about food and plumbing had been “blown out of proportion”. Food on these vessels in general, she said, could be “pretty disgusting”.Eight USS Lincoln personnel have attempted suicide, US navy confirmsRead moreHer bigger concern was the length of the deployment, the lack of port visits, and the inability of sailors to receive mail and care packages from home for extended periods.“I can’t imagine not feeling the ground under my feet for that amount of time,” she said. She also worried about sailors on their first deployment and whether such an experience might influence their decision to re-enlist.For some families, the feeling of helplessness became overwhelming.In August, Jefferson Kelley, whose son is onboard the Lincoln, wrote to his senator, Bernie Moreno, a Republican from Ohio, offering to take his son’s place on the ship for the remainder of the deployment.In the letter, shared with the Guardian, Kelley proposed what he called a “parent swap”.“If there is any lawful way for me to serve in his place so that he may return home, I am asking for that opportunity,” he wrote.His son had never complained to him or his family about conditions on the ship, Kelley said, adding that he often responded that he was doing fine, but as a father, he said he couldn’t help by worry about his son, especially as the reports continued to emerge.“I was trying to show that I am someone that is willing to do more than just sit at home and say somebody should do something or complain on social media,” Kelley said, describing his son’s deployment amid the war in Iran as a “very, very difficult experience” for the family.View image in fullscreenThe USS Abraham Lincoln has been on a record-long deployment amid the US war on Iran.Photograph: Morteza Nikoubazl/NurPhoto/Getty ImagesOn 15 August, as headlines about conditions on the Lincoln intensified, and as Democratic lawmakersdemandedmore information from the Pentagon, Adm Cooper, who heads Central Command,visited the carrier.Notlong afterward, he released a statement, claiming that of the US navy’s 11 active aircraft carriers, the Lincoln “currently has among the lowest number of cases related to mental health”. But, he added, “this doesn’t mean that all is perfect”.A long deployment at sea, Cooper said, “is uniquely challenging and tough, and every single one of us, including me, reacts to stressors in different ways”.In anopinion piecein the Wall Street Journal that week, Cooper wrote that “the crew is tired, but they continue to fire on all cylinders”.“History will record this deployment as one of the most operationally intense and consequential of the modern era,” he said. In the essay, Cooper said that “recent media reporting has portrayed varying perspectives on operational tempo, crew morale and the realities facing our deployed forces”, adding: “What I found aboard the Lincoln is that many elements of those stories are old news.”That same month, for one sailor, the strain of being away from home was compounded by events happening there. In a post on social media, Joshua Aviles, a sailor onboard the Lincoln, wrote that he had just learned that his father wasdetained by federalimmigration authorities.Aviles said his father had a driver’s license, social security card and work permit, and that the family “had done everything through immigration to get his green card approved, and we are just waiting”.“I don’t know how I can mentally continue working 12+ hour days ‌knowing that my dad is somewhere, possibly being treated like a criminal,” he wrote in a Facebook post.US immigration officials said at the time that Aviles’ father had entered the country illegally, and that “having a family member in the military is not a free pass to violate our nation’s laws”.Several days later, Aviles said his father wasreleased.View image in fullscreenThe USS Abraham Lincoln approaches the port of Laem Chabang near Pattaya, Thailand, on 2 September 2026.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesIn late August, it was finally announced that another US aircraft carrier, the USS George Washington, had arrived to relieve the Lincoln, and that the Lincolnwould be heading backto San Diego.On the journey home, the Lincoln dockedin Thailand for several days, giving sailors a chance to walk on land and rest before beginning the final passage home.In Thailand, the Guardianspoke with several sailors, who requested anonymity, who described eating “uncooked beef” and sliced-up, uncooked potatoes during the deployment. One sailor said that in his opinion, the decline in living standards was down to the battle conditions imposed during the combat operation, dubbed Operation Epic Fury, rather than the unprecedented length of deployment.Another of the sailors said that the hardest part of the deployment was “pushing through, keeping the mentality”, while another serviceman hinted at the toll the long deployment had taken: “Some people adapt to it, but not everyone.”Shakeria Fairfax, whose daughter, Jada, is onboard the Lincoln, couldn’t pass up the chance to be reunited with her daughter after such an intense deployment. She flew to Thailand, and still, to this day, Fairfax struggles to describe the moment they saw each other.“The best way I could describe it is just kind of like when I first looked at her it was the overwhelming sense of love after having had so much time apart,” Fairfax said in an interview this week. “There was such a sense of pride, love and pride.”View image in fullscreenUSS Abraham Lincoln sailors arrive during their port call at the Hard Rock Hotel in Pattaya, Thailand, on 2 September 2026.Photograph: Anthony Wallace/AFP/Getty ImagesFor two days in Thailand, they played their favorite card game, went shopping and did what Fairfax called “girly things” – manicures, pedicures, facials and massages.“It felt like we had some normalcy back in our lives after having been apart,” she said.Like several other families the Guardian has spoken with, Fairfax did not want to disclose details of her daughter’s experience on the vessel, but described her as “extremely resilient”.The deployment was Jada’s first, her mother said. She had completed basic training in October before she was deployed in November. When Fairfax woke to the news in February that the US and Israel had launched their war against Iran, she “couldn’t believe it”.“We don’t come from a military family, and now my child is at war and I don’t know what that looks like,” she said.Not long afterward, Fairfax lost contact with her daughter for several weeks, receiving only a handful of emails saying that she was OK. Then, on Easter weekend, Jada finally FaceTimed her mother. “It was beautiful,” Fairfax said.Over the months that followed, Fairfax remembers only one occasion when her daughter told her she was feeling discouraged. Fairfax said she felt powerless, and asked her what she could do to help. Jada, who turned 25 onboard the ship in June, asked her mother to tell her stories about when she was growing up, she said.So she did. “I told her stories. I sent her photographs,” Fairfax said. “Some of them she received, some of them she didn’t.”View image in fullscreenBalloons forming a US flag adorn a bar to welcome the arrival of  personnel of the USS Abraham Lincoln in Pattaya, Thailand, on 2 September 2026.Photograph: Anthony Wallace/AFP/Getty ImagesJada told her mother about some sailors onboard the ship who did not have the same kind of support system – people who did not receive care packages or have family members sending them reminders of home. And as the deployment continued, Fairfax said she could only imagine how difficult that must have become for those sailors. She and her daughter have since talked about finding a way to help those who do not have that support, she said.For Fairfax, there was never much of a question about whether she would go to Thailand to see her daughter when she docked, as to her: “It was really about showing up for my daughter.”Now she hopes to be able to head toSan Diegoto welcome her home.The most serious disclosure about the deployment came after the Lincoln left Thailand.In aletterresponding to questions from the Democratic senator Kirsten Gillibrand of New York, Hung Cao, the acting US navy secretary,acknowledged thateight navy personnel in the Lincoln strike group hadattemptedto take their own lives during the deployment, but said that no sailor had died from the attempts.Cao said one sailor assigned to the air wing went overboard from the ship in early August but was “quickly recovered by an air wing search and rescue helicopter”. The sailor was treated by the vessel’s medical department and transferred off ship for follow-up care, Cao said, and the sailor’s family was notified.Another sailor, he said, attempted to go overboard in March, but was stopped by his shipmates. That sailor was “also provided immediate medical care and subsequently returned to home port”, he added.According to USDepartment of Defense data, there were 356 attempted suicides recorded in the navy in 2024. There were 287 in 2023, and 282 in 2022. This month,NPRreported that a 21-year-old sailor onboard the USS Fort Lauderdale, which had been deployed in the Caribbean as part of the Trump administration’s operation around Venezuela, died by suicide in June, a month before the vessel returned to Virginia.View image in fullscreenJD Vance greets the acting secretary of the navy, Hung Cao, on the USS Kearsarge in New York harbor on 4 July 2026.Photograph: Vincent Alban/Getty ImagesCaosaidthat the navy launched a suicide prevention and response taskforce earlier this year, and also said in the letter that the Lincoln had deployed with five chaplains, an embedded integrated prevention counselor, a psychologist, a clinical social worker, three behavioral health technicians and a facility dog.Cao said that the Lincoln “maintains adequate food supplies” but that due to the ship’s “participation in major combat operations with limited opportunities for resupply in a combat ‘environment, the number of main entree options served during regular meal hours was reduced from two to one for a short time”.“Four meals were served daily, and all meals provided were nutritionally balanced, with adequate calories per day made available to every sailor,” he said.Pedicures and a pair of socks: sailors from USS Abraham Lincoln go wild in party resort of PattayaRead moreThe navy also acknowledged that earlier in the deployment the ship had experienced “localized piping failures” and temporary issues with its desalination units but that “shipboard engineering teams successfully completed repairs, and the potable water supply remains safe and tested daily”.The new information prompted further calls from members of Congress for investigations and greater transparency.In astatement, Gillibrand, who is a member of the Senate armed services committee, criticized the Trump administration’s handling of the reports from the vessel.“What Trump andSecretary Hegsethdismissedas ‘fake news’ turned out to be serious and deteriorating conditions for our service members,” she said, adding: “Our troops and their families make immense sacrifices every single day, yet the president dismissed them with open disrespect.”In response, a White House spokesperson said that Trump has “rightfully restored a focus on readiness, lethality and supporting our war fighters at the Pentagon”.“The president cares about our troops more than anyone, and he is ensuring our brave service members have all the resources they need to be successful as the United States military continues to economically strangle the Iranian regime,” they added.Richard Blumenthal, the Democratic senator from Connecticut, alsorequestedthat navy leaders provide an “accounting of the eight suicide attempts”, including when they occurred and when senior navy leaders were informed of the incidents. He has also asked navy leaders to “detail the steps you will take to protect sailors’ mental health and wellbeing during future extended deployments”.View image in fullscreenRichard Blumenthal, the Democratic senator from Connecticut, asked US navy leaders to provide an accounting of the eight sucicide attempts among the Lincoln strike group.Photograph: Ken Cedeno/AFP/Getty ImagesIn an interview with the Guardian, Donald Guter, a retired navy judge advocate general, described the eight reported attempts as a “tremendously concerning number” but said that “given the operational tempo and the total lack of opportunity for port calls, in a way, it shouldn’t have surprised people”.He described the Lincoln’s deployment as “extraordinary”, saying that spending “that long at sea without any breaks, at that operational tempo, is stressing on anyone”.Carl Schuster, a retired US navy captain, said that during his long deployments, which lasted between six and seven months, it was not unusual to have one or two suicide attempts.But, he said, “keep in mind, the Lincoln spent over 250 days at sea in a nine-month deployment, which is a much longer deployment and much more time entirely at sea than I ever did, so I’m not surprised at the additional stress and the additional attempts”.“We’re asking the crews to sacrifice much more than was normal in my day,” Schuster said. “All of us have a breaking point.”Lory Manning, who served more than 25 years in the navy, said that given the size of the strike group and the unprecedented length of the deployment, she didn’t think it was that “far out of bounds to have that many attempts” across thousands of people who “have been bottled up on ships for 10 months”, particularly amid prolonged uncertainty, deployment extensions and intense combat conditions.“I’m very glad that nobody succeeded,” Manning said.John Cordle, who retired from the navy in 2013 after 30 years of service and served in a carrier strike group, said he could remember only one suicide attempt onboard a ship of the two that he was in command of, so to him, “eight seems like a lot”.Cordle said that his longest deployment had been seven and a half months and his longest period without a port call had been 110 days.“I never had to deal with conditions this extreme,” he said of the Lincoln’s deployment.He urged the navy in the future to be more transparent earlier about the conditions onboard, especially with the families, and said that he hoped the leaders learned from the Lincoln’s deployment.Several veterans also cautioned that the strain of these deployments could potentially affect enlistment in the future.“Given the history of what does and doesn’t make people re-enlist, it’s certainly quite possible that none of them want to go through that again,” said Manning, “and maybe not the sailors, maybe it’s their families that don’t want to have to go through it again.”View image in fullscreenGenerals John D Caine, Randy George and Eric Smith, and Adm Daryl Caudle, during a State of the Union address at the US Capitol on 24 February 2026.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesDuring atown hallin late August, Adm Daryl Caudle, the chief of naval operations, warned that long deployments could become more common. That warning came as, earlier this year, the USS Gerald Fordreturnedfrom a record-breaking326 daysat sea, marking thelongest deploymentby a US warship since theVietnam war.“In the short term, until I can grow the navy we need, I hate to admit it, but longer deployments are going to be probably part of that,” Caudlesaid.Matthew Brown, aUS navy reserve commanderand former captain of the USS Scout, said he visited the Lincoln in mid-September.Brown runsChimney Trail Health, a behavioral healthcare company that specializes “in creative adaptations of cognitive behavior theory”. He said the Lincoln’s captain had invited him to provide his company’s cognitive readiness training program to the sailors as the carrier headed home.He said he delivered an in-person seminar, “sort of like a tabletop workshop-type thing”, to those onboard, and that it was “well received”.At that time, the crew were on their journey home, and Brown said he observed that their “morale was that they were obviously quite tired because it was a very like rigorous deployment” but that “they were resolute”.The sailors, he added, “were strong, and many of them maintained a very good sense of humor”.For future deployments, Brown said that having more personnel onboard trained in the basics of cognitive behavior theory and equipped with evidence-based materials could help when it comes to addressing some of the mental health challenges that may arise.Later in September, the congresswoman Sara Jacobs, a Democrat representing California’s 51st district, which includes San Diego,saidshe joined a bipartisan delegation for in-person oversight of the Lincoln as it journeyed back to San Diego.View image in fullscreenCongresswoman Sara Jacobs.Photograph: Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc/Getty Images“I raised my concerns directly with the ship’s command and received a briefing on logistics, supply issues and lessons learned for future deployments,” she said. “I also met with sailors and marines onboard who painted a very different picture of this war; they shared stories of the deployment and their struggles to wash clothes, get medicine and healthcare, and eat enough food.”Jacobs said that she didn’t blame the ship’s leadership, saying they had done the best they could under difficult circumstances. Instead, she said she blamed the president, whom she accused of “knowingly launch[ing] a war without the required planning and strategy needed”.She said she would push for an investigation into the conditions and a House armed services committee hearing to hear directly from service members once they returned.Meanwhile, another US carrier, the USS Theodore Roosevelt, was justrecently dispatchedto the Middle East.In avideo statement in early September,navy leaders said that they were learning from the Lincoln’s deployment, and had loaded the Roosevelt up with additional food, hygiene products and other supplies before it got under way.“We’re also focused on quality of life,” they said, adding that they will provide additional entertainment and fitness equipment onboard, and said that they were improving communication with families throughout the deployment.“To the Lincoln team, thank you for what you accomplished, and for what you taught us, and to the Roosevelt team, we’re doing everything we can to make sure you are ready for the mission,” they said. “You and your families.”

title: Badenoch returns to Conservative conference much stronger than a year ago | Kemi Badenoch | The Guardian
description: Approval ratings for Tory leader and her party have crept up as she has asserted her style and authority but big challenges lie ahead
Author: Rowena Mason
Headline: Approval ratings for Tory leader and her party have crept up as she has asserted her style and authority but big challenges lie ahead
Content: Insiders say Badenoch has listened to people warning she needs to focus more on the economy and less on culture war talking points.Photograph: Dan Kitwood/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenInsiders say Badenoch has listened to people warning she needs to focus more on the economy and less on culture war talking points.Photograph: Dan Kitwood/Getty ImagesKemi BadenochAnalysisBadenoch returns to Conservative conference much stronger than a year agoRowena MasonWhitehall editorApproval ratings for Tory leader and her party have crept up as she has asserted her style and authority but big challenges lie aheadSat 3 Oct 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 3 Oct 2026 09.01 EDTShareA year ago, Tory MPs were braced for the prospect of yet another leadership battle to toppleKemi Badenochas the party sunk to historic lows of 14-16% in the polls.At the time, the word “November” was uttered in hushed tones – this being the decisive month when rebels would be able to mount a challenge, Badenoch having served 12 months in office.But times appear to have changed and – against the odds – the Tories have undergone what has been termed a “Keminisation”, with the leader asserting her style and authority on the party, despite its wider poor performance in the polls.“Right now, Kemi is the only thing that’s holding them up,” says Luke Tryl, the director of the More in Common thinktank, which conducts focus groups and polling. “If they ditched her, I think they’d be certain for electoral oblivion.”Badenoch is running a party still discounted as toxic and incompetent by much of the electorate, but polling numbers and focus groups suggest some of them have recently begun to give her more of a hearing.The party has crept up from the teens to the low 20s – occasionally edging ahead of Reform UK for the first time in almost two years.“It’s not great for them, but it’s a lot better,” says Tryl. “The problem is the party brand. She is now in our approval ratings net neutral and has been net 1 or net 2. She was in the minus 30s and now only her and Burnham have positive approval.“Progressives don’t like her, but when you come to those who might conceivably be Tory voters there’s a lot of ‘like her, don’t like the party, she tells it like it is, wish she was in another party’. I do think the Kemi bounce is real. People talk about her having improved and they have seen her PMQs clips.”Data from the other pollsters backs up the idea that the public is more open to Badenoch than before. James Crouch, the head of policy and public affairs at Opinium, said Badenoch’s approval rating had been rising since May 2025, when she was at -27, to -3 in its latest poll. He said that among 2024 Conservative voters she had the approval of 64%, compared with just 8% who did not approve, while of those who voted Conservative in 2019, 56% approved of her, while 16% did not.Further research from YouGov this week found four in 10 people used at least one negative term to describe the Tory leader, one of the most common themes being a perceived unpleasantness. But three in 10 included one or more positive terms in their description, strong and intelligent being the main compliments.Some Tory MPs attribute Badenoch’s improvement over the last year to a willingness to learn and take advice on her performance. This is in spite of her having the preternatural public self-confidence to claim to theFT this weekendthat she couldn’t think of any mistakes she had made, saying everyone makes them but “nothing comes to mind”.But insiders say she has listened to people warning she needs to focus more on the economy and less on culture war talking points, with the party’s conference slogan set as “Stronger economy, stronger country”.She has also improved her prime minister’s questions appearances, partly with help on preparation from Conservative grandees such as David Cameron.Tory MPs believe a turning point for Badenoch was the defection of Robert Jenrick and Suella Braverman to Reform – because their departure removed a source of destabilisation on the right, and it gave her an opportunity to show decisiveness in pushing Jenrick before he jumped. She has also been aided by the increasing questions over Nigel Farage and Reform UK’s finances, with the party’s dominance in the polls slipping.However, the arrival of Andy Burnham on the scene for Labour has changed things.Giles Kenningham, the former Conservative director of communications who now leads the Trafalgar Strategy advisory firm, says Burnham “raises the bar … he’s a great communicator and comfortable in his own skin”.“It’s a harder ask now. Starmer was not a great orator or someone who electrified voters … Burnham has had a great conference but all eyes are now on the budget, so her conference needs to be on the economy and welfare. John Healey’s speech didn’t say anything, and there is an opportunity for Badenoch to put pressure on them and drive the agenda.”Badenoch’s star has also risen further with the membership of the party, the most recent ConservativeHome poll showing she has a 87% net satisfaction rating with the party faithful.Despite this, a number of Conservative aides and insiders believe that Badenoch’s future is still not totally secure if the party does not start to creep above Reform UK on a sustained basis. One pointed to the Tory selection races – excluding some high-profile former MPs from standing – as a sign of perceived weakness that those around Badenoch are worried about her being challenged. “She is not alone among politicians in not liking tall poppies,” said one Conservative strategist.“Ultimately, she is not immune from a challenge,” said another. “The shelf life of politicians is getting shorter and shorter. Leaders are much more exposed and the job is precarious. The thing most in her favour is that there are currently no other obvious contenders.”Explore more on these topicsKemi BadenochConservativesConservative leadershipConservative conferenceOpinion pollsanalysisShareReuse this content

title: When is the right time to compare US politics to the Nazi era? This expert on Christian nationalism says: now | Books | The Guardian
description: Robert P Jones argues that declining white Christian influence has fuelled an alliance with Trump, and warns it is reshaping US democracy
Author: David Smith
Headline: Robert P Jones argues that declining white Christian influence has fuelled an alliance with Trump, and warns it is reshaping US democracy
Content: Donald Trump delivers the keynote address at the Faith & Freedom Coalition's Road to Majority Policy Conference on 22 June 2024 in Washington DC.Photograph: Samuel Corum/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDonald Trump delivers the keynote address at the Faith & Freedom Coalition's Road to Majority Policy Conference on 22 June 2024 in Washington DC.Photograph: Samuel Corum/Getty ImagesBooks interviewBooksWhen is the right time to compare US politics to the Nazi era? This expert on Christian nationalism says: nowRobert P Jones argues that declining white Christian influence has fuelled an alliance with Trump, and warns it is reshaping US democracyDavid Smithin WashingtonSat 3 Oct 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 3 Oct 2026 09.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe lawyerMike Godwinfamously came up with the “law” that, as an online discussion grows longer, the probability of a comparison involving Nazis or Hitler approaches one (or 100%).Robert P Jonesthought long and hard about whether to go there in his latest book. But the more he studied US demographic numbers, considered the rise of Christian nationalism and heard Donald Trump use the language of racial purity, he found the conclusion inescapable. “This is our 1933,” he writes.So it is thatBackslide: Reclaiming a Faith and a Nation After the Christian Turn Against Democracybegins with the rise of the Nazi party and the complicity of the German people, including German Christians and churches.Jones citesMartin Niemöller, a Lutheran pastor imprisoned for opposing Hitler, remembered for the poem First They Came. But for the first four years of Hitler’s reign, he notes, Niemöller did not fully oppose the Nazis. He later regretted that he and the Protestant German church did not speak out sooner.Backslide returns to the analogy in its epilogue. He writes: “Just as God asked Niemoller where he was between 1933 and 1937, God will ask us where we were between 2025 and 2028. Just as Germans who backed Hitler and the Nazi Party after 1933 were fully aware of what they were joining, so Christians who have backed Trump and the MAGA movement a second time know and bear responsibility for what they are now endorsing.”Sitting in his downtown Washington office, the president and founder of thePublic Religion Research Institute(PRRI) contends that US democracy is experiencing a severe “backslide” that is directly aided and abetted by an “apostate” white Christianity, including Trump’s language on the campaign trail.“This dehumanising language, talking about immigrants as vermin, and this racial purity language, like they’re ‘poisoning the blood of our country’. What does that mean? If they’repoisoningthe blood, what’s thepureblood? We know where that story goes,” he said.Trump has repeatedly used the concept of genetic inheritance. In 2020, addressing a mostly white crowd in Minnesota,he declared: “You have good genes, you know that, right? You have good genes. A lot of it is about the genes, isn’t it, don’t you believe? The racehorse theory, you think we’re so different? You have good genes in Minnesota.”Normalisation is a perennial danger.“If don’t want to live in a place where we have a thuggish police force that’s kidnapping people off the street in masks and killing US citizens in the streets, now’s the time to speak up,” Jones said.Backslide cites historian and philosopher Hannah Arendt’s 1950The Aftermath of Nazi Rulereport for Commentary magazine based on interviews with postwar Berliners: “A great number of Germans, especially among the more educated, apparently are no longer capable of telling the truth even if they want to.”Jones grew up a Southern Baptist inJackson, Mississippi, went to church five times a week and earned a master of divinity degree. His previous books include The End of White Christian America in 2016, White Too Long in 2020 andThe Hidden Roots of White Supremacy and the Path to a Shared American Futurein 2023. He called this one Backslide very deliberately.The Hidden Roots of White Supremacy review: necessary chronicle of US racist historyRead moreIn international political science, “democratic backsliding” has become the established academic term for the systematic erosion of democratic norms, judicial independence and voting rights. Yet Jones recognises that the term carries an even older resonance.“In the evangelical world I grew up in, backslide was a word we heard all the time – a theological word about the fear of falling away from the faith,” he says, tracing the word’s history back through the Oxford English Dictionary to the 16th-century Protestant reformer John Knox.In Jones’s diagnosis, white American Christianity has committed a profound act of apostasy by trading its spiritual core for political dominance. By endorsing anti-democratic tactics, white Christian institutions have become the primary engine behind the country’s autocratic slide.View image in fullscreenBackslide: Reclaiming a Faith and a Nation After the Christian Turn Against Democracy by Robert P Jones.Photograph: Macmillan PublishersTo understand how a major religious tradition arrived at this moral impasse, Jones turns to the arithmetic of demographics. When Barack Obama was elected president in 2008, white Christian Americans still constituted 54% of the US population. By 2014, that figure had dropped to 47%. Today, white Christians account for 41% of the country.The decline among white evangelicals, long considered a bedrock of conservative politics, is even steeper. At the turn of the 21st century, white evangelicals represented a quarter of all Americans; today, they make up barely 13%. TheSouthern Baptist Convention, the country’s biggest evangelical denomination, has lost more than 3 million members since its 2006 peak.Faced with shrinking numbers and cultural marginalisation, white evangelicalism embraced not spiritual renewal, but existential panic – creating fertile ground for Trump’s demagoguery.“Trump loves to talk aboutthe art of the dealand, in many ways, there’s been a massive quid pro quo deal struck between a declining white evangelical population and Trump,” Jones observes. “His big appeal to them was less about policy and more anti-immigrant: I’m going to restore an America that looks like you, and I’m going to restore power to the Christian churches.“He was literally saying on the campaign trail: this is a quid pro quo deal. Give me your votes and you won’t even have to vote again. I’ll fix it so you don’t have to vote again.’”This transactional alliance marks a complete departure from the religious right of the late 20th century, which wrapped its political ambitions in the language of morality.“You don’t hear those words any more,” says Jones, contrasting today’s movement with Jerry Falwell’s Moral Majority or the “Values Voters” summits of the George W Bush era. “What we have now is an overtly anti-democratic Christian nationalism flying under the banner of: ‘We believe this country belongs to us, and we’re going to use the power we can to claim it.’”This Faustian bargain relies purely on power rather than shared theology – a dynamic starkly highlighted by the contrast between Trump and his running mate, JD Vance. WhileVance recently discussedthe End Times with 22-year-old evangelical podcaster Bryce Crawford, awkwardly reflecting on his evangelical upbringing and subsequent conversion to Catholicism, Trump operates largely without theological pretence.Jones continues: “He makes straight appeals to self-interest: if you’re for me, I’ll be for you. Evangelicals are willing to forgive a whole host of sins for the idea that he is going to bring them back into power as their numbers are dwindling.”The real world manifestation of this transaction plays out every Sunday across thousands of congregations. While high-profile megachurches such asFirst Baptist church in Dallasmake their political allegiance explicit, Jones contends that overt political sermonising is rarely needed.“Once you have churches that are largely segregated by race and increasingly segregated by partisanship, all you really have to do is keep out any critique. It’s reinforced by Fox News, Christian radio and going home to people of like mind. You don’t have to overtly teach Christian nationalism; you just keep it from being critiqued.”PRRI’s extensive empirical data undermines the widespread belief that religious attendance automatically fosters civic tolerance or democratic values.Jones says: “Particularly among white evangelicals, on several measures around Christian nationalism, anti-immigrant views, anti-Black views, and anti-Muslim views, going to church actually makes your views more extreme. It’s not the case that more church is the answer to democracy.”The dangerous potential of this theological radicalisation materialised dramatically during the January 6, 2021 attack on the US Capitol. Christian symbols were displayed prominently throughout the insurrection, including wooden crosses set up on Capitol grounds and rioters holding “Jesus Saves” banners alongside Confederate flags.Yet official investigationslargely overlooked this central element, influenced in part by political figures like Congresswoman Liz Cheney on the House select committee. “I was stunned to see very little of it in the House select committee report,” Jones recalls. “It was a huge loss and a huge skewing of public perception that we didn’t take those Christian symbols at the riot seriously.”Today, this blend of Christian nationalism and military authority reaches into the upper echelons of the national security apparatus.The defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, sports tattoos featuring Crusader iconography – including the medieval battle cryDeus Vult(“God wills it”) next to a Jerusalem cross – while renaming the Department of Defense as the “Department of War”. Hegseth has welcomed vocal Christian nationalists such as Pastor Doug Wilson to lead a worship service at the Pentagon.Jones comments: “I can’t imagine much more dangerous than somebody who thinks, ‘I am the instrument of God, I alone understand how the forces of good and evil are aligned,’ while holding the power to deploy the most powerful military force the world has ever seen. WhileGeorge W Bushtook care after 9/11 to explicitly state that the US was not at war with Islam, today we are making radicalisation propaganda films for extremists by presenting ourselves as a Christian nation at war with Islam.”Behind the public spectacle of rallies and political theatre, ideologues such asRussell Vought, a key architect of Project 2025 and advocate of the “unitary executive” theory, are laying the groundwork for a government rooted in Christian nationalist principles. “They are building an apparatus designed to institutionalise this worldview across the federal government,” Jones warns. “It is an intentional, long-term project to reshape American democracy in their own image.”Despite the alarming trajectory detailed in Backslide, Jones resists total pessimism. The central message of his book is that “backsliding is not irreversible” and that national recovery remains possible through honest confrontation with history and sincere repentance.Across the country, alternative Christian voices are beginning to organise against Christian nationalism. Figures such asJames Talarico, a Presbyterian seminarian running for the US Senate in Texas, and Methodist pastor Adam Hamilton in Kansas are offering a pro-democracy theological vision.“For a long time, mainline Protestants were taught propriety and politeness, leading to a reticence to speak out,” Jones notes. “If we don’t want the public and future face of Christianity to be only Christian nationalism, we have to present a public version of Christianity that is compatible with democracy – one that leans into care for the orphan, the widow and the immigrant.”Ultimately, Jones argues, neither sacred texts nor historical precedents will dictate the future of US democracy. He hopes his book will make white Christians realise they face a decision similar to the one that confronted the establishment Christian church in Nazi Germany in 1933.“It’s a wake-up call to see the bright lines that are being crossed, to be clear-eyed about how dangerous that is, and for those readers who are Christian – particularly white and Christian – to realise we have a particular responsibility to offer a different version of faith. Because it is our faith that’s been hijacked and used to legitimise this illiberal, anti-democratic, authoritarian movement that’s running rampant and taking over in the US.”Explore more on these topicsBooksBooks interviewRace & religionHistory booksTrump administrationRepublicansReligion (World news)Donald TrumpfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The moment I knew: As a reality TV contestant, I was allowed one 15-minute call a week. Even at 3am, Chris would always pick up | Australian lifestyle | The Guardian
description: Conor Curran’s first date with Chris lasted nine hours but their relationship remained casual. Then, when Conor was at his most vulnerable, Chris was there for him
Author: Doosie Morris
Headline: Conor Curran’s first date with Chris lasted nine hours but their relationship remained casual. Then, when Conor was at his most vulnerable, Chris was there for him
Content: Chris and Conor: ‘In the final week of the competition … I wrote to Chris, and all my feelings came flooding out.’Composite: Guardian design/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenChris and Conor: ‘In the final week of the competition … I wrote to Chris, and all my feelings came flooding out.’Composite: Guardian design/Getty ImagesThe moment I knewAustralian lifestyleThe moment I knew: As a reality TV contestant, I was allowed one 15-minute call a week. Even at 3am, Chris would always pick upConor Curran’sfirst date with Chris lasted nine hours but their relationship remained casual. Then, when Conor was at his most vulnerable, Chris was there for himFind more stories fromthe moment I knew seriesConor Curran, as told toDoosie MorrisSat 3 Oct 2026 15.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 3 Oct 2026 18.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAt 29 I had lost my career in hospitality because of Covid and decided to throw my hat in the ring as a contestant on MasterChef Australia. By the time I was eliminated in 2021, restaurants still weren’t open and I didn’t know what to do with my life. My lease was coming to an end in Melbourne and I wasn’t doing well with the lockdowns and people recognising me from TV. So I decided to retreat to my father’s place in Adelaide for a while.By early 2022 I was dating a guy but, after a few months, he ghosted me suddenly.One sunny autumn weekend as I was miserably assembling some flatpack furniture at Dad’s, I realised I had to get out of the house. I got on Grindr and this lovely guy, Chris, fresh from England, started messaging me.View image in fullscreenChris and Conor in Melbourne in the early years of their relationshipI’d lived in the UK in my early 20s and I knew how hard it was to make friends in a new city. Still processing the shock ghosting, I invited Chris for a drink – just as mates – so neither of us had to be lonely on such a beautiful day. He said he couldn’t imagine anything better.We met at Brighton beach and had a beer. What followed was one of the most wonderful and unexpected dates of my life. It went for nine hours! We chatted and chatted, not wanting it to end. I wasn’t anticipating any chemistry but it was there, and we spent the night together.The next day I took him on a tour of Adelaide’s wine regions and then sent him on his way. He was only in town for two days, en route to his new life in Sydney. I didn’t think I’d ever see him again.But we stayed in touch as he settled into the harbour city. One thing led to another and, by May, little more than a month after we’d met, we both wound up in Melbourne. Chris had been offered a job and I had always planned to return at some point. So without ever having discussed the details, or even admitting to ourselves we’d caught real feelings, we’d moved to the same city and became a sort-of-couple, while still keeping things casual.In July I was scheduled to be on this reality show, The Challenge, that was filming in Argentina. The show had a Survivor/Big Brother vibe and I didn’t think I was going to do very well. I figured I’d be eliminated within a week but, much to my surprise, I turned out to be quite the Challenge beast and made it all the way to the final.We were only allowed one 15-minute video call a week and in that month I used 53 of my 60 allotted minutes talking to Chris.View image in fullscreen‘We have both found exactly what we were looking for’: the couple in 2025I’m not a person who likes to show vulnerability but the demands of the show broke me in ways I wasn’t expecting. Being filmed 24/7 and doing all these insane challenges put my mental health on a knife’s edge. We weren’t even “official” but Chris would pick up the phone at 3am and just be there for me. No games, no bullshit: he was my support when I needed someone the most.In the final week of the competition we were given time to write a letter to someone in our life. I wrote to Chris and all my feelings came flooding out. I told him I was falling for him and that if he ever read this letter it meant I was no longer just falling. I was, for sure, in love. I tucked it away and made my way back to Melbourne to recover.Once home it became clearer that the reality TV filming had taken a real toll on my mental health and the network started paying for my therapy. Chris was with me all the way.A few months later I gave him the letter. And he told me he loved me too.
