The result is an impressive record but one that’s less immediately appealing … All Set the Bone contains fewer fireworks than Burnover, but Freeman still has plenty of spark.”Shaad D’SouzaRead the full reviewOn tour…Paraorchestra; Sinfonietta/Jonny GreenwoodSouthbank Centre, London; touring nowView image in fullscreenThe Reich stuff … Paraorchestra performing in London last week.Photograph: Siân O’ConnorSummed up in a sentenceParaorchestra’s immersive performance of Music for 18 Musicians was immaculate and exhilarating; London Sinfonietta and the Radiohead guitarist’s vibrant tribute to the almost 90-year-old composer followed.What our reviewer said“Doing the honours was Paraorchestra, Charles Hazlewood’s enterprising collective of disabled and non-disabled musicians, who brought Reich’s kaleidoscopic music to life with ironclad discipline … Line dancing, disco lights – this exhilarating performance had it all.”Clive PagetRead the full reviewExplore more on these topicsCultureThe week in reviewsTelevisionfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Tuchel convinced England have buried World Cup woes with Croatia thrashing | England | The Guardian
description: Thomas Tuchel said England have moved on from their World Cup pain after seeing his side hand Croatia their biggest ever defeat
Author: Jacob Steinberg
Headline: Thomas Tuchel said England have moved on from their World Cup pain after seeing his side hand Croatia their biggest ever defeat
Content: ‘This dominant performance is the way to move on’: Thomas Tuchel with Bukayo Saka after England’s 7-0 rout of Croatia in Rijeka.Photograph: Bradley Collyer/PAView image in fullscreen‘This dominant performance is the way to move on’: Thomas Tuchel with Bukayo Saka after England’s 7-0 rout of Croatia in Rijeka.Photograph: Bradley Collyer/PAEnglandTuchel convinced England have buried World Cup woes with Croatia thrashing‘We’ll always have a scar, but this is how we move forward’Manager praises ‘complete package’ Scott on full debutJacob Steinbergat Stadion HNK RijekaSat 3 Oct 2026 15.50 EDTLast modified on Sat 3 Oct 2026 19.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThomas Tuchel said England have moved on from their World Cup pain after seeing his side deliver a statement performance in Rijeka and hand Croatia their biggest ever defeat.Tuchel was delighted after hisfront four combined to devastating effectat Stadion HNK Rijeka, where 6,200 local schoolchildren were allowed in free of charge even though the game was supposed to take place behind closed doors after Croatia were punished by Uefa for racist and discriminatory fan behaviour last year.Kane and Saka double up as England school Croatia in historic Nations League routRead moreEngland, who have a firm grip on second place in theirNations Leaguegroup and are confident of reaching next year’s finals, saw Harry Kane and Bukayo Saka each score twice and Jude Bellingham become the first midfielder to register four goal involvements in a game since David Platt against San Marino in 1993.Anthony Gordon and Morgan Rogers were also on the scoresheet and Tuchel believes his players have used this extended international break to consign their limp World Cup semi-final defeat to Argentina to the past.“If you feel pain you have to lay with the pain,” the manager said. “The same with disappointment. It was not easy at the beginning of the camp. We had an excellent performance against Spain. The focus in the meetings, the translation of the meetings on the pitch, to bring it within these circumstances inCroatia, to win this dominant performance is the way to move on. We’ll always have a scar, feel pain, but this is the way to move forward. We’ve played in the same manner all three matches.”Tuchel called it a complete performance.Englandpressed hard, offered invention in possession and were rapid on the counterattack. Kane, who will equal Peter Shilton’s record of 125 caps when England host Czechia in their and fourth final game of the camp on Tuesday, felt it had the power and physicality of a Premier League performance.“They just want to play like this, it’s their belief and wish, their conviction,” Tuchel said. “We don’t have to convince them. Harry plays a very intense game at Bayern. We still think we have a certain edge if we play on the front foot. If we push as often as possible in man for man it’s what the team likes. We have to manage these risks.”View image in fullscreenEngland’s Alex Scott (left) said it was a ‘great honour’ to share the field with Croatia’s Luka Modric (right), one of the Bournemouth midfielder’s favourite players as a child.Photograph: Bradley Collyer/PAThere was also an impressive performance from Alex Scott, who made his full debut in midfield. “First start and what a start,” Tuchel said of the 23-year-old. “He is so smooth on the ball, his decision making. He plays with so much confidence. He is so active. The work rate off the ball makes him the complete package. We had a lot of variety in the centre of the pitch.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionScott was buzzing about facing Luka Modric, who struggled for Croatia. “It’s pretty surreal,” the Bournemouth midfielder said. “Probably one of my favourite players growing up because I had seen him as a boy. One of the best players in the world on his day. To be on the pitch with him and competing is a great honour and thankfully we got the win today.”Kane, who is up to 89 international goals, was delighted with England’s attitude. Croatia, 13th in the world, were looking to bounce back after losing 4-1 to Spain on Tuesday.“Every man was at the highest level,” the captain said. “They rested a lot of players on Tuesday. I feel they saw this as their best opportunity to get into those top two spots. During the week it was beautiful weather, an amazing hotel, looking out to the ocean. We could have fallen into that holiday mode.”Explore more on these topicsEnglandNations LeagueThomas TuchelCroatianewsShareReuse this content

title: Wakefield dominate Warrington in Grand Final to claim fairytale Super League title | Super League | The Guardian
description: Wakefield’s dominant first-half performance crushed Warrington’s hopes to secure their first Super League Grand Final with a 23-10 victory at Old Trafford
Author: Aaron Bower
Headline: Wakefield’s dominant first-half performance crushed Warrington’s hopes to secure their first Super League Grand Final with a 23-10 victory at Old Trafford
Content: Wakefield Trinity players lift the Super League trophy to complete a remarkable rise after relegation in 2023.Photograph: News Images/NurPhoto/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenWakefield Trinity players lift the Super League trophy to complete a remarkable rise after relegation in 2023.Photograph: News Images/NurPhoto/ShutterstockSuper LeagueWakefield dominate Warrington in Grand Final to claim fairytale Super League titleGrand Final: Warrington 10-23 WakefieldTrinity are champions for first time since 1968Aaron Bowerat Old TraffordSat 3 Oct 2026 16.51 EDTFirst published on Sat 3 Oct 2026 15.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDo not let anyone tell you fairytales do not exist. This is not just a maidenSuper Leaguetitle, or indeed a first major trophy for almost 60 years. This is the culmination of one of the most remarkable sporting stories of our time: from the unfashionable, second tier side nobody really spoke about to the champions of England.Matt Ellis promised things would change. When he took ownership of his belovedWakefield Trinityin 2023, he inherited a club on its knees. Just relegated to the Championship, with a stadium that resembled a building site and a squad of players nobody wanted a piece of. But he insisted that within five years, Wakefield would win their first major trophy since 1968 with his investment.Super League Grand Final: Warrington Wolves v Wakefield Trinity – liveRead moreIn the end, he lied: it took him only three. As Wakefield lifted rugby league’s most prestigious prize aloft inside Old Trafford on Saturday evening, surely not even Ellis could have foreseen how quickly all this could have happened. It is not an exaggeration to suggest Trinity have long been seen as one of Super League’s laughing stocks; now, they are the club everyone has to catch.Most of their recent history has been dominated by financial problems, and, year after year, simply surviving was seen as an achievement. That is not an indictment on those who came before Ellis, with the previous custodian of Wakefield, Michael Carter, playing just as key a role in this moment. Without him, this night would not have become a reality.Two years ago this week, Wakefield were preparing for the Championship play-offs with promotion to Super League the prize. Just making the playoffs this season would have been regarded as an achievement but, instead, Trinity have defied all odds and, in truth, all sporting logic to win their first trophy for a long, long time.Perhaps the most staggering thing about this night, though, was how Wakefield managed the occasion. After dismantling Wigan in the semi-finals last week, the biggest question mark over Trinity was their inexperience in games like these. But they looked like a side who have been walking out in Grand Finals for years.View image in fullscreenCam Scott dives over to score a try for Wakefield.Photograph: Olly Hassell/SWpix.com/ShutterstockThey comprehensively outplayedWarringtonfrom start to finish, leading 19-0 by half-time and never really looking back. Tries from Cam Scott, Isaiah Vagana and Jazz Tevaga put Trinity in complete control – with Jack Sinfield’s drop goal in the moments before the half-time hooter establishing a four-score lead. In games like these, they are often insurmountable cushions. That proved true here.What a moment for the Sinfield family too, with Jack winning his first Super League title on the day his father, Sir Kevin, seven times a winner here himself, delivered the match ball after completing his latest ultra-marathon fundraising challenge. That story was just one of several on the night: with seven of this team with Wakefield in the Championship just two years ago.“It’s pretty sweet for me as an individual but for the club, the players, everything we’ve built up over the last three years is phenomenal,” said Daryl Powell, beaten here in 2017 with Castleford. “This club can go as far as it wants and do anything it wants. It shows you that special things can be achieved.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe RecapThe best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFor every winner though, there is a loser. Warrington were looking for their first league title since 1955 but they have now lost five straight Old Trafford deciders. It is hard to imagine when a better opportunity will come around. “It’s not the result we were after,” Sam Burgess admitted. “The further you go, the deeper the wound. There’s a lot of disappointed men.”There was no shortage of effort from his side after half-time, epitomised by the early Arron Lindop try which briefly raised hopes of the greatest of comebacks. But Wakefield extinguished any momentum quickly, reasserting their control on the contest as Johnstone – who won the Rob Burrow Award for man of the match – finished a fine move for his second try and put the game beyond doubt.1968 was the last time the Wakefield City Hall steps were filled with a Trinity squad celebrating silverware. They will finally return on Sunday as heroes. You would suspect it will not be 58 years between drinks this time around. This club are here to stay.Explore more on these topicsSuper LeagueWakefield TrinityWarringtonRugby leaguematch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Bowie gets Pocognoli off mark with Scotland victory in North Macedonia | Nations League | The Guardian
description: Sébastien Pocognoli secured his first win in charge of Scotland with Kieron Bowie scoring in a 2-0 win in North Macedonia despite a late red card for Scott McKenna
Author: Ewan Murray
Headline: Sébastien Pocognoli secured his first win in charge of Scotland with Kieron Bowie scoring in a 2-0 win in North Macedonia despite a late red card for Scott McKenna
Content: Kieron Bowie celebrates with Andy Robertson after Scotland’s breakthrough goal.Photograph: Andrew Milligan/PAView image in fullscreenKieron Bowie celebrates with Andy Robertson after Scotland’s breakthrough goal.Photograph: Andrew Milligan/PANations LeagueBowie gets Pocognoli off mark with Scotland victory in North MacedoniaEwan MurraySat 3 Oct 2026 17.01 EDTLast modified on Sat 3 Oct 2026 17.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis was an occasion on which Scotland dare not stumble. By the time Kieron Bowie smashed home a seventh minute opener against aNorth Macedoniaside not without its troubles to seek, it was already clear they would not. Bowie afforded Sébastien Pocognoli his first goal as the Scotland manager. Later, the Belgian had his maiden victory confirmed. Anything else, against such a dismal level of opposition, would have been worthy of significant Scottish embarrassment.John McGinn’s 22nd goal for his country, coming from the penalty spot, meant the scoreline at least almost reflected Scotland’s dominance. Only Scott McKenna’s late sending off and a failure to notch three, four or five could have irked Pocognoli. Scotland remain alive and kicking in section B1 of theNations Leaguewhile aware they will face far, far stiffer challenges. Scotland needed to be professional in North Macedonia and met that task appropriately.Lamine Yamal stars again as Spain see off Czechia and maintain perfect startRead moreOn the occasion of Andy Robertson’s 100th cap, it appeared in the early stages that the Tottenham full-back had been stung by criticism of recent performances inScotlandcolours. Robertson marauded forward at will, including inside five minutes where he forced Stole Dimitrievski into a fine save. McGinn, like Robertson, has been the subject of some scathing words. McGinn’s response was as forceful as his teammate.It was Bowie, though, who afforded Scotland crucial early leeway. Jack Hendry’sred card in the early stagesof Tuesday’s loss to Switzerland led to Bowie being withdrawn from the Scotland attack. Pocognoli retained faith in Bowie in Skopje. Bowie had plenty to do when collecting Billy Gilmour’s pass, 25 yards from goal and with two defenders in close proximity. He set himself before firing a terrific left-foot shot beyond the helpless Dimitrievski.McGinn’s outrageous pass from the right-back position to Robertson, who was operating as a left winger, should have ensured a Scotland second. Robertson opted to shoot and dragged his shot wide when a square pass to Oli McBurnie was the more sensible option. As Ben Gannon-Doak and Bowie missed opportunities, North Macedonia opted for two substitutions with just half an hour played.View image in fullscreenKieron Bowie fires Scotland ahead during the first half.Photograph: Andrew Milligan/PAScotland’s lack of ruthlessness was their only concern. Gannon-Doak was clean through on Dimitrievski within five minutes of the restart but shot tamely at the goalkeeper. Gannon-Doak and Scotland soon believed they had won a penalty, only for the video assistant referee to rightly highlight the Bournemouth player had stood on the foot of Matej Gashtarov rather than vice versa. North Macedonia were clinging on as Bowie tested Dimitrievski from close range.Officialdom was soon to smile on Scotland. The match referee had originally given a foul against McKenna as the centre-back nodded the ball down towards Bowie from a Scotland corner. Not only was that decision reversed but Bojan Miovski was penalised for blocking Bowie’s shot with an arm. McGinn finished low and hard to close this game as a contest. Only three players have scored more Scotland goals than the Aston Villa midfielder.Ryan Christie’s arrival at half-time added composure and creativity to the Scotland midfield. He looks the ideal candidate to link play in Pocognoli’s final third. It will be a surprise if Christie does not start when Slovenia visit Glasgow on Tuesday. Angus Gunn, whose position as the Scotland goalkeeper was questioned before this game, had nothing whatsoever of consequence to do.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMcKenna will miss Slovenia’s visit after upending Agon Elezi, six minutes from time. The episode was regarded as the denial of an obvious scoring opportunity. Robertson’s slack pass had landed his teammate in bother.Robertson later admitted he owes McKenna an apology before reflecting on his cap milestone. “It means everything to me and my family,” said the 32-year-old. “It has been an unbelievable journey. It is emotional for me because I love this country and this is a special achievement. I believe I still have a lot to give.”Handily for Pocognoli, Scotland did not need 11 men to win. McGinn was denied his second of the evening in stoppage time. North Macedonia, who have now gone seven games without scoring a goal, are a desperate lot.Explore more on these topicsNations LeagueNorth MacedoniaScotlandmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Verstappen ends pole wait at Bahrain GP in Malaysia but Russell risks losing more ground | Formula One 2026 | The Guardian
description: Max Verstappen claimed pole position for the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia in Sepang, taking the top spot for Red Bull for the first time this season
Author: Giles Richards
Headline: Max Verstappen claimed pole position for the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia in Sepang, taking the top spot for Red Bull for the first time this season
Content: Red Bull's Max Verstappen raises a first in celebration after finishing qualifying 0.298sec faster than Ferrari’s Lewis Hamilton.Photograph: Jakub Porzycki/ReutersView image in fullscreenRed Bull's Max Verstappen raises a first in celebration after finishing qualifying 0.298sec faster than Ferrari’s Lewis Hamilton.Photograph: Jakub Porzycki/ReutersFormula One 2026Verstappen ends pole wait at Bahrain GP in Malaysia but Russell risks losing more groundFerrari’s Lewis Hamilton starts second on the front rowKimi Antonelli in fourth, George Russell down in eighthGiles RichardsSat 3 Oct 2026 05.47 EDTLast modified on Sat 3 Oct 2026 11.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe wait has been long forMax Verstappenbut when the Dutchman finally claimed his first pole position of the year he did it in no little style. Taking the top spot for Red Bull at the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, Verstappen was all but untouchable.However, what was of greatest import for theFormula Oneworld championship was the gulf between the title leader, Kimi Antonelli, and his Mercedes teammate, George Russell. The latter, somewhat floundering in Sepang, is now in danger of losing further points he can ill afford in pursuit of the Italian.Formula One 2026: Max Verstappen takes pole for Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia – liveRead moreVerstappen delivered a commanding performance in taking Red Bull’s first pole of the season, beating the Ferrari ofLewis Hamilton, who also delivered a mighty lap, into second by three-tenths of a second. Antonelli was fourth but crucially his title rival Russell could mange only eighth.Red Bull’s Isack Hadjar qualified third but has a five-place grid penalty for taking a new engine, meaning Antonelli will start third on the grid and Russell seventh. Charles Leclerc was fifth for Ferrari and the defending world champion, Lando Norris, sixth for McLaren.Verstappen, who has been wrestling with a recalcitrant Red Bull all season and is out of the title fight, has yet to take a win and was understandably pleased with pole. Not least in that his team have done so well to develop the car – and that he could take advantage of it with the control and confidence he has demonstratedso far in Malaysia.“It is fantastic,” Verstappen said. “To finally get it from where we started this season, pretty incredible. I am happy with today and I am going to try to win tomorrow. When you start first, that is the target.”Few would bet against him, although a jubilant Hamilton, taking his best qualifying result since the Hungarian GP, will expect to mix it with the Dutchman from the off, setting up a mouthwatering opening to the race. However, it is in their wake where the title is at stake.Afterhis victory at the last round in Baku, Russell had closed the gap to Antonelli to 66 points with eight rounds remaining and was hopeful of increasing the pressure. Yet he could not hook it up in Malaysia, while Mercedes were also left a little perplexed as to why the swathe of upgrades they brought to the race did not deliver.View image in fullscreenLewis Hamilton will start second on the grid for Sunday’s grand prix at Sepang.Photograph: Robbie Hoad/Every Second Media/ShutterstockNonetheless it was Antonelli who still had a marked advantage over his teammate, despite an unforced error going too wide in Q2 that proved costly. The pressure is now on Russell to try to come back at his teammate, who has every opportunity to further extend his lead.Antonelli conceded that pole might have been beyond him but also noted that the high tyre degradation in Malaysia could yet play a part in what is likely to be a two or even three-stop race.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe RecapThe best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“It’s a shame for the mistake, but with a clean qualifying without the track limit, maybe P2, P3 on the road would have been possible,” said Antonelli. “Max did an incredible job and alsoFerrari. We have to be happy because it could have been much worse. It’s going to be interesting but I think Max has the edge on pace. Tomorrow, the tyre deg is going to be huge.”Red Bull had been hoping to continue to bring their car on in the second half of the season and, although Verstappen’s dissatisfaction with energy-management has remained throughout, he will be buoyed by the advances the team are making – and perhaps even more importantly that they are coming to terms with their car, which bodes well for next season. On this form in qualifying, Verstappen has every chance to claim his first win of 2026 on a track where he was the last driver to win a grand prix, in 2017.Antonelli’s crucial error occurred when he had his first time in Q2 deleted for exceeding track limits. He had to go again, using up another set of the soft tyres he could not afford and leaving him with only one set of the new rubber to use in Q3. He was therefore able to make only one attempt at a hot lap and then with care to avoid another deleted time. It was perhaps moot, so good was Verstappen, who improved on both his decisive laps, finishing with an inch-perfect 1min 35.130sec run to put him three-tenths in front of Hamilton.The race, branded as the Bahrain GP, is being held in Malaysia to replace the meeting that was cancelled earlier this year because of the war in the Middle East. Sepang was the venue for the Malaysian GP between 1999 and 2017.Explore more on these topicsFormula One 2026Max VerstappenLewis HamiltonFormula OneRed BullMercedes GPFerrarinewsShareReuse this content

title: Let there be blanks instead of Manchester City’s name on trophies: there was no honour | Manchester City | The Guardian
description: The spaces can stand as a memorial to these lost years both as a rebuke to an era of greed but also a tribute to the Premier League’s hunt for justice
Author: Jonathan Wilson
Headline: The spaces can stand as a memorial to these lost years both as a rebuke to an era of greed but also a tribute to the Premier League’s hunt for justice
Content: Manchester City lift the Premier League trophy in 2018 after the club finished 19 points clear at the top.Photograph: Martin Rickett/PAView image in fullscreenManchester City lift the Premier League trophy in 2018 after the club finished 19 points clear at the top.Photograph: Martin Rickett/PAInside footballManchester CityLet there be blanks instead of Manchester City’s name on trophies: there was no honourJonathan WilsonThe spaces can stand both as a rebuke to an era of greed but also a tribute to the Premier League’s hunt for justiceSat 3 Oct 2026 15.00 EDTShareAt half-time in the 2014 League Cup final, Sunderland led Manchester City 1-0. Yaya Touré equalised with a casually brilliant 30-yard clip 10 minutes after the break, and City went on to win 3-1. City, we now know from the independent commission, were at the time involved ina prolonged and calculated act of cheating, while Touré, the leaks in Der Spiegel suggested, was being paid via a dual contract to disguise exactly how much City were spending. Although precise details were left to the appendices, the commission’s report refers to payments “not recorded in an employment contract … but instead recorded in a consultancy agreement”.Had Sunderland won, they would not merely have ended a 41-year wait for a trophy but would have qualified for the following season’s Europa League. It’s possible, of course, that the strain the extra games placed on the squad would have led to relegation in 2015, rather than the familiar trope of sacking a manager, in this case Gus Poyet, midway through the season, and surviving thanks to a bump under his successor, Dick Advocaat.But it’s also possible that the greater exposure brought by European football, the surge of positivity engendered by unfamiliar and unexpected silverware, may have led toPremier Leagueconsolidation, stability and semi-regular European qualification.Manchester City fans are right to feel angry – now they need to direct it at the owners | Will UnwinRead moreShould Sunderland feel cheated? Of course they should, just as those who came second behind Lance Armstrong should feel cheated; just as Liverpool and Arsenal should feel cheated over the League Cup finals of 2016 and 2018; just as Stoke should feel cheated over the 2011 FA Cup final; just as Manchester United should feel cheated over the Premier League titles in 2012 and 2018 and Liverpool should in 2014; just as every club who played in the same competitions as City between 2009 and 2018 should feel cheated. But does that mean the 2014 League Cup should be taken from City and awarded to Sunderland?These are two different questions, and it’s probably best to deal with the latter first – and this, unfortunately, is where subjectivity is unavoidable. I can’t speak for other Sunderland fans but, personally, I wouldn’t want it.Perhaps this comes from never having seen my club win a major trophy. If it happens, I want it to be pure. I want images that will be remembered down the generations, like the highlights of 1973 – Ian Porterfield’s goal, Jim Montgomery’s save and Bob Stokoe’s celebratory skip across the pitch in mac and trilby.I want the surge of adrenaline when a goal is scored, the agonised wait of injury time, the rush of the final whistle. I want tears and hugs and community and togetherness, all the things my dad’s generation banged on about. I want to get drunk and sing on a train. I don’t want to find out via an alert on my phone 12 years after the fact as I unpack the dishwasher.View image in fullscreenManchester City’s Yaya Touré equalises against Sunderland in the 2014 League Cup final.Photograph: Eddie Keogh/ReutersOthers may feel differently but the arithmetic of trophies won seems far less important than the experience of winning and the memories and sense of comradeship it provokes. Glory denied cannot be rectified a generation later by an independent commission, no matter how august.Awarding rivals league titles seems even less satisfactory. In the 2017-18 season, for instance, the league was effectively over by the end of January with City 15 points clear.As City went on to amass 100 points, there was little point in the four sides behind them – Manchester United, Liverpool, Chelsea and Tottenham, who were separated by five points – exerting themselves to try to rein City in.Their priorities changed. United, Chelsea and Spurs all reached the FA Cup semi-finals. Liverpool got to the Champions League final. In those circumstances, why would any of them have prioritised the league? To award United, who finished second, the title, would seem not just empty but arbitrary.That, though, does not mean City should not be stripped of those titles. They won them unfairly; why on earth should they be allowed to keep them? (And yes, something similar could be said of Chelsea, but that’s an argument for why Chelsea should also have been stripped of titles, not for why City should not be).How can those trophies be left in the record books for future generations unquestioningly to see? How can City stand as the fourth-most successful side in league history when so much of that success was achieved by cheating?skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe argument will be made that City’s players strived hard for those trophies. But so did players for those other teams, the ones who weren’t cheating. And how much easier to win in a deep squad full of high-grade players, drawn to City by the money they were offering, money whose source, the independent commission concluded, had been disguised in contravention of Premier League regulations.View image in fullscreenManchester City with the League Cup in 2014, one of seven major trophies won between 2009 and 2018.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianEuphoric memories cannot be expunged, but it is for City fans (and players and coaching staff and directors) to decide what to do with them. If they still want to exult in Sergio Agüero’s 94th-minute winner to claim the 2012 Premier League title, nobody can stop them. But the rest of the world knows what it was based on, that as the rest of the Premier League played to regulations voted in by the clubs themselves, City did not.That would mean that there was no Premier League champion in 2012, 2014 or 2018, no FA Cup winner in 2011 and no League Cup winner in 2014, 2016 or 2018 (and it does not seem unreasonable to wonder, when all this is done, whether there might be more to be investigated after 2018). If there are blanks on the roll of honour, let them be; there was no honour there.Let the spaces stand as testimony to what those seasons were. Let them stand as a memorial to the years when a foreign entity tried to subvert English football, when a foreign entity took this country’s greatest cultural mode, and all the passion and all the feeling, all the sorrow and all the joy, all the love it has entailed, and tried to twist it for its own political ends. Let them stand as a warning of the dangers of laissez-faire capitalism, when everything, no matter how beloved, could be sold off to the highest bidder.And let them stand as a monument to a Premier League that finally – belatedly? – took action, to a process that maintained its independence, to an institution that, at no little risk to its own wellbeing – a risk that has not gone away – in the end preferred justice and fairness and decency over grubby deals with the rich and powerful.Let the years without a champion stand for ever vacant, both as a rebuke and as a tribute. Sometimes, emptiness can be the most eloquent statement of all.Explore more on these topicsManchester CityInside footballPremier LeaguecommentShareReuse this content

title: Louis Rees-Zammit scores two tries as Bristol defeat champions Northampton | Prem Rugby | The Guardian
description: Bristol overcame a nasty-looking head injury to their centre Benhard van Rensburg to clinch an impressive victory over last year’s champions Northampton
Author: Gerard Meagher
Headline: Bristol overcame a nasty-looking head injury to their centre Benhard van Rensburg to clinch an impressive victory over last year’s champions Northampton
Content: Bristol’s Louis Rees-Zammit (front) shouts in celebration after scoring his second try at Ashton Gate.Photograph: Paul Rubery/Focus Images Ltd/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenBristol’s Louis Rees-Zammit (front) shouts in celebration after scoring his second try at Ashton Gate.Photograph: Paul Rubery/Focus Images Ltd/ShutterstockPrem RugbyLouis Rees-Zammit scores two tries as Bristol defeat champions NorthamptonPrem Rugby: Bristol 41-26 NorthamptonBears win opening two games for first time since 2023Gerard Meagherat Ashton GateSat 3 Oct 2026 14.34 EDTFirst published on Sat 3 Oct 2026 13.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLouis Rees-Zammit may have been denied a hat-trick againstNorthamptonbut there is no doubting who stole the show as Bristol maintained their flying start to the season by downing the champions. The Wales winger scored twice, earned the Bears’ late penalty try and, just to make clear that there is more than one showman in town, produced his own version of Henry Pollock’s pulse celebration.“I obviously know Pollock has done that before so I thought I’d just give it a little bit back,” said Rees-Zammit. “Me and Pollock are really close. He’s doing great things for the sport. If we’re going to grow this game we need personalities, he’s definitely one and he’s got to do something next week after the forfeit we spoke about yesterday.”‘They said I ran away from rucks’: Emmanuel Iyogun on going from reluctant prop to England debutRead moreAll things told, it was a fine day forBristol– a nasty-looking head injury to Benhard van Rensburg aside – and a pretty miserable one for Northampton. The Bears helped themselves to six tries with Gabriel Oghre, Tom Jordan and the excellent Harry Randall also on the scoresheet but it is the defensive resilience that will please Pat Lam most. Back in May, Bristol shipped 94 points to the Saints at Northampton but there is far more steel about them on this evidence.“I’ve watched that game five times,” said Bristol’s director of rugby Lam. “I never watched a game five times in the off-season. Though it hurt, I watched it and built the whole pre-season around that in a sense.”View image in fullscreenBristol’s Louis Rees-Zammit (centre) steams through the Northampton defence before going over to score the first of his two tries.Photograph: Andrew Matthews/PAThe downside was Van Rensburg’s injury. He received lengthy treatment and was taken off on a stretcher just before half-time and appeared to be knocked out cold. The South-African born centre is all-action but suffered the same fate during England’s summer victory over Argentina. He was seen by the Bristol dugout in the second half, however, allaying fears that the injury was serious.For the champions, it was a day to forget. For the first hour, pretty much everything that could go wrong did. Balls were dropped, sitters were missed, tries were disallowed and the lineout went horribly awry. Pollock began brightly but endured a disappointing afternoon too, taking a painful looking low blow in the first half for good measure.Quick GuidePrem roundup: Gloucester thrash hapless QuinsShowGloucestercontinued their impressive start to the Prem Rugby season by handing out a 48-0 thrashing to hapless Harlequins at Kingsholm.The hosts' eight-try win followed up their impressive opening day victory over Exeter at Sandy Park. Quins were without a few leading players including England internationals, Marcus Smith and Alex Dombrandt, but were outplayed in every aspect of the game and failed to get on the scoreboard.Ben Loader collected a crossfield kick from Charlie Atkinson to score the first try, with Jac Morgan finishing off a driving lineout for Gloucester's second after Will Evans was yellow carded. Will Trenholm surged over from close range and Atkinson added the bonus-point try as the hosts took a 24-0 half-time lead.Seb Atkinson and Caolon Engefield [pictured] raced in to score within four minutes of the restart, with Will Joseph and George Barton also on the score sheet. Barton added four conversions as Gloucester joined local rivals Bath and Bristol at the top of the table with two wins from two.Leicester bounced back from their opening defeat to Saracens with a 24-19 victory atNewcastle. New recruit Obi Ene crossed early on for the hosts, but the Tigers took control as tries from Samiuela Moli and Adam Radwan along with a Billy Searle penalty handed them a 17-5 lead at the break.George McGuigan went over in the second half forNewcastle, but Will Hurd’s try extended the visitors' advantage. Leicester withstood a late scare after Cam Jordan crossed  in the last 10 minutes.Press AssociationPhotograph: Luke Hastings/Shutterstock EditorialWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Then came Alex Mitchell from the replacements bench and Northampton briefly threatened the unlikeliest of comebacks but two late yellow cards – the second for Tommy Freeman for a bodycheck on Rees-Zammit which led to a penalty try – put paid to that. “I’m not going to lie, I was devastated,” said Rees-Zammit. “It was just fire in my belly to score a hat-trick. I’m good friends with Tommy and it’s all love after but in the moment I was a bit gutted.”Fitz Harding was a constant presence at the breakdown for the Bears and his early turnover gave Bristol a lineout deep in Northampton’s 22, from which there was no stopping the lineout drive with Oghre dotting down. However, Northampton hit back almost immediately with George Hendy going over on the left after a burst from Pollock.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe BreakdownThe latest rugby union news and analysis, plus all the week's action reviewedEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenNorthampton’s Henry Pollock reacts as referee Ian Tempest disallows a try on a rare quiet afternoon for the 21-year-old England star.Photograph: Tom Sandberg/PPAUK/ShutterstockBristol seized the initiative thereafter and Rees-Zammit eventually went over after a smart pass from Oghre. Northampton had endured a pretty torrid first 39 minutes and Ollie Sleightholme’s fumble on the right with the try-line beckoning just about summed up their first-half performance. They probed just before the interval, however, and it was then that Van Rensburg’s head struck a stray knee.The match restarted with a Northampton scrum. Another strike move, another try for Hendy and suddenly it was a one-point game at half-time. To the Bears’ credit, they raised their game again with Jordan stretching to the line before Randall sniped over from close range. Rees-Zammit splashed over for his second to give Bristol breathing space after a touch of good fortune, with James Williams’ penalty striking a post before Mitchell inspired a mini-revival from Saints.First he scooted under the posts before teeing up Josh Kemeny in the left corner, but Fin Smith pulled the conversion to keep Bristol’s lead at eight points. And after Northampton’s replacement prop Ion Neculai was shown a yellow card, the Bears finished the game on top.Max Pepper had a try disallowed before Rees-Zammit was cynically denied a hat-trick by Freeman, who was sent to the sin-bin, with the referee, Ian Tempest, choosing to award a penalty try. “I’d hate to think we would ever panic, regardless of the result,” said Northampton’s director of rugby, Phil Dowson. “The overwhelming feeling is frustration. There’s no panic but we don’t want to make the same mistake twice.”Explore more on these topicsPrem RugbyBristolNorthamptonRugby unionmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Celtic fans throw tennis balls at club owner Dermot Desmond during golf tournament | Celtic | The Guardian
description: Celtic’s principal shareholder Dermot Desmond had tennis balls thrown towards him during the Alfred Dunhill Links golf tournament at St Andrews in a protest from fans
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Celtic’s principal shareholder Dermot Desmond had tennis balls thrown towards him during the Alfred Dunhill Links golf tournament at St Andrews in a protest from fans
Content: Dermot Desmond (centre) leaves St Andrews with security after Celtic fans staged a protest.Photograph: Stuart Wallace/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenDermot Desmond (centre) leaves St Andrews with security after Celtic fans staged a protest.Photograph: Stuart Wallace/ShutterstockCelticCeltic fans throw tennis balls at club owner Dermot Desmond during golf tournamentDesmond escorted off St Andrews course by securityCeltic say the protest ‘brought shame upon the club’Press AssociationSat 3 Oct 2026 18.24 EDTFirst published on Sat 3 Oct 2026 14.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCeltic’s principal shareholder Dermot Desmond had tennis balls thrown towards him during his visit to the Alfred Dunhill Links golf tournament at St Andrews in a protest from fans.The 76-year-old – who has been criticised by supporters for an apparent lack of progress on the pitch – was taking part in the pro-am event on Saturday when the disruption happened on the green of the 15th hole.Tennis balls with pictures of Desmond’s face crossed out were thrown on to the green, with Desmond then escorted off the course by security.The Celtic Fans Collective laterreleased a statement on X, which included video and pictures of the protest, calling for change at the top of the club.View image in fullscreenDermot Desmond is driven away from the course after the fans’ protest.Photograph: Stuart Wallace/Shutterstock“Dermot Desmond has essentially been allowed to run Celtic Football Club whilst using his wealth to hide from supporters and accountability,” the statement said. “Fans took the chance today to send a message that this arrangement cannot continue.”On Saturday evening, Celtic issued a lengthy and strongly-worded statement against the “premeditated action” which “brought shame upon” the name of the club.The statement read: “Celtic Football Club has never sought to prevent supporters from expressing criticism of the club, its board or its shareholders. Supporters are entitled to disagree with decisions, to make their views known and to protest peacefully. What occurred at St Andrews represents a significant and unacceptable escalation.“Those responsible have brought shame upon the name of Celtic Football Club and upon a reputation which generations of Celtic supporters have spent more than a century building. The club no longer accepts that the Celtic Fans Collective can credibly claim to represent the wider Celtic support. Those responsible for today’s events certainly do not speak for the many thousands of Celtic supporters who express their views passionately, peacefully and responsibly.”Celtic said the club would not be “intimidated or coerced by organised acts of disruption”, adding “there is a line between protest and deliberate disruption. Today that line was crossed … The club will protect its employees, directors, shareholders and supporters. The reputation of Celtic Football Club is non negotiable.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMartin O’Neill’s side – who claimed the Premiership title ahead of Hearts after a final-day decider last season as part of a domestic double – currently sit top of the table, two points clear of rivals Rangers.Celtic, though, lost the last three games before the international break, including two defeats by Rangers,one at Parkhead, and were also beaten 3-1 at home by Ferencvaros in their opening Europa League fixture.Explore more on these topicsCelticnewsShareReuse this content

title: Lamine Yamal stars again as Spain see off Czechia and maintain perfect start | Nations League | The Guardian
description: For the third consecutive game the teenager scored inside six minutes, curling in another outrageous goal as Spain shone on their World Cup homecoming
Author: Sid Lowe
Headline: For the third consecutive game the teenager scored inside six minutes, curling in another outrageous goal as Spain shone on their World Cup homecoming
Content: Lamine Yamal opens the scoring for Spain against Czechia in Oviedo.Photograph: Manu Fernández/APView image in fullscreenLamine Yamal opens the scoring for Spain against Czechia in Oviedo.Photograph: Manu Fernández/APNations LeagueLamine Yamal stars again as Spain see off Czechia and maintain perfect startSid LoweSat 3 Oct 2026 17.13 EDTLast modified on Sat 3 Oct 2026 18.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLamine Yamal says he feels like Superman or Spider-Man sometimes, and Spain’s fans are starting to wonder if he just might be. There is something comic book hero about what the teenager is doing right now, some unexplained super power swelling inside him. For the third consecutive game he scored inside six minutes, curling in another outrageous goal as Spain completed their World Cup homecoming in Oviedo with a 3-1 win over Czechia that leaves them a single point from theNations Leaguequarter finals already. Spain’s manager, Luis de la Fuente, put it simply: “Lamine Yamal is on course to become a legend.”Lamine Yamal: ‘Football is mechanised but players like me have that special spark’Read moreAnd yet in a game which seemed to have been done at half-time, when Spain led 2-0 after Rodrigo Hernandez had added the second and Lamine Yamal was withdrawn, his show seemingly over, the danger returned.Czechia, vastly improved after the break, pulled one back through Jiri Slama on 69 and then were denied a 79th-minute equaliser when Vassilis Fotias, the referee, who rescued Spain, harshly ruled out a Ryan Naderi goal – apparently for a foul on Robin Le Normand as the free-kick that led to it was swung in.Reduced to 10 men soon after, still furious, Czechia finally fell with two minutes left when Mikel Merino madeSpainsafe. Theseleccion’sfirst visit to the Carlos Tartiere in 11 years had ended the way they had hoped. Welcomed back as world and European champions once more, they were applauded off as winners again. A night that had begun with Rodri being presented with the World Cup by Santi Cazorla and Juan Mata, academy products at Real Oviedo and members of the generation to which all others would forever be compared, ended with a jeopardy no one anticipated when it started in a way that has become implausibly, absurdly familiar.Lamine Yamal had scored after 104 seconds at Wembley and 70 in Seville, as Spain defeated England and Croatia. And the silly thing was that here, his goal might have come even sooner. Fifteen seconds in, the first frisson of excitement went round this place as he chased down the goalkeeper and after just fifty-seven Oviedo almost exploded. But, running on to a Dani Olmo pass, Lamine Yamal calmly guided a shot past the goalkeeper Antonin Kinsky … and past the post.He would just have to wait until the sixth minute was up instead. Playing a quick one-two with Dani Olmo, Lamine Yamal took possession on the top right corner of the area and curled another outrageous shot into the far corner, the ridiculous becoming routine. They had been playing five minutes 20 seconds, another stadium letting out a roar that spoke of delight but also a kind of disbelief. 320 seconds he had been out there, taking him to 494 seconds to score three.View image in fullscreenRodri reacts after scoring Spain’s second in OviedoPhotograph: Petr David Josek/APSpain weren’t hurrying but they were controlling, and the chances were accumulating: by half-time they had taken 13 shots to one, and enjoyed 70% of possession. They had also added a second on 32 minutes. Rodri collected near the centre circle and did something he rarely does. The man who sometimes seems to be walking, effortlessly controlling the game with his mind and without fuss, happy enough to drop the ball off to others to do their thing, went off on a run. Advancing through the midfield, he slotted to Pedri whose return, with the help of a defender’s touch, set him up to shoot high into the net.Next Lamine Yamal slipped in Alex Baena, denied by Kinsky. A little dinked pass from Baena then found Lamine whose shot, slightly scuffed, went wide. At the break Baena, who had drawn “oohs” with one glorious touch, was withdrawn and so too was Lamine Yamal, his work here done, another show over. The game, on the other hand, was not. That at least was Czechia’s intention and it should probably have been their reward too, the visitors taking a decisive step forward and a degree of control. They also reduced the deficit with 20 minutes to go.The move began deep: as it progressed up the right and through the middle, Jiri Slama was sprinting to catch up. Adam Hlozek saw him coming and played the ball into his path for him to steer it low and true beyond David Raya.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionA first error from Spain’s keeper almost gave Czechia an equaliser when Raya stepped out to play and his misplaced pass only found Ondrej Lingr, and a second error really should have done soon after. But if there was relief for Spain when Lingr’s shot drifted wide of an unguarded goal, it was even greater when the referee ruled out Ryan Nadel’s effort.For Czechia there was disbelief. Michal Sadilek’s long cross had been headed goalwards by Ladislav Krejci, and Raya, reaching by the bar, could not hold on. The ball dropped on the line, where Nadel nudged it in. The referee, though, had blown. For Santi Denia on the touchline it was hard to take and it was equally difficult not to feel sympathy. All the more when Krejci was soon sent off and then Víctor Muñoz was sent clear, dashed into the area where Kinsky blocked and Merino, forever alive, finished off the festivities.Explore more on these topicsNations LeagueSpainCzechiamatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Zigiotti Olme capitalises on Liverpool mistake to keep Manchester United moving up WSL | Women's Super League | The Guardian
description: Julia Zigiotti Olme  scored the only goal of the game as Manchester United edged to a 1-0 victory over Liverpool at the Unity Stadium
Author: Guardian sport
Headline: Julia Zigiotti Olme scored the only goal of the game as Manchester United edged to a 1-0 victory over Liverpool at the Unity Stadium
Content: Manchester United’s Julia Zigiotti Olme celebrates after scoring the only goal of the game at the Unity Stadium.Photograph: Poppy Townson/MUFC/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenManchester United’s Julia Zigiotti Olme celebrates after scoring the only goal of the game at the Unity Stadium.Photograph: Poppy Townson/MUFC/Getty ImagesWomen's Super LeagueZigiotti Olme capitalises on Liverpool mistake to keep Manchester United moving up WSLGuardian sportand Press AssociationSat 3 Oct 2026 10.52 EDTLast modified on Sat 3 Oct 2026 12.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJulia Zigiotti Olme’s sixth-minute lob proved enough to earn the Manchester United coach, Eva Olid, a second Women’s Super League victory of the season with a 1-0 home win over Liverpool.Zigiotti Olme capitalised on a mistake by Liverpool goalkeeper, Khiara Keating, and, despite some late pressure by Gareth Taylor’s side, United held on to make it back-to-back league wins.Slegers feels support from Arsenal hierarchy despite dismal run but biggest test loomsRead moreAfter a shaky start under the new head coach, Olid, the Spaniard has now masterminded four consecutive victories in all competitions and United are unbeaten in five matches.This was United’s 250th match since the team reformed in 2018 and Olid watched her side mark the occasion with the breakthrough after six minutes.It was a moment to forget for England goalkeeper Keating after her pass out from the back was intercepted by Zigiotti Olme, who composed herself and chipped home in superb fashion.Liverpool pushed for a leveller and drew a double save from the United goalkeeper, Phallon Tullis-Joyce, midway through the first half. Cornelia Kapocs had a low effort saved by Tullis-Joyce, who got up quickly to deny Beata Olsson on the rebound as well.United’s Jess Park hit the crossbar before half-time with a left-foot strike from the edge of the box before Keating saved at her near post from Andrea Medina on the rebound. Liverpool’s best chance of an equaliser came 20 minutes from time when Jenna Clark found herself free at a corner but she could not direct her header on target.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMoving the GoalpostsNo topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe win moves United level with Liverpool in the WSL, with both teams three points off the European places.Explore more on these topicsWomen's Super LeagueManchester United WomenLiverpool FC WomenWomen's footballmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: We live in a rape-prone society. The horrific Cornell case reveals what that looks like | Rebecca Solnit | The Guardian
description: Public outcry to punish the alleged perpetrators in the Cornell case misses the point – the only solution is political, legal and cultural equality of women
Author: Rebecca Solnit
Headline: Public outcry to punish the alleged perpetrators in the Cornell case misses the point – the only solution is political, legal and cultural equality of women
Content: ‘Sexual assault arises in part through both the entitlement and the desire to abuse and dehumanize women, which is in part about definitions of both masculinity and femininity.’Photograph: Lauren Petracca/ReutersView image in fullscreen‘Sexual assault arises in part through both the entitlement and the desire to abuse and dehumanize women, which is in part about definitions of both masculinity and femininity.’Photograph: Lauren Petracca/ReutersOpinionUS universitiesWe live in a rape-prone society. The horrific Cornell case reveals what that looks likeRebecca SolnitPublic outcry to punish the alleged perpetrators in the Cornell case misses the point – the only solution is political, legal and cultural equality of womenSat 3 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 3 Oct 2026 06.02 EDTShareSometimes a story is so so appalling, it captures the public’s attention, including the attention of people who don’t focus on the issue otherwise. Such is the case with the alleged 2024 gang rape at Cornell University.For feminists who focus on violence against women or anyone who has ever cared about campus rape, the claims made in Jane Doe’scivil lawsuitagainst the alleged perpetrators may be unusual in its severity – but we know the statistics that show that somewhere between20% and 25% of women college studentswill be the victim of a sexual assault (no statistics tell us what percentage of men students will be rapists).This makes the public outcry to punish seven male students miss the point, which is that there are tens of thousands of campus rape stories, few of which make the news.We know that nearly every campus in the US has a plethora of rape victims and rapists. We also know how it often happens. The Johns Hopkins University “student well-being” blogsummarizesa key aspect:“The ‘Red Zone’ is a period of time that lasts from the start of the fall semester through Thanksgiving break when the majority of sexual assault occurs on college campuses ... It’s a six-to-10-week time frame when many students are going to parties, gatherings, and other social events to celebrate their return to campus. Data shows that over 50% of sexual assaults that occur on college campuses occur during this time. New students can be especially vulnerable during this period, due to their unfamiliarity with the campus, new social experiences, and the resources available to survivors.”The horror of the Cornell rape case is how ordinary it is | Moira DoneganRead moreWe know that the Greek system that sets the rules for most sororities and fraternities does not permit alcohol at sororities, which makes fraternities the hosts of the alcohol-saturated parties, which sends young women into enemy territory, which is where they are sometimes manipulated to get them drunk and stranded and abused.The Hopkins blog notes: “Alcohol is the tool that is most commonly used by perpetrators in cases of sexual assault ...A person who is incapacitated by drugs or alcohol is not able to consent.” We know that fraternities often make the news for their excesses and abuses, including sometimes-harmful-to-fatal hazing of their own potential members.We know the Cornell student newspaper editorial that brought this case to lightdeclaresthat 15% of all students there have experienced “nonconsensual sexual contact” and a disproportionate fifth of those incidents took place at fraternities.The Cornell fraternity in question was suspended from campus for a period, as a November 2024 Guardian piece about the incidentreports. Meanwhile, campus rape is a nationwide issue, and the Trump administration’s assaulton Title IX continues.The non-profit organization Human Rights Campaignreportsthat the Department of Education just rescinded a Biden-era Title IX rule: “Specifically, this move puts back in place rules for colleges and universities from the first Trump administration that suppress the voices of survivors of rape and sexual assault and make it easier for their perpetrators to get away with their actions.” It also affects LGBTQ+ students.The Trump administration appears comfortable in the company of alleged perpetrators. Last year, itintervened on behalf of Andrew Tate, who ischarged withseveral counts of rape, trafficking and assault against women. This past week, administration membersselectedRussell Brand, likewiseawaiting trialon multiple charges of sexual assault, to co-moderate a panel at a Maha conference on 29 September, and then there’s Trump, who has been held liable for sex abuse, and theallegationsagainst the defense secretary, Pete Hegseth. (All of the men deny wrongdoing.)While the criminal justice system should address reports of rape, we know that rates of conviction are appallingly low for a number of reasons. Although, thanks to feminist interventions, the legal system is better equipped to understand this crime and less prejudiced against victims, we will not change the world through that means.After rape allegations at Cornell University, why are women again being urged to talk to their sons? Why not men? | Gaby HinsliffRead moreSexual assault arises in part through both the entitlement and the desire to abuse and dehumanize women, which is in part about definitions of both masculinity and femininity: masculinity in that domination, violation and degradation are seen as status-enhancing, femininity in the perception that women’s bodies are for men to use, women’s voices and rights to be ignored.The most compelling thing I’ve read in response to the Cornell case is in anessayby feminist writer Soraya Chemaly. She cites anthropologist Peggy Sanday, who told her that there are “rape-prone” and “rape-free” societies: “She found that in rape-free cultures, women have far more authority, status, safety and freedom.”They’re societies in which women’s rights to bodily and social self-determination are respected, and a man who violates those rights would face severe consequences. “Rape-prone cultures, on the other hand, treat rape as an entitlement in a system that revolves around masculine contests and hierarchies.”Sanday alsowrotea book titled Fraternity Gang Rape, documenting “daily life in the fraternity, highlighting the role played by pornography, male bonding, and degrading, often grotesque, initiation and hazing rituals”. In 2020, an 18-year-old Cornell freshmandiedfrom an alcohol-intensive hazing ritual at the Phi Kappa Psi fraternity, neighbor to the fraternity where the 2024 gang rape allegedly took place.The only effective, lasting, far-reaching solution is the political, legal, economic and cultural equality of women. This requires the liberation of men from the kind of misogynistic male supremacy Sanday describes in the fraternities, which may give them power and status in the context of that supremacy, but also corrupts and distorts their psyches into the kind of dehumanized grotesquery described in the Cornell case.Rebecca Solnit is a Guardian US columnist. She is the author of Orwell’s Roses and co-editor with Thelma Young Lutunatabua of the climate anthology Not Too Late: Changing the Climate Story from Despair to PossibilityExplore more on these topicsUS universitiesOpinionUS educationRape and sexual assaultWomenLaw (US)commentShareReuse this content

title: Burnham must remember: more regulation is not the best way to improve public services | Phillip Inman | The Guardian
description: In the NHS as in the private sector, the measure of success should be customer satisfaction and not just box-ticking
Author: Phillip Inman
Headline: In the NHS as in the private sector, the measure of success should be customer satisfaction and not just box-ticking
Content: Satisfaction levels are rising in the NHS when talking about GP and hospital visits.Photograph: Nick Moore/AlamyView image in fullscreenSatisfaction levels are rising in the NHS when talking about GP and hospital visits.Photograph: Nick Moore/AlamyViewpoint columnEconomicsBurnham must remember: more regulation is not the best way to improve public servicesPhillip InmanIn the NHS as in the private sector, the measure of success should be customer satisfaction and not just box-tickingSat 3 Oct 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 3 Oct 2026 11.10 EDTShareAndy Burnham said he wanted to “rewire” the economy. Then he seemed to slam on the brakes, kicking most reforms into the 2030s.Local government reorganisation is on hold, along with an overhaul of the much-maligned water industry. Social care and significant welfare reform are matters to be resolved by the next government.A delay is understandable when the issues are knotty and plans on the left to replace the word “rewire” with “renationalise”, stir up accusations of taking Britain back to the 1970s. And yet delay is unnecessary when the knowledge is available now to get on with the kind of changes that rebuild public trust in time for a 2029 election.There are oblique ways of achieving success, and the measure of success should be customer satisfaction. Without this aim, the hopes of reform are lost.The case for Labour to introduce a wealth tax has never been stronger | Phillip InmanRead moreThe economist Sir John Kay, a fellow of St John’s College, Oxford and former head of the Institute for Fiscal Studies, is a keen advocate of organisations that remember for whose benefit they exist. That means their primary aim should be to achieve customer satisfaction. In the private sector, profits will follow. In the public sector, there will be savings.In his book Obliquity, Kay shows how those companies that pursued shareholder value as their primary aim failed. And those that wanted to produce the best product secured long-term success.Just as a devotion to shareholder value – a financial metric of the benefit to investors -proved a blind alley for thousands of now-deceased companies, so the reliance on protocols in the public sector as a substitute for understanding the task in hand leads to failed outcomes and wasted money.You can see it now in the NHS, wheresatisfaction levels are risingin relation to GP and hospital visits. The new system for booking appointments has its drawbacks, but people are finding doctors are available more quickly, especially for GP and outpatient appointments.You can see the failures in theNHSfrom the cover-ups by maternity unit managers of rising mortality rates.Neither the success nor the failure can be attributed to the regulation of the health service. Regulation is an extra layer of cost that has, time after time, been shown to undermine productive behaviour, either because private providers and managers find they can game the system or it stifles innovation.Another example can be found in two unconnected government agencies. Last week, the Environment Agency said it would fund the planting of half a million trees, giving funds to councils and mayors and other government bodies to carry out the work. Surely this is a good thing?View image in fullscreenNational Highways planted 850,000 saplings in 2020 along a widened stretch of the A14 north of Cambridge – but three-quarters of them died.Photograph: Sean Smith/The GuardianOn the other hand, you might think it a complete waste of time and money when National Highways, the main road builder in England, planted 850,000 saplings in 2020 along a widened stretch of the A14 north of Cambridge, only to report three years later, in an internal review, thatthree-quarters of them had died.These failures are about the way public sector departments and agencies go about their work. Regulation only adds to a tick-box culture that asks: “Did you follow the protocol? If so, everything’s fine.”Eminent figures in Whitehall, from the former mandarin and Bank of England deputy governor Sir Jon Cunliffe to the House of Lords industry and regulators committee believe the answer is more intensive oversight.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionKay has many examples of companies that grew because the boardroom was dominated by people who were more obsessed about delivering the best service or product than rewarding their shareholders as the chief metric. Profits and improvements in things such as market share were not the dominant metrics in companies that expanded.The aircraft maker Boeing succeeded before it lost its way chasing quarterly profit targets. ICI, once the UK’s largest industrial company, was broken up and faded away after a higher stock market value became the main target.The management consultant John Seddon, whose Vanguard consulting firm has adapted the Toyota systems method, supports Kay’s studiously well-informed analysis of what it takes to make a successful organisation. Seddon puts flesh on the bones with the kind of practical systems approach that has helped Portsmouth city council’s housing department win international awards for its repairs service.He has seen many new initiatives in public sector management from grand strategies to more prosaic schemes for benchmarking services against the private sector. All have failed to improve services.Seddon isnot in favour of ditching regulation altogether. Regulation based on how well an organisation achieves the purpose will, he says, avoid the persistent problem of regulation “running behind events, shutting the stable door after another horse has bolted”.He adds: “Having a clear statement of purpose will enable regulators to apply sanctions immediately if and when an organisation is found to be undermining its allotted purpose.“It is time to liberate public servants from the prison of suspicion and distrust that our current method of regulation locks them in, demeaning their professionalism and casting them as part of the problem rather than as active creators of solutions.”Burnham’s staff should avoid letting the debate about ownership dominate – ignoring a maxim that says “private bad, public good.”. They should work more closely on how public sector organisations achieve better outcomes. The evidence is available. They don’t need to look very far.Explore more on these topicsEconomicsViewpoint columnLabourHealthNHSHospitalsHealth policyRegulatorscommentShareReuse this content

title: What do Britain’s death-penalty cheerleaders have to say about Christa Pike? | Maya Foa | The Guardian
description: Her harrowing botched execution is a reminder of why we must not even entertain the idea of restoring capital punishment, says Maya Foa, CEO of the human rights charity Reprieve
Author: Maya Foa
Headline: Her harrowing botched execution is a reminder of why we must not even entertain the idea of restoring capital punishment, says Maya Foa, CEO of the human rights charity Reprieve
Content: Witness Catherine Sweeney recounts the planned execution of Christa Pike at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville, Tennessee, 30 September 2026.Photograph: Denny Simmons/THE TENNESSEAN/ReutersView image in fullscreenWitness Catherine Sweeney recounts the planned execution of Christa Pike at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville, Tennessee, 30 September 2026.Photograph: Denny Simmons/THE TENNESSEAN/ReutersOpinionCapital punishmentWhat do Britain’s death-penalty cheerleaders have to say about Christa Pike?Maya FoaHer harrowing botched execution is a reminder of why we must not even entertain the idea of restoring capital punishmentMaya Foa is the CEO of the human rights charity ReprieveSat 3 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 3 Oct 2026 06.28 EDTShareIn recent months, there has been a resurgence of interest in the death penalty among rightwing politicians in the UK. The leader of Restore Britain, Rupert Lowe,has made a manifesto commitment to holding a legally binding referendum on bringing backcapital punishment. The Reform MP Lee Anderson isalso in favourof a referendum, arguing that the public would vote in favour of the death penalty.Such supporters of capital punishment in Britain point to polls such as this “bombshell survey” that supposedly showed 47% of students favoured bringing back the death penalty. But these headlines are misleading, as surveys rarely include details about the grim administration of capital punishment and only present a binary choice of the options.The more information you give the public about the reality of the death penalty, the less support it enjoys. In the UK, when people are offered specific alternative punishments, the death penaltyhas historically failed to get majority support, regardless of the crime. Only35% of respondentsbelieve it should be available as a punishment in all cases of murder, according to YouGov. And in the US, support for capital punishment hassteadily declined, from 80% in 1994 to 52% in 2025.The horrific failedexecution of Christa Pikeis only the most recentstate-sanctioned killing that has gone badly wrong. Lethal injection commands higher support than other methods of execution because it has a medical veneer that makes it seem more “humane”. This myth has sustained the death penalty in the US.Polling suggeststhat if states were to switch methods, support would decline.Christa Pike survived her execution attempt. Tennessee must not try again | Austin SaratRead morePike is a woman who sufferedhorrific traumafrom a young age and ended up being tortured by prison officials for more than an hour in a failed attempt to kill her. Campaigners have long argued that Pike,who was sentenced to death in 1996at the age of 20, shouldn’t be on death row. At trial, she was presented to jurors as a dangerous killer, rather than a teenager who hadsuffered extreme, violent abusesince she was a child, including being raped by several strangers.Her ordeal in the execution chamber was a visceral demonstration that there is nothing medical or humane about execution by lethal injection. What we saw was the awful, ugly, indefensible reality of the death penalty. It should make pro-capital punishment politicians in the UK urgently reconsider their positions.Great Britain abolished thedeath penalty for murder in 1965, in the outcry that followed a fatal miscarriage of justice when Timothy Evans was hanged for murdering his wife and daughter. They were actually both victims of the serial killer John Christie, who lived downstairs. This was not an anomaly. Countries that have the death penalty inevitably execute innocent people:one studyestimates that at least one in every 25 people sentenced to death in the US is likely innocent.British supporters of the death penalty look to the US as the model of a democratic society that practices capital punishment. But the case of Christa Pike should force them to pause. More than 200 people have been exonerated from death row in the US –one for every eight people executed. And there is clear evidence that capital punishment does not deter crime: in 2024, of theeight most-violent statesin the US measured by the murder rate, seven had the death penalty.In April, the US Department of Justice published adeath penalty reportthat brazenly claimed that all methods of execution available to US states are humane, from lethal gas to the electric chair, the firing squad to lethal injection. This is despite decades of evidence to the contrary, bothstatisticaland found on thebodiesofthosetorturedto death.Proponents of capital punishment often claim that it will be reserved for the “worst of the worst” mass murderers. Research shows that in reality the death penalty is disproportionately reserved for the most vulnerable, including people withmental illnessand intellectual disability, and people whocan’t afford a lawyer.Ruth Ellis, the last woman executed in the UK, in 1955, was punched, pushed down the stairs and threatened with murder by the man she shot dead. This summer, she wasgranted a conditional pardon by King Charlesin light of evidence that she was a victim of domestic abuse and coercive and controlling behaviour. It was a tiny measure of justice, 71 years too late, for a woman who should never have been executed.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIn 1956, as parliament debated abolition, public opinion was divided. Lord Mancrofttold peersthat one poll showed 73% support for capital punishment in 1953, while another, after the execution of Ellis, found only 50% in favour. In the Commons, Sydney Silverman MPsummed upthe moral obligation of politicians to lead, not follow, opinion, asking MPs if they would kill a man “whom they knew it would be wrong to kill … if there were violent public pressure” to do so.As the list of countries rejecting capital punishment growsever-longer, it is increasingly used as a tool by authoritarian regimes. The overwhelming majority ofglobal executions last yearwere carried out by China, Iran and Saudi Arabia. Iran reportedly executed more than 2,000 people – many for participating in protests calling for more equal rights for women. Is this the kind of company Lowe and Anderson think the UK should be keeping?In the US, numerous top lawyers and doctorsare demandinga moratorium on the death penalty in the wake of Pike’s botched execution.Here in the UK, each time Lowe, Anderson or any of their fellow travellers say they want to bring back a debate about capital punishment, they should be forcefully reminded of the horrific reality of what it means in practice.Maya Foa is the CEO of the human rights charity ReprieveDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Pete Hegseth just took his personal crusade to a new level | Arwa Mahdawi | The Guardian
description: The US defense secretary who hates ‘beardos, weirdos and wimps’ has announced an Office of Religious Affairs at the Pentagon
Author: Arwa Mahdawi
Headline: The US defense secretary who hates ‘beardos, weirdos and wimps’ has announced an Office of Religious Affairs at the Pentagon
Content: ‘I’m an atheist but the way things are going the end times are beginning to sound appealing.’Photograph: Alex Wong/Pool Getty Images North America/APView image in fullscreen‘I’m an atheist but the way things are going the end times are beginning to sound appealing.’Photograph: Alex Wong/Pool Getty Images North America/APThe Week in PatriarchyTrump administrationPete Hegseth just took his personal crusade to a new levelArwa MahdawiThe US defense secretary who hates ‘beardos, weirdos and wimps’ has announced an Office of Religious Affairs at the PentagonSat 3 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 3 Oct 2026 08.03 EDTShareApart from money andMcDonald’s, there’s nothing Donald Trump seems to love more than a “big, beautiful” wall. The government is currently spending billions of taxpayer dollars to fulfill the president’s fantasy ofliningthe US-Mexico border with 30ft steel bollard walls and high-tech surveillance.What the Trump administration is apparently not so keen on is the wall of separation between church and state. While the president mayhawk biblesas a side hustle, he is not exactly devout; he serves only mammon. The top levels of his government, however, are stuffed full ofreligious fanaticswho appear hellbent on remaking the country as a Christian theocracy.Chief among these is the defense secretary and former Fox News personalityPete Hegseth. When he isn’tscreechingabout “beardos, weirdos, and wimps”, the man is cosplaying as a megachurch pastor. Hegseth, who has been married three times and paid $50,000 to a woman whoaccusedhim of rape in 2017 (he denies the accusation), found God relatively recently. He joined an evangelical church in2018and is now busy imposing his own brand of religion on the Pentagon, framing the war on Iran as a modern crusade and instituting monthly prayer services.Sometimes he blendsPulp Fictionwith the Bible at these services; other times heprays for“overwhelming violence of action against those who deserve no mercy”. The Jesus that told people to love their enemies, it seems, is far too woke (andbearded) for Hegseth.This week, Hegseth took his personal crusade to a whole new level,announcinga new Pentagon Office of Religious Affairs, which reports directly to him. The military he said, was putting on “the full armor of God”. The Pentagoninsiststhat it will not “compel religious participation”, but given Hegseth’s broader efforts to imbue Christianity into the armed forces, it’s hard not to be alarmed. Americans United for Separation of Church and State, which has sued the Pentagon over its worship services, is certainly worried. “All of [Hegseth’s] actions combined with this latest announcement make clear that Hegseth is advancing a Christian Nationalist agenda in the military,” the group saidin a statement.And that agenda seems to go well beyond the military. Hegseth has close ties to Doug Wilson, an extremist pastor and self-described Christian nationalist who thinks that women should not beallowed to vote. In an interview with NPR, Wilson said he doesn’t think his full vision for turning the US into a Christian theocracy will be realized for about 250 years, but he’s taking it step by step. His main focus now is banning abortion and same-sex marriage. While he’s still not a mainstream figure, the likes of Hegseth are pushing him out of the fringes fast.
