The defense secretaryinvited Wilsonto lead a worship service at the Pentagon in February and hasamplifieda CNN video where the pastor said women should submit to their husbands.It’s also not just Hegseth and his extremist pastor that we have to worry about. The Missouri senator Josh Hawleyproudly saidin a 2024 speech that he is “advocating Christian nationalism” and has been pushing tooverturn accessto abortion medication in the name of these beliefs. The House speaker Mike Johnson isconnected tostrongly Christian nationalist views. Meanwhile, JD Vance recently appeared on anevangelical podcastwhere he said is doing as much of “God’s work as possible” and is OK “if that leads to theend times”, which are apparently “coming”.I’m an atheist, but the way things are going, the end times are beginning to sound appealing. Let’s just pray it starts with the end of this administration.The underground world of US abortion pill mulesNineteen states and Washington DC have codifiedshield lawsthat protect health providers who prescribe and mail the abortion medications mifepristone and misoprostol to people in states with abortion bans. But these protections are under attack: in thelatest attemptto curtail access to the medication, three attorneys general in anti-abortion states (Louisiana, Alabama, Arkansas) filed a lawsuit with the US supreme courtchallengingthese laws. It’s not surprising then that some activists are bypassing the legal and medical systems and taking matters into their own hands: using volunteers to obtain abortion pills abroad and then distribute them to community support networks across the US. “It really doesn’t matter what [state and federal authorities] do legally – we will continue,” one activisttold Mother Jones. They added: “There may come a time where we are one of the only, if nottheonly, option for the nation.”Margot Robbie is changing her legal name after a decade of marriage“We don’t know why she has done this, but it has nonetheless caused a stir,” writes the always hilariousRebecca Shaw in the Guardianabout Margot Robbie becoming Margot Ackerley. “We got the usual discourse of blah blah tradition, blah blah patriarchy, blah blah women’s individual choice and so on.” Instead of engaging in this discourse, Shaw has a very practical solution for how married couples should choose a surname.Laws on intoxication and consent scrutinized after Cornell rape allegationsNew York is one of19 statesthat has “voluntary intoxication” laws, which some people argue effectively serve as alegal loopholeprotecting sexual offenders. If you as a victim were voluntarily under the influence of drugs or alcohol, you cannot claim that you were mentally incapacitated during an assault unless you can show that you were unconscious or otherwise physically helpless. After the Cornell gang-rape allegations became national news, this law is now facingincreasing scrutiny. The prosecutor Matthew Van Houtenhas saidthat that the fact the Jane Doe in the case voluntarily took drugs is partly why criminal charges were never brought. Kathy Hochul, New York’s governor, has criticized this aspect of the law and appointed the state attorney generalLetitia James to overseethe case after she “lost faith” in Van Houten.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe Week in PatriarchyGet Arwa Mahdawi’s weekly recap of the most important stories on feminism and sexism and those fighting for equalityEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe horror of the Cornell rape case is how ordinary it is“Sexual assault … reveals that law is applied selectively, according to the needs of power,”writes Moria Donegan. “Every court and every university, and every institutionwill say: ‘We take sexual violence extremely seriously.’ And every one will find, with uncanny consistency, reasons not to take it very seriously at all.”Take a look at the latest Google Mapssatellite imagesof Gaza… and then tell me this isn’t a genocide. While it isn’t a mainstay of the news, South Lebanon is alsosystematicallybeing wiped off the map by Israel.Influencer Alix Earle says she’s never read a book“Like, maybe Dr Seuss,” she added in achatwith Interview Mag. I had never actually heard of Earle before seeing this headline, but I have certainly heard about the USliteracy crisis. No doubt Earle is exaggerating forattention, but this sort of proud anti-intellectualism is so depressing. No wonder Trump is the president.The US is spelled wrong in a White House accord on ‘super intelligence’The president and some top tech titans signed avoluntary accordon “super intelligence” this week to allay fears about AI. Alas, they managed to misspell the United States as “Unites States”. Is the “super intelligence” in the room with us now? Forget AI, it’s Trump’s intelligence I’m worried about.Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsTrump administrationThe Week in PatriarchyPete HegsethUS militaryReligionDonald TrumpcommentShareReuse this content

title: The expansion of Heathrow would be an expensive disaster for Britain and the world. Burnham needs to block it | George Monbiot | The Guardian
description: A third runway would fly in the face of reason. If we are to prioritise human life over short-term ‘growth’, we need to use planes less, not more, says Guardian columnist George Monbiot
Author: George Monbiot
Headline: A third runway would fly in the face of reason. If we are to prioritise human life over short-term ‘growth’, we need to use planes less, not more, says Guardian columnist George Monbiot
Content: Illustration: Nathalie Lees/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Nathalie Lees/The GuardianOpinionHeathrow third runwayThe expansion of Heathrow would be an expensive disaster for Britain and the world. Burnham needs to block itGeorge MonbiotA third runway would fly in the face of reason. If we are to prioritise human life over short-term ‘growth’, we need to use planes less, not moreSat 3 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 3 Oct 2026 12.47 EDTShareIf a third runway is built at Heathrow, what will be the impact on the wealth of the nation? It will cost us somewhere between £23.4bn and £62.5bn. These are not myfigures; they weren’t calculated by environmental groups, but by the Department for Transport.For decades, government ministers have told us that airport expansion is essential for “growth”. As chancellor, Rachel Reeves claimed that a third runway at Heathrow would add0.43% to GDP, figures we later discovered came from a report commissioned by the airport. The transport department’s ownanalysisconcluded that the real addition to GDP would be between 0.03% and 0.05%: eight to 14 times less. Against this, it weighed the social and environmental costs of the project, to reveal a massive net loss. It found that a third runway would cause major harm to the health and wellbeing ofup to 3 million local people.But even these figures don’t capture it. The climate breakdown caused by the runway affects the entire planet, yet the costs to other countries aren’t counted. So again we must ask, why does the government support it?Or does it? Though Heathrow expansion remainsofficial policy, when asked at the weekend,Andy Burnham saidthe runway was “contested” and “principally it’s a matter for London and London MPs”. That sounds hopeful.We also learned that the project has been delayed yet again. Though Heathrowannouncedlast year that its plans were “shovel-ready”, it nowadmitsthe runway would take four years longer to build than it claimed: the estimated completion date is now 2039.By then, or so we must hope, a government might have decided to take the climate impact seriously. If so, the new runway would need to be shuttered the moment it opened. Otherwise, according to the government’sClimate Change Committee, “almost all CO2emissions in 2050 will be from aviation”. Heathrow’s expansion alone, the committee says, would cause more carbon emissions by 2054 than “any other sector of the economy”.And even this is not the end of it. The committee considers only the carbon dioxide planes produce, but the other impacts are even greater. A paper in the journalAtmospheric Environmentsuggests that, over 100 years, the nitrogen oxides, carbon monoxide, soot, volatile organic products, water vapour and other compounds released or formed in the upper troposphere and lower stratosphere by planes raise the heating caused by flying by 115%. Over 20 years, they raise it by an astonishing 517%.Given that crucial Earth systems may be approaching theirtipping points,and heating today triggers further greenhouse gas releases from forests, wetlands and permafrost, the 20-year horizon is crucial. But these other compounds are considered in neither international treaties nor the UK’s Climate Change Act. The impact of flying is officially and massively underestimated.Driving that’s too fast, too dangerous and utterly lawless: why do we tolerate this petro-masculinity? | George MonbiotRead moreWhile the heating effects of almost all other sectors can be greatly reduced by technology, there are simply no good solutions for aviation. Successive governments have justified airport expansion plans with the promise of “sustainable aviation fuel”. Mostly they mean turning biomass into kerosene, which is even worse than using fossil fuels. If this substitute is to reach any kind of scale, it will either swallow up existing cropland, driving starvation, or it will cause the expansion of cropland into forests, wetlands and other habitats, accelerating the environmental crisis. An analysis by theRoyal Societyfound that meeting existing UK aviation demand (never mind future growth) with energy crops “would require around half of UK agricultural land”. That’s the opposite of sustainable.“Sustainable aviation fuel” can also mean synthetic fuels made from captured CO2and green hydrogen. But the Royal Society found that for existing aviation, we’d need to use between five and eight times the UK’s entire renewable electricity capacity. And still, aeroplanes would release a lethal chemical cocktail – not just CO2but those other compounds – into the high atmosphere, so only afraction of the problemwould be solved. Worldwide, a paper in the journalOne Earthfound that even with a wildly unrealistic programme of technological change, in which fossil jet fuels were phased out completely by 2040, the global heating caused by aviation would more than double by 2070, thanks to rising demand.As for hydrogen-, ammonia- or battery-powered commercial aircraft, they all fail on technical or safety grounds, even before we ask where the power comes from. The “prototypes” endlessly showcased by the airlines, which never get beyond the artist’s impression, are nothing but “perceptionware”, designed to solve political problems, not technical ones.If Heathrow expansion goes ahead, passenger numbers in the UK areforecastto rise from 299 million in 2025 to 491 million in 2050. As other sectors decarbonise, the proportion of climate breakdown caused by flying climbs and climbs, until planes account for almost all of it.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe only effective strategy is to reduce demand. There’s a progressive means of doing so: thefrequent flyer levy. Wealth and flights are strongly linked. In 2024,48% of England’s population did not fly at all. But 5% of the population took five or more flights abroad, and these account for 33% of all journeys. Increasing demand has been almost entirely driven by frequent flyers, who are highly concentrated in the highest income quintile. The levy would not be charged on the first flight someone took in any year, but it would escalate with every additional flight.This is just, proportionate and – unlike all the techno-bollocks – immediately dispatchable. Otherwise, we continue to subsidise a wealthy, selfish minority with our money, our health, our wellbeing and the degradation of the living planet. How is that fair?What government support for airport expansion shows is that “growth” is simply an excuse for giving powerful lobby groups what they want. When asked whether growth was more important than net zero,Reeves replied: “Well, if it’s the No 1 mission, it’s obviously the most important thing.” That’s another way of saying money is more important than human life. But, as the figures show, it was never about growth at all. It was always about meeting the demands of the airport lobby and wealthy passengers.Now we wait on Burnham. Will the flight of reason continue? Or will human and planetary welfare at last outweigh the lobbyists?George Monbiot is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsHeathrow third runwayOpinionClimate crisisHeathrow airportAir transportTransportTravel and transportcommentShareReuse this content

title: I’m not buying into the ‘Keminaissance’. If the Tories lowered the bar any further, they’d be Reform UK | Frances Ryan | The Guardian
description: Rather than ridding the Conservatives of their ‘nasty party’ status, Badenoch has a plan – to cut benefits for young people and demonise the unemployed, says Guardian columnist Frances Ryan
Author: Frances Ryan
Headline: Rather than ridding the Conservatives of their ‘nasty party’ status, Badenoch has a plan – to cut benefits for young people and demonise the unemployed, says Guardian columnist Frances Ryan
Content: Kemi Badenoch visits an Oil States Industries site in Aberdeen, Scotland on 5 June 2026.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianView image in fullscreenKemi Badenoch visits an Oil States Industries site in Aberdeen, Scotland on 5 June 2026.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianOpinionKemi BadenochI’m not buying into the ‘Keminaissance’. If the Tories lowered the bar any further, they’d be Reform UKFrances RyanRather than ridding the Conservatives of their ‘nasty party’ status, Badenoch has a plan – to cut benefits for young people and demonise the unemployedSat 3 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 3 Oct 2026 06.26 EDTShareKemi Badenoch is considering doing her job. With her second Conservative party conference as leader looming on Sunday, and her rival Nigel Farage finally losing some ground, the provocateur with a reputation fordodging media roundsand beingill-prepared for briefshas seemingly cured her camera shyness.In recent days, Badenoch has touted a policy to give the unemployed a “subsistence allowance” that would prevent them from buying booze or cigarettes, sought to bar benefits fromyoung peoplewho are straight out of school, accused Andy Burnham of wanting to take Britain “back to the 1970s” with public control of utilities, and enjoyed somemixedpolling.That the rightwing press has greeted this with a relief bordering on delusion (theTelegraphwent as far to suggest the Conservatives could win a snap election) gives a hint of how dismally low the bar is in parts of the Tory camp.More than two years since the Conservative’s crushing general election defeat, it is not simply that the most successful electoral force in the democratic world has collapsed into irrelevance – but that it has happened with barely a whimper. The juggernaut success of Reform UK, mixed with Badenoch’s unwillingness to fully engage, has given large sections of the media licence to treat Farage as unofficial leader of the opposition, with theConservativesgetting most column inches when another one of them defects to Reform.The so-called natural party of government is essentially now an afterthought in the national conversation, throwing out ananti-migrant comment hereand anableist speechthere in the hope of just getting some attention.Meanwhile, the country quietly gets on with the day-to-day consequences of the last time it let the Tories govern:fundraisingto patch up the roof at their children’s school, waiting a year to get a hospital scan, or walking past their now closed local library.There has been an audible sigh of relief from Badenoch’s team as her personalpoll ratingsmarkedly improved over the past year, even as the Conservative’s image has tanked (as of last month, only19% of Britonsfeel the party is ready for a return to government). But talk of a “Keminaissance” misses the point: it means little that the electorate are slightly less put off by the captain if they still wouldn’t get on the ship for fear of drowning.That, as of last week, Badenoch – nostalgic for the days the Tories were a main player in a two-party system – is still ruling out anelectoral pact with Reformis only further weakening her chances of ever seeing No 10.It’s not as if the Conservatives have made any substantive efforts for reputation rehabilitation. Are they regretful of Brexit? What about Partygate? If re-elected, would they repeat Liz Truss’s deep tax cuts or George Osborne’s austerity? As the public faces mounting crises, from gutted living standards to long NHS waiting lists, Badenoch has largely kept stumm rather than offer any meaningful solutions. Indeed, on a rare occasion she has spoken out on a pressing issue – namelysocial care– it was to refuse to engage with Burnham’s reforms if paying for it involved tax rises.You could argue that it would have made sense to regroup after such a large-scale loss – not least when Keir Starmer was expected to fulfil a five-year term – or that it is rather difficult to propose solutions for problems that your party has largely caused. There is truth in both. And yet it is telling what Badenoch chooses to spend her energy on. While the former minister has told her MPs not to expect big policy plans until2027, she has found time to wade into culture wars including, but not limited to: why she hatescritical race theory; a U-turn on the Conservative commitment to meetnet zeroby 2050; and why she wants the UK to withdraw from theEuropean convention on human rights.It’s not a coincidence that Badenoch’s main policy intervention ahead of gathering in Birmingham for conference is auniversal credit cutthat would shame unemployed people not trusted to spend cash to have to use a special debit card while saving a paltry £538m a year for the taxpayer (As context, thestate pension billis now £154bn annually.) It is less a substantive socioeconomic policy and more a wink to the audience, a casual cruelty that would make already hard lives even harder for the vague promise of a point in the polls. That Badenoch presumably genuinely believes in this stuff is a grim added bonus.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe Conservatives will clearly be hoping that Reform’s downward spiral continues and in the meantime, the benefits bill – much like immigration – seems easy pickings. The proposed universal credit cut is the latest in their package of welfare cuts worth £23bn.But that Reform recently announced a plan to slice a staggering£50bnfrom the social security budget shows that as extreme as Badenoch continues to go in the coming months, Reform will go further. That Farage is now being clipped by Rupert Lowe’s Restore shows neatly enough that no matter what depths you are willing to sink to, someone out there will dig their way lower still. Britain’s hard right in 2026 is effectively a Russian doll: each party pushes the previous one inside, only to reveal an even worse version underneath.In another timeline, Badenoch would be pivoting to the centre, or at least the centre right, picking up traditional Conservative voters who fear Burnham’s threat ofhigher taxesand squirm at Reform’s race-baiting. But Badenoch is not the candidate for that fight. For all her inaction, she has been clear about her direction: centrist ideas are no longer wanted in the Conservative party, she has said, and if one-nation Tories have qualms about her rightward push, they “need to get out of the way”.This is not the opposition era of David Cameron withhuskies, or William Hague on a log flume wearing abaseball cap. Badenoch has no interest in ridding the Conservatives of their “nasty party” image. She is rejuvenating it. This is the party of theWindrush scandal, mass disability benefit cuts, and“go home” vansrepackaged for an even more toxic climate. The only question is: will it actually work? It is hard to say what’s worse: selling your soul for power or selling it and still losing.Frances Ryan is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsKemi BadenochOpinionConservativesConservative conferenceFar rightWelfarecommentShareReuse this content

title: ‘This can’t go on’: tens of thousands protest against housing crisis in Spain | Spain | The Guardian
description: Demonstrators take to the streets of Madrid ⁠and other Spanish cities ⁠after ​new legislation fails to pass
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Demonstrators take to the streets of Madrid ⁠and other Spanish cities ⁠after ​new legislation fails to pass
Content: Demonstrators fill a Madrid city square during a housing protest on Saturday.Photograph: Juan Barbosa/ReutersView image in fullscreenDemonstrators fill a Madrid city square during a housing protest on Saturday.Photograph: Juan Barbosa/ReutersSpain‘This can’t go on’: tens of thousands protest against housing crisis in SpainDemonstrators take to the streets of Madrid ⁠and other Spanish cities ⁠after ​new legislation fails to passStaff and agenciesSat 3 Oct 2026 10.19 EDTLast modified on Sat 3 Oct 2026 17.33 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTens of thousands of people have taken to the streets of Madrid ⁠and other Spanish cities as they step up demands for action to tackle ⁠a mounting housing crisis ⁠after ​government measures were struck down by the opposition.Demonstrators on Saturday waved posters calling for a general strike ⁠after the measures drawn up to address mass anger over the eviction of an 87-year-old woman in ⁠Madrid, and other housing issues,were rejected in parliamenton ​Friday.Authorities said 70,000 people were protesting. Organisers put the figure at 500,000.“It’s a shame,” Nando ‌de Anguulo, 26, ‌who joined the protest in Madrid, told Reuters. “It only proves that it ‌is us, the people, who have to adapt to the political parties, and not the politicians to what the people want, and this can’t go on like that.”Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, may call a snap election for November after the ‌legislation failed to pass, Spanish media reported on Friday, and would be watching the strength of Saturday’s ​protests before making a decision.View image in fullscreenThousands of demonstrators took to the streets of Madrid.Photograph: Alejandro Martinez Velez/ReutersThe demonstrations have dominated the national conversation, breathing new life intoSánchez’s beleaguered governmentand shifting attention away from the lingering impact ofrecent events in Ceuta.Protests on Saturday were peaceful in 50 Spanish cities. In the south-eastern city of Valencia, demonstrators clashed with police who fired rubber bullets and teargas ⁠to break up the protests.About 30 people managed to get inside ​the City ​of Arts and Sciences, a ​landmark cultural building in the city, before they were ​ousted by ‌police.One protester in Madrid, Marcos Sainz, a librarian, 26, said he used to rent a two-bedroom apartment with friends for a monthly rent of 900 euros ($1,000) but that a one-bedroom flat often now cost 1,000 euros – or half the median monthly salary in the capital.He told AFP he would protest rental spikes “until someone dares to regulate it all, as (otherwise) we’ll all have to leave Madrid and that would be a shame as I am from Madrid”.Javier, 31, a solar panel installer, said: “We are demanding a fundamental right: decent housing, stability and conditions allowing us to construct a decent life project.” He added: “I spend half of my salary on a tiny room.”“What we are feeling in the streets is a new energy that we haven’t seen in a long time, an energy that is showing that eight days of people power can achieve more than eight years of progressive government,” Valeria Racu, one of the spokespeople of the Tenants’ Union organising the protest, said in a statement.“Now begins real politics – politics which has always belonged to the people and which will return once and for all to the streets,” she said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenProtesters clash with police during the demonstration in Valencia.Photograph: Kai Forsterling/EPALate on Saturday groups of far-right protesters, some of them performing Nazi salutes, tried to get to the camp in Madrid but were blocked by police.One video posted on the website of Spanish daily El País showed police chasing some members of the group through the streets and the newspaper also reported that officers had made three arrests.On Friday, Sánchez’s Socialist-led coalition put forward two decrees that included a range of measures aimed at improving access to housing, from a ban on evictions until 2030 to the regulation of temporary lettings and lettings by room.Despite the anger of the protesters outside parliament, the conservative People’s party, the far-right Vox and the Catalan pro-independence party Junts voted against both decrees.The People’s party said it had voted in line with its belief that building, rather than regulating, was the best way to address the crisis. “Housing doesn’t become more affordable through decrees; it becomes more affordable by building ​more homes,” said the lawmaker Juan Bravo.View image in fullscreenA demonstrator holds up a sign reading ‘Right to a Roof’ on Plaza de Espana in Madrid.Photograph: Javier Soriano/AFP/Getty ImagesNews of the package’s rejection was met with boos and cries of “shame” outside. “Your profits, our misery,” the protesters chanted.The long-simmering anger at soaring housing costs boiled over late last month, when 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal, who uses a wheelchair, wasevicted from the home she had lived in for 70 years. The octogenarian said she was unable to afford the 230% rent hike demanded by the investment fund that bought her apartment.Reuters and AFP contributed to this report.Explore more on these topicsSpainEuropeRenting propertyHousingProtestnewsShareReuse this content

title: Greece returns priceless relics – and suggests UK should follow suit with Parthenon marbles | Bulgaria | The Guardian
description: Greek PM hopes handover of Tsar Samuel to Bulgaria will persuade Britain that time has come for ‘truth, reason, justice and morality’
Author: Helena Smith
Headline: Greek PM hopes handover of Tsar Samuel to Bulgaria will persuade Britain that time has come for ‘truth, reason, justice and morality’
Content: Statue of Tsar Samuel in Sofia, Bulgaria. As part of the agreement, Bulgaria is returning relics taken from Greek monasteries during the first world war.Photograph: Lambros Kazanas/AlamyView image in fullscreenStatue of Tsar Samuel in Sofia, Bulgaria. As part of the agreement, Bulgaria is returning relics taken from Greek monasteries during the first world war.Photograph: Lambros Kazanas/AlamyBulgariaGreece returns priceless relics – and suggests UK should follow suit with Parthenon marblesGreek PM hopes handover of Tsar Samuel to Bulgaria will persuade Britain that time has come for ‘truth, reason, justice and morality’Helena Smithin AthensSat 3 Oct 2026 10.46 EDTFirst published on Sat 3 Oct 2026 06.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn a ceremony replete with the sort of fanfare usually reserved for great events, Greece andBulgariahave formally exchanged “a treasury” of relics and bones, sealing a cultural deal negotiated over decades.The handover involved priceless religious objects removed fromGreeceat the height of the first world war, as well as remains thought to belong to Tsar Samuel, Bulgaria’s revered medieval warrior ruler.Greece hailed the exchange as emblematic of the headway countries could make in similar repatriation disputes, with the prime minister, Kyriakos Mitsotakis, saying he hoped the accord would bolster Athens’ campaign to retrieve the Parthenon sculptures and send a clear message to Britain.“The global community is essentially re-evaluating its longstanding stance on protecting cultural heritage,” he told a crowd gathered for the ceremony in Thessaloniki on Saturday. “This shift is embodied by today’s initiative, which rests on the obvious principle that monuments and historical heirlooms cannot be treated as spoils of war, nor as the result of circumstances subsequent to their creation.”Greek PM: deal to return Parthenon marbles could still be reached with ‘political will and courage’Read moreThe Greek-Bulgarian deal, reached after 50 years of intense cultural diplomacy between the two neighbours, was also an example of the “political will” needed to settle the west’s longest running cultural row, Mitsotakis said, referring to the fifth century BCParthenon marbles. “It took time, and above all, political will and determination to overcome the obstacles of the past,” he added.Under the agreement, 48 relics, including icons, crosses and ornate ecclesiastical vessels, pillaged by Bulgarian troops from churches and monasteries in northern Greece during the first world war, will be returned to Athens. In the more than 100 intervening years, they had been safeguarded at the National History Museum in Bulgaria.Meanwhile, the remains of Tsar Samuel, regarded as a national hero for his role in battling to preserve his country’s independence from the Byzantine empire, were discovered by archaeologists more than 60 years ago in a border area of Greece.Authorities arranged a homecoming with full state honours, with the tsar’s bones flown to Sofia, the Bulgarian capital, on a military aircraft accompanied by an escort of jet fighters and a 21-gun salute upon arrival. Free transport had been organised for pilgrims to pay their respects.In his own address at the handover, Bulgaria’s prime minister, Rumen Radev, a former air force officer, said: “These are items that belong to both our peoples; they constitute our memory and our bond, and our compatriots and future generations deserve, and must have, the opportunity to pay tribute to their ancestor. If in the past Tsar Samuel divided us, I can say that today he unites us. He strengthens our strategic cooperation and makes the historical relations between our states and peoples even stronger.”View image in fullscreenBulgaria’s military personnel carry a coffin with the remains of medieval ruler Tsar Samuel during a handover ceremony in Thessaloniki.Photograph: Giannis Papanikos/APMitsotakis emphasised that Greece’s campaign to win back the Parthenon marbles was neither “dictated by a vague national claim, nor does it call into question the mission of museums worldwide”.Athens remained committed to repatriating the sculptures, he said, because it would allow viewers to fully enjoy what has long been seen as the high point of classical art if the masterpieces were reunited.“It is precisely this same principle – the principle of the integrity of a monument – that underpins our continuous efforts to reunite the Parthenon sculptures. The Parthenon constitutes a unique and singular case,” he said of the building that is the predominant temple on the Acropolis of Athens.“[The campaign] is about the restoration of a universal monument that remains violently dismembered. My country will not accept arrangements that imply recognition of foreign sovereignty or the supposed borrowing of its own treasures. On the contrary, it now believes that the time has come for truth, for reason, for justice and morality.”The fifth century BC carvings were sawn from the Parthenon on the order of Lord Elgin, Britain’s then ambassador to the Sublime Porte, in what have since become highly contentious circumstances.They were acquired by the British Museum in 1816 after the bankrupt peer was forced to sell them and have been on display there ever since.Explore more on these topicsBulgariaEuropeGreeceArchaeologyParthenon marblesHeritageSculpturenewsShareReuse this content

title: Episcopal bishop who urged Trump to ‘have mercy’ to resign post in Washington DC | Washington DC | The Guardian
description: Mariann Budde gained national attention for calling on US president to consider immigrants and LGBTQ+ people
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Mariann Budde gained national attention for calling on US president to consider immigrants and LGBTQ+ people
Content: Mariann Budde at the Washington National Cathedral after Trump’s second inauguration, on 21 January 2025.Photograph: Evan Vucci/APView image in fullscreenMariann Budde at the Washington National Cathedral after Trump’s second inauguration, on 21 January 2025.Photograph: Evan Vucci/APWashington DCEpiscopal bishop who urged Trump to ‘have mercy’ to resign post in Washington DCMariann Budde gained national attention for calling on US president to consider immigrants and LGBTQ+ peopleKeely AougaSat 3 Oct 2026 17.21 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRev Mariann Edgar Budde, the Episcopal bishop of Washington DC who gained national attention when she called on Donald Trump to “have mercy” on the country’s immigrants and LGBTQ+ community after his second inauguration, is resigning.Budde shared in herresignation letterthat she will be leaving her post on 3 June 2028 after the consecration and ordination of the new diocesan bishop.“I write today because I have discerned, in consultation with diocesan leadership and the Presiding Bishop’s office, that it is time to begin preparing for the election of your next bishop. I have not come to this decision lightly or alone, and it will not be easy to say goodbye to the diocese I love,” her letter said.Next week, the standing committee will outline the steps required, which include the appointment of two committees to undertake this work, the letter added.Budde, 66, is thefirst woman to serveas the spiritual leader of the Episcopal diocese of Washington. She has been leading the diocese since her election to the role in 2011. Before that, she served as the rector of St John’s Episcopal church in Minneapolis for 18 years.She made headlines for urging Trump duringher sermonto show mercy to “gay, lesbian and transgender children” from all political backgrounds, some of whom, she said, “fear for their lives”.View image in fullscreenBudde arriving for the National Day of Prayer service, with Donald Trump beyond, in Washington on 21 January 2025.Photograph: Kevin Lamarque/ReutersTrump demanded an apology in apost shared on social media.“She brought her church into the World of politics in a very ungracious way. She was nasty in tone, and not compelling or smart,” the president said.“Apart from her inappropriate statements, the service was a very boring and uninspiring one. She is not very good at her job! She and her church owe the public an apology!”It was not the first time Budde had called out and clashed with Trump.During Trump’s first term, she published anopinion piecein the New York Times, expressing outrage over Trump’s appearance in front of St John’s Episcopal holding up a Bible for a photo after federal officers hadused force to clear a crowd of peaceful protestersdemonstrating against the police killing ofGeorge Floydthe previous week.Budde wrote that Trump had “used sacred symbols to cloak himself in the mantle of spiritual authority, while espousing positions antithetical to the Bible that he held in his hands”.Looking towards the future of the Episcopal diocese of Washington, Budde wrote, she is committed to ensuring a strong and healthy transition for her successor.“Alongside the diocesan staff and leadership bodies, I will do everything in my power to ensure that the diocese is as strong and healthy as possible for this leadership transition. I am praying for all involved, and especially for the one God is preparing to serve as the tenth bishop of the Diocese of Washington,” Budde concluded.Explore more on these topicsWashington DCReligionTrump administrationChristianityDonald TrumpUS politicsShareReuse this content

title: Women given free cycling shorts to prevent upskirting on Oktoberfest amusement ride | Germany | The Guardian
description: Investigation revealed thousands of voyeuristic videos taken on Munich beer festival’s Teufelsrad, or Devil’s Wheel
Author: Jessie Williams
Headline: Investigation revealed thousands of voyeuristic videos taken on Munich beer festival’s Teufelsrad, or Devil’s Wheel
Content: The ride’s operator has given out more than 100 pairs of shorts to women and girls wearing dresses.Photograph: Anna Szilágyi/EPAView image in fullscreenThe ride’s operator has given out more than 100 pairs of shorts to women and girls wearing dresses.Photograph: Anna Szilágyi/EPAGermanyWomen given free cycling shorts to prevent upskirting on Oktoberfest amusement rideInvestigation revealed thousands of voyeuristic videos taken on Munich beer festival’s Teufelsrad, or Devil’s WheelJessie WilliamsSat 3 Oct 2026 11.10 EDTLast modified on Sat 3 Oct 2026 12.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWomen have been given free cycling shorts to prevent upskirting on a famous amusement ride at the Oktoberfest in Munich, after an investigation revealed tens of thousands of voyeuristic videos circulating online.TheTeufelsrad,or Devil’s Wheel, which rapidly spins around while people try to sit on it for as long as they can, is one of the beer festival’s oldest rides. But many of the videos discovered by German journalists focus on women whose traditional dirndl dresses have ridden up, often showing their underwear.The findings have revived concerns about upskirting – secretly filming or taking photos under someone’s skirt without consent, which has been illegal inGermanysince 2020. It is punishable by a fine or up to two years in prison. But some women’s rights advocates have said the law is not enough to stop the abuse.According tothe researchby the Munich daily newspaper Süddeutsche Zeitung, more than 32,000 videos linked to the Teufelsrad were found on Meta platforms alone, some of them with millions of views.The operator of the ride, Elisabeth Polaczy, told the BBC she has been handing out free cycling shorts to women and girls wearing dresses to protect them from people filming them. She has given out more than 100 pairs during this Oktoberfest, which finishes on Sunday. “I want to do everything I can to make people feel secure,” she said.There are signs and police posters in German and English around the tent where the Teufelsradis located that warn against filming under people’s skirts. But Polaczy, 80, said it was difficult to control everyone filming with smartphones.A spokesperson for the Bavarian police told the BBC they have put up posters at the Oktoberfest warning against upskirting since 2025.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionPolice arrested a 45-year-old Swiss man for filming under a German woman’s dirndl at this year’s festival. In 2025 there were 10 arrests for upskirting and seven in 2024.Explore more on these topicsGermanyEuropeWomen's rights and gender equalitynewsShareReuse this content

title: They embraced the Fiat 500, the Vespa, even tuk-tuks. But will Romans draw the line at the golf cart?  | Italy | The Guardian
description: Authorities crack down on trade they says risks spiralling out of control – but operators say they are being targeted unfairly
Author: Angela Giuffrida
Headline: Authorities crack down on trade they says risks spiralling out of control – but operators say they are being targeted unfairly
Content: A tourist golf cart passes in front of the Colosseum.Photograph: Victor Sokolowicz/The GuardianView image in fullscreenA tourist golf cart passes in front of the Colosseum.Photograph: Victor Sokolowicz/The GuardianItalyThey embraced the Fiat 500, the Vespa, even tuk-tuks. But will Romans draw the line at the golf cart?Authorities crack down on trade they says risks spiralling out of control – but operators say they are being targeted unfairlyAngela Giuffridain RomeSat 3 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 3 Oct 2026 09.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOn the edge of Piazza Navona, one of the grandest squares in central Rome, Barry and Linda, visitors from Texas in the US, stepped out of a golf cart. They planned to cross the square on foot, perhaps stopping to admire Lorenzo Bernini’s 17th-century Fountain of the Four Rivers, before being picked up by their driver at the opposite end.The couple had already done a walking tour on day one of their trip, and had been so exasperated by a stifling three-hour shuffle along a corridor towards the Sistine Chapel on day two that by the third day they wanted to give their tired feet a rest.View image in fullscreenAmerican tourists Barry and Linda on foot in Piazza Navona.Photograph: Victor Sokolowicz/The Guardian“When I first heard you could do golf cart tours in Rome, I thought to myself: that sounds a little weird,” said Barry. “But then we decided to try it out.” He said the most enjoyable thing about the experience was “feeling the breeze”.Rome is a difficult city to navigate, noted Linda, especially its ancient narrow streets in the centre. “There are no sidewalks,” she said. “Our feet were hurting and we needed a break.”For visitors, golf cart tours offer respite from the heat, crowds and cobbles. For residents, however, their proliferation in recent years has become another source of frustration in a city already wrestling with traffic and overtourism.View image in fullscreenRome’s leaders are pushing for regionwide measures to properly regulate the carts.Photograph: Victor Sokolowicz/The GuardianTaxi drivers are especially incensed, accusing golf cart operators of stealing their business, while one local newspaper said the city had been “taken hostage” by the vehicles.Now Rome authorities are cracking down on the burgeoning trade. Police intensified checks this week after the news agencyAdnkronosreported that 90% of the roughly 500 golf carts circulating in the city were operating without authorisation.In recent days, police stopped 131 carts around Piazza Navona, the Pantheon, Circo Massimo and the Spanish Steps, issuing €38,000 of fines for offences ranging from unlicensed driving to illegal parking.Rome’s leaders are pushing for regionwide measures to properly regulate an activity that “risks spiralling out of control”, Eugenio Patanè, a councillor for mobility, told the news agency Adnkronos.View image in fullscreenA golf cart in traffic in Rome.Photograph: Victor Sokolowicz/The GuardianPrices vary based on the type of tour and duration, but the cost per person can start at €100 and exceed €400 for a half-day trip. Barry and Linda paid €310 for their three-hour ride. “But it’s worth it,” said Barry.Rome’s traffic problem is hardly new. Julius Caesar tried to tackle the issue more than 2,000 years ago by banning private vehicles and commercial carts from the city’s streets during the day. Today, pedestrians, cars, scooters, delivery vans and the occasional roguehorse-drawn carriageall jostle for space.View image in fullscreenNora and Carlo outside their shop Trevimage near the Pantheon.Photograph: Victor Sokolowicz/The GuardianTourists can also take tours in Fiat 500s, on Vespas with sidecars, and even in tuk-tuks. But the golf carts seem to have drawn a special kind of wrath.“There are too many of them,” said Nora Fahmi, who works at Trevimage, an art photography shop behind the Pantheon. “We’ve had this shop for 13 years and have seen all sorts of things, but the golf cart situation is kind of wild.”Nearby, two teenagers from Israel were taking a rest on a parked cart. “We just want a lift to the Colosseum but you have to book online,” said their mother, Miri. “Rome is too crowded and it’s difficult to walk.”View image in fullscreenTwo young tourists rest in a golf cart parked in the town centre.Photograph: Victor Sokolowicz/The GuardianElisa Isacco, who lives in the Monti area, spares no sympathy for the weary tourists. “What do they actually see or learn about Rome when they are on one of these things?” she said. “I find myself having to dodge them all the time – Rome is chaotic, it’s like a jungle.”Amid the clampdown, several golf cart tour operators have banned staff from speaking to the press. But Leo Pavoncello, a driver for an operator in the Jewish Ghetto area, was happy to publicly defend the trade.“Golf carts are silent and eco-friendly,” he said. “Rome is not an easy city to visit but these vehicles allow people with disabilities and families with children to see the sites in a comfortable way. On top of that, they provide jobs for young people.”View image in fullscreenA golf cart waiting for a group of tourists in Piazza Navona.Photograph: Victor Sokolowicz/The GuardianPavoncello, who was subjected to the police checks and was found to be operating fully legitimately, argued that a few rotten apples were giving the business a bad name.“I don’t understand why they are targeting us,” he said, although he suspects “taxi lobbies” are piling on the pressure. “But Rome is a touristic city that has always been full of traffic, and the golf carts are simply another mode of transport.”Explore more on these topicsItalyOvertourismEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Whales on Australia’s ‘humpback highway’ are at growing risk of injury from boat and propellor strikes | Whales | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Images show deep cuts and damage to tails and fins, as experts warn the migrating species often aren’t able to avoid a collision
Author: Graham Readfearn
Headline: Exclusive: Images show deep cuts and damage to tails and fins, as experts warn the migrating species often aren’t able to avoid a collision
Content: The fluke of a female humpback whale first seen in Hervey Bay, Queensland in 2004 as a subadult. In 2026 her calf was seen with propeller injuries.Photograph: Isabel Taylor Pacific Whale Foundation Eco Adventures AustraliaView image in fullscreenThe fluke of a female humpback whale first seen in Hervey Bay, Queensland in 2004 as a subadult. In 2026 her calf was seen with propeller injuries.Photograph: Isabel Taylor Pacific Whale Foundation Eco Adventures AustraliaWhalesWhales on Australia’s ‘humpback highway’ are at growing risk of injury from boat and propellor strikesExclusive:Images show deep cuts and damage to tails and fins, as experts warn the migrating species often aren’t able to avoid a collisionGraham ReadfearnClimate and environment correspondentSat 3 Oct 2026 15.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 3 Oct 2026 20.27 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGruesome images of adult and juvenile humpback whales along Australia’s east coast with slash and gouge injuries from boat and propeller strikes highlight what experts say is a growing problem, as the population booms 60 years after the ban on whaling.Missing tail parts, deep red lacerations and shocking injuries to the spine of a whale calf can be clearly seen on the images, gathered by WWF Australia and shared with the Guardian.One image of fresh and broad cuts on the back of a calf was taken last month in Hervey Bay in Queensland, where many mothers choose to bring their calves for rest and shelter on the long migration down to Antarctica.The atmosphere on the town’s whale-watching boats is often one of heightened excitement and elation, as the majestic mammals come to the surface, says Isabel Taylor, a senior naturalist with the Pacific Whale Foundation’s whale-watching tours.Last month, Taylor saw two mothers with calves come to the surface, but all was not well with one pair.“The others were very surface active and putting on a show, but this other mum and calf were more reserved,” she says.Clearly visible on the calf’s back were slash marks from a boat propeller. “The mood on the boat changed a bit,” says Taylor.View image in fullscreenThis female humpback has become known as ‘bladerunner’ because of the deep slashes from a propeller blade on her back and tail thought to have been sustained more than 20 years ago.Photograph: oceanspray_photography“We get people from all over the world and some say it’s the best day of their lives. So to have this on the other end of the spectrum was quite profound.”Another image taken in June by drone off Sydney’s Bondi beach shows a humpback with lacerations and exposed red flesh that appear to have been caused by repeated sweeps of a propeller blade.An image from 2024 shows a female humpback off the coast of southern New South Wales that has become known as “bladerunner” because of a highly distinctive sequence of deep slashes from a propeller blade on her back and tailthought to have been sustained more than 20 years ago.“These images really bring home the physical and direct impact we’re having on these animals, especially on animals that size,” says Dr Raphael Mayaud, a marine ecologist at Griffith University and a member of an expert group advising the InternationalWhalingCommission (IWC) on vessel strikes.After a dead whale washed up at a Perth beach, some took selfies. Others held their nose from the stenchRead moreRebecca Dunlop, an associate professor and humpback expert at the University of Queensland, says most of the images showed injuries to the back and rear of the whales, “suggesting they are surfacing as the boat propeller goes past and over their back”.“When migrating humpbacks travel and surface like clockwork they don’t seem to be able to change their dive and travel behaviour to avoid an intercept pathway – this could be due to a boat approaching the intercept point at speed where they just don’t have the time to make an avoidance decision,” Dunlop saysConservation success storyThe IWC banned humpback whaling in the southern hemisphere in 1963 – after numbers had already crashed.Soviet whalers continued to hunt them in the Southern Ocean until the early 1970s. Estimates from the 1960s put their numbers off the east coast of Australia at less than 300.View image in fullscreenAn adult humpback whale with its right fluke chopped off. As populations have increased alongside boating and water recreation, the numbers of vessel strikes have also probably increased, whale experts say.Photograph: Isabel Taylor Pacific Whale Foundation Eco Adventures AustraliaBut as the threat of the harpoon was progressively removed, the population rebounded. Onestudy based on observations of whalessuggested that by 2004 the east coast humpbacks numbered 7,800.It is seen by many conservationists as one of the planet’s great wildlife recovery stories.By 2015, their numbers had more than trebled to 25,500. Estimates now suggest between 40,000 and 50,000 whales are migrating up and down the coast each year. Some modelling has suggested numbers will peak and plateau this year.Dunlop and Mayaud both observe that, as populations have increased alongside the rise in popularity of boating and water recreation, the numbers of vessel strikes have also likely increased.View image in fullscreen‘Humpbacks have been one of the great conservation success stories. But along Australia’s humpback highway, there’s growing risk for them to be hit by vessels,’ says WWF’s Chris Johnson.Photograph: Tracey HarrisOne in 10 Australians have a boat licence and of themore than 970,000 registered boats, more than half a million are in Queensland and New South Wales.But it is difficult to know how many collisions there are with both large and smaller boats, experts say.The IWC says that globally, “most collisions go unseen and unreported”. On Friday, it passed a resolution to work with all parties around the world to reduce “vessel strikes” which, the meeting agreed, was a “priority concern” for the commission.Chris Johnson, the WWF’s global lead on initiatives to protect whales, who was at the meeting, says it is an important step for the IWC.“Humpbacks have been one of the great conservation success stories. But along Australia’s humpback highway, there’s growing risk for them to be hit by vessels,” he says.View image in fullscreenAn injured humpback calf. Injuries such as this could affect migration, feeding, body condition and reproduction.Photograph: Isabel Taylor Pacific Whale Foundation Eco Adventures Australia“Those strikes [in the images] would have been incredibly painful. We can see the evidence, but we have a black hole of information.”Experts say cutting speed limits for all vessels moving along migration routes, and making boats and ships more aware of the riskiest places and times of the year, would help.In California, for example, Johnson says shipping companies compete with each other to win high grades on public scorecards that assess how well they stick to speed limits during high-risk periods for whale strikes.In San Francisco Bay,AI-assisted whale-spotting camerasare being trialled to give captains more notice about whales in their path.1:13Humpback whale filmed apparently grieving its stillborn calf – videoWhile Australian law in theory requires that collisions with protected species like humpbacks be reported, Mayaud says most are either undetected or are never documented.“The big thing is that a strike doesn’t have to kill a whale to have a serious impact,” he says.“If a whale loses part of its fluke [tail] it may still survive, but swimming is likely to become less efficient and more energetically costly. That can then have knock-on effects on things like migration, feeding, body condition and potentially reproduction.“There’s also the immediate trauma – the pain, blood loss, infection – and then the possibility the animal is carrying the effects of that injury for years afterwards.“So I think the welfare issue is really about both the initial injury and the longer-term energetic and physical consequences for animals that survive.”Explore more on these topicsWhalesWhalingCetaceansWildlifeMarine lifeConservationAnimal welfarefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Bangkok at breaking point as floods turn streets into stagnant lakes | Extreme weather | The Guardian
description: With 40 dead and a disaster declared across all 50 city districts, experts warn extreme flooding will only worsen across south-east Asia
Author: Oliver Holmes
Headline: With 40 dead and a disaster declared across all 50 city districts, experts warn extreme flooding will only worsen across south-east Asia
Content: People wade through a flooded street in Bangkok. Photograph: Patipat Janthong/ReutersWith 40 dead and a disaster declared across all 50 city districts, experts warn extreme flooding will only worsen across south-east AsiaByOliver HolmesandAjit NiranjanFri 2 Oct 2026 22.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBangkok is used to absorbing the sudden afternoon downpours that inundate the city during the rainy season. Even streets in many central high-rise districts can briefly turn into rivers, with rats and cockroaches racing out of sewers and taking temporary refuge on trees and buildings as the subterranean world is flushed out.But every city has a breaking point, and this year rain fell so fast and so hard that whole neighbourhoods of the Thai capital have been transformed, not into rivers, but stagnant lakes. In parts of the city, roughly 300mm of rain – the equivalent of half a year of average rainfall in London – fell in about two days.View image in fullscreenA person wades through flood water in Lat Krabang district, Bangkok.Photograph: Rungroj Yongrit/EPAAbout 40 people died in flood-related incidents, according to the government. A number of the deaths were from drowning and several from accidental electrocution. Thousands of people stayed in more than 230 shelters across the city, authorities said.Suleemas Kurangkul, a 73-year-old resident of a block of flats whose ground floor stairs are still under water, said last weekend’s rain was not the usual evening storm but was constant, “like all day, all night”.“The water just kept rising,” said Suleemas, whose flat is above the waterline on the second floor. By the time she and her neighbours received a mobile phone warning, it was too late, and the street-level water was waist-high.The 1970s Khlong Chan flat compound in north-east Bangkok where Suleemas lives has become a symbol of the disaster. Photos have been shared acrossThailandof the flats rising out of the brownish water, with the rooftops of parked cars barely peeking above the surface, although the authorities had managed to drain away the worst of it by Thursday.Later in the week, during a brief respite in the rain, Suleemas said the water had receded somewhat. “People are so happy to see the sunshine,” she said. “Yet, the smell is getting stronger. So much debris and rubbish floating all over the place.”Built on a vast floodplain of the Chao Phraya River, Bangkok, a megacity of millions, relies on a network of muddy canals to drain water, as well as pumps and dikes. But concrete construction has destroyed much of the canal network, and the city is unable to cope.The government has declared a flood disaster across all 50 of the city’s districts. Some neighbourhoods have turned into dystopian scenes, with people using blow-up paddling pools or, in one case, a floating fridge, as boats to reach their homes. One man wasarrested for riding a jetskialong a main road.View image in fullscreenA resident uses a floating fridge as a boat.Photograph: Rungroj Yongrit/EPA“It’s a lesson,” said Chaleerat Chamrasporn, 55, a resident. “The kids are into doomsday-themed content, so now they can see what the ‘end of the world’ is actually like, or rather, that this is just the beginning.”Flooding has also disrupted Bangkok’s main Suvarnabhumi airport, with about half ⁠of Thai Airways’ workforce unable to report for work at one point this week, causing thousands of items of luggage ​to pile up and forcing flight ​cancellations. Many schools have closed, and with much of the capital in gridlock even people in less affected areas have been stuck at home.Thailand’s prime minister, Anutin Charnvirakul, told reporters that Bangkok’s metropolitan area was still at risk from flood waters flowing in from ​the north, and said a war room had ‌been set up to monitor ‌the situation. Thailand’s weather ⁠agency has forecast more ​heavy rain for next week.View image in fullscreenPeople stand on benches on the flooded pavement in Ramkhamhaeng in Bangkok.Photograph: Lillian Suwanrumpha/AFP/Getty ImagesIt is part of a pattern that seems to be setting in this part of the world. South-east Asia has already seen a worsening of extreme floods, scientists say, a trend that is set to worsen as fossil fuel pollutants bake the planet further. Hot seas evaporate more water and warm air can hold more moisture, allowing downpours to crash down with far more force.“In central Thailand, I can see from my maps, we have already seen a small but significant trend towards extreme rainfall,” said Nikolaos Skliris, an ocean scientist at the University of Southampton who hasstudiedheavy rain in the region. “In the long-term, all models show this will be amplified – more rainfall, and more extreme rainfall.”It is too early for scientists to attribute these particular rains to climate breakdown without doing a study. They were caused by a low-pressure system that moved from an unusually warm South China Sea over Cambodia and Vietnam before getting stuck above Bangkok, which was fairly cool, data from Copernicus Climate Pulse showed.The picture is complicated by the emergence of an abnormally strongEl Niño, a cyclical weather patternthat brings record heat and more violent extremes around the world. Its presence typically leads to drier summer conditions in south-east Asia but recent research suggests it still exacerbates days with extreme rainfall.Naim Laeni, a consultant and part-time university lecturer who co-authoreda study on Bangkok’s flood resilience, said authorities had underestimated the strength of the rains, which persisted for days. The city’s drainage canals can handle about 60mm of rain an hour, rising to 80mm in upgraded sections, but localised bursts exceeded this while leaving too little time between periods of stress.“The government did not communicate the seriousness,” said Laeni. “Usually in Bangkok we receive heavy rain for a few hours, not for days.”View image in fullscreenPeople wade through a flooded area during heavy rain in Bangkok.Photograph: Patipat Janthong/ReutersNeighbouring Myanmar has suffered from the same weather system, with flash floods and blocked roads complicating rescue efforts in the country.Rescuers were pulling bodies from a landslide that devastated the village of Ka Det Nge Htein in Myanmar’s south at the weekend. That disaster had already claimed nine lives, and eight more people are missing under the mud in another village, local officials said.Civil war across the country, and a junta that restricts the media, have made it hard to get information, and hampered aid organisations.Back in Bangkok, pumping stations have been operating at full capacity, but it could be days before the waters fully drain.At her apartment complex, Suleemas said she would stay where she was with her neighbours.“It’s hard, yes, very hard,” she said. “But together we are fighting and biting through it. When we get together to help one another like this, our spirit can keep us on our feet; we can get through it all together.”Agence France-Presse contributed to this reportExplore more on these topicsExtreme weatherThailandAsia PacificFloodingEl Niño southern oscillationClimate crisisfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘It’s shocking really’: Devon community tracks River Dart sewage spills | Water | The Guardian
description: Citizen environmentalists create online platform that flags spills in real time and highlights repeatedly polluted spots
Author: Steven Morris
Headline: Citizen environmentalists create online platform that flags spills in real time and highlights repeatedly polluted spots
Content: Ben Brierley, of Sea Kayak Devon, said the hub could help him work out when and where it would be safe for his clients to enter the river.Photograph: Jim Wileman/The GuardianView image in fullscreenBen Brierley, of Sea Kayak Devon, said the hub could help him work out when and where it would be safe for his clients to enter the river.Photograph: Jim Wileman/The GuardianOur riversWater‘It’s shocking really’: Devon community tracks River Dart sewage spillsCitizen environmentalists create online platform that flags spills in real time and highlights repeatedly polluted spotsSteven MorrisSat 3 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 3 Oct 2026 07.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe easy thing for the people who live on the banks of the River Dart inDevonmight have been to grumble and groan about the sewage spills that blight their beloved waterway.Instead, citizen environmentalists in the area have created a unique online platform that flags up spills in real time, highlights spots that are repeatedly polluted, and sets out where improvement work is planned – and where it isn’t.Friends of the Dart (FOD), an independent, not-for-profit organisation, says itsRiver Hubis the first platform to pull together, overflow by overflow, such a sweep of granular detail about how one British river is being polluted.It argues it should be up to water companies or theEnvironment Agencyto provide this sort of information in a user-friendly way – but claims they don’t – so it has done the digging and provided what it believes is a vital service.View image in fullscreenRob Worthington, one of the designers of the River Hub platform, said it was built to ‘help channel’ anger over sewage pollution.Photograph: Jim Wileman/The GuardianRob Worthington, one of the designers of the platform, said there was a lot of justified anger about sewage. “We built River Hub to help channel that constructively: to show where the problems are and why, so communities can help decide what gets fixed first.”The launch comes in the week that South West Water (SWW)was fined almost £8m for sewage spills,including in Cornwall’s River Camel, which like the Dart rises on the moors and plunges down to cherished tourist hotspots.It also coincides with the prime minister, Andy Burnham, telling the Labour conference that water was a symbol of what had gone wrong with Britain and promising to reverse Margaret Thatcher’s “ideological ban” on the public ownership of water companies.Worthington told the Guardian about River Hub while sitting on a bench at Steamer Quay on the Dart in the market town of Totnes. This is adesignated bathing water spot– but Worthington says he would not swim there, knowing about what goes on a little farther upstream.View image in fullscreenThe Kilbury wastewater treatment works, near Buckfastleigh, upstream of Totnes.Photograph: Jim Wileman/The GuardianThe hub has a page that people can check to find out where spills are happening right now and where they stopped in the last 12 hours. There is also information about “dry spills” –discharges when there was no or little rain.Worthington acknowledged other independent sewage maps, such asTop of the Poops, also do this job. “But River Hub takes this a lot further,” he said.A section called Why it keeps happening? probes issues such as whether sewage treatment works have the capacity to deal with the sewage produced by the size of the population it serves. The hub concludes that not all do.In Who is fixing it?, the hub spells out works that are taking place or planned, with the dates they are due to be completed, and also draws attention to problem spots where there is no planned remedial work.A lengthy How we know? section sets out the hub’s methodology – for example, where the rainfall data it uses to classify each dry spill comes from.View image in fullscreenPeople who live in and around Totnes tell tales of falling ill after swimming in the Dart and its tributaries.Photograph: Jim Wileman/The GuardianMuch of the data used, such as SWW spill information and permits, is in the public domain but some of it can be difficult to spot, and FOD had to extract some through freedom of information requests.Worthington has worked on the hub alongside his day job as a business analyst and accepted that the picture the platform provided was incomplete and there could be inaccuracies. He and the rest of the team are happy to be corrected when they have got something wrong.They are offering the model for free to any groups who want to do the same thing on their local river. Organisations FOD has links with have already shown an interest.People who live in and around Totnes tell tales of falling ill after swimming in the Dart and its tributaries.View image in fullscreenEmma Roberts ended up in hospital with anE coliinfection after swimming in the Dart.Photograph: Jim Wileman/The GuardianEmma Roberts, an interfaith minister and theatre director, said she ended up in hospital with anE coliinfection after a dip. “It’s shocking really. The river is alive and we should all be protecting it, not putting poo into it.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionShe is not a member of FOD but thinks the hub will help. “The more information people have, the more pressure that we can put on.” A quick check of the hub reveals that place where she got ill was close to a treatment work that FOD believes does not have sufficient capacity.Olivia Doherty, who works in children’s rights and participation, said her son Seamus, 17, recently suffered stomach problems after swimming in the Dart.She said the United Nations had made it clear that young people had a right to safe spaces. “For me that includes our rivers. Getting into the river is a big thing for children here. It’s so wrong if they miss out because it’s too dirty.”View image in fullscreen‘Getting into the river is a big thing for children here,’ said Olivia Doherty. ‘It’s so wrong if they miss out because it’s too dirty.’Photograph: Jim Wileman/The GuardianBen Brierley, who runs kayak tours and courses on the Dart, said the hub could help him work out where and when it was safe for his clients to be submerged in the river.Brierley expressed frustration that water companieshave been given a deadlineof 2035 by the UK government to reduce sewage flowing into bathing water and areas of ecological importance, and 2050 for other places. “It’s bonkers that we’ll be putting sewage into our rivers until 2050,” he said.SWW said it welcomed people taking an interest in rivers’ health. A spokesperson said itsWaterFit Live siteprovided customers with a wide range of information, including near real-time storm overflow data, bathing water information and details about investment programmes.The spokesperson said: “We are committed to making information accessible and continue to develop the platform to help customers better understand our work to improve river health.”An Environment Agency spokesperson said it was taking action to tackle pollution on the Dart and welcomed the initiative from local communities to use data to raise standards.The agency said: “100% of storm overflows are now monitored and the data is publicly available. As part of the government’s storm overflows reduction plan, a record £10.2bn is also being invested over the next five years to improve more than 2,500 storm overflows inEngland. We will continue to hold water companies to account where performance falls short.”View image in fullscreenHannah Pearson said the idea of the hub and other Friends of the Dart project was ‘taking responsibility’ and bringing about change.Photograph: Jim Wileman/The GuardianHannah Pearson, a healer, coach and a founding director of FOD, said the hub built on other initiatives such as water monitoring and installing river “guardians” in parishes along the Dart.Pearson was keen to stress that they met dedicated professionals who wanted to do the right thing within organisations such as SWW and the Environment Agency. “But they are working in a dysfunctional system,” she said.She said the idea of the hub and other FOD projects was to find a way to bring about change, not to moan. “We’re not saying: ‘This is terrible.’ We’re taking responsibility and saying: ‘What can we do?’”Explore more on these topicsWaterOur riversDevonPollutionRiversEnvironment AgencyWater industryEnglandfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Country diary: The breathtaking sight of a tuna taking flight in British waters  | Fish | The Guardian
description: South Hams, Devon: These are monstrous animals, growing to 3 metres and reaching 40mph, and I was lucky enough to see a pack in hunting mode
Author: Anita Roy
Headline: South Hams, Devon: These are monstrous animals, growing to 3 metres and reaching 40mph, and I was lucky enough to see a pack in hunting mode
Content: Bluefin tuna … ‘Dark on top, with fins like daggers, its silver underside is lit up by the sun.’Photograph: Ray Harrington/Devon Sea SafarisView image in fullscreenBluefin tuna … ‘Dark on top, with fins like daggers, its silver underside is lit up by the sun.’Photograph: Ray Harrington/Devon Sea SafarisCountry diaryFishCountry diary: The breathtaking sight of a tuna taking flight in British watersSouth Hams, Devon: These are monstrous animals, growing to 3 metres and reaching 40mph, and I was lucky enough to see a pack in hunting modeAnita RoySat 3 Oct 2026 00.30 EDTLast modified on Sat 3 Oct 2026 02.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt is a perfect autumn day for a clifftop walk: sea and sky blend into a veil of baby blue, and the water is calm and dazzling. A motorboat unzips the ocean as we squint out over the bay.My companion points to a dark line snaking along in the water. It seems to intensify for a moment, then erupts in a silver commotion. Through binoculars I can make out the frantic leaping of a shoal of eel-like fish. “Garfish,” he says. “Now just watch.”Suddenly, the water erupts as a monster bursts into the air, scattering the garfish like sequins. Dark on top, with fins like daggers, its silver underside is lit up by the sun, massive as a billboard caught in headlights. It crashes down, swallowed up by its own whirlpool. Another leaps, and another. Tuna!View image in fullscreenAtlantic bluefin tuna chasing garfish off the Devon coast.Photograph: Ray Harrington/Devon Sea SafarisBy the time I’ve remembered to breathe again, the surface of the water is still and twinkling once more, as if I’d hallucinated the whole thing. Atlantic bluefin tuna (Thunnus thynnus) have, as I’ve just found, made an astonishing return to British waters. And what astonishing animals they are – they can live up to 50 years, grow to 3 metres and reach speeds of more than 40mph. This apex predator hunts in packs, herding its prey to the surface. I’m glad I’m not a garfish.‘Success story’ hailed as bluefin tunas caught off Yorkshire for first time since 1960sRead moreA common sight off England’s south coast until the 1950s, overfishing then pushed them almost to extinction here. In the early 2000s, strict regulations were introduced – andthe results are clear to see. This shows “the power of effective management”, as Chris Graham of theMarine Conservation Societyputs it.But Chris also identifies the “background issue” of global warming, which is changing the migration patterns of tuna and their prey. Bluefin tuna need warm water and, after this year’s heatwaves, the Devon coast must be like heaven.The multiple catastrophic effects of the climate crisis on ecosystems are … well, too horrific to look at head-on. So let’s focus, if only for today, on this astonishing good news story. In 2021, Atlantic bluefin tuna were reclassified on the IUCN red list from “critically endangered” to “least concern”. It’s a giant leap.Under the Changing Skies: The Best of the Guardian’s Country Diary, 2018-2024, is available now atguardianbookshop.comExplore more on these topicsFishCountry diaryRural affairsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Two Iranian men identified Manchester synagogue as site for alleged bomb plot, court hears | UK news | The Guardian
description: Rahman Salehi, 34, and Salam Ahmadyan, 36, were charged with preparing attacks on city’s Jewish community, including Heaton Park synagogue
Author: Sammy Gecsoyler
Headline: Rahman Salehi, 34, and Salam Ahmadyan, 36, were charged with preparing attacks on city’s Jewish community, including Heaton Park synagogue
Content: Salam Ahmadyan (left) and Rahman Salehi are alleged to have carried out ‘hostile reconnaissance’ within Manchester’s Jewish community.Photograph: Elizabeth Cook/PAView image in fullscreenSalam Ahmadyan (left) and Rahman Salehi are alleged to have carried out ‘hostile reconnaissance’ within Manchester’s Jewish community.Photograph: Elizabeth Cook/PAUK newsTwo Iranian men identified Manchester synagogue as site for alleged bomb plot, court hearsRahman Salehi, 34, and Salam Ahmadyan, 36, were charged with preparing attacks on city’s Jewish community, including Heaton Park synagogueSammy GecsoylerSat 3 Oct 2026 08.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTwo Iranian men identified a Manchester synagogue previously subjected to a fatal terrorist attack as a target for an alleged homemade bomb plot, a court has heard.Rahman Salehi, 34, from Salford, and Salam Ahmadyan, 36, from Liverpool were charged with preparing to commit an act of terrorism or assisting another to commit an act of terrorism on Friday.The two men appeared in Westminster magistrates court on Saturday morning. They wore grey overalls in the dock while and, through a Kurdish interpreter, spoke to confirm their names, dates of birth and addresses.The pair were alleged to have carried out “hostile reconnaissance” within Manchester’s Jewish community and identified a number of potential targets including the city’s Jewish museum and Heaton Park synagogue.The court heard the pair came to the UK illegally via small boats. Salehi arrived in 2020 before being granted leave to remain in 2023. Ahmadyan came in 2023 and has an outstanding asylum claim.They were in contact with a third party, believed to be operating from within Iran, who “directed and coordinated” the planned attack and sent them “instructions on how to prepare an explosive device”.Prosecutor Mark Luckett told the court: “Both defendants are accused of preparing acts of terrorism targeting the Jewish community in Manchester through the use of a homemade explosive device.“The defendants were observed carrying out, what the prosecution say, is a hostile reconnaissance within Manchester’s Jewish community, identifying attempted targets such as the Jewish Museum and Heaton Park synagogue.”“They were in contact with a third party who is alleged to have directed and coordinated the planned attack and provided instructions on how to assemble a homemade explosive device,” he said.“It is assessed this individual is also an Iranian national and most likely operating from within Iran.”The two men were arrested on 20 September 2026 in broad daylight, just before the festival of Yom Kippur, widely regarded as the holiest day in the Jewish calendar.Before coming to the UK, Salehi lived in Germany for five years. The men are accused of acquiring a document entitled Steps for Making [a] Powder Chlorine and Car Brake Oil/Fluid Bomb and video material on how to manufacture or assemble an improvised explosive device. They are also accused of acquiring liquids, components and equipment required in order to manufacture or assemble an improvised explosive device.They are also accused of using the internet to identify and research potential targets, acquiring images, plans and maps of potential targets and conducting reconnaissance of potential locations for attack.District judge Nina Tempia remanded the two men into custody to appear at the Old Bailey on 23 OctoberExplore more on these topicsUK newsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Half of UK wants to rejoin EU and backing it could drive up Labour vote, megapoll finds | European Union | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Findings will bolster those in No 10 who want to negotiate on re-entry but some senior figures remain wary
Author: Pippa Crerar
Headline: Exclusive: Findings will bolster those in No 10 who want to negotiate on re-entry but some senior figures remain wary
Content: Pro-EU campaigner calling on Andy Burnham to rejoin the bloc, in Parliament Square last month.Photograph: Vuk Valcic/Zuma Press Wire/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenPro-EU campaigner calling on Andy Burnham to rejoin the bloc, in Parliament Square last month.Photograph: Vuk Valcic/Zuma Press Wire/ShutterstockEuropean UnionHalf of UK wants to rejoin EU and backing it could drive up Labour vote, megapoll findsExclusive: Findings will bolster those in No 10 who want to negotiate on re-entry but some senior figures remain waryPippa CrerarandRowena MasonSat 3 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast
