modified on Sat 3 Oct 2026 01.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndy Burnham’s personal preference to rejoin theEuropean Unionafter the next election is supported by almost half of all voters, a new megapoll has found, although cabinet ministers concerned about reopening Brexit divides are privately urging him to proceed with caution.The poll by the Messina Group (TMG) found that renegotiating the UK’s relationship with the EU could boost Labour’s vote share by as much as seven points, if the prime minister offered a fresh referendum in which he campaigned to re-enter the bloc.Almost a third of voters said an in-out referendum would be needed first, while more than one in six felt that a general election mandate would be sufficient, and the same proportion thought parliament could make the decision.The overall findings will bolster the case of those inside Downing Street who want to promise at the next election that Labour would at least negotiate over re-entry, which the prime minister has said he wants to see “in his lifetime”.chartBurnham used hisfirst Labour conference speechas leader on Tuesday to announce a review ofthe optionsfor Britain’s future relationship with Europe, andsubsequently addedthat these should include rejoining entirely.However, there are nerves among some Labour MPs, especially those with constituencies that voted forBrexit, that even testing out public support for the move would be fraught with political risk and a potential boost to Reform.Two-thirds of cabinet ministers, including Burnham himself, his first secretary, Louise Haigh, chancellor, John Healey, and foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, represent seats that backed Brexit, and previously said they would respect the 2016 vote. However, public opinion has shifted.Before Burnham’s speech, several ministers had publicly cautioned against the move. Lucy Powell, Labour’s deputy leader, said while the defence and security relationship could be better, going beyond EU reset plans inherited from Keir Starmer was “not possible nor desirable”.2:20Andy Burnham fights tears as he speaks of his dad at Labour conference – videoThe trade secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, said “constitutional questions” around Britain’s EU relationship were causing uncertainty for business. The home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, said rejoining was “not a simple, straightforward thing” and the costs might be unacceptable.Downing Street’s strategy appears to be to put the focus on those who made big promises on Brexit but then failed to deliver, rather than accusing those who voted to leave the EU of making the wrong decision. But the government’s shift in position has caused some anxiety among Burnham’s team.One cabinet minister told the Guardian: “Brexit clearly hasn’t worked and the promises made haven’t been kept so Andy is right to open up the question of what the future relationship looks like. But he definitely needs to proceed with caution because we don’t want to restoke division”.A second said: “Andy is right to say we need some clarity around our long-term relationship. Security and trade cooperation are higher up the agenda than they were 10 years ago. But whether that adds up to a real desire for big change in the population I don’t know. My constituents will be cautious.”A third added: “There are obviously different views across cabinet about it, but theMade in Europe agendameans we do need to talk to the EU about what relationship they want with us long term, as what they are currently proposing is very challenging.”Another cabinet source said: “There’s an awareness among a number of cabinet ministers with leave voting seats that opinions are going to differ and the arguments about the future will have to be carefully made about the national interest.”chart 2A fifth said there were genuine questions about the best option on the table. “I’m sceptical if we go back in, about the terms we’d be going back in on, and whether that can really resolve the problems in people’s lives. But if you look at the global context you cannot start to solve things for people without having a closer relationship with the EU.”TMG polled 11,461 people, weighted by referendum result, from 12-24 September on seven different options for relationships with the EU. The most popular was rejoin, with 49% in favour and 28.5% against.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe second was to keep the existing relationship but cut as many trade barriers as possible – as the government is attempting to do with its reset – and which was supported by 48.2%, with 20.9% against. A customs union came next, on 47.1% versus 20.7%.Joining the single market and associate membership were virtually neck and neck – 45.1% and 45.5% of respondents respectively support them – while sticking with the existing relationship was backed by 42%. The seventh option – the UK moving further away from the EU – was supported by only 27.9%, with 41.2% against.A plurality of voters – 25.9% – said they wanted the UK to rejoin the EU immediately, while a slightly lower proportion – 22.9% – said it should happen in the next three years, and 8.4% over the next decade, while 23% said they did not want a closer relationship at all.TMG also tested political messaging for each of the options to see how they could affect Labour’s vote share in an election, and found that it went up – by between 4.3 and 7.4 percentage points – for all the scenarios that resulted in closer ties, with most votes coming from the Greens and Lib Dems.The polling showed that more than two-thirds of voters thought that trading with the EU was more important than the US or China, in the event the UK had to choose; four in five people want to keep the pound; and a majority want to stay in the ECHR – 53.4% versus 24.2% against.However, it also found that Brexit arguments over immigration control and sovereignty still resonated.Senior Downing Street officialshave beenin contact with thinktanks and pollsters as they look to test public support for the UK rejoining the EU. The TMG research is expected to be shared with the current operation.Some inside No 10 are nervous, however, that promising to renegotiate entry into the bloc could revive the flagging political fortunes of Nigel Farage, who said on Thursday Burnham had given him “the biggest boost in my career” byreviving the Brexit debate.The TMG research found that 29.7% people thought the UK had been right to leave the EU, while 52.4% said it had been wrong, and 17.9% didn’t know. On whether it had been a success or failure, 12.2% said a success, 54.9% a failure, 23.2% said neither and 9.7% did not know.Ben Judah, a visiting fellow at Chatham House who was an adviser to David Lammy as foreign secretary, told the Guardian: “These polls are a massive validation of Andy Burnham’s boldness on Europe. There is close to a national consensus that Brexit was not a success.“Against this background these results show thatEuropeas an issue has a unique ability to unite the left and grow the Labour vote share among swing voters. The bolder the stance towards rejoin, the bigger Labour’s reward.”Explore more on these topicsEuropean UnionLabourBrexitForeign policyEuropeAndy BurnhamnewsShareReuse this content

title: UK urged to act as Polymarket takes bets on whether HSBC and Lloyds will fail | Banking | The Guardian
description: Revelation comes amid mounting concern over online prediction market’s effects on integrity of financial system
Author: Kalyeena Makortoff
Headline: Revelation comes amid mounting concern over online prediction market’s effects on integrity of financial system
Content: Residents from UK, US, Canada and EU are banned from betting on Polymarket’s offshore platform.Photograph: Samuel Boivin/NurPhoto/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenResidents from UK, US, Canada and EU are banned from betting on Polymarket’s offshore platform.Photograph: Samuel Boivin/NurPhoto/ShutterstockBankingUK urged to act as Polymarket takes bets on whether HSBC and Lloyds will failRevelation comes amid mounting concern over online prediction market’s effects on integrity of financial systemKalyeena MakortoffBanking correspondentSat 3 Oct 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleUK authorities are being urged to intervene after it emerged that the online prediction marketPolymarkethas been taking thousands of dollars worth of bets over whether HSBC and Lloyds will fail.Polymarket – the US-owned company which holds bets on anything from football matches, to the existence of aliens, towhen a bomb drops on a city– has allowed users to take $77,507 (£58,530) worth of positions on whether the world’s biggest banks will go under by the end of this year.That includes lenders ranging from JP Morgan to BNP Paribas, as well as two of the largest on UK high streets: HSBC andLloyds Banking Group.Will prediction market ‘catch fire’ in UK, replicating US boom?Read moreWhile residents from UK, US, Canada and EU are banned from betting on Polymarket’s offshore platform, it leaves punters from across roughly 150 countries in a position to monetarily benefit from events that would create huge financial instability and threaten the health of entire economies.In a sign that authorities are taking the issue seriously, the UK’s Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) told the Guardian it had been speaking to international regulators about prediction markets, as part of efforts to protect “market integrity”.There are growingconcerns over insider trading and market manipulationon Polymarket by bad actors hoping to win big on online bets.That raises the stakes for the banking industry, which has already been toldto prepare for the risk of social media-fuelled bank runs, where customers withdraw cash at speed. Silicon Valley Bank and Credit Suisse collapsed in 2023 after big stock sell-offs and bank runs, both of which were accelerated by a frenzy of speculation on platforms such as X and WhatsApp.The Treasury committee member and Liberal Democrat MP Bobby Dean said UK authorities should intervene. “Polymarket has a poor reputation for stopping insider trading or bad actors placing bets on their platform, so it’s easy to see how it could be exploited to try to aggravate real shifts in market sentiment,” he said.“If the bank-related activity grows on the platform and then a particular market was to escalate rapidly, it could even trigger bank runs,” Dean added.“I would urge our regulators to get in contact with their counterparts in the US to raise concerns. We should not turn a blind eye to the risks because they are relatively small today, we’ve all seen how quickly things can move in this sector.”Polymarket bosses said they did not see a problem with the bets themselves, arguing they were democratising markets that were previously restricted to elite traders and institutions.The company’s chief legal officer, Neal Kumar, said: “The information in these markets is already public. Banks, hedge funds and credit professionals have had access to credit default swap markets for years. You shouldn’t need to work at an institution like that to have access to information on a topic of this importance like bank failures.“Polymarket simplifies the question, providing a much larger audience with information, and markets serve as a powerful source of information and combating disinformation.”However,academics have warnedthese platforms are creating a serious moral hazard, giving market participants “an incentive to engage in corrupt, illegal, or dangerous actions in order to rig the outcome of the contract”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMeanwhile, the European Securities and Markets Authority (ESMA)used its twice-yearly risk report last monthto warn that “a growing number of incidents illustrates that prediction markets are rife with inside trading”.“Market manipulation and insider trading risks reach new levels in the context of prediction markets, particularly on DLT-based [distributed ledger technology] platforms such as Polymarket, which operate with limited identity verification and where the platform itself may not know who is behind a given wager.”Polymarket’s offshore platform is built on a blockchain. Accounts are linked to crypto wallets that can be publicly traced but are difficult to link back to an individual.While Polymarket is headquartered in the US, its markets are international and its users are anonymous. Some users from restricted countries can find workarounds via virtual private networks (VPNs), despite this violating Polymarket’s terms of use.ESMA’s report pointed to cases such as the US-Israel strike on Iran in February, when several newly created wallets reportedly generated $1.2m profits shortly before the military operation became public. That followed the US capture of Venezuela’s leader, Nicolás Maduro, in January, wherea US soldier was criminally chargedfor allegedly using classified information to place profitable bets on Polymarket ahead of the operation.And, in April this year, police were notified oversuspected tamperingof weather sensors at the Charles de Gaulle airport that were used to settle Polymarket weather contracts.The Bank of England said its supervisors engage regularly with companies on a wide range of market developments and emerging risks. Lloyds andHSBCdeclined to comment.The Treasury did not respond to requests for comment.Explore more on these topicsBankingHSBCLloyds Banking GroupPolymarketPrediction marketsGamblingBanks and building societiesnewsShareReuse this content

title: UK-Iran national arrested over alleged bomb plot at RAF Fairford released on bail | UK news | The Guardian
description: The 25-year-old was the sixth man detained as counter-terrorism police investigate ‘possible foreign state involvement’
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The 25-year-old was the sixth man detained as counter-terrorism police investigate ‘possible foreign state involvement’
Content: Police patrol the perimeter of RAF Fairford as a US bomber lands.Photograph: Ben Birchall/PAView image in fullscreenPolice patrol the perimeter of RAF Fairford as a US bomber lands.Photograph: Ben Birchall/PAUK newsUK-Iran national arrested over alleged bomb plot at RAF Fairford released on bailThe 25-year-old was the sixth man detained as counter-terrorism police investigate ‘possible foreign state involvement’PA MediaSat 3 Oct 2026 09.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA sixth man who was arrested in connection with a suspected terrorist plot at RAF Fairford has been released on bail.The 25-year-old, a dual UK-Iranian national, was arrested on suspicion of preparing terrorist acts under section 5 of the Terrorism Act 2006.He was detained on Thursday in the borough of Westminster, London, where searches of two properties have now concluded.The investigation into the incident is still under way, counter-terrorism police said.Last weekend, five British nationals, all in their mid-20s, were arrested on suspicion of explosives offences and terrorism and then bailed.The arrests were made after three suspicious vans were spotted near the military site in Gloucestershire.View image in fullscreenFive men were arrested last weekend after police were alerted to suspicious vans near RAF Fairford.Photograph: BBCVicki Evans, the senior national coordinator for Counter Terrorism Policing, previously said the investigation was “hugely complex”, adding that specialist teams were “interrogating multiple lines of inquiry”.She said: “As we’ve made clear, we’re looking at all possible angles – including possible foreign state involvement.”The prime minister, Andy Burnham, has said there were “strong indications” Iran played a part in the incident near the Gloucestershire military base.RAF Fairford has been used in recent months by US bombers after former prime minister Keir Starmer granted Washington permission to use British bases for “defensive” strikes against Tehran.View image in fullscreenA B‑1B Lancer bomber departs RAF Fairford airbase after police declared a major incident at the base last weekend.Photograph: Toby Shepheard/ReutersCounter-terrorism police have said a quantity of petrol, but no explosive devices, was found in the vans that had sparked the security alert near the airbase.On Thursday, the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, claimed Israel handed Britain intelligence about the suspected terror plot.Netanyahu said his country warned UK authorities about the “Iranian-sponsored attack” shortly before Britain’s announcement of a ban on trade with illegal Israeli settlements in the West Bank.Explore more on these topicsUK newsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Can anything politicians say at Sunday’s election stop young people from leaving Bosnia? | Bosnia and Herzegovina | The Guardian
description: They are the support base for non-nationalist parties but are voting with their feet and not on ballot papers
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: They are the support base for non-nationalist parties but are voting with their feet and not on ballot papers
Content: Sarah Ćato, 19: ‘Young people don’t know who to vote for because nobody’s standing for us.’Photograph: Guy De Launey/The GuardianView image in fullscreenSarah Ćato, 19: ‘Young people don’t know who to vote for because nobody’s standing for us.’Photograph: Guy De Launey/The GuardianBosnia and HerzegovinaCan anything politicians say at Sunday’s election stop young people from leaving Bosnia?They are the support base for non-nationalist parties but are voting with their feet and not on ballot papersGuy de Launey in SarajevoSat 3 Oct 2026 05.35 EDTLast modified on Sat 3 Oct 2026 06.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOn a perfect October morning in Sarajevo, the motivation for young people to be leavingBosnia and Herzegovinain droves is not immediately apparent. The country’s capital is basking in the autumn sunshine and the pavement cafes in the shadow of the Sacred Heart Cathedral are packed. People lingering over coffee and cigarettes mix peacefully with the Swedish football fans in town for their team’s Nations League match.But Sarajevo’s many charms have not been enough to keep young people in Bosnia. One local organisation that tracks emigration estimated that more than 600,000 people had left the country in the decade after the 2013 census, when the official population was 3.5 million.View image in fullscreenPre-election billboards of various parties and candidates line the streets of SarajevoPhotograph: Elvis Barukčić/AFP/Getty Images“If I weren’t optimistic, maybe I would also move out,” said Timur Ilic, a 28-year-old municipal councillor in Sarajevo, who is standing on Sunday for election to the cantonal government. He represents Our Party – a multi-ethnic, non-nationalist, liberal movement that he admits faces a struggle to appeal to voters in a country dominated by ethnonationalist parties.View image in fullscreenTimur Ilic of Our Party: ‘People are not ready for a significant change.’Photograph: Guy De Launey/The Guardian“People are not ready for a significant change,” he said. “They’re afraid of uncertainty. I think there needs to be a new generation which doesn’t understand why people are willing to put up with this situation and who are willing to maybe vote for us to try something different.”The problem for Our Party – and other non-nationalist movements – is that the young people who make up their support base are voting with their feet, rather than making their mark on ballot papers. In theory, Sunday’s vote should be one of the great European festivals of democracy, with the election of no fewer than 14 prime ministers and five presidents. But the plethora of posts on offer reflects a fiendishly complicated system of governance.The Dayton agreement’s creation of two powerful regional “entities” – with a weaker central government – was intended as a stopgap to ensure peace after the ruinous conflict of the 1990s. Instead, it has perpetuated the divisions in the country. Most Serbs live in the Republika Srpska (RS), while the Federation is home to most of Bosnia’s Croats and Bosniak Muslims. There is no incentive for the ethnonationalist leaders to change that situation – or to appeal to young people who see a brighter future outside the country.View image in fullscreenAjna Mesic: ‘Our parents tell us to go.’Photograph: Guy De Launey/The Guardian“They don’t want young people to be interested, and young people are not interested in politics,” said Sarah Ćato, gesturing over her shoulder to a banner of the unsmiling leader of the Bosniak SDA party looming over the cafe tables in central Sarajevo. The 19-year-old student of political science and international relations is eligible to vote on Sunday for the first time – but she says that her age group feels unseen by the political mainstream.“Young people don’t know how to vote or who to vote for because nobody’s standing for us,” she said, adding that the reluctance to engage in politics reflects its status as a “taboo subject” after the end of the conflict in 1995. “I think educating youth from middle school on how to be a good citizen should be mandatory.”View image in fullscreenA drone view shows a campaign billboard featuring Darijana Filipovic, a candidate of the Croat Democratic Union of Bosnia and Herzegovina (HDZ BiH) in Mostar.Photograph: Amel Emrić/ReutersBut there seems little chance of that happening, given that Bosnian children learn different versions of their country’s recent history depending on whether they are Serbs, Bosniaks or Croats. Indeed, the curriculum in the RS now celebrates Radovan Karadzic and the late Ratko Mladić – both convicted of genocide by an international tribunal in The Hague – as “national heroes”.View image in fullscreenDijana Papaz in East Sarajevo, where young people grow up ‘surrounded by murals of war criminals’.Photograph: Guy De Launey/The GuardianEast Sarajevo is just a short drive from the centre of the capital – but it is on the other side of the “entity line” that divides the Federation from the RS. The road signs are written in Serbian Cyrillic, and young people grow up “surrounded by murals of war criminals”, as 23-year-old local resident Dijana Papaz put it. She worked on an exhibition with Sarah Ćato called What If the Border Is Within You?, looking at the divisions between Sarajevo and East Sarajevo – and how young people overcome them.Papaz rejects ethnic labels, referring to herself as “Bosnian”, but she concedes that theglorification of Mladićfollowing his death in August reflects both enduring divisions and the need for change.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“We need to do something about our constitution, because Dayton wasn’t supposed to last 30 years,” she said. “It was supposed to be a temporary thing after the war while we made the country better, but that never happened.”View image in fullscreenCampaign posters by the river in SarajevoPhotograph: Guy De Launey/The GuardianPeople born since 1995 may have no memories of the conflict or its causes, but they do hear plenty about it from family members. And Ajna Mešić from the Youth Initiative for Human Rights says the continuing exodus of Bosnia’s brightest prospects can also be put down to pressure at home.“Our parents tell us to go,” she said. “Growing up, my destiny was to be a lawyer in Germany. Then somewhere in high school, I remembered I have free will. But a lot of parents will tell you that they fought the war for nothing and they don’t want us also to live here.”View image in fullscreenBenjamin Ahmedbegovic of the non-nationalist SDP does not expect the polls to change anything.Photograph: Guy De Launey/The GuardianYoung faces were thin on the ground at a pre-election rally for the non-nationalist Social Democratic party (SDP) opposite Sarajevo’s historic city hall, with red flares reflecting off the Miljacka River as party activists put on a show. But 23-year-old Benjamin Ahmedbegovic, the vice-president of the local branch of the SDP’s youth forum, admitted he did not expect the polls to change the country’s situation – or the propensity of its young people to leave.“Political instability has been one of the main drivers of migration from Bosnia and Herzegovina,” he said, pointing to the phenomenon of people “voting for their own” as an aggravating factor. “Everyone just wants someone who has the same ethnic label to be in power, rather than judging whether they do something well or not.”That means the elections are unlikely to bring any surprises – or any reasons to make young Bosnians who are thinking of leaving change their minds. They may, as Ilic puts it, “miss the coffee”. But they certainly will not feel the same way about the divisive politics that leave their country stuck in the past.Explore more on these topicsBosnia and HerzegovinaEuropeYoung peoplefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Brazil’s neck-and-neck election offers test for growing pro-Trump Latin American bloc | Brazil | The Guardian
description: Sunday’s poll pits the leftist incumbent Lula against the son of a former far-right president convicted of staging a coup
Author: Tiago Rogero
Headline: Sunday’s poll pits the leftist incumbent Lula against the son of a former far-right president convicted of staging a coup
Content: President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, a candidate for re-election for the Workers' party, attends a rally in São Gonçalo, Brazil. Photograph: Tita Barros/ReutersSunday’s poll pits the leftist incumbent Lula against the son of a former far-right president convicted of staging a coup‘No one disrespects Our Lady’: fears for Brazil’s patron saint grip country ahead of electionByTiago Rogeroin Rio de JaneiroSat 3 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 3 Oct 2026 03.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleShortly after hiscontroversial speechto the United Nations general assembly in September, Donald Trump gathered a dozen like-minded Latin American leaders and boasted that rightwing candidates had won all seven presidential elections held in the region since he began his second term.“Everybody I’ve endorsed has won,” the US president said in New York to most of the leaders of the Shield of the Americas, ananti-drug cartel coalitionof 15 countries governed by the right or far right.View image in fullscreenA giant balloon of Donald Trump holding Brazil’s President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva during a Flávio Bolsonaro rally in São Paulo.Photograph: Miguel Schincariol/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDonald Trump departs a meeting of the multinational coalition Shield of the Americas on the sidelines at the UN general assembly in New York.Photograph: Julia Demaree Nikhinson/APThose electoral victories – and theUS takeoverof Venezuela after capturing Nicolás Maduro – have left just six Latin American countries under leftwing governments: regional heavyweights Brazil and Mexico, small Uruguay and Guatemala, and the isolated regimes of Cuba and Nicaragua.On Sunday, Brazilians go to the polls in apresidential electionthat many believe will determinemore thanLatin America’s largest country’s fate for the next four years.View image in fullscreenSupporters Lula gather at a political rally in São Paulo.Photograph: Brian Snyder/ReutersGiven Mexico’s geographic proximity and unique economic relationship with the US, analysts see Brazil as perhaps the last country in the regionstill capableof saying “no” to Trump’s whims – something that could change dramatically depending on the election result.Polls indicate aneck-and-neck racebetween Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva,the 80-year-old leftist incumbentwho is seeking a fourth non-consecutive term, andFlávio Bolsonaro, 45, the far-right senator son of former president Jair Bolsonaro.“Trump really does take seriously the idea that theAmericasshould be his back yard,” said Pedro Telles, a professor at the School of International Relations at Brazil’s FGV university.View image in fullscreenPresident Claudia Sheinbaum leads her morning press conference at the National Palace in Mexico City, marking two years in office.Photograph: Luis Marin/Clasos/Zuma Press/Shutterstock“Mexico will remain relevant, and its president,Claudia Sheinbaum, is one of themost popularleftwing leaders. But if Flávio wins, it would be a real blow to the left and a major boost to the far-right agenda globally,” added Telles.“There is a lot at stake,” said Sandra Borda Guzmán, an associate professor of political science at Colombia’s Universidad de los Andes. “Instead of taking the opportunity to expand our region’s autonomy, a far-right victory would align the region unconditionally with the dictates of the US,” she added.View image in fullscreenA street vendor sells campaign flags of the presidential candidates Bolsonaro and Lula.Photograph: Eraldo Peres/APLula and Bolsonaro differ sharply on the US, including over what has become Trump’s main foreign policy for the region: theso-called “war on drugs” used to justify dozens of airstrikes on boats that havekilled more than 230 peopleand joint operations involving US military personnelon land.While Bolsonaro has pledged to join the Shield of the Americas and to follow an“iron fist” approachto crime, Lula has raised concerns about sovereignty and said it is “sad to see theinferiority complexof Latin American presidents” who are part of the Trump-created coalition.Brazil attorney general says meddling ‘cannot be tolerated’ after Trump funding plans revealedRead moreLula and Trump’s relationship hasswungbetween not speaking andpublic displays of warmth, but it is currentlyat a low point, with the Brazilian president andDemocratic membersof the US Congress accusing Washington oftrying to interferein Bolsonaro’s favour.“Brazil is a big prize,” said Michael Shifter, adjunct professor at Georgetown University’s School of Foreign Service, adding that amid endless conflicts in Iran, Ukraine and Israel-Palestine, “US foreign policy is going very badly in the rest of the world.”A victory for Bolsonaro in Brazil, he said, would be used “triumphantly” by Trump for producing an “almost completely aligned region”.At the latest Shield of the Americas meeting, Trump made clear that it was not all about security. The US president also referred to the “tremendous natural wealth” of Latin American countries, which he said could not “be taken over by hostile outside powers” – widely understood as a reference to China.View image in fullscreenPosters for Lula  in the streets of the Cajazeiras neighborhood in Salvador, Bahia state.Photograph: Amanda Cotrim/AFP/Getty ImagesPrivileged access to Brazil’s rare earths and critical minerals wasone of the conditionsWashington imposed in exchange for not applying tariffs, which Lula rejected. Bolsonaro, on the other hand,has offeredthose natural resources as the “solution” to help the US “break its dependence on China”.“Democracy is also kind of on the line here,” added Shifter, noting that Bolsonaro was only running because his father cannot – Jair Bolsonaro is under house arrest after being convicted ofattempting a coupto overturn his defeat by Lula in the 2022 election.“So it’s not just a question of one more country moving to the right, but of a right that has a very problematic relationship with democracy,” he said.As in recent elections across Latin America, the race includes other candidates but is polarised between two leading candidates. Lula and Bolsonaro have alternated as frontrunners in the final stretch, making the outcome unpredictable; if neither wins 50% plus one of the votes, there will be a runoff on 25 October.Bolsonaro’s only previous bid for an executive role in government ended ignominiously when he tookfourth placein Rio’s 2016 mayoral race. But analysts say there are several reasons why a congressman best known for his family name and corruption allegations – someshelved, othersstill under investigation– has emerged as a serious challenger to a three-time president.Unemployment, poverty and inflationhave fallen, and average incomes have risen, but so hashousehold debt– something many attribute to online betting, which the older Bolsonaro left unregulated andLula banneddays before the vote.The incumbent’s campaign has also been hit by corruption allegations – stillunder investigation– involving his son and a former aide, while ascandal involving supreme court justiceswith no connection to Lula may have rubbed off on the president.View image in fullscreenBolsonaro waves at supporters during a campaign rally at the São Paulo Municipal Market in São Paulo.Photograph: Miguel Schincariol/AFP/Getty ImagesMany therefore see Bolsonaro’s support as coming both from asimple transferof his father’s voter base and from ananti-Lula vote.“I’m going to vote for Flávio, but not because I think he’s the best option,” said Bruna Arguello, 34, a businesswoman from Santana de Parnaíba, whose first choice would be Ronaldo Caiado, a far-right former governor of Goiás, polling at 4%. “Unfortunately, he has no chance of winning, so I’m going with Flávio so we can get Lula out,” she said.View image in fullscreenThe presidential candidate for the Social Democratic party (PSD), Ronaldo Caiado, speaks at a press conference in Rio de Janeiro on Thursday.Photograph: Andre Coelho/EPAActor Docy Moreira, 59, will vote for Lula. In 2018, she was so dismayed byJair Bolsonaro’s electionthat she decided to leave her home town of Belo Horizonte, where two-thirds of voters backed the far-right leader. “I couldn’t understand how people, including the vast majority of my family, were choosing so much violence and authoritarianism,” she said.She Googled which cities had given Bolsonaro the lowest share of the vote, chose one about 1,550 miles away and moved north to Luís Correia, in Piauí.She eventually returned home, and most of her family will now vote for Bolsonaro’s son. Still, Moreira remains confident Lula will win.“If not, it will be devastating, but I’m not going to move again. I’m stronger now. I’ve learned that I can find refuge within myself,” said Moreira.Explore more on these topicsBrazilLuiz Inácio Lula da SilvaAmericasJair BolsonaronewsShareReuse this content

title: Libyan unity talks upended as warlord’s son linked to drone attacks on fuel facilities | Libya | The Guardian
description: Western Libya’s GNU say working with Saddam Haftar ‘impossible’ as US-backed merger plan breaks down
Author: Patrick Wintour
Headline: Western Libya’s GNU say working with Saddam Haftar ‘impossible’ as US-backed merger plan breaks down
Content: Four people were arrested after drones attacked the Zawiya oil station, causing a fire. Three Libyans were arrested and have been linked to Saddam Haftar.Photograph: Mahmud Turkia/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenFour people were arrested after drones attacked the Zawiya oil station, causing a fire. Three Libyans were arrested and have been linked to Saddam Haftar.Photograph: Mahmud Turkia/AFP/Getty ImagesLibyaLibyan unity talks upended as warlord’s son linked to drone attacks on fuel facilitiesWestern Libya’s GNU say working with Saddam Haftar ‘impossible’ as US-backed merger plan breaks downPatrick WintourSat 3 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 3 Oct 2026 05.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAllegations that the son of the Libyan warlord Khalifa Haftar oversaw a “terror cell” that launched drone attacks on fuel storage facilities and power stations in westernLibyahave upended plans for the Tripoli-based government of national unity (GNU) to continue cooperating with Haftar on a plan to unify the country.Saddam Haftar, the deputy commander of the so-called Libyan National Army (LNA), has increasingly been seen by the US as an important figure in its plans to unify Libyan security, judicial and political institutions.But a round of drone attacks in August worsened electricity blackouts in the west of the country, putting intense popular pressure on the GNU led by the prime minister, Abdul Hamid Dbeibah.Libya has been split between the east, dominated by Haftar, and the west, governed by the GNU, since the fall of Col MuammarGaddafi in 2011, leaving the oil-rich country at the mercy of corruption, militia, migrant traffickers and myriad external actors.View image in fullscreenKhalifa Haftar.Photograph: Esam Omran Al-Fetori/ReutersDonald Trump’sAfricaadviser, Massad Boulos, has hatched a plan to unify the two Libyan governments in which Haftar from the east would take on the role of president and a member of the Dbeibah family from the west would become prime minister.Boulos has insisted he is not trying a quick fix that entrenches family elites in Libya. “It’s not about families or names,” Boulos said when asked about the reported Haftar-Dbeibah deal, before adding: “At the end of the day, those are individuals that have to be in one position or the other.”But the drone strikes, it is claimed, were prompted by Haftar’s anger at Dbeibah apparently stalling on the Boulos merger plan and by Tripoli allegedly encouraging tribes in southern Libya to attack and kill his forces.Over more than five days in August, drones attacked the Zawiya oil station and fuel storage facilities in western Libya. The drone strikes hit the gasoline-storage tank at the Zawiya oil complex, west of Tripoli, causing a large fire and the tank’s collapse. The tank held approximately 4.5m litres of fuel when it was struck, according to Libya’s National Oil Corporation.0:25Libyan oil refinery engulfed in flames after drone attack – videoOn 5 September, three Libyans and one Spanish citizen were arrested in southern Tripoli by the GNU for their alleged role in a plot that was intended to include an attack on Tripoli airport. It was thought the whole group involved five Spaniards and four Libyans. The three arrested Libyans were allegedly affiliated with the Tareq ben Ziyad brigade, an LNA formation. Information that has emerged from interviews about the plot, and Saddam Haftar’s alleged role, not just in Libya, has been described as a goldmine, capable of weakening Khalifa Haftar.Sources in the GNU said the alleged plotters were working for Saddam Haftar. “No formal decision has been made, but in light of what has been discovered it is impossible to work with Saddam,” the sources said.The claims not only damage Saddam Haftar’s role in the Boulos plan but also the parallel UN sponsored 4+4 talks involving the main four political institutions in Libya that led to an August agreement to stage elections within two years. The deal endorsed by the UN security council overcomes previous obstacles to elections, and had been backed by the main actors capable of delivering the change.Walid Ellafi, minister for state for political affairs in the UN-backed Libyan GNU and an enthusiast for elections, said: “Our support for the 4+4 process is rooted in its role as a UN sponsored framework offering a new approach to achieving practical results that pave the way for elections and institutions whose political legitimacy derives from the will of the people – not as a political settlement that overlooks violations or sets aside the rights of those affected.”He opposes an elite east-west political deal that brushes aside longstanding grievances such as the displacement of 9,000 families in Benghazi during the 2014 war.The allegations about the sabotage operation may intensify a power struggle between the three sons of Khalifa Haftar in the east.Saddam Haftar is seen as his father’s most likely heir, possesses the most resources, enjoys the backing of the United Arab Emirates and has so far dominated the political tracks. But his brothers, Khaled and Belqasim – more allied with Egypt than the United Arab Emirates – have recently started to challenge his dominance.Explore more on these topicsLibyaMiddle East and north AfricaAfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: BT accused of ‘bullying’ customers by pausing broadband in digital landline push | BT | The Guardian
description: Companies race to switch households to ‘voice over internet protocol’ services by the end of January
Author: Mark Sweney
Headline: Companies race to switch households to ‘voice over internet protocol’ services by the end of January
Content: About 1.3m copper-based landlines are yet to be migrated to digital.Photograph: Ian Rutherford/AlamyView image in fullscreenAbout 1.3m copper-based landlines are yet to be migrated to digital.Photograph: Ian Rutherford/AlamyBTBT accused of ‘bullying’ customers by pausing broadband in digital landline pushCompanies race to switch households to ‘voice over internet protocol’ services by the end of JanuaryMark SweneySat 3 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBT has been accused of “bullying” customers by temporarily cutting off their broadband to pressure them to upgrade to a digital landline, as providers race to switch households over before the January deadline.Telecoms companies have so far migrated 16-17m lines from the old copper network to digital voice over internet protocol (VoiP), which uses a broadband connection instead, in the biggest technological upgrade since the early 00s, whenanalogue TV was switched off.However, as the date for the retirement of the old public switched telephone network (PSTN) approaches, Openreach, the BT subsidiary that maintains the vast majority of the UK broadband and telephony network, says there are still about 1.3m copper-based landlines yet to be migrated.To hit the end-of-January deadline telecoms companies have started to ramp up pressure after years of direct customer communications and awareness campaigns – in BT’s case including using personalitiesincluding Moira Stuartand Clare Balding– have failed to prompt some to engage in the migration programme.“I’m getting increasing evidence that there is some bullying behaviour going on in order to try to force people to switch over,” said Dennis Reed, the founder of the campaign group Silver Voices.“I have heard of cases that some with a contract with BT for broadband, who have not been particularly proactive or cooperative over a date to switch their landline, have been threatened with their internet being cut off. I am also fearful that, because targets have to be met, a lot of people are going to fall through the cracks.”It is understood that BT did recently “temporarily pause” broadband services for a small group of customers who had not responded to any communications about the copper landline switchover for two years.They were given five days’ notice of the planned outage to encourage them to contact BT and take action to avoid the “pause” in broadband service. Landline connections and mobile services remained intact, meaning services such astelecare devicesremained operational.More than 80% of the previously unresponsive customers are understood to have subsequently taken the steps needed to switch over.“Throughout this transformation BT has been raising awareness of the switchover, supported by local events, advertising campaigns and partners – as well as direct communications to our customers,” said a BT spokesperson.“A small minority of customers are yet to move and haven’t responded to repeated communications about the change. The temporary broadband pause we have introduced for this small minority is intended to help prevent a complete loss of service when the old, analogue network is retired.“In the final months of the programme, it’s critical that customers take action when contacted about the switchover – failing to do so could result in the loss of their services when the outdated network retires.”Campaigners are concerned that the 1.3 million households still on copper lines include vulnerable individuals, such as elderly people with only a landline and no internet andthose in rural areaswith patchy, or no, broadband and variable mobile coverage who worry about being able to call emergency services if there is a power cut.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThere are alsoaround 2 million users of telecareservices, most commonly personal pendant alarms or buttons that have traditionally relied on copper landlines, which are unaffected if the internet goes down.In December, Virgin Media wasfined £23.8mfor leaving thousands of customers, typically older and disabled people, without access to their alarms as it was transitioning customers in 2023.Theissue of vulnerable customersresulted in a pause of non-voluntary migrations to digital landlines, and ultimately resulted in the industry moving the copper landline retirement date from December last year to the end of this coming January.For most customers, the switch involved just plugging their existing home phone handset into the back of their broadband router rather than into the phone socket on the wall.Caroline Abrahams, the charity director at Age UK, said: “As the January 2027 deadline gets closer the telecoms providers should commit to ensuring that no older person is cut off if they haven’t yet switched. It should not mark a hard-and-fast cliff edge. We know that older people are overrepresented among those who are yet to switch.”Explore more on these topicsBTTelecommunications industryOlder peopleBroadband (Money)Broadband (Technology)InternetConsumer affairsnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I was making no money’: Travel agent side hustle promoted by influencers criticised over fees | Consumer affairs | The Guardian
description: Would-be marketers enticed by online talk of entering a world of travel and easy cash find that the reality is rather different
Author: Sarah Marsh
Headline: Would-be marketers enticed by online talk of entering a world of travel and easy cash find that the reality is rather different
Content: Influencers promote InteleTravel and PlanNet Marketing to large audiences, with slogans such as ‘normalise working from anywhere’.Photograph: Westend61/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenInfluencers promote InteleTravel and PlanNet Marketing to large audiences, with slogans such as ‘normalise working from anywhere’.Photograph: Westend61/Getty ImagesConsumer affairs‘I was making no money’: Travel agent side hustle promoted by influencers criticised over feesWould-be marketers enticed by online talk of entering a world of travel and easy cash find that the reality is rather differentSarah MarshSat 3 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMonths before she entered the Love Island villa, the content creator Yasmin Hadlow promised viewers of her online videos that they could “catch flights and get paid mid-air”. All they had to do, she said, was send her a direct message with the word “freedom”.The 23-year-old is among several influencers and celebrities, including the former Geordie Shore star Vicky Pattison, working for PlanNet Marketing, which recruits people to work as independent travel agents with a separate US business, InteleTravel.Pattison’s Instagram page, Vickys Vacays, says it helps women “build confidence, income and freedom through a supportive online travel business”.View image in fullscreenYasmin Hadlow in series 13 of Love Island.Photograph: ITV/ShutterstockIt sounds like a great way to make money. But the Guardian has spoken to seven people who were recruited as InteleTravel agents by PlanNet Marketing reps, not the influencers mentioned above, who said they struggled to make money once sign-up costs and monthly fees were taken into account.Some of them said the people who recruited them encouraged them to sign up as PlanNet Marketing reps and recruit others, and that became their main focus rather than selling holidays.‘I was making no money’Mark* always wanted to be a travel agent. He was recruited by a PlanNet rep to work with InteleTravel in 2021 when he was 28. He had just been furloughed during Covid, wanted a career change and was looking at different routes to his dream job.He paid InteleTravel a sign-up fee of about £150, plus £30 to £40 a month for access to its booking system and training.Agents earn about 70% of the roughly 10% commission suppliers pay on bookings. So, if they sell £10,000 worth of holidays, the supplier pays out £1,000 in commission and the agent gets £700.After about 18 months working long days, Mark had only made a handful of sales. “I was making no money on the travel side,” he says, adding that the PlanNet rep who recruited him told him “to try recruitment instead, by signing up with PlanNet Marketing”.View image in fullscreenPlanNet Marketing recruits people to work as independent travel agents with a separate US business, InteleTravel.Photograph: Hotel Photography SrlIf you are an InteleTravel agent, joining PlanNet Marketing is optional. Those who do so pay PlanNet Marketing a separate monthly fee of about £14. They then get roughly $4, or about £3, for every new person they recruit as an active travel agent, plus referral bonuses and rank-based payouts as their “downline” (number of recruits) grows.“I ended up with a team of 10 people, but it never felt like me,” Mark says. “The whole point of joining was to be a travel agent, not a recruiter.”PlanNet Marketing’s annual income disclosure statement suggests earnings from recruitment are typically very low. Its most recent figures show average annual earnings across its general base of representatives are about $40.Mark was with InteleTravel and PlanNet Marketing for about two years. “I made about three bookings and maybe £1,000 in commission, but I was paying £32 a month in fees, plus about £100 to sign up,” he says. “That wasn’t because I was bad at it. It’s not set up for people to succeed.”A spokesperson for InteleTravel said: “As with any self-employed business owner, there can be no guarantee of continuous profit and success when starting a business … An unwavering guarantee of significant profit is not a foregone conclusion and cannot be guaranteed, as is the case with any form of self-employment.”The spokesperson said joining fees covered regulatory licensing and memberships, operational insurance, mandatory training and booking systems, to enable travel advisers to make bookings in accordance with the UK’s travel regulatory requirements.View image in fullscreenThe homepage of the InteleTravel websitePhotograph: Inteletravel websiteInteleTravel offers a 30-day money-back guarantee so agents can cancel for a refund. Any travel commissions earned during that first month are deducted from the returned amount.The company also offers a “first-year profit guarantee”, which pledges to refund the difference if an agent doesn’t earn back their fees in their first 12 months, as long as they meet certain contractual conditions.For example, according to its website, the agent must have “completed one full year of valid adviser status”, purchase branded business cards, create a website, successfully book one completed hotel stay every quarter, and submit their written refund claim within a 30-day window after their one-year anniversary.Shelley, 52, a nurse from Suffolk, signed up to InteleTravel during the pandemic in 2021 after seeing a Facebook advert. She says: “I’d always loved travelling, and with everything shut down during Covid, I thought: ‘Why not build up some knowledge and training for when things reopened?’”She says that after filling out a form, she was approached online by a local PlanNet recruiter advertising support, training and “excellent commission”, before being introduced to the recruiter’s manager (also a PlanNet person) on social media. “It was sold really well – the impression given was that you really couldn’t lose anything,” she says.But she says the reality fell short almost immediately. “The moment you’re out of the money-back guarantee period – I paid a £142 joining fee, which at the time came with a 30-day guarantee – you’re on your own. If I had a question, the manager would say to go and watch the training videos yourself.”View image in fullscreenSome critics have suggested that the arrangement is a multi-level marketing (MLM) operation – a legal, but controversial, model in which agents make money through recruitment rather than through selling a product.Photograph: Shiiko Alexander/AlamyAfter accounting for spending on business cards, flyers and a website, Shelley estimates her total profit over roughly two years was between £500 and £1,000. “I was told [by the recruiter] I could earn a living from it … I was misled into thinking this could be a full-time job,” she says.‘Exclusive partner’PlanNet Marketing says it only works for InteleTravel and is described on the InteleTravel sign-up page as its “exclusive enrolment partner”.Some critics have suggested that the arrangement is a multi-level marketing (MLM) operation – a legal, but controversial, model in which agents make money through recruitment rather than through selling a product.PlanNet Marketing did not comment on whether it is an MLM. InteleTravel denies that it is, saying that the two are separate businesses, and that signing up with PlanNet Marketing to do recruitment is an individual’s choice.On its website, PlanNet Marketing sets out strict rules on how representatives should promote the InteleTravel opportunity. Representatives are told to promote the “income opportunity” rather than travel discounts or perks, and to keep the roles of PlanNet Marketing representatives and InteleTravel travel agents separate.For example, an Instagram post in August from a PlanNet Marketing and InteleTravel agent promoting the opportunity online said she had booked her “own holidays for years”, never realising “there was another way”.She said: “Now I still book with those exact same trusted suppliers, but through my own travel platform instead … The only difference is I have access to an even wider range of suppliers, and I earn the commission on every booking.”View image in fullscreenOn its website, PlanNet Marketing sets out strict rules on how representatives should promote the InteleTravel opportunity.Photograph: imageBROKER/ShutterstockAnother former InteleTravel agent, Claire*, joined PlanNet Marketing in early 2024 and left this February. She became a one-star director – a leadership rank awarded after recruiting 100 people that PlanNet Marketing says guarantees a minimum monthly income of $1,000 (£754). Claire says she never received that sum.“By the time I left, I’d recruited about 150 people and was making about $800 a month. Over two years, more than 700 people came through – most didn’t stay because most weren’t making money.”Claire says many PlanNet Marketing agents recruiting for InteleTravel promoted the opportunity of working as a travel agent as a way for people to save money on their own holidays by earning commission on personal travel and accessing exclusive discounts. But she believes people could frequently find cheaper deals elsewhere.Appealing to womenWhen recruiting for PlanNet Marketing, Vicky Pattison’s page specifically appeals to mothers on maternity leave. In one story, she describes the opportunity as “your dream come true”, adding: “Some mummies have even started this on maternity leave and been so successful they haven’t returned to their nine-to-five.”The Guardian found recruiting accounts that mentioned women, mothers and those with a chronic illness. One account appealed to “fellow chronically ill girlies” who wanted to “put their health first” while working remotely.View image in fullscreenVicky Pattison works for PlanNet Marketing.Photograph: Maureen McLean/ShutterstockThe influencers promote InteleTravel and PlanNet Marketing to large audiences. Hadlow leads a team of more than 100 agents. One of her final posts before entering the Love Island villa showed her posing in a series of swimsuits alongside the caption: “Normalise working from anywhere.”Hadlow and Pattison did not respond to requests for comment.A spokesperson for InteleTravel said: “While it’s regrettable that certain individuals experience struggles trying to launch a travel career, there are thousands of successful award-winning advisers who have taken the time to use the vast array of resources provided by InteleTravel to build their career in a responsible and dedicated fashion.”Amanda Restivo, the vice-president of compliance at PlanNet Marketing, said: “PlanNet Marketing and InteleTravel are two completely separate companies … People are not required to enrol with both companies; they can choose to be only a rep with PlanNet Marketing or only a travel adviser with InteleTravel.”Restivo then added: “It takes hard work to make substantial income in this business. Success requires personal effort and dedication.”* Name has been changedExplore more on these topicsConsumer affairsTravel & leisureDigital mediaMarketing & PRSocial mediafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: OpenAI says its review into hacks, including on Australian government sites, is costing $500,000 a day | OpenAI | The Guardian
description: Company says it is reviewing 50 petabytes of data after its agents accessed websites including Medicare without authorisation
Author: Josh Taylor
Headline: Company says it is reviewing 50 petabytes of data after its agents accessed websites including Medicare without authorisation
Content: OpenAI has warned that its review may identify more organisations that have had websites accessed by its AI agents without authorisation.Photograph: Dado Ruvić/ReutersView image in fullscreenOpenAI has warned that its review may identify more organisations that have had websites accessed by its AI agents without authorisation.Photograph: Dado Ruvić/ReutersOpenAIOpenAI says its review into hacks, including on Australian government sites, is costing $500,000 a dayCompany says it is reviewing 50 petabytes of data after its agents accessed websites including Medicare without authorisationGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastJosh TaylorTechnology reporterSat 3 Oct 2026 01.39 EDTLast modified on Sat 3 Oct 2026 01.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOpenAI says its review in response to the Medicare and Hugging Face agent attacks is costing the company more than US$500,000 per day, as it deploys AI to examine data that would take a human 66m years to read.The company has warned the review is ongoing, and more organisations may be informed they’ve been targeted in the near future.OpenAI’s Medicare attack has exposed Australia’s ‘tech debt’. Fixing it could bring a big bill for taxpayersRead moreOn Friday evening,OpenAI revealedagents had hacked into a New South Wales government website in June and accessed historical non-public data on bushfires without authorisation.It is thesixth government website in Australiato be notified by the AI giant since last month of agent activity on their services, after the prime minister, Anthony Albanese,announced OpenAI’s agentshad hacked into Services Australia’s Medicare statistics portal.The reason for the delay compared to the revelation of the Medicare attack is due to the sheer volume of data OpenAI needs to review.In a blog postthis weekthe company revealed the large amount of work involved in reviewing its agents’ activity.OpenAI said it has to review 50 petabytes of data – roughly 50m gigabytes.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email“We’re working back through the records month by month, looking for potential unintended activity beyond the cases we’ve already found,” the company said.“To put that in perspective, if that were all plain English text, it would take one person about 66 million years to read it at 240 words a minute, reading nonstop without ever sleeping or taking a break.”The company is searching records for where models accessed and changed websites, or took actions involving passwords, application programming interface (API) access or other sensitive credentials.AI is being used to help sift through the records, and it was costing the company more than half a million US dollars per day to go through. OpenAI said it also plans to increase its computing power as the process is refined.As of late last month, more than 100 organisations had been notified of having being targeted by OpenAI’s agents, but the company said notifying an organisation does not mean private information was accessed or that their system was compromised.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionOpenAI said it expects to find more cases and notify more organisations about events that may have occurred months ago.Australia is run on legacy systems that AI agents can easily exploit, former UN cyber negotiator warnsRead moreOrganisations will be informed privately if they need to investigate and address potential security issues, and OpenAI has said it will publicly report findings about agent behaviour and identified weaknesses in safeguards for the broader AI sector.“We err on the side of notification when our models’ activity exposes a potential security vulnerability, even in cases where it is unclear if the information accessed was intended to be public, so the organization can investigate and take appropriate action,” OpenAI said.OpenAI discovered the latest NSW government website breach on Tuesday, and informed the state government and the Australian Signals Directorate after a 48-hour review.The Medicare breach has prompted the Australian government to require departments and agencies to undertakea stocktake of legacy technologyto reduce the number of ageing systems within government and reduce the cybersecurity risk they may present in the event of an AI agent attack.Executives from OpenAI, Anthropic, Microsoft and Google will front a joint parliamentary committee on artificial intelligence in Sydney on Tuesday.Explore more on these topicsOpenAIAI (artificial intelligence)Australian politicsMedicare AustralianewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Happy Christmas, Ange’: why we have always loved a dramatic TV divorce | Television | The Guardian
description: Untying the knot is having a television moment with the launch of the HBO legal thriller War and BBC’s The Split Up
Author: Michael Hogan
Headline: Untying the knot is having a television moment with the launch of the HBO legal thriller War and BBC’s The Split Up
Content: Leslie Grantham and Anita Dobson as Den and Angie Watts: 30.1m viewers saw him serve her with divorce papers on Christmas Day.Photograph: BBCView image in fullscreenLeslie Grantham and Anita Dobson as Den and Angie Watts: 30.1m viewers saw him serve her with divorce papers on Christmas Day.Photograph: BBCTelevision‘Happy Christmas, Ange’: why we have always loved a dramatic TV divorceUntying the knot is having a television moment with the launch of the HBO legal thriller War and BBC’s The Split UpMichael HoganSat 3 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 3 Oct 2026 07.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere were105,002 divorcesin England and Wales last year, according to the Office for National Statistics (ONS). Right now, it feels like there are almost as many on TV.The new HBOlegal thriller War, which launched on Sky Atlantic on Friday night, chronicles what it calls “the highest-profile divorce case in UK history”. This enjoyably juicy eight-parter is joined in the weekend schedules by the BBC ​dramaThe Split Up– a Manchester-based spin-off from Abi Morgan’s The Split – following a British Asian family law firm specialising in elite divorces.In broadcasting terms, untying the knot is definitely having a moment. With about four in 10 real-life marriages ending in divorce, it’s no wonder viewers can’t look away.War traces the cataclysmic break-up between a narcissistic Hollywood star, Carla Duval (played by Sienna Miller), and her philandering tech billionaire husband Morgan Henderson (Dominic West). Their split sparks a ruthless battle between two rival law firms as they fight for the considerable spoils.“If they play dirty,” says one bloodthirsty brief, “we will be totally and utterly filthy.” Cue honey traps and underhand tactics. The bitter fallout is all played out in the public eye as the celebrity couple come under intense media scrutiny. With its illicit office affairs and drug-fuelled toilet cubicle romps, TV lawyers haven’t been this sexy since This Life.The series is created by George Kay, whose previous credits include Lupin, Hijack and The Long Shadow. When Kay hit upon the premise of a high-stakes divorce, he realised this was a world ripe with dramatic potential. The prenups and property disputes reminded Kay of the glossy legal procedurals he grew up watching, such as Ally McBeal and LA Law. More recent reference points include Suits and The Good Wife.It might have the aspirational sheen and starry cast of a US prestige drama but War is set in London, widely acknowledged as the divorce capital of the world. English courts have a reputation for fairness, expertise and generosity to the financially weaker party. Foreign wives fight to have their claims heard in London. In turn, this has spawned an entire industry of specialist ​practices, forensic accountants and private investigators.Leading man West did his research by listening to theBBCpodcast Good Bad Billionaire and by picking the brains of rich divorcees. “I asked one wealthy guy how brutal it gets,” West told this week’s Radio Times. “He said, ‘It gets absolutely awful.’ I suppose the richer they are, the more appalling the divorce is.”His co-star Miller agrees that marriage becomes a “a commodity to be bartered with – and the more acrimonious, the more money for the lawyers”. Top divorce solicitors have a £1,200 hourly rate. Barristers can charge £10,000 a hearing. Costs soon add up. With an increasing number of long marriages ending in divorce, contested cases can become even more tangled.ONS data shows that couples who divorced in 2025 had been married for an average of 13 years, the longest since records began in 1963. Jess Knauf, the director of client strategy at the mediation service Mediate UK, said: “A 13-year marriage usually means a shared home, pensions and children. When couples separate later in life, there is simply more to sort out.”Writer Kay had plenty of real-life cases to go to for inspiration, from multibillion-pound claims against Russian oligarchs to tech moguls Bill Gates and Jeff Bezos’s record-breaking settlements. He lifted one memorable scene – in the opening episode, Carla is served with divorce papers on the red carpet at her movie premiere – directly from the headlines. In 2022, Olivia Wilde was served child custody papers from her ex-fiance the Ted Lasso star Jason Sudeikis while speaking on stage at a cinema convention, introducing her film Don’t Worry Darling.Full of double-crossing and delicious plot twists, War makes for addictive viewing. In fact, fictional divorces have long kept audiences entertained and enthralled. Here are just a few all-time favourites.Den and Angie Watts (EastEnders)“Happy Christmas, Ange!” On Christmas Day 1986, the Queen Vic landlord Dirty Den exacted revenge for his wife, Angie, faking terminal cancer by gifting her divorce papers. A mind-boggling 30.1 million tuned in, making it the most viewed British TV programme ever.Don and Betty Draper(Mad Men)They looked picture perfect but the marriage between adulterous ad exec Don (Jon Hamm) and icy blonde Betty (January Jones) was a messy one. They split during the third season, with Don angrily insisting that Betty “won’t get a nickel”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe GuideGet our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every FridayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBlake and Alexis Carrington (Dynasty)Much action in the 80s supersoap was driven by the feud between the oil magnate Blake (John Forsythe) and his scheming ex Alexis (Joan Collins in her shoulderpadded pomp). Her rivalry with his new wife, Krystle (Linda Evans), descended into camp catfights.Walter and Skyler White (Breaking Bad)When the terminally ill chemistry teacher Walt (Bryan Cranston) became a drug lord, his wife, Skyler (Anna Gunn), widely reviled for putting a damper on his activities, demanded a divorce in exchange for her silence.View image in fullscreenFrasier and Lilith Crane in Cheers.Photograph: Maximum Film/AlamyFrasier and Lilith Crane (Cheers/Frasier)The mismatched psychiatrists married, then split, on Cheers. It wasn’t until Kelsey Grammer’s spinoff that their divorce was confirmed. Even Eddie the dog was scared of formidable Lilith. Frasier’s brother, Niles, had his own nemesis ex, the much-feared but never seen Maris.Ken and Deirdre Barlow(Coronation Street)“Don’t make me walk out that door, Ken!” Somehow the cobbles stalwarts rode out the nation-gripping scandal of Deirdre’s steamy affair with Mike Baldwin. The final straw came when Ken slept with his secretary, Wendy Crozier. Ken and Deirdre remarried 15 years later.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionDivorceHBOBBCOffice for National StatisticsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: I craved a mean girl’s approval until My Little Pony broke the spell | Television | The Guardian
description: I didn’t realise my school infatuation was just making fun of me, but then an episode of the cartoon series taught me the attributes of true companionship
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: I didn’t realise my school infatuation was just making fun of me, but then an episode of the cartoon series taught me the attributes of true companionship
Content: ‘I lived for that cartoon. It had all the things I loved’ … My Little Pony: Friendship Is Magic.Illustration: Martin O'Neill/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘I lived for that cartoon. It had all the things I loved’ … My Little Pony: Friendship Is Magic.Illustration: Martin O'Neill/The GuardianMy cultural awakeningTelevisionI craved a mean girl’s approval until My Little Pony broke the spellI didn’t realise my school infatuation was just making fun of me, but then an episode of the cartoon series taught me the attributes of true companionshipFatimah MerchantSat 3 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen I was seven, I was obsessed with one particular classmate. She was the only girl taller than me and she never let me forget it. She was allowed to wear colourful nail polish and had shiny Lelli Kelly shoes, while I had short, plain nails and had to make do with classic black Clarks. I craved her approval.That spring she got an iPhone, and deliberately shunned me for a while afterwards. I cried for hours, but I wasn’t confused. I understood, and even respected it. Why would she grace me with her aura? I was lucky she let me sit at her table at all, even if it was only to taunt me for still bringing in a packed lunch. She was my best friend – I was always holding out hope that one day I would be hers.Growing up neurodivergent, I struggled to recognise when someone was making fun of me. I had sat through the same anti-bullying assemblies as everyone else, but I could not understand what that looked like in practice. So each day I would come home upset from school, kick off my stupid, ugly Clarks shoes, and tumble on to the sofa with my little sister to watch My Little Pony: Friendship Is Magic.I lived for that cartoon. It had all the things I loved: talking creatures, bright colours, catchy songs and a multitude of branded dolls, clothes and stationery that I begged my parents for. But what fascinated me most were the Elements of Harmony. Each of the “Mane Six” ponies represented an “Element” that made her a good friend: honesty, kindness, laughter, generosity, loyalty and magic.double quotation markI tried to assign her elements of a good friend: Honesty? No. Kindness? No. Loyalty? Definitely notI started assigning the Elements to my own friends, a little game I played in my head. One friend was definitely kindness. That one was honesty. My sister was so funny that she could only be laughter. I went through my friends one by one, trying to work out which quality best represented them.Then I got to her. I couldn’t think of one. I went through the list again. Honesty? No. Kindness? No. Generosity? Not really. Loyalty? Definitely not. Laughter? Not when she was the only one laughing.My favourite song was A True, True Friend from the season three finale. In the episode, Twilight Sparkle and her friends have their identities mixed up, and the ponies work together to help one another become themselves again. The song is essentially a celebration of showing up for your friends, unique as they are. They all have their specific traits, their own things they are good at. The true, true friend is someone who helps you find and access your own talents, without overshadowing you or making you feel bad for not having the same things they do.Eurovision made me realise that I was autistic at 34Read moreOne morning, in the car on the way to school, I started singing that song in my head. My inner voice grew louder as I walked towards the corner of the playground where the subject of my devotion was telling a story to her admirers, gesticulating wildly. As I looked at them, the chorus ricocheted around in my head.Then I simply turned around and walked away. I joined a girl I knew slightly who was reading a wildlife book alone on a bench. I asked her if she liked ponies.More than a decade later, I still feel guided by the Elements of Harmony. I love my friends for their quirks, the things that are just them. My best friend from sixth form is so clever she is like Twilight Sparkle in the flesh. My university roomie sends me weird reels and buys me takeaways when I’m skint. When I need brutal honesty, I know my sister will be more than eager to serve it to me.I even think about that girl from primary school. I worry about whether she was hurt when I walked away from her that day. We just weren’t right for each other. And that’s OK. Maybe her elements are different. But I have my people.Share your cultural awakeningsYou can tell us how a cultural moment has prompted you to make a major life change by filling in the form below or emailing us on cultural.awakening@theguardian.com.Please share your story if you are 18 or over, anonymously if you wish.
