title: ‘We swept a lot under the carpet’: Vichy regime film hits home in France of 2026 | France | The Guardian
description: Movie about Nazi-collaborating administration strikes chord during what director calls ‘time of great uncertainty’
Author: Angelique Chrisafis
Headline: Movie about Nazi-collaborating administration strikes chord during what director calls ‘time of great uncertainty’
Content: A still from Notre Salut, which is poised to become a box office hit.Photograph: Kidam & Michigan FilmsView image in fullscreenA still from Notre Salut, which is poised to become a box office hit.Photograph: Kidam & Michigan FilmsFrance‘We swept a lot under the carpet’: Vichy regime film hits home in France of 2026Movie about Nazi-collaborating administration strikes chord during what director calls ‘time of great uncertainty’Angelique Chrisafisin ParisSat 3 Oct 2026 00.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt is the story of how a lowly state administrator unthinkingly becomes a cog in the machine of an authoritarian regime, embracing the bureaucracy and logistics of sending people to their deaths – and it is drawing in audiences to French cinemas.The French filmNotre Salut(Our Salvation), with its modern lighting, improvised scenes and anachronistic 1980s Europop soundtrack, is far from the standard historical costume drama about the second world war.But the award-winning film about the daily lives of ordinary people participating in the puppet Vichy regime that collaborated with the Nazis – and ensured the deportation of a quarter of France’s Jewish population to concentration camps – is poised to become a box office hit.View image in fullscreenRounding up of Jewish people in Paris in May 1941.Photograph: LAPI/Roger Viollet/Getty ImagesThe film, which has been given the English-language title A Man of His Time, had a strong cinema opening in France this week, particularly among young audiences, at a time when the country is soul-searching ahead of next spring’s presidential election.Marine Le Penof the far-right, anti-immigration National Rally (RN) continues to top the polls for the presidential race despite the political fallout from an investigation byMediapartalleging that her party leader,Jordan Bardella, published antisemitic commentsas a young party member, which he denies.Notre Salut comes amid a boom in films about France during the second world war, including more than 5m ticket sales for the two-part biopic ofCharles de Gaulle, as well the controversialLes Rayons et les Ombresabout the press baron and Nazi collaborator Jean Luchaire, and the forthcomingMoulin, about the last days of the French resistance leader Jean Moulin.View image in fullscreenA scene from Notre Salut. The film was inspired by a stash of family letters found by director Emmanuel Marre that shed light on the life of his great-grandfather, a Vichy administrator.Photograph: TCD/Prod.DB/AlamyBut rather than tackling well-known heroes or monsters, Notre Salut focuses instead on the role of ordinary people in the Vichy regime that, underMarshal Philippe Pétain, collaborated in the deportation of 76,000 Jewish people to Nazi concentration camps.The film was inspired by a stash of family letters found by its writer and director, Emmanuel Marre, that gave insight into the life of his great-grandfather Henri Marre, who worked as an administrator under the authoritarian puppet regime.“There are great figures who make history, but history is also made by the second-players, the grassroots who act on the ground, and that is what is interesting about this film,” said Marc Olivier Baruch, a historian and specialist on state administrators in the Vichy regime.View image in fullscreenJewish deportees in the Drancy transit camp in France during the second world war.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesFor Baruch, the most chilling scene in the film is the bureaucratic nitpicking about the costs incurred by providing Jews on cattle trucks with straw and chamber pots. The central character in the film, the administrator Henri Marre, “never chooses to reflect on things or look at what he’s doing, to wonder what his room for manoeuvre is”.Baruch said the film’s sense of unease was a pull for modern of audiences because today France was “in atime of great uncertainty… There’s a strong lack of confidence among French people in their elites and in their state and that has been going on for a long time.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenA notice in a restaurant window banning Jews from entering, German-occupied Paris, July 1940.Photograph: Art Media/Print Collector/Getty ImagesHe said the Vichy regime had resonance today as a period in history. “The Pétain dictatorship is the only moment when the far right was in power since 1820. There were these four years at the heart of the 20th century when the far right was in power and clearly for French people in 2026 and 2027 that is interesting … There has been a certain unease in modern France that it would be better to stop talking about Vichy, to draw a line under it, stop the masochism [of looking back]. That of course is stupid, and not possible.”Film critics suggested modern audiences were seeking to better understand the rise of the far right acrossEuropeand in France.Henry Rousso, a historian who has studied the place of the Vichy regime in collective memory, wrote of the film inLe Monde: “The RN is not the fascism of the 1930s, nor a resurgence of the Pétain regime, but knowing this history allows an understanding of what [the RN] is the heir to, and how the mechanisms of gradually renouncing democratic and republican values led to disaster.”View image in fullscreenEmmanuel Marre won the screenplay prize for Notre Salut at the 2026 Cannes film festival.Photograph: SOPA Images Limited/AlamyEmmanuel Marre, the film’s writer-director, who won the best Screenplay prize at the Cannes film festival, began working on the story more than a decade ago after the discovery of the letters from his great-grandfather that his family had kept in a drawer.He told France Inter radio: “There are [similar] drawers everywhere in France … there is a phantom memory of the collaboration. With this film, we wanted to prise open those drawers and allow all families to look at that – not as flagellation, [but] because after the war France pushed a lot of it under the carpet to survive.”He said it was crucial to look at the nuance of what led people to collaborate or take a stand. “In between resistance and in collaboration, there is a whole range of human emotions, even the most ambiguous.”Explore more on these topicsFranceSecond world warEuropeAntisemitismWar filmsThe far rightnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Brave from the beginning’: 20 years of Friday Night Lights – the sports drama that dared to be different | Television | The Guardian
description: It launched the careers of Jesse Plemons and Michael B Jordan, and let its stars improvise in a way that was fresh and new. This show about smalltown US football was confident, trailblazing – and wonderful
Author: Michael Hann
Headline: It launched the careers of Jesse Plemons and Michael B Jordan, and let its stars improvise in a way that was fresh and new. This show about smalltown US football was confident, trailblazing – and wonderful
Content: Power couple … Kyle Chandler and Connie Britton in Friday Night Lights (2006).Photograph: Album/AlamyView image in fullscreenPower couple … Kyle Chandler and Connie Britton in Friday Night Lights (2006).Photograph: Album/AlamyTelevision‘Brave from the beginning’: 20 years of Friday Night Lights – the sports drama that dared to be differentIt launched the careers of Jesse Plemons and Michael B Jordan, and let its stars improvise in a way that was fresh and new. This show about smalltown US football was confident, trailblazing – and wonderfulMichael HannSat 3 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 3 Oct 2026 10.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleI’ve been around the south of the US enough to have seen the importance of football: little burgs where the high-school football field has stands that wouldn’t disgrace a League Two soccer club in the UK. Friday Night Lights, which was first broadcast 20 years ago, is set in the most fervent edges of that world, smalltown Texas, where what happens under the floodlights at the end of the working week defines the mood of the place for days to come.Britt Daniel, the frontman of the Texas band Spoon, grew up in one such town, Temple. “Friday Night Lights is based on Odessa, and Odessa and Temple are very, very similar,” he told me in 2017. “The high schools used to play each other at football, and they’re the kind of towns where everything happens on Friday because it’s the football game. I didn’t really think about it until many years later, but you really risked being beaten [up]. Not just harassed, but beaten. Everywhere you went, you really had to look over your shoulder. If you were at the mall, if you were at the parking lot, if you were at a party – people really wanted to fight.”That was the world into which the Pulitzer-winning reporter HG “Buzz” Bissinger inserted himself. In 1988, he moved to Odessa with his family to write a book about smalltown football. He expected something folksier than he ended up with, which was a portrait of young men being simultaneously revved up like boxers and told to be gentle like priests, all the while burdened with the expectations of their whole community and the pressure to win college scholarships.View image in fullscreenField of dreams … the Dillon Panthers in Friday Night Lights.Photograph: Bill Records/Nbc-Tv/Kobal/REX/ShutterstockIt was also a portrait of a town riven with racism, where football sucked precious resources from classroom budgets, and where evidence was everywhere that football was a broken dream, especially in the former golden boys, with their state championship rings, still hanging around Odessa rather than lighting up the NFL.The book came out in 1990 and was acclaimed everywhere except Odessa. In 1993, it inspired a TV series, Against the Grain, that lasted a single series, and propelled the young Ben Affleck nowhere. There was a 2004 movie that stuck more closely to the book, and was pretty good. And then there was the 2006 series – created by the director of the movie, Peter Berg – which used the book as a starting point for something wonderful: Friday Night Lights.double quotation markThey’re the kind of towns where everything happens on Friday night because it’s the football gameOdessa became Dillon, home of the Dillon Panthers. In came characters, some clearly based on their counterparts in the book, others entirely new. Out went some of Bissinger’s more troubling reporting, but the thrust of his discomfort with much of life in Odessa was reflected in Dillon.Friday Night Lights ended up being so good that it transcended difficulties, some of its own making, that might have killed it. Its second season was cut short by a writers’ strike, but was also hampered by melodramatic plotlines. After that second season, with ratings low despite critical acclaim, NBC planned to scrap the show before coming to a co-production deal that saw it air first on cable for the remaining three seasons. It was so good it was possible to forgive its fairytale elements – the show’s de facto hero, coach Eric Taylor (Kyle Chandler), moving to a school across town with no money and no football programme, and making them state champions inside two seasons.View image in fullscreenRising star … Michael B Jordan as Vince Howard, who appeared in the final two series of Friday Night Lights.Photograph: Album/AlamyEric and his wife Tami (Connie Britton, in the role of her lifetime – as was Chandler), a part-time counsellor who somehow becomes principal of Dillon High, are the moral heart of the show, he stern and hard but loyal and trusting, she softer and more empathetic but just as determined. They row, sometimes very badly; they struggle with bringing up their deeply irritating teenage daughter; they live with the insecurity that comes with being a coach at a school with high expectations, and the constant attention and demands it brings.The show was brave from the beginning. The pilot episode introduced us to the square-jawed leader, the quarterback Jason Street, and his sparkly toothed cheerleader girlfriend Lyla Garrity, our leading man and lady, surely. By the end of the episode, his back was broken. No more football, all hopes and dreams and expectations gone.View image in fullscreenYoung love … Jesse Plemons (left) and Adrianne Palicki in season two of Friday Night Lights.Photograph: NBC/Getty ImagesThe breakout star of the show was supposed to be Taylor Kitsch, playing brooding, handsome, drunken, violent, womanising Tim Riggins, in the vein of James Dean at his most sullen, so puppyish you could forgive him anything, even if Coach couldn’t. He’s the one who went straight to starring roles, but the real winner was the potato-ish actor playing an initially incidental character called Landry Clarke, who grew more central as the series progressed: that wasJesse Plemons, perfect as a teenager who’s clever but knows that is rarely an advantage and often a disadvantage in this world, especially when paired with a lack of the only thing that is respected: physical prowess. (Landry’s hapless and hopeless alt-rock band is just the perfect thing for his character.)A more likely star emerged inMichael B Jordan, making the transition from child soap player to dramatic actor as the quarterback Vince Howard in the final two series (his flirtation with Jurnee Smollett’s Jess Merriweather is one of the show’s most touching relationships).Berg encouraged his cast to improvise, had scenes filmed with handheld cameras and did away with “blocking” – the discipline of telling actors exactly where to move throughout a scene. As long as story beats were met, they could adapt dialogue and reactions. It gave the show a naturalism that felt new and fresh in a network drama: when characters paused to think of a reply, they were actually thinking, not just pausing.View image in fullscreenFresh-faced … Ben Affleck (left) in Against the Grain, a 1993 TV adaptation of the book that inspired Friday Night Lights.Photograph: Everett Collection Inc/AlamyThe female characters had lives of their own and weren’t simply adjuncts to the football (Britton had played coach Billy Bob Thornton’s wife in the movie, and had not been willing to return only to reprise looking pretty in the corner). Admittedly, except for quarterback Matt Saracen’s dementia-ridden grandma, they were all stunningly beautiful, but then so were pretty much all the men. Berg’s camera, though, had a covetous eye for its young cast, male and female alike: it’s hard not to look great through a filter against a Texas sunset, as Kitsch was so often shown, often muttering, “Texas f’rever.”Friday Night Lights didn’t overstay its welcome: 76 episodes over five seasons. At times it creaked, but its humanity always tethered it, and its sense of place was constant. If Buffy the Vampire Slayer’s Sunnydale was hilarious because it would just invent locations – here are some docks! Here’s an airport! – Dillon was the opposite. It had nothing. Fast food, a bar, a car dealership, and the open range. All it had was football, and the Friday night lights. Just like Odessa and Temple, towns where anything could go wrong.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionJesse PlemonsMichael B JordanConnie BrittonfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Get Jiro: Anthony Bourdain’s ultraviolent sushi chef makes for wild, pulpy television | Television | The Guardian
description: A love of food and a taste for bloodthirsty action collide as a very angry chef gets caught up in a brutal turf war between warring restaurants in LA
Author: Rhik Samadder
Headline: A love of food and a taste for bloodthirsty action collide as a very angry chef gets caught up in a brutal turf war between warring restaurants in LA
Content: Virtual reality … sushi chef Jiro voiced by Brian Tee in Get Jiro.Photograph: HBO MaxView image in fullscreenVirtual reality … sushi chef Jiro voiced by Brian Tee in Get Jiro.Photograph: HBO MaxThe watcherTelevisionGet Jiro: Anthony Bourdain’s ultraviolent sushi chef makes for wild, pulpy televisionA love of food and a taste for bloodthirsty action collide as a very angry chef gets caught up in a brutal turf war between warring restaurants in LARhik SamadderSat 3 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHas foodie culture gone too far? It’s a truism that to get to a lasagne recipe now, you have to wade through an essay about someone’s childhood in Tuscany. We talk about food sentimentally, consume TV about it fetishistically, slavering over slow-motion shots of chopped pepper falling on to stainless steel. We enjoy judging the food of others. We talk about the provenance of our ingredients with a kind of purity fixation. It strikes me that there’s a totalitarianism to it.So it was bracing to watch Get Jiro (from Sunday 4 October, HBO Max), an adult animation that pairs a love of food with a taste for ultraviolence. It’s the story of a sushi chef, caught up in a bloodthirsty turf war between warring restaurants. It is set in a dystopian near-future Los Angeles, in which all human desires “including companionship, travel and sex, can be experienced … virtually”. (The episodes I’ve seen don’t go into this, explaining for example how chiropody could be experienced virtually, but that’s beside the point.)Food is the holdout: a sensual pleasure the digital world cannot colonise. As a result, master chefs have gained great power – operating like crime lords, while people kill for reservations at their restaurants. Having spent four years failing to get a table at the Sportsman for the slip sole with seaweed butter, I get it.Jiro himself is a taciturn, exacting sushi chef and biker, who knows how to use a knife and is no innocent bystander. In the first scene, he decapitates a customer for the crime of dipping his fish in soy sauce. Elsewhere, the violence is cartoonish yet gory. There is cheese-grater violence, custard violence, creme brulee blowtorch violence. Bones are snapped off, faces deep-fried. There are bloodthirsty, militant vegans. “It’s one thing to take out a few low-level busboys. But Monty was a made chef,” growls one proprietor.It’s not for the squeamish, clearly. But the hardness with which Get Jiro leans into its satire is part of the fun. One of the characters trying to get Jiro is Cynda, a detective with the City of Angels Health Department. CAHD pack heat, drive armoured squad cars, and work out of a Fritz Lang skyscraper emblazoned with their initials. They have beef with the Alcohol, Firearms and Food agency, or AFF. Both desks have real power in a town where control of food supply lines is crucial, and hospitality staff headhunting takes on new meaning. The streets here run redder than a rib-eye.It’s an inherently funny idea, that the refined language of restaurant criticism could hit the streets like this. “You gotta try these anchovy toasts! They make them with Calabrian chilli butter,” drools one law-enforcement meathead, pronouncing it “calla-bryan” and “budda”. “Unless you want some chilli butter up your ass, get to work,” shoots back Cynda. That’s a spicy workplace threat. I guess when the robots came, HR were the first to leave the CAHD building.In classic comic-book style, men are barrel-chested, jaws squared off like anvils. Women are coke bottles. Subtlety is not the dish of the day; except presumably for the texture of Jiro’s nigiri, over which every diner has a Proustian meltdown. Tenderness is reserved for the food scenes, disquisitions on pot-au-feu, spaghetti con la bottarga, katsu sando. I ate Haribo through most of it, and hated myself.Get Jiro is camp and in on the joke, tongue firmly in its pig cheek. It is produced by and based on a graphic novel co-written by Joel Rose and, ah! –Anthony Bourdain. A man whostirred machismowith empathy, and was as interested in people as the primal energy of kitchens. His influence shows: beneath the pulpy twists and action hits, politics simmers. The story is an indictment of how food becomes class currency, and can be wielded as a weapon.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toWhat's OnGet the best TV reviews, news and features in your inbox every MondayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionOne can’t help but think of a meditative 2011 documentary, and wonder if there’s a connection.Jiro Dreams of Sushi?Jiro Dreams of Slicing Clean Through Your C-5 Vertebra, more like. But this is its own, provocative concoction – a dash of Sweeney Todd, a tablespoon of Batman: Caped Crusader, and a quarter cup of Grand Theft Auto. You thought Seinfeld’s Soup Nazi had high standards? You ain’t seen nothing.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionThe watcherAnthony BourdainfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘My hips can’t help but move’: readers on the songs that always get them dancing | Music | The Guardian
description: From Northern soul and 90s bangers to disco classics and indie anthems, readers share the floorfillers that never fail to start the party
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: From Northern soul and 90s bangers to disco classics and indie anthems, readers share the floorfillers that never fail to start the party
Content: Wedding crashers … Scissor Sisters on stage at  Wilderness Festival, Oxfordshire, 1 August 2026.Photograph: Jim Dyson/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenWedding crashers … Scissor Sisters on stage at  Wilderness Festival, Oxfordshire, 1 August 2026.Photograph: Jim Dyson/Getty ImagesMusic‘My hips can’t help but move’: readers on the songs that always get them dancingFrom Northern soul and 90s bangers to disco classics and indie anthems, readers share the floorfillers that never fail to start the partySat 3 Oct 2026 00.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleI Don’t Feel Like Dancin’ – Scissor SistersMy now-husband and I attended a wedding. The reception was boring. No one was dancing and people were wondering if it was too early to leave. We sat at our table thinking what song would get everyone up on to the dancefloor. We chose I Don’t Feel Like Dancin’. When I asked the DJ to play it he laughed and said: “That’s appropriate.” We danced by ourselves and people started joining us. The party kicked off and we all had a great time. Years later, we played the song at our own wedding. It makes me happy.Rachael,46,WarringtonCelebrity Skin – HoleI used to go to rock clubs in the early 2000s and this was the only song they’d play with a female vocalist. Me and my friend danced like maniacs, forcing the guys off the dancefloor.Heather, LondonReturn of the Mack – Mark MorrisonIt’s a guilty pleasure for sure, but Return of the Mack always gets me out there. It has been a favourite of mine and my twin brother’s since we first heard it. The melody transcends the cheese and lyrics to make it a booty bopper I can’t resist. The last time my brother and I were back home at a very stodgy bar, this surprisingly came on and we immediately transformed the bar into our dancefloor. Some others actually followed. Music truly does transcend all.Dave, 56, Portland,USI Bet You Look Good on the Dancefloor – Arctic MonkeysIt’s a song that I’ve grown up with and was a staple at the nightclub Welly in Hull that I used to go to when I was in sixth form and university. It was the first song I put down when my wife and I were choosing our wedding evening playlist. It’s timeless.Chris Brough,31,YorkTemptation – New OrderAn extremely danceable classic from an iconic band, which is guaranteed to get everybody up and moving.Calle Jershed, 55,Gothenburg, SwedenRock Lobster – The B-52sView image in fullscreenHere comes a stingray … The B-52s: Fred Schneider, Kate Pierson, Ricky Wilson, Keith Strickland and Cindy Wilson.Photograph: Lynn Goldsmith/Corbis/VCG/Getty ImagesThis is the one that always gets me up, wherever I am. It’s like I was hypnotised way back when I first heard it – I always immediately spring up from my seat when it’s on.Julie Gibson,61,NorthamptonshireI Believe in Miracles – The Jackson SistersIt’s soulful, funky and utterly hypnotic – the song grabs me instantly.Bernd Wagner,Mainz, GermanyGroove Is in the Heart – Deee-LiteIt is still sensational, and so inventive. It pops and crackles along at a rollicking pace, Lady Miss Kier’s vocals give way to insane drum breaks, and it never grows old. It’s funky as hell and just wonderful.Alex,52,SouthamptonLast Dance – Donna SummerWhen I was a college student in the 70s, I loved going to discos. This is such a joyful song. To this day, when I hear it I cannot sit still.Terry Heimbaugh, 70,Illinois,USSex & Drugs & Rock & Roll – Ian DuryOpening with an ambitious drum roll, it moves instantly into a killer riff. This song combines whimsical lyrics with tightly executed funk that’s an absolute joy to dance to.Kate, East CambridgeshireBlinding Lights – The WeekndView image in fullscreenGorgeous … The Weeknd live in Atlanta, 21 August 2025.Photograph: Prince Williams/WireImageMy taste is eclectic, but rarely includes songs that chart. This is a gorgeous exception. The composition is so simple but it’s combined into something so full and rich. Immediately I’m dancing.Jack, 32,BristolMan 2 Man Meets Man Parrish – Male StripperThis song will always get me on the dancefloor. It’s so catchy and the opening few bars are so distinctive that it puts a massive smile on my face.Tim,60,PrestwickButter – BTSButter has a great beat and has also helped me introduce more people to the world of K-pop. It holds great memories for me, of connecting to other people when I was feeling low. This song just has a way of bringing people together, no matter what genre they like.Gwen, Sydney, AustraliaRocks – Primal ScreamYes, it’s a Rolling Stones rip-off but it is pure adrenaline and rock’n’roll euphoria.Dave Ross,GlasgowCalifornia Love – 2Pac ftDr DreView image in fullscreen‘Shake it, shake it, baby’ … Tupac Shakur live in Chicago, March 1994.Photograph: Raymond Boyd/Getty ImagesAs soon as I hear those first few notes, my hips can’t help but move. 2Pac’s “shake it, shake it, baby” is a command I cannot deny. Something about this song reminds me of being 18, hitting the dancefloor and being carefree.Rachael, 39,Sydney, AustraliaDo I Love You (Indeed I Do) – Frank WilsonI have always loved Northern soul and Do I Love You (Indeed I Do) is the song which always gets me dancing. I will often request it at wedding functions. It brings back memories of a bygone age, growing up in a deprived area where music was a way of gathering together at the local youth club.Julie, 68, ShropshireBrimfulof Asha – CornershopWhen I hear it, I absolutely can’t stay still, no matter how knackered I am. And I can listen to it time after time and not get sick of it.Barbara Manighetti, 65,Wellington, New ZealandMoveon Up – Curtis MayfieldIt’s the greatest song ever written in my opinion – it has just four main chords, but it’s so uplifting.Michael, 43, Madrid, SpainJump Around – House of PainThe distinctive horn at the beginning is like a calling, and then the hip-hop beat starts, and you’re already a goner within the first few seconds. There’s something about the track: not only do you jump, but you also want to shout out the chorus on the dancefloor. It’s a 90s banger with attitude.Sofia Ilyas, 45,LondonIce Ice Baby – Vanilla IceI remember my two sisters and I dancing to this song when it played on MTV back in the 90s. We would jump around the living room. I still listen to it now, dancing around the house with my dogs watching curiously. It triggers a happiness switch in my mind.Lara, 39,Bengaluru, IndiaLet Me Be Your Fantasy – Baby DI only have to hear the whisper of “Let me be your fantasy” at the beginning and I’ll be on the floor dragging anyone in my path. This track is such a mood booster.Debbie, 51,LondonMr Brightside – The KillersIt was once played at a friend’s wedding – I maniacally jumped up and down on the dancefloor and the bride audibly guffawed.Neil Vicker, 63, NewburyPeople featured in the article responded to a Communitycallout. You can contributehere.Explore more on these topicsMusicPop and rockPlaylistsDance musicIndiefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘I thought, if I’m going to die, I’m going to write a book first’: Pachinko author Min Jin Lee | Fiction | The Guardian
description: Her last novel sold 5m copies and was adapted into a hit series. Nearly 10 years on, the Korean-American author has written another epic. She discusses ambition and the diagnosis that inspired her to leave work and write
Author: Lisa Allardice
Headline: Her last novel sold 5m copies and was adapted into a hit series. Nearly 10 years on, the Korean-American author has written another epic. She discusses ambition and the diagnosis that inspired her to leave work and write
Content: Min Jin Lee, author of Pachinko photographed in New YorkPhotograph: Benedict Evans/The GuardianView image in fullscreenMin Jin Lee, author of Pachinko photographed in New YorkPhotograph: Benedict Evans/The GuardianFictionInterview‘I thought, if I’m going to die, I’m going to write a book first’: Pachinko author Min Jin LeeLisa AllardiceHer last novel sold 5m copies and was adapted into a hit series. Nearly 10 years on, the Korean-American author has written another epic. She discusses ambition and the diagnosis that inspired her to leave work and writeSat 3 Oct 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBack in 1995, when she was in her mid-20s, Min Jin Lee quit her job as a corporate lawyer. As a teenager she had been diagnosed as a hepatitis B carrier and doctors told her she was highly likely to develop liver cancer in her 20s or 30s. “I thought, if I’m going to die, I’m going to write a book first,” the now 57-year-old Korean-American author says of her decision to turn her back on a regular pay cheque and healthcare. “I was told so many times that I was going to get sicker and sicker, that I’ve always felt that if I can get a really good book out then I’m done.”Lee, looking very much alive and well, is on a video call from her home in Harlem, New York, floor-to-ceiling bookshelves behind her. We are meeting to discuss the publication of her third novel, American Hagwon, the final part in what she calls her “Korean trilogy”, following Free Food for Millionaires in 2007 and her 2017 international bestseller,Pachinko, stylishlyadapted for Apple TVin 2022. “Korean quartet!” she corrects me now. Thanks to experimental drugs, she is now so healthy she can commit to another book. “Before I turn 70, I should turn in my manuscript,” she jokes. “I’m writing the four books that I wanted to write and after that I’m going to take a long nap.”Lee averages a book a decade. It took 11 years of writing before Free Food for Millionaires, about the children of Korean immigrants in New York in the 90s, was published. She worked on Pachinko, which spans nearly a century, and ranges from a fishing village in Japanese-occupied Korea to Wall Street in the 1980s, for 20 years. It was voted one of the New York Times 100 best books of the century and has sold more than 5m globally. American Hagwon, which follows one family from Seoul to Sydney to California in the years leading up to and after the Asian financial crisis of 1997, was bought in a 12-way publishing auction. She has recently returned from Germany on a research trip for her next book, her “European novel”, which already has a title: Marshall Plan. Its starting point is the 1963 bilateral agreement when thousands of Koreans were sent to West Germany to work as miners or nurses to boost the economy back home. The only thing all four novels have in common is the Korean diaspora.View image in fullscreenSungkyu Kim, Eunchae Jung and Minha Kim in Pachinko.Photograph: Apple TV“I’ve had to have lessons to do this, to talk to you,” Lee confesses, smiling into the screen. A once desperately shy and poor girl from Seoul, she is both modest about her success – “I’m used to feeling unwanted” – and proud that she has pulled it off. “Wow, I have done this. I have fucking done this. I would love to know how many Asian American women have been published in the New York Review of Books,” Lee told the Believer Magazine. Her NYRB essay was an indepth appraisal of the work of fellow novelist Han Kang, who became the first Korean Nobel prize for literature laureate in 2024. While Lee’s sprawling multi­generational epics couldn’t be more different from Han’s slim, poetic novels, they both tackle periods of their country’s troubled history that the world has chosen to forget. Ironically, they have come to prominence on the crest of hallyu, the Korean Wave, the government-sponsoredcultural pushthat has given the west K-pop bands and Squid Game.double quotation mark‘I would love to write a short novel, but I don’t know how with these subjects’Each weighing in at more than 500 pages, Lee’s novels take up as much space on a bookshelf as the life’s work of other writers. “I would love to write a short novel, but I don’t know how with these subjects,” she says. “I always think: ‘God, pick something easier. What is the matter with you? How about two people having feelings at a kitchen table?’”As big-hearted as they are physically hefty, her books have the immersive narrative drive, social conscience and moral purpose of the Victorian classics, on which she trained herself as a writer. “Almost all the people that I admire the most in terms of writers are old dead British writers,” she says. “Austen and Eliot, they have enormous hearts, they’re so romantic in terms of what they think human beings can be.”If her first two novels dealt with assimilation and colonisation, respectively, American Hagwon takes on one of the most important things to Koreans around the world: education. “Hagwon” is the term for private cram schools that are ubiquitous inSouth Korea. “If there was one word that I wanted you to know, that it’s so important for you to understand any Korean person you’ll ever meet, it’s ‘hagwon’,” Lee says. “In Korea that word is almost like the word water.” Some publishers were uneasy with Pachinko as a title, because it was unfamiliar to western readers. But this noisy pinball machine found in pachinko parlours across Korea was the perfect metaphor for the unpredictability of success, especially when the odds are stacked against you, as they were for the Korean-Japanese immigrants.In American Hagwon, John and Helen Koh are forced to uproot their family after a business betrayal: John swaps a well-paid job in insurance to manage a nail bar in LA, and their three children – Bo, DH and Mido – have to learn harder lessons than those taught in any classroom. More than 600 pages devoted to studying, tutoring and the establishment of a hagwon business, a concept unfamiliar to most readers outside Korea, might be a tough sell. But American Hagwon is about much more than swotting for exams. Lee wants to show the true cost of the overachieving Asian stereotype, the sacrifices of the “tiger mom” and the inequities of the elite education system. “How do you live a wise life?” the novel asks. It is a story of “power and ambition and getting to your goals”, she says. “In America, we really worship work but we also really worship success. We don’t always worship how people get there. In Korea, people really do examine how you get there.”She likes to set out her thesis in the opening line of each of her novels: “Competence can be a curse” in Free Food for Millionaires; “History has failed us, but no matter” in Pachinko. “The rules of engagement have changed already,” she declares at the start of American Hagwon. “There was a time when we felt we could sort of predict things,” she says now. “But right now most people are feeling: ‘I have no idea what just happened, no idea what will happen. I don’t know how to raise my children or plan my career because shit just keeps happening. And the people who are changing the rules aren’t sending us memos.’ I think that is where advanced economies are right now. Of course,” she adds, “people who are not from advanced economies have always felt this way.”View image in fullscreenLee in New York.Photograph: The GuardianAll her novels take the Asian immigrant experience from the margins to the mainstream. “In my pages, I want to be the centre,” as she puts it. But she is also reflecting our global contemporary predicament. Diaspora “is a permanent condition for every single person in the world,” she says. “Now we have economic diaspora and we also have environmental diaspora. The people that I focus on are obviously Koreans, but what I’m really writing about is when you have to leave because you’re no longer useful or you’re no longer wanted, what do you do? You have to adapt.”Lee’s own story has the epic sweep of her novels. Her father was a war refugee who fled North Korea when he was 16, never to see his family again. He met her mother, a piano teacher, in Seoul. The family moved to the US when Min was seven, where they lived in an apartment in Elmhurst, Queens. The middle of three sisters, she remembers it as an “ugly little hovel”, with mice and bugs. Her father bought a newsstand, where the young Min would sit on the weekends. After a year, they bought a wholesale jewellers, not much bigger than the newspaper kiosk, selling costume jewellery to street pedlars. Both her parents worked in the shop six days a week. Her father is now 91, her mother 86, and she visits them in New Jersey after church each Sunday.“I didn’t have any friends and I really couldn’t get on,” she says of her own school days. Things improved when she got into Bronx High School of Science (also attended by NYC mayor Zohran Mamdani). But she felt out of her depth once again at Yale, where “there were so few Asians and everybody was so much wealthier”. Her two years as a lawyer, condensing boxes of documents into 20-page memos, proved a perfect training for a novelist intent on taking on huge hunks of Korean history. She married her husband, Christopher Duffy, who is half Japanese and half European, when she was 24, and their son was born when she was 29. “I really did think I was going to die,” she says. “I thought I had to get everything done.”Walking home from the subway one day after reading VS Naipaul’sA House for Mr Biswas, she realised that here was her subject. “I had to write about the disgraced, the poor and the earnest strivers of Queens,” she wrote in an essay in the New York Times. She took classes at Harvard Business School and a whole semester in millinery at a fashion college as research for Free Food for Millionaires.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIn 2007, the year it was finally published, Duffy was relocated to Tokyo. The seed for Pachinko had been sown 20 years earlier at Yale, when she attended a lecture by a visiting Japanese missionary about a Korean immigrant boy in Japan who killed himself because he was bullied. She had a draft of a novel, entitled Motherland, but it was too “dry” and “angry”. Living in Tokyo and talking to hundreds of Korean immigrants – street sellers, security guards, Uber drivers – Pachniko came to life. “Literary fiction must incorporate those stories,” she says. “Writing about work is something that social novelists must do.”double quotation mark'Humans have a kind of buoyancy – because we adapt and we have humour'It is no surprise that these epic novels about ordinary people at the mercy of cataclysmic social and economic changes have struck a chord right now. “The thing that I’ve always been able to do is to listen. And I’m willing to listen if someone will tell me how difficult their lives are,” she says. But she also wants to capture the resilience and joy of the people she speaks to. “There’s a wish for more love and recognition that regular human beings have and also a kind of buoyancy,” she says. “You read the dismal horrible stuff, but then we still have sex and have children. How do I connect that? The way I see it is because we adapt and we have humour.”She has no truck with the vogue for autofiction – “It’s for a certain reader. I’m probably not her” – which she feels has no place for the people she writes about. Having been on judging panels for many book prizes in the US, she has come to the conclusion that she doesn’t fit in with other contemporary writers. “My peers are writing wonderful, incredibly moving things, but I don’t know how to write like that.”She survived her wilderness years by following American author Grace Paley’s advice to writers to “keep a low overhead”, and also by having “a low overhead for expectations of recognition”. Today, she still leads a very quiet life. “I’m not a cool literary It person,” she says. “But I get to do what I want to do.” Her working day begins by reading and making notes on a chapter of the Bible, which Willa Cather used to do before writing. She diagrams everything – character outlines, plot – and looks for gaps. When she has a first draft she is happy with, she throws it away. Her manuscripts push 200,000 words. “I’ll just start all over,” she says, breezily. “It’s so much cleaner when you do it that way.”It is only since the success of the Pachinko TV series (on which she is remaining tight-lipped, after withdrawing as an executive producer) that she feels part of the publishing scene. “It’s like I’m visiting. I feel like, they’re letting me come and I’ll behave myself and I’ll be on time, but if I’m not asked again, I will just be grateful for the opportunity.” But there is nothing modest about her literary ambitions. “I want to build a palace,” she says of her novels. “I want to build a palace that stands.”In return for the commitment of their time, she wants the reader to feel changed by the experience, just as she has been by reading 19th-century novels. “I probably feel more British than anything because I’ve read so much British literature, over and over again,” she says. “That is what I am trying to do, in some ways. I’m trying to make you Korean.”American Hagwon by Min Jin Lee is published by 4th Estate. To support the Guardian, order your copy atguardianbookshop.com. title: Deepfake review – ingenious interview with a PM who dances around every issue | Dance | The Guardian
description: An interrogater tries to get to the bottom of a surreal scandal while green screen actors meddle with the story in Jess and Morgs’ inventive production
Author: Sanjoy Roy
Headline: An interrogater tries to get to the bottom of a surreal scandal while green screen actors meddle with the story in Jess and Morgs’ inventive production
Content: Unravelling … Kennedy Muntanga as the prime minister with dancers Cathy Grealish, Dylan Springer and Tommi Sutton in Deepfake at Sadler’s Wells East, London.Photograph: Foteini ChristofilopoulouView image in fullscreenUnravelling … Kennedy Muntanga as the prime minister with dancers Cathy Grealish, Dylan Springer and Tommi Sutton in Deepfake at Sadler’s Wells East, London.Photograph: Foteini ChristofilopoulouDanceReviewDeepfake review – ingenious interview with a PM who dances around every issueSadler’s Wells East, LondonAn interrogater tries to get to the bottom of a surreal scandal while green screen actors meddle with the story in Jess and Morgs’ inventive productionSanjoy RoySat 3 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhat audiences remember most from a political interview, a voiceover tells the prime minister (Kennedy Muntanga) as he prepares to face his TV interrogator (Rebecca Bassett-Graham, coiffed à la Emily Maitlis), is less the words themselves than the tone of voice and the tenor of the body. Muntanga is on point, then: his arms sweep, his fingers beetle and his hands spread out, as if he were wordlessly fielding fly-by questions and offering open statements. It’s the moves and the staging that count.This setup lands right in the zone for creative duoJess and Morgs(Jessica Wright and Morgann Runacre-Temple), whose turf is a congenial mix of choreography, film and theatre. In Deepfake, along with writerJeff James, they explore the various unravellings of an encounter in which the interviewer tries to find the truth behind a surreal – but maybe real? – story in which the PM was seen variously spattered with yellow paint, with his flies undone, and partaking in a ritual involving a deer’s head.View image in fullscreenEmily Maitlis-alike … Rebecca Bassett-Graham in Deepfake.Photograph: Foteini ChristofilopoulouThe content of these scenarios perhaps matters less than the ingenious manner of their staging (props to the design team too), which deploys green screen, live relay and other film and stage effects to storify the interview with simulated settings, duplicates of the figure of the PM, selective perspectives and closeups of the central encounter. Spidering about the main characters and manipulating the sets are a team of seven dancers in green body stockings, anonymously blending into the background but integral to the whole media matrix.‘This gap opens up of doubt and scepticism about everything’: Jess and Morgs confront the politics of deepfakesRead moreInitially the tone is paranoid and conspiratorial, the dancers syncing to voiceovers that then start to glitch (a signature device ofworks by Crystal Pite and Jonathon Young). There are ambiguous, unvoiced duets which intimate, intriguingly, that interviewer and interviewee may not only be playing the same game of moves and countermoves, but might sometimes even be on the same side. Later, the piece starts shifting gears, swerving through farce, parody (there’s some delightful and very unexpected play with 19th-century ballet), absurdism, and ultimately a kind of comic bathos, equally unexpected.It’s inventive, clever, exactly executed and quite a lot of fun, but the tone is also scattershot, and the piece ends up feeling more lightweight than its deepfake premise had promised – as if it wasn’t quite convinced by its own story.AtSadler’s Wells East, London, until 3 OctoberExplore more on these topicsDanceTheatreSadler's WellsreviewsShareReuse this content
