title: The Guide #263: How Claudia Winkleman ​became TV’s ​perfect ‘bad’ gameshow host | Culture | The Guardian
description: In this week’s newsletter: As The Celebrity Traitors returns, Winkleman once again proves herself the show’s secret weapon​, becoming heir to a distinctly British TV tradition
Author: Gwilym Mumford
Headline: In this week’s newsletter: As The Celebrity Traitors returns, Winkleman once again proves herself the show’s secret weapon​, becoming heir to a distinctly British TV tradition
Content: Stern-faced and slightly sadistic … Claudia Winkleman on The Celebrity Traitors.Photograph: BBC/Studio Lambert/Euan Cherry/PAView image in fullscreenStern-faced and slightly sadistic … Claudia Winkleman on The Celebrity Traitors.Photograph: BBC/Studio Lambert/Euan Cherry/PAThe Guide newsletterCultureThe Guide #263: How Claudia Winkleman ​became TV’s ​perfect ‘bad’ gameshow hostIn this week’s newsletter: As The Celebrity Traitors returns, Winkleman once again proves herself the show’s secret weapon​, becoming heir to a distinctly British TV traditionDon’t get The Guide delivered to your inbox? Sign up hereGwilym MumfordSat 3 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 3 Oct 2026 02.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Celebrity Traitors has returned and, as ever, its pleasures are manifold: the coming together of very different types of famous people (what other show gives you the chance to see mathematician Hannah Fry chatting with Jerry Hall); the now obligatory series-upending first-episode twist; Richard E Grant careering around trying to break the game; Ross Kemp, eyes wide with terror, convinced that anyone who touches him, talks to him or blows on him is his killer.There’s so much to enjoy in fact, that you almost overlook the heavy-fringed host at the show’s centre. By this pointClaudia Winklemanfeels undeniably core to the series, in both its Celebrity and civilian guises – as much a part of the furniture as that mustard armchair where faithfuls learn that they have been murdered. So much so, in fact, that it feels jarring – just plainwrong– when you watch one of the international variants of the Traitors and see someone else attempting to play the part of the pantomimish master or mistress of ceremonies; Alan Cumming, Siobhan McSweeney, or any of the other non-Claudias. They all make a decent fist of it, but none of them manage it quite like her.It was a bit of a punt to cast Winkleman in the role, really. She was certainly famous and likable enough, but daffy too: you probably wouldn’t have envisioned her as the Traitors’ stern-faced, slightly sadistic host– goth-tinged haircut aside. She actually turned the role down originally, not willing to trudge up to the Highlands for filming while her daughter was doing GCSEs, and only relented after binging the original Dutch version of the show, De Verraders. But once installed she made the role her own. She does a lot with not that much screen time: for large chunks of the show she’s not present at all, but when she does rock up, she’s able to shift the entire mood. Faithfuls and Traitors alike fall into terrified silence when she enters.In her Traitors role, Winkleman is continuing a peculiar TV tradition: that of the ‘bad’ gameshow host. Usually the role of the host is a supportive one, encouraging contestants when they’re weighing up a key question, consoling them when they inevitably get it wrong. Think of Alexander Armstrong doing his crumpled “there there” face as someone spectacularly botches the final round of Pointless. The ‘bad’ gameshow host upends all that, transforming the role from confidant to tormentor.View image in fullscreenPitiless … Anne Robinson on the Weakest Link.Photograph: BBC Picture PublicityIt’s a role that has existed in some form for decades – Des O’Connor definitely had a bit of the devil in him on Take Your Pick. But it came into its own in the 90s and 00s with the twin terrors of Jeremy Paxman, on University Challenge, and Anne Robinson (pictured above), on the Weakest Link, two pitiless interrogators (it’s not coincidental that both were once journalists, as was Winkleman) with the power to turn contestants to jelly with just a stern look. If Paxman’s role as ‘bad’ host was largely the product of him being a bit of a grump (in a way that his avuncular predecessor Bamber Gascoigne never was), Robinson’s performance was baked into the show from its outset and proved a sensation. People would tune in primarily to see her eviscerate members of the public (andfuture Guardian employees), her catchphrase was repeated in offices and school playgrounds across the country, and the show’s success (moving from daytime to primetime) would see Robinson afforded a chance to crack America – though they didn’t quite appreciate her schoolmistress shtick in the same way.There’s definitely a hint of the Robinson in Winkleman’s Traitors performance, but the show lets her take the role of the ‘bad’ host to a new level. Where Paxman and Robinson were merely savaging contestants for incorrect answers, Winkleman is actively meddling with the mechanics of the game itself, introducing nefarious twists and tweaks to its format (on behalf of its producers of course), and conspiring with the show’s titular villains. All that while still having time to deliver a Robinson-style tongue-lashing: her post-round table scoldings are enough to make you the viewer feel a degree of contact shame, so lord knows how the actual people receiving them are feeling.Winkleman’s Traitors turn has been nothing short of a sensation, arguably launching her to the very top tier of celebrity in the UK. But it comes with a hint of risk attached: once you’ve put on the mask of ‘bad’ host, is it possible to take it off again? Perhaps part of the failure of her talkshow this year – a strange, stilted programme that has already been consigned to the cancellation dustbin – was that she just didn’t look quite right as a friendly chat-facilitator. Shouldn’t she be forcing Lisa Kudrow or James McAvoy to climb into a coffin or run through a haunted wood, rather than just, you know,talkingto them?Still, being typecast as the host of the biggest, most beloved show on British TV probably isn’t a bad place to be, all things considered. This series of the Celebrity Traitors will be the most viewed and nattered-about TV show this year, and then the civvy version will return to attract similar numbers of eyeballs in January. And Winkleman will be right there in the middle of it, talking to owls, being held aloft by shirtless hunks, and hurling photographs of deceased faithfuls to the floor with a smile. Long may she reign.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe GuideGet our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every FridayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTo read the complete version of this newsletterplease subscribeto receive The Guide in your inbox every FridayExplore more on these topicsCultureThe Guide newsletterClaudia WinklemanAnne RobinsonGame showsTelevisionnewslettersShareReuse this content

title: ‘I waited patiently, hoping he might make the jump’: Mirna Abass’s best phone picture | Photography | The Guardian
description: As a fan of Henri Cartier-Bresson, the Egyptian photographer was determined to capture his own ‘decisive moment’
Author: Grace Holliday
Headline: As a fan of Henri Cartier-Bresson, the Egyptian photographer was determined to capture his own ‘decisive moment’
Content: Freedom, 2024, shot on iPhone 13 in Ezbet El Borg, Egypt.Photograph: Mirna AbassView image in fullscreenFreedom, 2024, shot on iPhone 13 in Ezbet El Borg, Egypt.Photograph: Mirna AbassSmart shotPhotography‘I waited patiently, hoping he might make the jump’: Mirna Abass’s best phone pictureAs a fan of Henri Cartier-Bresson, the Egyptian photographer was determined to capture his own ‘decisive moment’Grace HollidaySat 3 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMirna Abass regards his small Egyptian city as “heaven for street, travel and documentary photography”. At the intersection of the Nile and the Mediterranean, the governorate of Damietta is home to Ezbet El Borg, a shipbuilding and fishing port. Abass describes it as “a colourful hub of daily fishing life; fishers and their nets, boats being built, maintained and painted”.‘The balloons made me smile but his expression made me stop’: Harivansh Verma’s best phone pictureRead moreOn the day he took this shot, Abass had joined a walk with the EgyptianCamera Crewphotography club. Abass works as an agricultural engineer, but describes film and photography as his true passions. Henri Cartier-Bresson is one of his biggest inspirations, and he is often guided by the pioneering photographer’s concept of thedecisive moment.“As we explored the shipyard, I saw this teenage fisher jumping between several boats,” Abass says. “I set up my iPhone 13 to capture these two contrasting boats, side by side, and waited patiently, hoping he might eventually make the jump in front of me. I was elated when he did, and went to show him our very own decisive moment.“The human element gave a sense of scale, of how large these ships are, and I loved how I captured him leaping from the white ship to the colourful ship,” he adds. “It is almost as if he is escaping from pale life to fruitful life.”Explore more on these topicsPhotographySmart shotArtEgyptfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Blind date: ‘He asked if my disco ball tattoo was an onion’ | Dating | The Guardian
description: Shahar, 29, a graphic designer and music label manager, meets Stephen, 34, a product designer
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Shahar, 29, a graphic designer and music label manager, meets Stephen, 34, a product designer
Content:
Composite: Sophia Evans and Christian SinibaldiView image in fullscreenComposite: Sophia Evans and Christian SinibaldiBlind dateDatingBlind date: ‘He asked if my disco ball tattoo was an onion’Shahar, 29, a graphic designer and music label manager, meets Stephen, 34, a product designerSat 3 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleShahar on StephenView image in fullscreenWhat were you hoping for?I’d never been on a blind date, so a good story, and a new connection.First impressions?Kind, a bit nervous. Very engaged, but kind of in awe of the situation.What did you talk about?Our careers in design. Music. What we like to cook. Artwork and posters we own. His extensive cap collection. Films (lots of movies I need to add to my watchlist).Most awkward moment?He asked me if my disco ball tattoo was an onion.Good table manners?Excellent. At one point, talking to the waiter, he referred to me as “the lady”, which we had a good laugh about.Best thing about Stephen?He was really engaged, easy to talk to, made me laugh – and very generous with compliments. He’s good at leading the conversation, but also at recollecting details and circling back.Would you introduce Stephen to your friends?After a while, yeah. It’s quite a compliment, introducing someone to your circle – gotta earn that trust!Q&AFancy a blind date?ShowBlind date is Saturday’s dating column: every week, two 
strangers are paired up for dinner and drinks, and then spill the beans 
to us, answering a set of questions. This runs, with a photograph we 
take of each dater before the date, in Saturday magazine (in the
 UK) and online attheguardian.comevery Saturday. It’s been running since 2009 – you canread all about how we put it together here.What questions will I be asked?We
 ask about age, location, occupation, hobbies, interests and the type of
 person you are looking to meet. If you do not think these questions 
cover everything you would like to know, tell us what’s on your mind.Can I choose who I match with?No,
 it’s a blind date! But we do ask you a bit about your interests, 
preferences, etc – the more you tell us, the better the match is likely 
to be.Can I pick the photograph?No, but don't worry: we'll choose the nicest ones.What personal details will appear?Your first name, job and age.How should I answer?Honestly
 but respectfully. Be mindful of how it will read to your date, and that
 Blind date reaches a large audience, in print and online.Will I see the other person’s answers?No. We may edit yours and theirs for a range of reasons, including length, and we may ask you for more details.Will you find me The One?We’ll try! Marriage! Babies!Can I do it in my home town?Only if it’s in the UK. Many of our applicants live in London, but we would love to hear from people living elsewhere.How to applyEmailblind.date@theguardian.comWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Describe Stephen in three wordsThoughtful, authentic, curious.What do you think he made of you?I hope he thought I was funny. I did make him laugh quite a few times.Did you go on somewhere?We spent four hours over dinner and it was a Sunday, so we called it a night.And … did you kiss?We did not.If you could change one thing about the date, what would it be?I wish I’d come across as slightly more curious and not drawn a blank about recent albums I liked. Also, I wish I’d had more room to finish dessert!Marks out of 10?8 (8.5 really, but I’m honouring Stephen’s dislike of .5 ratings).Would you meet again?We did chat about maybe going to a gig or the cinema.View image in fullscreenStephen and Shahar on their date.Stephen on ShaharView image in fullscreenWhat were you hoping for?Some cute flirting with someone my judgmental female friends would approve of.First impressions?Gorgeous hair, an American accent.What did you talk about?We compared graphics, recent albums, films and cinema etiquette. Then moved on to how fancy the venue was, our favourite things to cook, the perils of dating apps and the lost art of flirting.Most awkward moment?Nothing major. I did refer to Shahar as “the lady”, but only because the place was so fancy!Good table manners?Perfect, nothing spilled, many well-shared drinks and plates.Best thing about Shahar?I admired her passion and approach to design – and again, great hair!Would you introduce Shahar to your friends?I reckon they’d yap up a storm.Blind date: ‘He probably thinks I hold a lot of strong opinions on frivolous matters’Read moreDescribe Shahar in three wordsElegant, chatty, curly.What do you think she made of you?A film nerd with a large hat collection.Did you go on somewhere?I suggested another drink, but it was too late. To be fair, we did stay at the restaurant for almost five hours.And … did you kiss?The vibe didn’t lend itself to kissing, and that’s OK; there was lots to take in.If you could change one thing about the date, what would it be?Our seats being so far apart and not meeting on a school night.Marks out of 10?8 for the date. I couldn’t judge a person like that.Would you meet again?I gave her my number, so let’s see. There are lots of gigs and films we could watch.Shahar and Stephen ate atCooper’s Cut, LondonEC3.Fancy a blind date? Emailblind.date@theguardian.comExplore more on these topicsDatingBlind dateRelationshipsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Fashion designer Henry Holland: ‘I’ve thought about a nose job but everyone says I’ll look different. That’s the point!’ | Life and style | The Guardian
description: Holland on his dashed Olympic dreams, ranking the Real Housewives shows, and a terrifying taxi ride
Author: Rosanna Greenstreet
Headline: Holland on his dashed Olympic dreams, ranking the Real Housewives shows, and a terrifying taxi ride
Content: Henry Holland: ‘Who would play me in a film of my life? A young Sean Penn.’Photograph: Instar ImagesView image in fullscreenHenry Holland: ‘Who would play me in a film of my life? A young Sean Penn.’Photograph: Instar ImagesThe Q&ALife and styleInterviewFashion designer Henry Holland: ‘I’ve thought about a nose job but everyone says I’ll look different. That’s the point!’Rosanna GreenstreetHolland on his dashed Olympic dreams, ranking the Real Housewives shows, and a terrifying taxi rideSat 3 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBorn in Greater Manchester, Henry Holland, 43, worked as a stylist and fashion editor for Smash Hits magazine. In 2006, he gained attention for his witty slogan T-shirts which were worn during London fashion week. Two years later, he founded his fashion label, House of Holland, and in 2020, he established Henry Holland Studio, which specialises in ceramics and homewares. He has curatedThere’s No Place Like It, an exhibition at The Royal Society of Sculptors in London, which runs until 28 November. He is married and lives in London.When were you happiest?In my late teen years, on that verge of having independence and no responsibilities.What is your greatest fear?Going through grief and the loss of a parent was one of the toughest things I’ve ever done, so it happening again is my biggest fear.What is the trait you most deplore in yourself?Procrastination.What is the trait you most deplore in others?Laziness.What is your most treasured possession?This chain I wear round my neck, which was my mum’s.Describe yourself in three wordsPlayful, ambitious, silly.What makes you unhappy?A lack of connection to people.What is your guiltiest pleasure?The Real Housewives – all franchises but primarily Salt Lake City, Beverly Hills and Orange County.What do you most dislike about your appearance?My nose – it’s big and it’s got a lump in the middle. I’ve thought about a nose job. But everyone says no, I’ll look different. I’m like: that’s the point!Who would play you in the film of your life?A young Sean Penn.What is your most unappealing habit?Vaping.What did you want to be when you were growing up?Famous.Would you choose fame or anonymity?Now, anonymity, for sure.Have yousaid ‘I love you’ and not meant it?Yes, probably to a girl.Which living person do you most despise, and why?It’s a three-way tie between Elon Musk, Donald Trump and Nigel Farage.Which words or phrases do you most overuse?Yes.Adele Parks: ‘If I could ​edit my pas​t, I’d be fitter younger – I​ would have been hotter’Read moreWhat has been your biggest disappointment?Not becoming an Olympic gymnast.How often do you have sex?Do you speak to your mother with that mouth? None of your business.What is the closest you’vecome to death?My Uber driver lost consciousness at the wheel. I’d just started my ceramics business and the car was full of pots that were destined for Liberty. I had to reach through and drive the car from the back seat. We ended up crashed into a bollard and all the air bags came up and the window smashed. It was quite intense. And do you know what? Uber charged me for the trip!What has been your closest brush with the law?Lots of speeding tickets.What is the most important lesson life has taught you?Do things your way.Explore more on these topicsLife and styleThe Q&AHenry HollandCeramicsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘A hefty umami punch’: the best (and worst) supermarket light soy sauce, tasted and rated | Sauces and gravies | The Guardian
description: Which salty condiment nails that deep flavour profile, and which is saltier than the sea? Our resident taster tries 10 soy sauces straight from the bottle
Author: Tom Hunt
Headline: Which salty condiment nails that deep flavour profile, and which is saltier than the sea? Our resident taster tries 10 soy sauces straight from the bottle
Content: Soy much flavour …Photograph: Robert Billington/The Guardian. Food styling: Robert BillingtonView image in fullscreenSoy much flavour …Photograph: Robert Billington/The Guardian. Food styling: Robert BillingtonGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The FilterSauces and graviesReview‘A hefty umami punch’: the best (and worst) supermarket light soy sauce, tasted and ratedWhich salty condiment nails that deep flavour profile, and which is saltier than the sea? Our resident taster tries 10 soy sauces straight from the bottleThe best supermarket kimchiTom HuntSat 3 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSoy sauce was created in China about 2,200 years ago, as a means to preserve food and to zhoosh up the humble vegetarian Buddhist diet. It’s a demonstration inkokumi– literally “rich taste” – a flavour sensation that’s often called the sixth taste.I tested all of today’s soy sauces straight from the bottle, in all their intensity. I first identified distinctive aromas such as cooked potato, sulphur and broth (all typical in soy sauce and not as off-putting as they sound), alongside caramel and malty notes. The best ones are more nuanced, with fruity high notes and vinous tones.The best supermarket light soy sauceBest overall:Poon’s premium first extract soy sauceView image in fullscreen£16.30 for 250ml at Ocado (£6.52/100ml)£18.99 for 250ml at Selfridges (£8/100ml)★★★★★A delightful, wildly complex aroma with a fruity note of banana blossom and forest-floor undertones. Hits the palate with a broad flavour profile, astringent with roasted popcorn and caramel, then salt and acidity, and a strong bean base. Made from non-GMO soya beans grown in southern Taiwan, pressed only once and naturally fermented with no additives. Well worth the price.Best bargain:Yutaka organic tamari soy sauceView image in fullscreen£2.35 for 150ml at Sainsbury’s (£1.57/100ml)★★★★★A wonderfully deep flavour profile with notes of dark malt, green vegetables and molasses. Salt-forward with an intense, rounded mouthfeel and a beany mushroom base note. Naturally fermented for eight months and gluten-free. Just four ingredients and a high ratio of organic soybean (45%). Incredible value.And the rest …Kikkoman soy sauceView image in fullscreen£3 for 150ml at Tesco (£2/100ml)£3 for 150ml at Sainsbury’s (£2/100ml)★★★★☆A deep, beany aroma with meaty notes and a sweet, fruity caramel finish. Massive flavour that fills the mouth with an intense, salty, soy-forward, umami complexity that’s like the scrapings off a sticky roast beef rib. Just four ingredients – water, soybeans, wheat, salt – and naturally brewed and fermented for six months. Zero additives.Clearspring organic yaemon tamari soya sauceView image in fullscreen£3.80 for 150ml at Ocado (£2.54/100ml)★★★★☆A sweet, malty, caramel aroma with deep savoury notes of mushroom and potato. An intensely rich, salt-forward taste with a hefty umami punch and balanced acidity. Double-strength gluten-free organic tamari aged in cedarwood kegs over two summers, with a high ratio of soya beans (52%) and zero additives.Amoy light soy sauceView image in fullscreen£2 for 150ml at Tesco (£1.34/100ml)£2.10 for 150ml at Waitrose (£1.40/100ml)★★★☆☆A deep, meaty, cooked-mushroom aroma with notes of caramel, potatoes and cheese. Salt-forward with a sharp high note of alcohol and beany mushroom undertones. Made with more soy sauce extract (51%) than the other cheaper products, and six additives, including colour, acidity regulators, preservative (potassium sorbate) and flavour enhancers.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe FilterGet the best shopping advice from the Filter team straight to your inbox. The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSainsbury’s light soy sauceView image in fullscreen55p for 150ml at Sainsbury’s (37p/100ml)★★☆☆☆A sweet and floral mirin aroma with a synthetic, meaty undertone. Sweet-forward on the palate, with a strong, caramel flavour and malty cola notes. Made with 15% soy sauce extract and three additives (colour, acidity regulator, preservative).Morrisons light soy sauceView image in fullscreen90p for 150ml at Morrisons (60p/100ml)★★☆☆☆A dark, meaty, Bovril aroma with an intensely salty taste and a strong but one-dimensional caramel, brothy flavour. At just 3%, it has the lowest stated soybean content of any product in this lineup and contains three additives (colour, acidity regulator, preservative).Waitrose light soy sauceView image in fullscreen£1.35 for 150ml at Waitrose (90p/100ml)★★☆☆☆A mushroomy Bovril aroma and an intense salty, bitter flavour with notes of smoke, caramel and brassica. A low soy sauce extract percentage of 6%, and three additives (colour, acidity regulator, preservative).M&S light soy sauceView image in fullscreen£1.20 for 150ml at Ocado (80p/100ml)★★☆☆☆A sweet, fruity floral aroma with mushroom and meaty caramel undertones. Intensely salty and powerful, with a deep but one-note umami base. Made in Malaysia using Chinese soy sauce extract, with only 8% soybeans, and three additives (colour, acidity regulator, preservative).Co-op Chinese Menu light soy sauceView image in fullscreen74p for 150ml at Co-op (50p/100ml)★☆☆☆☆An intense, malty, caramel aroma with a hint of smoke. Intensely salty and powerful, with a meat and potato umami, sulphuric notes and a sweet aftertaste. Use sparingly. Made with 20% soy sauce extract, otherwise made up from water, salt, caramelised sugar syrup, acidity regulator (lactic acid) and preservative (potassium sorbate).For more, read thebest hot sauces, tasted and ratedExplore more on these topicsSauces and graviesThe FilterFoodChinese food and drinkJapanese food and drinkfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Henry Harris’s recipe for vegetarian endive au gratin | Food | The Guardian
description: A worthy, meat-free version of the best comfort dish ever, this French classic is best served with a chilled red and a crisp salad
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: A worthy, meat-free version of the best comfort dish ever, this French classic is best served with a chilled red and a crisp salad
Content: Henry Harris’ vegetarian endive au gratin.Photograph: Louise Hagger/The Guardian. Food styling: Emily Kydd. Prop styling: Jennifer Kay. Food styling assistant: Laura Lawrence.View image in fullscreenHenry Harris’ vegetarian endive au gratin.Photograph: Louise Hagger/The Guardian. Food styling: Emily Kydd. Prop styling: Jennifer Kay. Food styling assistant: Laura Lawrence.FoodHenry Harris’s recipe for vegetarian endive au gratinA worthy, meat-free version of the best comfort dish ever, this French classic is best served with a chilled red and a crisp saladHenry HarrisSat 3 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis is the best comfort dish on planet Earth. Cauliflower cheese held that title when I was a child, but I still remember the first time I ate this gratin, made bySimon Hopkinsonat his restaurant Hilaire in London, and wanting to take it away and eat it in a quiet corner. Endive when braised well retains a gentle bitterness that contrasts beautifully with a cheese-heavy bechamel. This dish is traditionally made with comté and with each endive wrapped in a slice of cooked ham, but some dark, crisp-fried mushrooms and emmental serve very well as good, savoury vegetarian alternatives.Endive au gratinA chilled beaujolais and a salad are good friends to serve alongside.Prep10 minInfuse1 hrCook1 hr, plus coolingServes4600ml milk1 bay leaf6 black peppercorns1 small onion, peeled and sliced2 parsley stalks(if you have them)2 large flat mushrooms120g unsalted butterSalt and black pepper4 heads endiveNutmeg50g plain flour1 pinch cayenne pepper, to taste200gemmental(suitable for vegetarians), gratedHeat the oven to 180C (160C fan)/350F/gas 4. Put the milk in a saucepan with the bay, peppercorns, sliced onion and parsley stalks, if using. Bring to a boil, then take off the heat and leave to infuse for an hour.Finely slice the mushrooms. Melt a third of the butter in a shallow pan on a gentle heat, then add the mushrooms, season and cook until they release their juices. Turn up the heat just enough so the liquid simmers and evaporates, leaving you with just the mushrooms and melted butter. (Don’t be tempted to tip out those juices, because they are full of flavour and need returning to the mushrooms.) Keep cooking the mushrooms, stirring from time to time, until they brown and turn a little leathery, then transfer to a plate lined with kitchen towel to absorb the excess butter.Melt another third of the butter in a heavy, ovenproof pan and, when it’s just starting to foam, add the endives and season with salt, pepper and a good rasping of freshly grated nutmeg. Turn down the heat and cook gently, turning frequently, until nicely coloured all over. Cover loosely with foil and transfer to the oven for 40 minutes to an hour, until completely tender. Remove from the oven and leave to cool a little. (The outer leaves will probably need pulling off, because they’ll be quite brown and crisp by now.)While the endive is roasting, make the bechamel. Reheat the infused milk. Melt the remaining third of the butter in a saucepan, add the flour and cook, stirring, for two minutes. Strain the hot milk into a jug, then whisk it into the flour mixture and keep whisking over a gentle heat for a good five minutes, until you have a thick, glossy sauce. Season with a pinch of cayenne, then stir in two-thirds of the cheese, until it melts. Taste and adjust the seasoning as needed.Heat the grill. Scatter the fried mushrooms over the base of four individual gratin dishes (or one large one), and top with the braised endives. Spoon over the hot bechamel, scatter over the remaining grated cheese and grill until bubbling and golden. Serve immediately.Henry Harris is chef/co-owner ofBouchon Racine, London EC1. His book, The Racine Effect, is published by Quadrille at £40. To order a copy for £36, go toguardianbookshop.comExplore more on these topicsFoodFrench food and drinkVegetablesStarterSnacksMain courseVegetarian food and drinkrecipesShareReuse this content

title: From the Bayeux tapestry to Glastonbury: top tips and tricks to grab the hottest tickets | Consumer affairs | The Guardian
description: Nothing is guaranteed but there are ways to boost your chances of experiencing such in-demand events
Author: Rupert Jones
Headline: Nothing is guaranteed but there are ways to boost your chances of experiencing such in-demand events
Content: The British Museum is making the most of having been loaned the Bayeux tapestry.Photograph: Amer Ghazzal/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenThe British Museum is making the most of having been loaned the Bayeux tapestry.Photograph: Amer Ghazzal/ShutterstockConsumer affairsFrom the Bayeux tapestry to Glastonbury: top tips and tricks to grab the hottest ticketsNothing is guaranteed but there are ways to boost your chances of experiencing such in-demand eventsRupert JonesSat 3 Oct 2026 03.36 EDTFirst published on Sat 3 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhether your passion is the battle of the bands or the Battle of Hastings, what are probably Britain’s hottest cultural tickets are about to go on sale – and to be in with a shout of going, there are insider tips that will get you a good spot in the queue.General admission tickets to theGlastonbury festivalnext June go on sale online at 9am on Sunday, while the next tranche of tickets to view the Bayeux tapestry at the British Museum will be released to members on Tuesday 6 October before a public on-sale on 21 October.If you are planning to try your luck, get your fastest finger ready and check out our tips for how to increase your chances of bagging tickets for the most in-demand events.Join the clubMembership of an organisation or venue often includes priority booking, giving you early access to tickets. However, the cost will be beyond many people’s budgets.The next member priority booking window for theBayeux tapestry– for slots from 1 January to 31 March 2027 – opens on Tuesday 6 October at noon. That is for members who joined up to 16 September. If you join now, you can book before the public in January for April to July 2027 dates. However, standard individual membership starts at £82.View image in fullscreenThe next member priority booking window for the Bayeux tapestry opens on Tuesday.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianSometimes you don’t have to pay to get priority booking for hot-ticket events. Some theatres (such as those run by the LW Theatres group) and gig promoters (such as Live Nation) offer presale access to people who sign up for email alerts or newsletters.Assemble your squadPlanning to try for Glastonbury tickets? One person can book up to six per transaction, and this year, when the sale begins, everyone who is already on the glastonbury.seetickets.com page will be assigned a place in a queue to access the booking process.The six-ticket limit means that if there are a lot of you who want to go, the best way to maximise your chances is to split into one or more groups of six. They need to all be logged on before 9am.View image in fullscreenThe Glastonbury festival is scheduled for June next year.Photograph: Anthony Devlin/Hogan Media/ShutterstockThe festival says you only get five minutes on the booking page, and there’s a lot of information to input.If and when one of the six people gets through, they will need the registration details, including postcodes, of everyone in their party in order to book tickets. (Registration for this year is now closed.) Everyone shouldcheck their registration detailsare still correct ahead of the sale.So, before things kick off, get a spreadsheet going with everyone’s details on it that everyone can access, and set up a group chat on WhatsApp or wherever so you can message each other instantly. To speed up the checkout process, everyone should consider having their debit or credit card details saved in their browser.For the Glastonbury general admission sale, you pay a £100 deposit a person now, so everyone needs to have enough cash in their account, or a big enough credit limit on their card, to pay for all the tickets. They must have their mobile phone charged and ready to approve the payment by entering a code if necessary.Multiple devices and browsers?In theory you can increase your chances of getting a good spot in the queue for in-demand tickets by using multiple web browsers or several devices. However, ticket websites often warn there is a risk you will be identified as an automated bot and blocked from making a purchase.The ticketing company AXS is known to be particularly strict about this sort of thing.View image in fullscreenLog on early to be in with a chance of tickets.Photograph: Dominic Lipinski/PACrucially, it appears that for this year, Glastonbury ticket hunters must enter their registration number before entering the queue. They then get a unique queue ID linked to that. So it appears that means one queue spot only per person, and means the end of being able to use multiple devices and/or browsers for Glastonbury.Be readyIf it says the tickets go on sale at 9am, don’t log on to the site at 8.58am. Go on at perhaps 8am or even earlier. It means you are in the website, just in case it starts to buckle later when everyone else tries to log on.Some ticketing and venue websites will let you create an account and add your address and payment card details in advance. That will mean a quicker checkout if you get through.Hold your nerveSo the tickets for that gig or show, etc went on sale at 9am but a few minutes later the website says it is sold out.Don’t give up: keep refreshing the page for at least a few minutes. In that 9am scramble, some people’s purchases won’t have gone through. Perhaps there was a technical glitch or they took too long inputting their details and were “timed out”, or their bank card was rejected.In such cases, their tickets will go back on sale – maybe immediately or a little while later.Once you’re done, don’t hang aroundYou got through, and the tickets are in your basket. Pay for your tickets and get out quick. Don’t tempt fate by hanging around: sometimes websites crash when they are overloaded, causing people to lose the tickets in their basket.Resale sitesand‘wait lists’Did you end up missing out? Secondary ticketing websites such as Viagogo and StubHub are not popular with everyone.However, there are more palatable options – notably Twickets, an “ethical” fan-to-fan marketplace enabling people to sell spare tickets at no more than face value (plus fees). Twickets is an app and website and is well worth checking regularly if you are hunting for tickets for a gig, show or sporting event.View image in fullscreenSome venues such as the Royal Albert Hall in London use Twickets as their official ticket resale partner.Photograph: Graham Turner/The GuardianSome venues such as the Royal Albert Hall in London use Twickets as their official ticket resale partner.Meanwhile, you may be able to join a waiting list for tickets that have been returned by people who can no longer attend a sold-out event. Some theatres operate waiting lists, as does the gig tickets app Dice. On Dice, if something is sold out, it will usually say “Wait list” under the event information. Once you join this, you will be sent an email or push notification if tickets become available, and you will have a short window to buy them.Get help from AIAccording to Ticketmaster, music fans “are increasingly using AI assistants to discover live events, compare options and make purchasing decisions”.If you have your eye on a gig or event that is sold out, a tool such as ChatGPT can now “work in the background” and check the relevant ticketing or venue website from time to time. So you could ask it to alert you if tickets become available or extra ones are released (or if prices fall below a specific amount).For example, if it’s an arena or stadium event, extra “production seats” – also known as “production holds” – are often released nearer the time, when they have got the staging finalised. Similarly, theatres will sometimes only put certain seats (such as the front row) on sale once they have sorted out the staging and sightlines.Explore more on these topicsConsumer affairsTravel & leisureBayeux tapestryGlastonbury festivalFestivalsMusic festivalsBritish MuseumfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Bailiffs and 100 unpaid teachers: inside the collapse of ‘groundbreaking’ yoga studio Triyoga | Yoga | The Guardian
description: Formerly a favourite of the A-list, the chain has abruptly ceased trading, leaving teachers and customers blindsided
Author: Rachel Hall
Headline: Formerly a favourite of the A-list, the chain has abruptly ceased trading, leaving teachers and customers blindsided
Content: Yoga teachers who spoke to the Guardian said they had been left struggling to pay essential bills.Photograph: Yuri Arcurs/AlamyView image in fullscreenYoga teachers who spoke to the Guardian said they had been left struggling to pay essential bills.Photograph: Yuri Arcurs/AlamyYogaBailiffs and 100 unpaid teachers: inside the collapse of ‘groundbreaking’ yoga studio TriyogaFormerly a favourite of the A-list, the chain has abruptly ceased trading, leaving teachers and customers blindsidedRachel Hall,Geneva AbdulandFrankie TobiSat 3 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 3 Oct 2026 14.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleKate Comer is a single mother with two children, so she is used to living on a financial knife-edge. But when the yoga studio at which she taught closed without warning in September, leaving her with two months’ worth of unpaid wages, it sent her anxiety skyrocketing.“I’m just reeling right now,” she said, estimating her loss at about £1,500. “I’m very concerned about the future.”Comer is one of an estimated 100 yoga teachers who were not paid for their final weeks of teaching before Triyoga, the cult London yoga studio, shut. Several instructors of barre, spin and box-fit classes who taught at its sister brands Barrecore, Boom Cycle, Kobox and Reformcore, which have also closed, have also said they have been left out of pocket.Yoga teachers who spoke to the Guardian said they felt blindsided by the sudden collapse, and are now struggling to pay essential bills. At least one says they are facing homelessness.“It’s absolutely disgraceful and there’s nothing we can do about it as freelancers,” said Comer, who is currently going through a divorce and fears that her sudden loss of income will mean she is considered unable to keep the family flat. She is searching for other work, but “the market is saturated with hundreds of teachers”.View image in fullscreenKate Comer: one of an estimated 100 yoga teachers who were not paid for their final weeks of teaching at Triyoga.Photograph: Graeme Robertson/The GuardianThe five fitness brands are all owned by Common Bond, which announced on 24 September that it was “temporarily suspending trading”.In August, bailiffs attended Triyoga’s Shoreditch studio. Shortly afterwards, Triyoga failed to pay its teachers on time, prompting instructors to threaten industrial action. Some teachers were paid late on 21 August, but none received their scheduled pay on 14 September, teachers said.Like many fitness studios, Triyoga struggled during Covid, closing its Soho studio in April 2022 after 17 years. The brand was bought by UnitedFitnessBrands (UFB) in January 2022. Following the liquidation of UFB in 2025, its assets were acquired by a new company, Common Bond, run by a former UFB director, Robert Rowland, and backed by the same investment firm, Nectar Capital.Rowland quit as director in May 2026 after the company went into financial difficulty. A winding-up petition was subsequently filed on 18 September. Rowland, whose LinkedIn profile describes him as a “C-suite executive” and is now chief of staff at wellness company Until, is also director of the Brown Dog pub in Barnes, which filed a winding-up petition to HMRC on 18 October 2025. He told the Guardian his resignation from Common Bond was planned from the start of his tenure.It is understood that Nectar Capital has launched an investigation into Rowland’s management of the business.Instructors from studios affected, and others close to Common Bond, have questioned whether its collapse is an example of “phoenixing”, in which directors close down a company to eliminate debts, and subsequently establish a new company to continue the same business. Phoenixing is legal unless there is evidence of deliberate abuse.Common Bond is currently undergoing an insolvency process in order to repay HMRC. It is understood that the fitness brands are for sale.Yoga teachers said cost-cutting measures had changed the atmosphere at Triyoga, which first opened in Primrose Hill in 2000. They said they were told to use AI-generated music instead of Spotify to avoid the cost of music licensing. Eco-friendly products were replaced with cheaper versions.Robin Catto, who has taught at Triyoga for 26 years, said the studio – which was popularised by celebrity clientele such as Kate Moss and Jude Law – was “groundbreaking” at the time for offering a mix of styles, and beloved for its “very strong sense of community”.Though UFB initially “saved” Triyoga, he said, “what became apparent quite quickly is that they didn’t really either get or care about the deeper element of yoga … it began to hollow out the vibe.”Davy Jones, chair of the Yoga Teachers’ Union, said it was now unlikely that any teachers would be paid. “I think it’s a wake-up call for yoga teachers to realise that they are actually part of that same gig economy [as Uber and Deliveroo drivers],” he said, adding that the union is bringing a test case in a bid to secure yoga teachers thesame workers’ rightsthat Uber drivers are now entitled to.He said that although “the yoga community tends to be a sort of trusting and, and – perhaps in business terms – slightly naive”, with profit-seeking multinational chains, private equity and hedge funds moving into the fitness industry, “they have to get organised in the same sort of way.”Students have also been impacted by the chains’ collapse. Ciara Regan paid for a year-long membership, at a cost of £180 per month, which she splurged on for its mental health benefits.She first felt that things were going downhill when classes were cancelled at the last minute, then she noticed that all the websites and social media accounts suddenly disappeared. “Everybody’s been left in the dark,” she said. “I wish there had been some sort of communication, but it’s careless.”Other studios in London including Home and Mission, which are run by former Triyoga staff, have offered to allow former Triyoga students to spend unused credits at their studios. Jonathan Sattin, the former founder of Triyoga who now runs Home, noted that studios are “challenging to run” due to the high business rates and VAT that they pay, which he would like to see reduced.With new gyms continually opening up on high streets across the country, the fitness industry has grown increasingly competitive. David Minton, an industry expert at Evolve, said boutique gyms which offer just one style – except the highly popular reformer pilates – “have seen a slowdown” compared with those that are expanding to include strength training, and sauna and cold plunge facilities.Nectar Capital declined to comment.Explore more on these topicsYogaGig economyJob lossesFitnessfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: In the footsteps of Wales’s heroic rebel prince: hiking Glyndŵr’s Way | Walking | The Guardian
description: As Michael Sheen prepares to bring Owain Glyndŵr to life on stage, our writer walks the peaceful national trail named after the last Welsh Prince of Wales
Author: Kevin Rushby
Headline: As Michael Sheen prepares to bring Owain Glyndŵr to life on stage, our writer walks the peaceful national trail named after the last Welsh Prince of Wales
Content: A section of Glyndŵr’s Way national trail that overlooks Clywedog reservoir.Photograph: Stephen Dorey/AlamyView image in fullscreenA section of Glyndŵr’s Way national trail that overlooks Clywedog reservoir.Photograph: Stephen Dorey/AlamyWalkingIn the footsteps of Wales’s heroic rebel prince: hiking Glyndŵr’s WayAs Michael Sheen prepares to bring Owain Glyndŵr to life on stage, our writer walks the peaceful national trail named after the last Welsh Prince of WalesKevin RushbySat 3 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBetween the treetops, I can see the towers of a distant mist-shrouded castle. Is it possible I could make contact with the spirit of the great Welsh hero Owain Glyndŵr so soon, at the very start of our hike? We are not even on the actual trail ofGlyndŵr’s Way. I’ve had to make a detour to find accommodation that takes dogs, as Stevie the terrier is with me.The Castle Innat Knucklas is a mile off the route, and two miles or so from the pretty border town of Knighton – where the 135-mile (217km) Glyndŵr’s Way officially begins.The towers slide away behind trees and a railway viaduct emerges. The medieval castle ruins, it turns out, are believed to have been plundered to build the viaduct in the 1860s, and the builders dropped in a couple of crenelated towers to honour the origins of the stone. I fear this may be an early omen: the spirit of Glyndŵr will be as elusive as the man himself was in his lifetime.View image in fullscreenAfter his great rebellion of 1400 devolved into a murderous guerrilla campaign, the last Welsh prince of Wales simply disappeared. His English adversaries thought he had supernatural powers. Writing two centuries after the events, Shakespeare has Glyndŵr declare (under the anglicised name Owen Glendower) in Henry IV: Part I that “the earth did shake when I was born” and “I can call spirits from the vasty deep”. The last known sighting was in about 1819, when William Blake saw him in a vision and sketched his gaunt head. Since then, nothing. If he’s been hard to pin down for six centuries, what chance now?View image in fullscreenWelsh rebel leader Owain Glyndŵr seen in battle in a painting by AC Michael.Photograph: Lordprice Collection/AlamyI plan to cover the 75-mile southern section of the national trail’s great horseshoe across mid-Wales, starting with a late afternoon two-mile warm-up from Knighton station up to Knucklas. On our first full day of walking, we head south out of Knucklas and soon reconnect with the main path. The hills are bone dry, lying like dead giants across our route, defended by armies of sheep. Stevie is nonchalant. He was born near Rhayader and is good friends with a tup called Patrick. Nevertheless, I keep him on a tight leash.The rebellion started with a land theft, an English lord helping himself to some of Glyndŵr’s hectares, a personal feud that laid bare a vast hinterland of Welsh disgruntlement. Men flooded back from England to join Glyndŵr. Edward I’s great fortress atConwywas captured; a battle near Knighton was won. It was all going well until the teenage son of Henry IV (the future Henry V) was put in charge of the English forces. Not for the first time, British history turned on an arrow: this one burying itself six inches into the young Henry’s skull at the Battle of Shrewsbury. He survived. The rebellion faltered.double quotation markOwain could only do the uprising because of that landscape; it enabled a guerrilla war and you still feel that todayMichael SheenIt is coming over Bailey Hill that Stevie gets the first hint of danger. A flock of sturdy old ewes spot him and form a tight huddle, atestudoformation, to slink up behind us. Stevie turns and does a comedy backwards leap of surprise. The ewes stamp their feet. Stevie hides behind a tussock. The ewes creep forward. I pull him through a gate. He has not barked or rushed at them. He has done well. Soon, we drop down into the hamlet of Llangunllo, where there is a pub. “It’s closed,” says a local woman. “Evenings and weekends, and for drinking only.” There is a dearth of facilities along Glyndŵr’s Way, widely considered the most remote of all 17 English and Welshnational trails, and I have brought a stove and teabags. This will prove a good decision. We set off up the lane and then on to the hills. It is quiet, very quiet. Nothing moves except the distant wind turbines.View image in fullscreenThe writer on remote Glyndŵr’s Way.Photograph: Kevin RushbyRebellion is in the air at the moment. The Uprising, a film about the 1381 Peasants’ Revolt, directed by Paul Greengrass, will be released in the UK on 9 October. And a new play by Gary Owen, Owain & Henry, opens on 5 November in Cardiff with Michael Sheen in the lead role. On a call before I set off, I ask Sheen why Glyndŵr remains such a potent hero. “His vision for a Welsh nation was based on a Welsh parliament, universities, religion and the laws ofHywel Dda,” he tells me. “It’s a vision that resonates. The play feels like a conversation between then and now.”Sheen himself has walked parts of Glyndŵr’s Way. He says: “Owain could only do the uprising because of that landscape; it enabled a guerrilla war and you still feel that today.”Stevie and I take a break in the Llangunllo bus shelter. There are no refreshments, but there are stacks of unwanted books. I find a copy ofFrancis Kilvert’s Diary, by the Victorian curate who kept a vibrant record of life in the Welsh borders. “Who died on the cross to save us all?” he asks one wild child from a remote Welsh farm. “Lord Chesterfield,” she replies. I tuck the book in my pocket.View image in fullscreenApproaching the hamlet of Llangunllo.Photograph: Simon Whaley Landscapes/AlamySoon we are climbing over hills where the heather and gorse is in glorious bloom and there are no roads except droving tracks. These green lanes were once used to send cattle and sheep across the border, a tough, brawling existence hinted at in Kilvert’s Diary. By then, however, the railways had arrived and the old droving life was doomed.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice a weekSign up toThe TravellerGet travel inspiration, featured trips and local tips for your next break, as well as the latest deals from Guardian HolidaysEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAt our first encounter with cattle, Stevie is happy to be carried. Different breeds, we soon learn, represent different threats: big cows can’t be bothered, small feisty ones are to be avoided. We take some long detours.Our second night is atBrandy House farm, a welcoming place with various types of accommodation. We choose the vintage caravan. Nearby Felindre has a simple pub, the Wharf Inn, serving one of my favourite beers, Wye Valley Brewery’s Butty Bach.Now the walk really begins to deliver. Majestic upland stages pass epic locations such as theCastell y Blaidd, the castle of the wolf, before arriving atAbbeycwmhir, the abbey that Glyndŵr reputedly sacked. I’m staying in a cabin atWales in the Woods, a couple of miles up the hill in a deep, silent pine plantation, perfect for Glyndŵr reflections.View image in fullscreenThe‘lovely, eccentric’town of Llanidloes.Photograph: Joe Dunckley/AlamyNext day, rain threatens, but we dodge all the showers, passing Saint Harmon, where Kilvert was briefly vicar, enjoying a stop at the superbWelsh Mountain Cider, then dropping down to Llanidloes. After three days on the trail, this lovely, slightly eccentric town seems like the big city, with so many pubs to choose from. We stay at theUnicorn. The following morning, we pass the Clywedog dam and climb toY Star Inn, one of the highest pubs in Wales, which has three smart new pods to stay in. From here, the path rises again on what, for me, is the greatest stage of all. Leaving the trail, Stevie and I climb the 564-metre hill of Foel Fadian, opening up great panoramas of Cadair Idris, Yr Wyddfa (Snowdon) and the Irish Sea. We follow the trail down and reach our destination, Machynlleth, a town that has the same eccentric edge as Llanidloes, with lots of interesting independent shops, pubs and cafes.It was in Mach (as the locals often call it) that Glyndŵr briefly set up his parliament, andthe building, albeit partially reconstructed in 1460, survives. It is an atmospheric spot and there, on the wall, charging into battle, is the great hero himself. Now I get the ghostly shivers. But it turns out the Victorian artist used the face of his patron,David Davies, the indefatigable railway builder of the 1850s and 60s. After five days of walking, Owain has eluded me yet again.The trip wasprovided byNational TrailsandNatural Resources Wales.Walking Glyndŵr’s Wayby Paddy Dillon is published by Cicerone (£16.95).To support the Guardian, order your copy atguardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.Owain & Henryruns from 5-28 November atWales Millennium Centre, CardiffExplore more on these topicsWalkingWalking holidaysWales holidaysMichael SheenfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Tim Dowling: nobody’s laughing – is the joke on me? | Family | The Guardian
description: By over-committing to the bit, I’m in danger of becoming the very thing that I mock
Author: Tim Dowling
Headline: By over-committing to the bit, I’m in danger of becoming the very thing that I mock
Content: Illustration: Selman Hosgor/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Selman Hosgor/The GuardianThe Tim Dowling columnFamilyTim Dowling: nobody’s laughing – is the joke on me?By over-committing to the bit, I’m in danger of becoming the very thing that I mockTim DowlingSat 3 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 3 Oct 2026 14.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere was a kid in my year in high school named Jimmy Tremarelli. We were in a couple of the same classes, and also had occasion to pass each other in the hall between bells about three times a day. Whenever we did Jimmy would nod and say, “Dr Dowling”, and I would say, “Dr Tremarelli”. And then we’d carry on in opposite directions.Over the years the pretence became gradually more elaborate. Sometimes Jim would steal up alongside me at the end of class, cupping my elbow in the palm of his hand.“Doctor,” he might say. “I know you’re busy, but I have a case I’d like to get your opinion on.” I would then stare at him gravely for a few seconds.“Call my secretary,” I would say. Then we’d nod and go our separate ways. We were 15.I can’t remember how or why it started, but in the hundreds of times Jim and I encountered one another over the course of three years, we never didn’t do it, not once. It wasn’t for anyone else’s benefit – I’m not sure anyone else even knew about it. I just remember students streaming round us, taking no notice as we stood there consulting in the corridor by the gym doors.double quotation markI never saw Jim again. But I think of him whenever I feel that same, slightly dangerous sense of commitment to a joke that has run its courseWhen it began we didn’t even know each other that well. Arguably we never really got to know each other any better. I don’t recall us ever having a normal conversation; we were just too committed to the bit.I never saw Jim again after graduation. But I think of him often, whenever I feel that same, slightly dangerous sense of commitment to a joke that has run its course – most recently whenever I refer to Sainsbury’s as “Saino’s”.I remember how this one started: I was striding across the kitchen with a shopping bag when I stopped short to pat myself for keys, wallet, and phone. The oldest one, sitting in front of his laptop, glanced up, taking me in.“You going Saino’s?” he said. I laughed. There was something in how he seemed to be mocking someone who would use such an abbreviation, while simultaneously taking an unbridled delight in it, that struck me as funny. But I accept that you had to be there, and that even if you had been it might not have been enough.That didn’t stop me from immediately adopting his diminutive. For the last two years I have never referred to Sainsbury’s as anything but “Saino’s”. No one else has ever laughed; the only thing my commitment has earned me is my wife’s contempt.“I’m off out,” she says, leaning her head through my office door. “Do we need anything you can think of?”I stare at the backs of my hands for a moment, weighing my options, one of which is, as always, a quiet life.“You going Saino’s?” I say.double quotation markI hope that sheer repetition will eventually open up some new vista of funniness. On that front I can only say: nothing so far.“If you call it that again I’m going to kill you,” she says. “But yes, probably.” Once more, I weigh my options.“Big Saino’s?” I say.In the absence of any potential for comic development, the only thing that makes my dedication worthwhile is the hope that sheer repetition will eventually open up some new vista of funniness. On that front I can only say: nothing so far.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTim Dowling: I’ve been replaced by a younger model … it’s a reliefRead moreThe real danger lies in commitment for commitment’s sake – that instead of passing comment on the sort of irritating person who exclusively calls Sainsbury’s Saino’s, I have simply become him.On a weekend away with another couple, my wife drives us back from a long dog walk on the beach – women in front, men in back.“Have we got enough wine?” says one friend.“Will anything be open?” says the other.“There’s a Saino’s on the way,” I say, without thinking.“Shut up!” my wife yells, turning to our friend in front. “I’m afraid he calls Sainsbury’s Saino’s.”“Why?” says our friend in front.“I don’t know,” my wife says.“Why?” says our friend, turning round toward me.“I’ll tell you,” I say. “But when I’m about halfway through my explanation 10 minutes from now, I want you to remember: you asked.”The other day I looked up Jimmy Tremarelli to see if, by any chance, he went on to become an actual medical practitioner. It would, if nothing else, constitute an unparalleled commitment to the bit. The truth is almost stranger: he’s a teacher, still working in the same high school that we attended together 45 years ago. I like to think that if I went there tomorrow and caught his eye as we passed each other in the crowded hall, he would just nod and say “Doctor”, and I would say it back.Explore more on these topicsFamilyThe Tim Dowling columnFriendshipComedyfeaturesShareReuse this content

The Saturday quizFrom the Geordie Springsteen to Bridalveil Fall and El Capitan, test your knowledge with the Saturday quizThomas EatonSat 3 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe questions1Whose funeral in 1989 attracted about 10 million mourners?2What is the only major river to cross the equator twice?3Which singer has been called the Geordie Springsteen?4What is the largest surviving carnivorous marsupial?5What was added to 30 June 2015?6Which sci-fi epic was inspired by the shifting sands of the Oregon coast?7Football and which other sport were banned in Scotland in 1457?8Which war memorial was designed by Yale student Maya Lin?What links:9Buzzard; Clair; Cygnus; Jackdaw; Rosebank?10Dis; Duat; Helheim; Irkalla; Mictlan?11England: 188,900; Scotland: 37,200; Wales: 21,100?12Susan Janet Ballion; Marianne Elliott-Said; Arianna Forster and Paloma Romero?13Bridalveil Fall; El Capitan; Half Dome; Mount Lyell; Sentinel Dome?14Saving Private Ryan; Pressure; The Longest Day?15Everton (currently); Arsenal; Southampton; Norwich City?View image in fullscreenFlagging over the Everton clue?Photograph: NurPhoto/Getty ImagesThe answers1Ayatollah Khomeini (Iran).2Congo.3Sam Fender.4Tasmanian devil.5Extra/leap second.6Dune (Frank Herbert).7Golf.8Vietnam Veterans Memorial, Washington DC.9Major UK oil and gasfields.10Underworld in various mythologies: Roman; ancient Egypt; Norse; Mesopotamian; Aztec.11Estimated total lengths of roads in Britain.12Original names of early punks: Siouxsie Sioux; Poly Styrene; Ari Up and Palmolive.13Natural landmarks in Yosemite national park, California.14Films about D-day.15Football allegiances of recent PMs: Burnham; Starmer; Sunak; Truss.Explore more on these topicsQuiz and trivia gamesThe quizquizzesShareReuse this content

title: Why do cats miaow and what’s the most powerful Pokémon? The kids’ quiz | Family | The Guardian
description: Five multiple-choice questions – set by children – to test your knowledge, and a chance to submit your own junior brainteasers for future quizzes ​
Author: Molly Oldfield
Headline: Five multiple-choice questions – set by children – to test your knowledge, and a chance to submit your own junior brainteasers for future quizzes ​
Content: Illustration: Hennie Haworth/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Hennie Haworth/The GuardianThe kids' quizFamilyWhy do cats miaow and what’s the most powerful Pokémon? title: ‘The enemy is tearing our city apart’: terror in Kyiv as Russia ramps up attacks | Ukraine | The Guardian
description: Mayor Vitali Klitschko says Kyivans can no longer pretend it is ‘peacetime’ amid strikes on school, hospital and bridge
Author: Pjotr Sauer
Headline: Mayor Vitali Klitschko says Kyivans can no longer pretend it is ‘peacetime’ amid strikes on school, hospital and bridge
Content: A woman and child passing the site of a Russian drone strike in Kyiv city centre this week.Photograph: Julia Kochetova/The GuardianView image in fullscreenA woman and child passing the site of a Russian drone strike in Kyiv city centre this week.Photograph: Julia Kochetova/The GuardianUkraine‘The enemy is tearing our city apart’: terror in Kyiv as Russia ramps up attacksMayor Vitali Klitschko says Kyivans can no longer pretend it is ‘peacetime’ amid strikes on school, hospital and bridgePjotr Sauerin KyivSat 3 Oct 2026 04.52 EDTFirst published on Fri 2 Oct 2026 10.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleValeriya Tkachenko was dropping her son off at school in central Kyiv when the air raid alert sounded. Staff hurried the children and parents into the shelter, where the frightened lawyer spent the next two hours with her son.“I’m scared to death all day about what could happen to my son,” she said as she emerged from the shelter, already late for work.A day earlier, a Russian jet-powered drone had struck a school nearby. “And I can’t plan anything any more,” she said. “It’s not sustainable like this.”View image in fullscreenSmoke rises after a Russian drone hit the Academy of Sciences building in Kyiv on Monday.Photograph: Julia Kochetova/The GuardianView image in fullscreenFirefighters tackling a blaze in the city centre.Photograph: Julia Kochetova/The GuardianAcross the city on Friday morning, Artem Marchenko, an IT worker, was forced to abandon his car and walk for 20 minutes across the Pivdennyi, or Southern, Bridge on his way to work after repeated Russian strikes damaged the crossing.He feared Russia would soon target Kyiv’s other bridges, paralysing movement across a city of about 3 million people, the two halves of which are divided by the Dnipro.On Saturday morning, Russia targeted a second major bridge connecting Kyiv, damaging the road surface on the Northern Bridge and temporarily halting traffic.Kyiv is entering its most difficult period since the early days of the invasion, asintensifying Russian attacksreshape everyday life in a capital that Moscow is seeking to plunge into darkness.MapFor weeks, the main worry in the capital had been the coming winter, when Russia is expected once again to try to plungeUkraineinto darkness and cold. But a sharp escalation in Russian attacks has left many residents feeling that some of the hardship they had been bracing for is already here.“The capital is in a very dramatic situation. And it’s no longer possible to pretend that we can live now as we do in peacetime,” the Kyiv mayor,Vitali Klitschko, said on Friday. “The enemy is tearing Kyiv apart.”View image in fullscreenRescue workers running to a shelter during an air threat.Photograph: Julia Kochetova/The GuardianThis week alone, Russian missiles and drones have struck offices, datacentres, a school and hospital and one of Kyiv’s main bridges. Moscow has also started its attacks on Ukraine’s energy, targeting a thermal power plant and other energy facilities, leaving several neighbourhoods without power and water by morning.Volodymyr Zelenskyy underlined the apparent shift in Russian tactics in aninterviewwith the Financial Times this week, saying Vladimir Putin had recently ordered his commanders to abandon the rules of war.“They want Ukrainians to leave the capital … and show that if you don’t have the capital you don’t have the country,” Zelenskyy said in separate comments to reporters.Until recently, Kyiv had retained a deceptively normal rhythm, while cities closer to the front, including Kharkiv and Dnipro, absorbed the brunt of daily missile and drone attacks. Now, residents joke grimly that the balance is beginning to shift, with those cities at times feeling safer than the capital.View image in fullscreenA volunteer medic crew on patrol in Kyiv.Photograph: Julia Kochetova/The GuardianThe city is confronting a particularly dangerous combination of an acute shortage of Patriot interceptors for ballistic missiles and a new generation of faster, jet-powered Russian drones that are harder to shoot down.‘We just have to adapt’: Kyiv residents prepare for a hard winter aheadRead moreKyiv is racing to fast-track a new generation of interceptor drones capable of taking down the jet-powered models. Several are already in use, according to three defence industry sources, though they said it could still take weeks or months to deploy them at a scale sufficient to provide meaningful protection for the capital.At the same time, Russia’s advances on the battlefield remain relatively slow and are coming at enormous cost.Moscow captured about 361 sq km in September, according to the military analyst Konrad Muzyka, an increase on recent months but still far short of the pace needed to seize the rest of the Donbas before winter, when offensive operations typically become more difficult.View image in fullscreenA man with a tattoo reading ‘immortal’ standing near the site of a Russian drone strike in Kyiv.Photograph: Julia Kochetova/The GuardianUkraine, meanwhile, has clawed back about 126 sq km in a series of counteroffensives in the east, being conducted under the codename Vivaldi. That slower-moving battle on the ground is increasingly at odds with what is happening far behind the front. The contrast reflects a broader shift in the war, as Ukraine’s major cities come under growing pressure.“You can be quite successful in the land domain, but if you are vulnerable in the air, especially in the rear, that is the vulnerability your opponent is going to exploit,” said Mykola Bielieskov, a military analyst at Ukraine’s government-run National Institute for Strategic Studies.Ukrainian officials have been warning their European counterparts about the scale of the looming threat. According to the New York Times, Ukraine’s energy minister, Denys Shmyhal, recently briefed European counterparts on an intercepted Russian plan to use as many as 1,000 missiles, drones and bombs against the country’s energy system. The targets included electrical substations, hydroelectric and thermal power plants and boiler houses, in what appeared to be an effort to plunge Ukrainian cities into darkness and cold and create a humanitarian crisis.“Russia plans to freeze Kyiv out, to throw it back into the stone age,” said one senior western diplomat in Kyiv, speaking on condition of anonymity.Western diplomats say publicly that they intend to remain in Kyiv, mindful that leaving would hand Moscow a propaganda victory and risk creating the impression that Ukraine was being abandoned. However, privately two senior diplomats said contingency plans were being drawn up to relocate embassies to Lviv or eastern Poland if Russia began deliberately targeting foreign missions.“The situation is obviously deteriorating fast,” the diplomat said.Explore more on these topicsUkraineRussiaEuropeVitali KlitschkonewsShareReuse this content

title: Libyan unity talks upended as warlord’s son linked to drone attacks on fuel facilities | Libya | The Guardian
description: Western Libya’s GNU say working with Saddam Haftar ‘impossible’ as US-backed merger plan breaks down
Author: Patrick Wintour
Headline: Western Libya’s GNU say working with Saddam Haftar ‘impossible’ as US-backed merger plan breaks down
Content: Four people were arrested after drones attacked the Zawiya oil station, causing a fire. Three Libyans were arrested and have been linked to Saddam Haftar.Photograph: Mahmud Turkia/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenFour people were arrested after drones attacked the Zawiya oil station, causing a fire. Three Libyans were arrested and have been linked to Saddam Haftar.Photograph: Mahmud Turkia/AFP/Getty ImagesLibyaLibyan unity talks upended as warlord’s son linked to drone attacks on fuel facilitiesWestern Libya’s GNU say working with Saddam Haftar ‘impossible’ as US-backed merger plan breaks downPatrick WintourSat 3 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 3 Oct 2026 05.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAllegations that the son of the Libyan warlord Khalifa Haftar oversaw a “terror cell” that launched drone attacks on fuel storage facilities and power stations in westernLibyahave upended plans for the Tripoli-based government of national unity (GNU) to continue cooperating with Haftar on a plan to unify the country.Saddam Haftar, the deputy commander of the so-called Libyan National Army (LNA), has increasingly been seen by the US as an important figure in its plans to unify Libyan security, judicial and political institutions.But a round of drone attacks in August worsened electricity blackouts in the west of the country, putting intense popular pressure on the GNU led by the prime minister, Abdul Hamid Dbeibah.Libya has been split between the east, dominated by Haftar, and the west, governed by the GNU, since the fall of Col MuammarGaddafi in 2011, leaving the oil-rich country at the mercy of corruption, militia, migrant traffickers and myriad external actors.View image in fullscreenKhalifa Haftar.Photograph: Esam Omran Al-Fetori/ReutersDonald Trump’sAfricaadviser, Massad Boulos, has hatched a plan to unify the two Libyan governments in which Haftar from the east would take on the role of president and a member of the Dbeibah family from the west would become prime minister.Boulos has insisted he is not trying a quick fix that entrenches family elites in Libya. “It’s not about families or names,” Boulos said when asked about the reported Haftar-Dbeibah deal, before adding: “At the end of the day, those are individuals that have to be in one position or the other.”But the drone strikes, it is claimed, were prompted by Haftar’s anger at Dbeibah apparently stalling on the Boulos merger plan and by Tripoli allegedly encouraging tribes in southern Libya to attack and kill his forces.Over more than five days in August, drones attacked the Zawiya oil station and fuel storage facilities in western Libya. The drone strikes hit the gasoline-storage tank at the Zawiya oil complex, west of Tripoli, causing a large fire and the tank’s collapse. The tank held approximately 4.5m litres of fuel when it was struck, according to Libya’s National Oil Corporation.0:25Libyan oil refinery engulfed in flames after drone attack – videoOn 5 September, three Libyans and one Spanish citizen were arrested in southern Tripoli by the GNU for their alleged role in a plot that was intended to include an attack on Tripoli airport. It was thought the whole group involved five Spaniards and four Libyans. The three arrested Libyans were allegedly affiliated with the Tareq ben Ziyad brigade, an LNA formation. Information that has emerged from interviews about the plot, and Saddam Haftar’s alleged role, not just in Libya, has been described as a goldmine, capable of weakening Khalifa Haftar.Sources in the GNU said the alleged plotters were working for Saddam Haftar. “No formal decision has been made, but in light of what has been discovered it is impossible to work with Saddam,” the sources said.The claims not only damage Saddam Haftar’s role in the Boulos plan but also the parallel UN sponsored 4+4 talks involving the main four political institutions in Libya that led to an August agreement to stage elections within two years. The deal endorsed by the UN security council overcomes previous obstacles to elections, and had been backed by the main actors capable of delivering the change.Walid Ellafi, minister for state for political affairs in the UN-backed Libyan GNU and an enthusiast for elections, said: “Our support for the 4+4 process is rooted in its role as a UN sponsored framework offering a new approach to achieving practical results that pave the way for elections and institutions whose political legitimacy derives from the will of the people – not as a political settlement that overlooks violations or sets aside the rights of those affected.”He opposes an elite east-west political deal that brushes aside longstanding grievances such as the displacement of 9,000 families in Benghazi during the 2014 war.The allegations about the sabotage operation may intensify a power struggle between the three sons of Khalifa Haftar in the east.Saddam Haftar is seen as his father’s most likely heir, possesses the most resources, enjoys the backing of the United Arab Emirates and has so far dominated the political tracks. But his brothers, Khaled and Belqasim – more allied with Egypt than the United Arab Emirates – have recently started to challenge his dominance.Explore more on these topicsLibyaMiddle East and north AfricaAfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: US Coast Guard searches for missing air ambulance off coast of Massachusetts | Massachusetts | The Guardian
description: The plane was undertaking a medical evacuation from Bermuda with six people onboard when it lost contact
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The plane was undertaking a medical evacuation from Bermuda with six people onboard when it lost contact
Content: A US Coast Guard ship patrols off the California coast in 2024.Photograph: APView image in fullscreenA US Coast Guard ship patrols off the California coast in 2024.Photograph: APMassachusettsUS Coast Guard searches for missing air ambulance off coast of MassachusettsThe plane was undertaking a medical evacuation from Bermuda with six people onboard when it lost contactKeely AougaSat 3 Oct 2026 13.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe US Coast Guard is searching for an air ambulance jet with six people onboard that lost contact with the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) during a flight fromBermudatoBostonearly on Saturday morning.In a statement to the Guardian, an FAA spokesperson said that the agency issued a search-and-rescue alert notice for a Gulfstream G-100 at about 1.20am local time on Saturday.The Canadian-registered air ambulance jet had four crew members and two passengers onboard when it departed Bermuda’s LF Wade international airport overnight for the flight to Massachusetts, according to a statement from the Bermuda airport’s operator, Skyport, obtained by theAssociated Press.NBC Newsreportedthat the plane was carrying out a medical evacuation in Bermuda, citing a statement from Clarence Togeretz, the director of flight operations at Latitude Air Ambulance, the aircraft’s operator.“We always get rather concerned when our crew doesn’t report to us in a timely manner,” he told NBC News. “But I will say that again, optimistically and positively, that doesn’t mean that the worst has happened.”NBC also reported that theMassachusettsport authority, which operates Boston Logan international airport, said the aircraft did not arrive as scheduled. A port authority spokesperson said: “Our thoughts are with those onboard and their loved ones as the search continues.”The FAA is coordinating with the Rescue Coordination Center and the US Coast Guard to locate the aircraft.The search area as of Saturday morning was off the coast of the island of Nantucket, Massachusetts, the coast guard said in astatement posted to X.Air and surface crews have launched in search of the aircraft, the statement added.Citing a source with knowledge of the investigation,ABC Newsreported there were no Americans onboard the plane, though the identities of those onboard were not immediately released.Officials believe the plane rapidly descended 7,500ft before hitting the water, according to the outlet’s source.Explore more on these topicsMassachusettsBermudaBostonPlane crashesAir transportAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: Brazil’s neck-and-neck election offers test for growing pro-Trump Latin American bloc | Brazil | The Guardian
description: Sunday’s poll pits the leftist incumbent Lula against the son of a former far-right president convicted of staging a coup
Author: Tiago Rogero
Headline: Sunday’s poll pits the leftist incumbent Lula against the son of a former far-right president convicted of staging a coup
Content: President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, a candidate for re-election for the Workers' party, attends a rally in São Gonçalo, Brazil. Photograph: Tita Barros/ReutersSunday’s poll pits the leftist incumbent Lula against the son of a former far-right president convicted of staging a coup‘No one disrespects Our Lady’: fears for Brazil’s patron saint grip country ahead of electionByTiago Rogeroin Rio de JaneiroSat 3 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 3 Oct 2026 03.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleShortly after
