hiscontroversial speechto the United Nations general assembly in September, Donald Trump gathered a dozen like-minded Latin American leaders and boasted that rightwing candidates had won all seven presidential elections held in the region since he began his second term.“Everybody I’ve endorsed has won,” the US president said in New York to most of the leaders of the Shield of the Americas, ananti-drug cartel coalitionof 15 countries governed by the right or far right.View image in fullscreenA giant balloon of Donald Trump holding Brazil’s President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva during a Flávio Bolsonaro rally in São Paulo.Photograph: Miguel Schincariol/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDonald Trump departs a meeting of the multinational coalition Shield of the Americas on the sidelines at the UN general assembly in New York.Photograph: Julia Demaree Nikhinson/APThose electoral victories – and theUS takeoverof Venezuela after capturing Nicolás Maduro – have left just six Latin American countries under leftwing governments: regional heavyweights Brazil and Mexico, small Uruguay and Guatemala, and the isolated regimes of Cuba and Nicaragua.On Sunday, Brazilians go to the polls in apresidential electionthat many believe will determinemore thanLatin America’s largest country’s fate for the next four years.View image in fullscreenSupporters Lula gather at a political rally in São Paulo.Photograph: Brian Snyder/ReutersGiven Mexico’s geographic proximity and unique economic relationship with the US, analysts see Brazil as perhaps the last country in the regionstill capableof saying “no” to Trump’s whims – something that could change dramatically depending on the election result.Polls indicate aneck-and-neck racebetween Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva,the 80-year-old leftist incumbentwho is seeking a fourth non-consecutive term, andFlávio Bolsonaro, 45, the far-right senator son of former president Jair Bolsonaro.“Trump really does take seriously the idea that theAmericasshould be his back yard,” said Pedro Telles, a professor at the School of International Relations at Brazil’s FGV university.View image in fullscreenPresident Claudia Sheinbaum leads her morning press conference at the National Palace in Mexico City, marking two years in office.Photograph: Luis Marin/Clasos/Zuma Press/Shutterstock“Mexico will remain relevant, and its president,Claudia Sheinbaum, is one of themost popularleftwing leaders. But if Flávio wins, it would be a real blow to the left and a major boost to the far-right agenda globally,” added Telles.“There is a lot at stake,” said Sandra Borda Guzmán, an associate professor of political science at Colombia’s Universidad de los Andes. “Instead of taking the opportunity to expand our region’s autonomy, a far-right victory would align the region unconditionally with the dictates of the US,” she added.View image in fullscreenA street vendor sells campaign flags of the presidential candidates Bolsonaro and Lula.Photograph: Eraldo Peres/APLula and Bolsonaro differ sharply on the US, including over what has become Trump’s main foreign policy for the region: theso-called “war on drugs” used to justify dozens of airstrikes on boats that havekilled more than 230 peopleand joint operations involving US military personnelon land.While Bolsonaro has pledged to join the Shield of the Americas and to follow an“iron fist” approachto crime, Lula has raised concerns about sovereignty and said it is “sad to see theinferiority complexof Latin American presidents” who are part of the Trump-created coalition.Brazil attorney general says meddling ‘cannot be tolerated’ after Trump funding plans revealedRead moreLula and Trump’s relationship hasswungbetween not speaking andpublic displays of warmth, but it is currentlyat a low point, with the Brazilian president andDemocratic membersof the US Congress accusing Washington oftrying to interferein Bolsonaro’s favour.“Brazil is a big prize,” said Michael Shifter, adjunct professor at Georgetown University’s School of Foreign Service, adding that amid endless conflicts in Iran, Ukraine and Israel-Palestine, “US foreign policy is going very badly in the rest of the world.”A victory for Bolsonaro in Brazil, he said, would be used “triumphantly” by Trump for producing an “almost completely aligned region”.At the latest Shield of the Americas meeting, Trump made clear that it was not all about security. The US president also referred to the “tremendous natural wealth” of Latin American countries, which he said could not “be taken over by hostile outside powers” – widely understood as a reference to China.View image in fullscreenPosters for Lula  in the streets of the Cajazeiras neighborhood in Salvador, Bahia state.Photograph: Amanda Cotrim/AFP/Getty ImagesPrivileged access to Brazil’s rare earths and critical minerals wasone of the conditionsWashington imposed in exchange for not applying tariffs, which Lula rejected. Bolsonaro, on the other hand,has offeredthose natural resources as the “solution” to help the US “break its dependence on China”.“Democracy is also kind of on the line here,” added Shifter, noting that Bolsonaro was only running because his father cannot – Jair Bolsonaro is under house arrest after being convicted ofattempting a coupto overturn his defeat by Lula in the 2022 election.“So it’s not just a question of one more country moving to the right, but of a right that has a very problematic relationship with democracy,” he said.As in recent elections across Latin America, the race includes other candidates but is polarised between two leading candidates. Lula and Bolsonaro have alternated as frontrunners in the final stretch, making the outcome unpredictable; if neither wins 50% plus one of the votes, there will be a runoff on 25 October.Bolsonaro’s only previous bid for an executive role in government ended ignominiously when he tookfourth placein Rio’s 2016 mayoral race. But analysts say there are several reasons why a congressman best known for his family name and corruption allegations – someshelved, othersstill under investigation– has emerged as a serious challenger to a three-time president.Unemployment, poverty and inflationhave fallen, and average incomes have risen, but so hashousehold debt– something many attribute to online betting, which the older Bolsonaro left unregulated andLula banneddays before the vote.The incumbent’s campaign has also been hit by corruption allegations – stillunder investigation– involving his son and a former aide, while ascandal involving supreme court justiceswith no connection to Lula may have rubbed off on the president.View image in fullscreenBolsonaro waves at supporters during a campaign rally at the São Paulo Municipal Market in São Paulo.Photograph: Miguel Schincariol/AFP/Getty ImagesMany therefore see Bolsonaro’s support as coming both from asimple transferof his father’s voter base and from ananti-Lula vote.“I’m going to vote for Flávio, but not because I think he’s the best option,” said Bruna Arguello, 34, a businesswoman from Santana de Parnaíba, whose first choice would be Ronaldo Caiado, a far-right former governor of Goiás, polling at 4%. “Unfortunately, he has no chance of winning, so I’m going with Flávio so we can get Lula out,” she said.View image in fullscreenThe presidential candidate for the Social Democratic party (PSD), Ronaldo Caiado, speaks at a press conference in Rio de Janeiro on Thursday.Photograph: Andre Coelho/EPAActor Docy Moreira, 59, will vote for Lula. In 2018, she was so dismayed byJair Bolsonaro’s electionthat she decided to leave her home town of Belo Horizonte, where two-thirds of voters backed the far-right leader. “I couldn’t understand how people, including the vast majority of my family, were choosing so much violence and authoritarianism,” she said.She Googled which cities had given Bolsonaro the lowest share of the vote, chose one about 1,550 miles away and moved north to Luís Correia, in Piauí.She eventually returned home, and most of her family will now vote for Bolsonaro’s son. Still, Moreira remains confident Lula will win.“If not, it will be devastating, but I’m not going to move again. I’m stronger now. I’ve learned that I can find refuge within myself,” said Moreira.Explore more on these topicsBrazilLuiz Inácio Lula da SilvaAmericasJair BolsonaronewsShareReuse this content

title: North Korea launches ballistic missile after Seoul demands apology over wounded soldiers | North Korea | The Guardian
description: Pyongyang fires towards sea a day after Kim Jong-un sister denounces South Korea for claiming North’s mines wounded South’s soldiers in DMZ
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Pyongyang fires towards sea a day after Kim Jong-un sister denounces South Korea for claiming North’s mines wounded South’s soldiers in DMZ
Content: A TV screen shows a file image of a North Korean missile launch during a news program at Seoul railway station in South Korea on Saturday.Photograph: Ahn Young-joon/APView image in fullscreenA TV screen shows a file image of a North Korean missile launch during a news program at Seoul railway station in South Korea on Saturday.Photograph: Ahn Young-joon/APNorth KoreaNorth Korea launches ballistic missile after Seoul demands apology over wounded soldiersPyongyang fires towards sea a day after Kim Jong-un sister denounces South Korea for claiming North’s mines wounded South’s soldiers in DMZReutersSat 3 Oct 2026 01.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNorth Korea fired a ballistic missile towards the sea on Saturday,South Koreaand Japan said, ⁠a day ​after it rejected Seoul’s accusation of its mines wounding soldiers.The missile was launched from the Wonsan area at about 6.30am towards the East Sea – also known as the Sea of Japan – and flew more than 700km (434 miles), the South Korean military said. Seoul and Washington were analysing the test for details, it added.Japan’s ⁠coast guard, citing the defence ministry, said the object may have been ​a ballistic missile and appeared to have come ‌down, warning ships to take ‌precautions.Why is South Korea so angry with Ukraine over two North Korean prisoners of war?Read moreSouth Korea’s military said it heightened its monitoring of any further missile tests and would share intelligence with the US and Japan. The South Korean presidential office’s national security council convened an emergency meeting on Saturday to assess the situation.Pyongyang’s Kim Yo-jong, the powerful sister of ruler Kim Jong-un, ​issued a statement on Friday that dismissedSeoul’s demand for an apologyfor what it said were North Korean mines that seriously wounded South Korean soldiers in the demilitarised zone – the heavily guarded buffer between the two Koreas.South Korea’s president, Lee Jae Myung, had urged Pyongyang on Thursday to return to dialogue, despite his military demanding an apology a day earlier. Kim Yo-jong responded by calling Seoul “really despicable” and ridiculing Lee’s latest overture, calling it “the climax of the farce that everyone should watch”.Kim also warned that Pyongyang was “ready for anything” Seoul might do over the mine blast – remarks followed the next morning by North Korea’s ballistic missile launch.South Korea said this week that North Korean mines caused the blast that injured ⁠three South Korean soldiers on a reconnaissance mission inside the 4km-wide buffer zone that stretches ​across the Korean peninsula.The missile ​test might be an attempt ​by Pyongyang to draw a response from South Korea to the sister’s statement, ​said Cheong Seong-chang, vice-president ‌at the Sejong ​Institute in Seoul, ​a research centre on North Korean affairs. North Korea might also have tested a new type of missile, he added.North Korea has launched missile tests on more than 10 occasions so far this year. Some came after North Korea protested against joint military drills between Seoul and Washington.North Korea has ramped up hostility against the South in recent years, disavowing unification as a national goal and calling South Korea its “primary foe”.With Agence France-PresseExplore more on these topicsNorth KoreaSouth KoreaAsia PacificnewsShareReuse this content

title: Bangkok at breaking point as floods turn streets into stagnant lakes | Extreme weather | The Guardian
description: With 40 dead and a disaster declared across all 50 city districts, experts warn extreme flooding will only worsen across south-east Asia
Author: Oliver Holmes
Headline: With 40 dead and a disaster declared across all 50 city districts, experts warn extreme flooding will only worsen across south-east Asia
Content: People wade through a flooded street in Bangkok. Photograph: Patipat Janthong/ReutersWith 40 dead and a disaster declared across all 50 city districts, experts warn extreme flooding will only worsen across south-east AsiaByOliver HolmesandAjit NiranjanFri 2 Oct 2026 22.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBangkok is used to absorbing the sudden afternoon downpours that inundate the city during the rainy season. Even streets in many central high-rise districts can briefly turn into rivers, with rats and cockroaches racing out of sewers and taking temporary refuge on trees and buildings as the subterranean world is flushed out.But every city has a breaking point, and this year rain fell so fast and so hard that whole neighbourhoods of the Thai capital have been transformed, not into rivers, but stagnant lakes. In parts of the city, roughly 300mm of rain – the equivalent of half a year of average rainfall in London – fell in about two days.View image in fullscreenA person wades through flood water in Lat Krabang district, Bangkok.Photograph: Rungroj Yongrit/EPAAbout 40 people died in flood-related incidents, according to the government. A number of the deaths were from drowning and several from accidental electrocution. Thousands of people stayed in more than 230 shelters across the city, authorities said.Suleemas Kurangkul, a 73-year-old resident of a block of flats whose ground floor stairs are still under water, said last weekend’s rain was not the usual evening storm but was constant, “like all day, all night”.“The water just kept rising,” said Suleemas, whose flat is above the waterline on the second floor. By the time she and her neighbours received a mobile phone warning, it was too late, and the street-level water was waist-high.The 1970s Khlong Chan flat compound in north-east Bangkok where Suleemas lives has become a symbol of the disaster. Photos have been shared acrossThailandof the flats rising out of the brownish water, with the rooftops of parked cars barely peeking above the surface, although the authorities had managed to drain away the worst of it by Thursday.Later in the week, during a brief respite in the rain, Suleemas said the water had receded somewhat. “People are so happy to see the sunshine,” she said. “Yet, the smell is getting stronger. So much debris and rubbish floating all over the place.”Built on a vast floodplain of the Chao Phraya River, Bangkok, a megacity of millions, relies on a network of muddy canals to drain water, as well as pumps and dikes. But concrete construction has destroyed much of the canal network, and the city is unable to cope.The government has declared a flood disaster across all 50 of the city’s districts. Some neighbourhoods have turned into dystopian scenes, with people using blow-up paddling pools or, in one case, a floating fridge, as boats to reach their homes. One man wasarrested for riding a jetskialong a main road.View image in fullscreenA resident uses a floating fridge as a boat.Photograph: Rungroj Yongrit/EPA“It’s a lesson,” said Chaleerat Chamrasporn, 55, a resident. “The kids are into doomsday-themed content, so now they can see what the ‘end of the world’ is actually like, or rather, that this is just the beginning.”Flooding has also disrupted Bangkok’s main Suvarnabhumi airport, with about half ⁠of Thai Airways’ workforce unable to report for work at one point this week, causing thousands of items of luggage ​to pile up and forcing flight ​cancellations. Many schools have closed, and with much of the capital in gridlock even people in less affected areas have been stuck at home.Thailand’s prime minister, Anutin Charnvirakul, told reporters that Bangkok’s metropolitan area was still at risk from flood waters flowing in from ​the north, and said a war room had ‌been set up to monitor ‌the situation. Thailand’s weather ⁠agency has forecast more ​heavy rain for next week.View image in fullscreenPeople stand on benches on the flooded pavement in Ramkhamhaeng in Bangkok.Photograph: Lillian Suwanrumpha/AFP/Getty ImagesIt is part of a pattern that seems to be setting in this part of the world. South-east Asia has already seen a worsening of extreme floods, scientists say, a trend that is set to worsen as fossil fuel pollutants bake the planet further. Hot seas evaporate more water and warm air can hold more moisture, allowing downpours to crash down with far more force.“In central Thailand, I can see from my maps, we have already seen a small but significant trend towards extreme rainfall,” said Nikolaos Skliris, an ocean scientist at the University of Southampton who hasstudiedheavy rain in the region. “In the long-term, all models show this will be amplified – more rainfall, and more extreme rainfall.”It is too early for scientists to attribute these particular rains to climate breakdown without doing a study. They were caused by a low-pressure system that moved from an unusually warm South China Sea over Cambodia and Vietnam before getting stuck above Bangkok, which was fairly cool, data from Copernicus Climate Pulse showed.The picture is complicated by the emergence of an abnormally strongEl Niño, a cyclical weather patternthat brings record heat and more violent extremes around the world. Its presence typically leads to drier summer conditions in south-east Asia but recent research suggests it still exacerbates days with extreme rainfall.Naim Laeni, a consultant and part-time university lecturer who co-authoreda study on Bangkok’s flood resilience, said authorities had underestimated the strength of the rains, which persisted for days. The city’s drainage canals can handle about 60mm of rain an hour, rising to 80mm in upgraded sections, but localised bursts exceeded this while leaving too little time between periods of stress.“The government did not communicate the seriousness,” said Laeni. “Usually in Bangkok we receive heavy rain for a few hours, not for days.”View image in fullscreenPeople wade through a flooded area during heavy rain in Bangkok.Photograph: Patipat Janthong/ReutersNeighbouring Myanmar has suffered from the same weather system, with flash floods and blocked roads complicating rescue efforts in the country.Rescuers were pulling bodies from a landslide that devastated the village of Ka Det Nge Htein in Myanmar’s south at the weekend. That disaster had already claimed nine lives, and eight more people are missing under the mud in another village, local officials said.Civil war across the country, and a junta that restricts the media, have made it hard to get information, and hampered aid organisations.Back in Bangkok, pumping stations have been operating at full capacity, but it could be days before the waters fully drain.At her apartment complex, Suleemas said she would stay where she was with her neighbours.“It’s hard, yes, very hard,” she said. “But together we are fighting and biting through it. When we get together to help one another like this, our spirit can keep us on our feet; we can get through it all together.”Agence France-Presse contributed to this reportExplore more on these topicsExtreme weatherThailandAsia PacificFloodingEl Niño southern oscillationClimate crisisfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Five-year-old girl in a coma and P-plater charged after car hits crowd of NRL fans in Newcastle | Newcastle and the Hunter | The Guardian
description: Man charged with nine offences after vehicle struck Knights fans attending grand final farewell, leaving 10 injured including three children
Author: Nino Bucci
Headline: Man charged with nine offences after vehicle struck Knights fans attending grand final farewell, leaving 10 injured including three children
Content: NSW police say 10 people were injured in the incident, prompting a major response from emergency services with four helicopters and 15 ambulances on scene.Photograph: Nine News/AAPView image in fullscreenNSW police say 10 people were injured in the incident, prompting a major response from emergency services with four helicopters and 15 ambulances on scene.Photograph: Nine News/AAPNewcastle and the HunterFive-year-old girl in a coma and P-plater charged after car hits crowd of NRL fans in NewcastleMan charged with nine offences after vehicle struck Knights fans attending grand final farewell, leaving 10 injured including three childrenGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastNino BucciSat 3 Oct 2026 18.32 EDTFirst published on Fri 2 Oct 2026 20.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTen people have been injured, one critically, after a car crashed into a crowd of people in Newcastle waiting to farewell the Knights team bus before theNRLgrand final.New South Wales police said a five-year-old girl remained in a critical but stable condition in an induced coma after the crash on Saturday morning.Initially a 67-year-old man was also in a critical. The man is now in a serious but stable condition.John Hunter hospital provided an update to Australian Associated Press on Saturday night confirming five other patients were in a stable condition and three others had been discharged.The injured were treated on the scene by NSW ambulance paramedics, before being taken to hospital.Police said the P-plate driver was an 18-year-old man who was arrested at the scene and taken to hospital for mandatory testing and subsequently charged with nine offences including dangerous driving occasioning grievous bodily harm, negligent driving and causing bodily harm by misconduct.He was refused bail to appear in court on Sunday.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailAssistant Commissioner Dave Waddell said two other people allegedly in the car were escorted from the crash scene after the crowd turned on them.Police did not believe the incident was deliberate but declined to comment on reports the vehicle was allegedly being driven erratically before the accident.“I’ll let the investigators from the crash investigation unit deal with that,” Waddell told reporters.The police minister, Yasmin Catley, said so many lives had been affected by a split-second decision, as she urged other drivers to take care over the NSW long weekend.“We have already started Saturday morning with this devastation,” she said.“Nobody can comprehend what has happened with this terrible tragedy.”The roads minister, Jenny Aitchison, said the incident could have been worse, with more than 1,000 people gathered in the area where it occurred.Emergency services were called to Newcastle Link Road at the Transfield Drive roundabout in Wallsend about 9.30am on Saturday after reports a vehicle struck multiple people in a crowd.“Several people have been injured and are currently receiving treatment at the scene,” police said.“Police have commenced an investigation into the circumstances surrounding the incident, with initial inquiries indicating it is not believed to be terror related.”Gavin Morris, the mayor of Newcastle, told the ABC that the driver, who he said was a Knights fan, lost control while revving his car shortly before the team arrived.“I’ve spoken to the authorities, a number of which, and look, first of all, it is under investigation, and the young driver is now with police, so it appears that he was revving the car in some form. He was excited. He was a supporter. He was, you know, a fan,” Morris said.“It appears that he’s lost control of the car, and he’s gone … sideways into the crowd.”Footage posted on social media appeared to show a car being driven quickly around a roundabout shortly before the crash.Other images showed it had careened off the road soon afterwards.A witness to the incident, Dylan Prior,told ABC Newsthat the car was “revving a bit” before it ran into a group of people.“I saw some young kids go flying, and people running to help the victims,” he said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“Everyone was yelling and hysterical, yelling at the driver.“They were screaming for help.”The Newcastle Link Road was closed in both directions, leading to the diversion of the Knights grand final procession.The club confirmed in an Instagram post that it had changed its route, apologising to fans who may have missed farewelling the team but saying “public safety is our priority”.Police appealed for fans to leave the area.“Police acknowledge many loyal supporters may have missed the opportunity to see the team and show their support.“Members of the public are asked to safely disperse from the area and keep roadways clear to assist emergency services and traffic management efforts.“Police thank the community for their patience, cooperation and assistance.”The NSW premier, Chris Minns, said his thoughts were with the families and friends of those injured.“It’s heartbreaking to see fans who were sending off their grand final team involved in such a terrible incident,” he said. “We’ve seen how this grand final has brought Newcastle together, and I hope the whole community remains united as we continue to respond.”The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, said he had spoken with Minns and offered the federal government’s support.“My thoughts are with everyone injured or involved in the horrible incident this morning in Newcastle,” Albanese said in a statement. “I want to acknowledge and thank emergency services and police for responding so quickly, and their ongoing work in treating the injured.“Rugby league brings people together, and this should have been a weekend of excitement and pride for Newcastle fans.”Multiple fundraisers were launched on Saturday afternoon by friends and loved ones of injured fans, including for a five-year-old child who was placed in an induced coma after suffering serious injuries.The child has already required multiple operations, according to organiser Ashleigh Gibbs.“Their mum was also seriously injured and will require multiple operations and a long period of recovery,” the fundraising page says.“Both mum and child now have a long road ahead of them, with ongoing surgeries, hospital stays, rehabilitation.”- Australian Associated Press contributed to this reportExplore more on these topicsNewcastle and the HunterNewcastle KnightsNew South WalesNRLnewsShareReuse this content

title: OpenAI says its review into hacks, including on Australian government sites, is costing $500,000 a day | OpenAI | The Guardian
description: Company says it is reviewing 50 petabytes of data after its agents accessed websites including Medicare without authorisation
Author: Josh Taylor
Headline: Company says it is reviewing 50 petabytes of data after its agents accessed websites including Medicare without authorisation
Content: OpenAI has warned that its review may identify more organisations that have had websites accessed by its AI agents without authorisation.Photograph: Dado Ruvić/ReutersView image in fullscreenOpenAI has warned that its review may identify more organisations that have had websites accessed by its AI agents without authorisation.Photograph: Dado Ruvić/ReutersOpenAIOpenAI says its review into hacks, including on Australian government sites, is costing $500,000 a dayCompany says it is reviewing 50 petabytes of data after its agents accessed websites including Medicare without authorisationGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastJosh TaylorTechnology reporterSat 3 Oct 2026 01.39 EDTLast modified on Sat 3 Oct 2026 01.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOpenAI says its review in response to the Medicare and Hugging Face agent attacks is costing the company more than US$500,000 per day, as it deploys AI to examine data that would take a human 66m years to read.The company has warned the review is ongoing, and more organisations may be informed they’ve been targeted in the near future.OpenAI’s Medicare attack has exposed Australia’s ‘tech debt’. Fixing it could bring a big bill for taxpayersRead moreOn Friday evening,OpenAI revealedagents had hacked into a New South Wales government website in June and accessed historical non-public data on bushfires without authorisation.It is thesixth government website in Australiato be notified by the AI giant since last month of agent activity on their services, after the prime minister, Anthony Albanese,announced OpenAI’s agentshad hacked into Services Australia’s Medicare statistics portal.The reason for the delay compared to the revelation of the Medicare attack is due to the sheer volume of data OpenAI needs to review.In a blog postthis weekthe company revealed the large amount of work involved in reviewing its agents’ activity.OpenAI said it has to review 50 petabytes of data – roughly 50m gigabytes.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email“We’re working back through the records month by month, looking for potential unintended activity beyond the cases we’ve already found,” the company said.“To put that in perspective, if that were all plain English text, it would take one person about 66 million years to read it at 240 words a minute, reading nonstop without ever sleeping or taking a break.”The company is searching records for where models accessed and changed websites, or took actions involving passwords, application programming interface (API) access or other sensitive credentials.AI is being used to help sift through the records, and it was costing the company more than half a million US dollars per day to go through. OpenAI said it also plans to increase its computing power as the process is refined.As of late last month, more than 100 organisations had been notified of having being targeted by OpenAI’s agents, but the company said notifying an organisation does not mean private information was accessed or that their system was compromised.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionOpenAI said it expects to find more cases and notify more organisations about events that may have occurred months ago.Australia is run on legacy systems that AI agents can easily exploit, former UN cyber negotiator warnsRead moreOrganisations will be informed privately if they need to investigate and address potential security issues, and OpenAI has said it will publicly report findings about agent behaviour and identified weaknesses in safeguards for the broader AI sector.“We err on the side of notification when our models’ activity exposes a potential security vulnerability, even in cases where it is unclear if the information accessed was intended to be public, so the organization can investigate and take appropriate action,” OpenAI said.OpenAI discovered the latest NSW government website breach on Tuesday, and informed the state government and the Australian Signals Directorate after a 48-hour review.The Medicare breach has prompted the Australian government to require departments and agencies to undertakea stocktake of legacy technologyto reduce the number of ageing systems within government and reduce the cybersecurity risk they may present in the event of an AI agent attack.Executives from OpenAI, Anthropic, Microsoft and Google will front a joint parliamentary committee on artificial intelligence in Sydney on Tuesday.Explore more on these topicsOpenAIAI (artificial intelligence)Australian politicsMedicare AustralianewsShareReuse this content

title: Magnitude 4.8 earthquake hits Victoria with tremors felt across Melbourne | Earthquakes | The Guardian
description: The epicentre was at Leongatha, 130km south-east of Melbourne, with residents reporting houses shaking just after 2am
Author: Martin Farrer
Headline: The epicentre was at Leongatha, 130km south-east of Melbourne, with residents reporting houses shaking just after 2am
Content: The grid of 'felt reports' of the Victoria earthquake showing the epicentre (red dot) of Leongatha.Illustration: Felt reportView image in fullscreenThe grid of 'felt reports' of the Victoria earthquake showing the epicentre (red dot) of Leongatha.Illustration: Felt reportEarthquakesMagnitude 4.8 earthquake hits Victoria with tremors felt across MelbourneThe epicentre was at Leongatha, 130km south-east of Melbourne, with residents reporting houses shaking just after 2amGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastMartin FarrerFri 2 Oct 2026 20.23 EDTFirst published on Fri 2 Oct 2026 15.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA magnitude 4.8 earthquake struck Victoria in the early hours of Saturday morning, shaking Melbourne and waking people across the whole region.Geoscience Australia said itdetectedan earthquake with a preliminary magnitude of 4.8 at 2.01am near Leongatha, 130km south-east of Melbourne, with the tremors felt across the city’s eastern suburbs.Geoscience Australia said it had received thousands of reports from people who said they had felt the earthquake.Posting on Facebook, Brian Morley in Narre Warren said “felt it and woke me up”, while Theresa Stevens said: “Shook our house in Garfield.”Other posts indicated the quake had been felt in Preston, Heidelberg Heights, Venus Bay and many other parts of Melbourne.The quake was estimated to have struck at about 10km below the Earth’s surface.Victoria’s State Emergency Service said the earthquake was a “timely reminder” to remember the drill to follow during an earthquake and that was drop to the ground, take cover under a sturdy piece of furniture and protect your head and neck, and hold on until the shaking stops.The Bureau of Meteorology said there wasno tsunami threatfrom the quake.The quake occurred in a region of South Gippsland considered to be amongst the most active seismic zones in Australia.Victoria’s two most recent quakes with magnitudes of 5 or above, however, were recorded elsewhere: a 5.9 magnitude in 2021 near Mansfield, in the state’s north-east, and a 5.0 on the Great Ocean Road in 2023.The quake on Saturday morning was the largest recorded in the state since that shock in 2023.An aftershock of 3.1 magnitude was recorded 55 minutes after the 4.8 magnitude earthquake early Saturday, with a magnitude 3.3 earthquake also recorded on Thursday morning at Yarram, about 80km east of Leongatha.Mark Quigley, associate professor of earthquake science at the University of Melbourne, said aftershocks could be felt for weeks in the region.“South Gippsland is one of our more seismically active parts of the country,” Quigley told the ABC.“We know it’s an area where seismicity is common, [and] we know we would expect aftershocks from an earthquake of that magnitude.”He said the earthquake was the result of a two by three kilometre area of rock about 10km below the surface slipping five to 10 cm rapidly, releasing seismic energy.Quigley said that earthquakes were not being recorded more often, despite a seeming increase in frequency in recent years.While the earthquake was “not an opportunity for people to panic or anything”, Quigley said it could be useful for people who lived in the region to consider whether they had items in their houses that could be damaged or create a safety risk in the event of a larger quake.“We know from the geological record we’ve had much larger in Gippsland in the past, larger than six and possibly as large as magnitude seven which I can assure you would cause widespread damage should they occur.”The last earthquake to cause property damage in Victoria wasthe 2021 quake, which resulted in tremors about 700km from the epicentre.Explore more on these topicsEarthquakesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Women given free cycling shorts to prevent upskirting on Oktoberfest amusement ride | Germany | The Guardian
description: Investigation revealed thousands of voyeuristic videos taken on Munich beer festival’s Teufelsrad, or Devil’s Wheel
Author: Jessie Williams
Headline: Investigation revealed thousands of voyeuristic videos taken on Munich beer festival’s Teufelsrad, or Devil’s Wheel
Content: The ride’s operator has given out more than 100 pairs of shorts to women and girls wearing dresses.Photograph: Anna Szilágyi/EPAView image in fullscreenThe ride’s operator has given out more than 100 pairs of shorts to women and girls wearing dresses.Photograph: Anna Szilágyi/EPAGermanyWomen given free cycling shorts to prevent upskirting on Oktoberfest amusement rideInvestigation revealed thousands of voyeuristic videos taken on Munich beer festival’s Teufelsrad, or Devil’s WheelJessie WilliamsSat 3 Oct 2026 11.10 EDTLast modified on Sat 3 Oct 2026 12.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWomen have been given free cycling shorts to prevent upskirting on a famous amusement ride at the Oktoberfest in Munich, after an investigation revealed tens of thousands of voyeuristic videos circulating online.TheTeufelsrad,or Devil’s Wheel, which rapidly spins around while people try to sit on it for as long as they can, is one of the beer festival’s oldest rides. But many of the videos discovered by German journalists focus on women whose traditional dirndl dresses have ridden up, often showing their underwear.The findings have revived concerns about upskirting – secretly filming or taking photos under someone’s skirt without consent, which has been illegal inGermanysince 2020. It is punishable by a fine or up to two years in prison. But some women’s rights advocates have said the law is not enough to stop the abuse.According tothe researchby the Munich daily newspaper Süddeutsche Zeitung, more than 32,000 videos linked to the Teufelsrad were found on Meta platforms alone, some of them with millions of views.The operator of the ride, Elisabeth Polaczy, told the BBC she has been handing out free cycling shorts to women and girls wearing dresses to protect them from people filming them. She has given out more than 100 pairs during this Oktoberfest, which finishes on Sunday. “I want to do everything I can to make people feel secure,” she said.There are signs and police posters in German and English around the tent where the Teufelsradis located that warn against filming under people’s skirts. But Polaczy, 80, said it was difficult to control everyone filming with smartphones.A spokesperson for the Bavarian police told the BBC they have put up posters at the Oktoberfest warning against upskirting since 2025.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionPolice arrested a 45-year-old Swiss man for filming under a German woman’s dirndl at this year’s festival. In 2025 there were 10 arrests for upskirting and seven in 2024.Explore more on these topicsGermanyEuropeWomen's rights and gender equalitynewsShareReuse this content

title: Greece returns priceless relics – and suggests UK should follow suit with Parthenon marbles | Bulgaria | The Guardian
description: Greek PM hopes handover of Tsar Samuel to Bulgaria will persuade Britain that time has come for ‘truth, reason, justice and morality’
Author: Helena Smith
Headline: Greek PM hopes handover of Tsar Samuel to Bulgaria will persuade Britain that time has come for ‘truth, reason, justice and morality’
Content: Statue of Tsar Samuel in Sofia, Bulgaria. As part of the agreement, Bulgaria is returning relics taken from Greek monasteries during the first world war.Photograph: Lambros Kazanas/AlamyView image in fullscreenStatue of Tsar Samuel in Sofia, Bulgaria. As part of the agreement, Bulgaria is returning relics taken from Greek monasteries during the first world war.Photograph: Lambros Kazanas/AlamyBulgariaGreece returns priceless relics – and suggests UK should follow suit with Parthenon marblesGreek PM hopes handover of Tsar Samuel to Bulgaria will persuade Britain that time has come for ‘truth, reason, justice and morality’Helena Smithin AthensSat 3 Oct 2026 10.46 EDTFirst published on Sat 3 Oct 2026 06.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn a ceremony replete with the sort of fanfare usually reserved for great events, Greece andBulgariahave formally exchanged “a treasury” of relics and bones, sealing a cultural deal negotiated over decades.The handover involved priceless religious objects removed fromGreeceat the height of the first world war, as well as remains thought to belong to Tsar Samuel, Bulgaria’s revered medieval warrior ruler.Greece hailed the exchange as emblematic of the headway countries could make in similar repatriation disputes, with the prime minister, Kyriakos Mitsotakis, saying he hoped the accord would bolster Athens’ campaign to retrieve the Parthenon sculptures and send a clear message to Britain.“The global community is essentially re-evaluating its longstanding stance on protecting cultural heritage,” he told a crowd gathered for the ceremony in Thessaloniki on Saturday. “This shift is embodied by today’s initiative, which rests on the obvious principle that monuments and historical heirlooms cannot be treated as spoils of war, nor as the result of circumstances subsequent to their creation.”Greek PM: deal to return Parthenon marbles could still be reached with ‘political will and courage’Read moreThe Greek-Bulgarian deal, reached after 50 years of intense cultural diplomacy between the two neighbours, was also an example of the “political will” needed to settle the west’s longest running cultural row, Mitsotakis said, referring to the fifth century BCParthenon marbles. “It took time, and above all, political will and determination to overcome the obstacles of the past,” he added.Under the agreement, 48 relics, including icons, crosses and ornate ecclesiastical vessels, pillaged by Bulgarian troops from churches and monasteries in northern Greece during the first world war, will be returned to Athens. In the more than 100 intervening years, they had been safeguarded at the National History Museum in Bulgaria.Meanwhile, the remains of Tsar Samuel, regarded as a national hero for his role in battling to preserve his country’s independence from the Byzantine empire, were discovered by archaeologists more than 60 years ago in a border area of Greece.Authorities arranged a homecoming with full state honours, with the tsar’s bones flown to Sofia, the Bulgarian capital, on a military aircraft accompanied by an escort of jet fighters and a 21-gun salute upon arrival. Free transport had been organised for pilgrims to pay their respects.In his own address at the handover, Bulgaria’s prime minister, Rumen Radev, a former air force officer, said: “These are items that belong to both our peoples; they constitute our memory and our bond, and our compatriots and future generations deserve, and must have, the opportunity to pay tribute to their ancestor. If in the past Tsar Samuel divided us, I can say that today he unites us. He strengthens our strategic cooperation and makes the historical relations between our states and peoples even stronger.”View image in fullscreenBulgaria’s military personnel carry a coffin with the remains of medieval ruler Tsar Samuel during a handover ceremony in Thessaloniki.Photograph: Giannis Papanikos/APMitsotakis emphasised that Greece’s campaign to win back the Parthenon marbles was neither “dictated by a vague national claim, nor does it call into question the mission of museums worldwide”.Athens remained committed to repatriating the sculptures, he said, because it would allow viewers to fully enjoy what has long been seen as the high point of classical art if the masterpieces were reunited.“It is precisely this same principle – the principle of the integrity of a monument – that underpins our continuous efforts to reunite the Parthenon sculptures. The Parthenon constitutes a unique and singular case,” he said of the building that is the predominant temple on the Acropolis of Athens.“[The campaign] is about the restoration of a universal monument that remains violently dismembered. My country will not accept arrangements that imply recognition of foreign sovereignty or the supposed borrowing of its own treasures. On the contrary, it now believes that the time has come for truth, for reason, for justice and morality.”The fifth century BC carvings were sawn from the Parthenon on the order of Lord Elgin, Britain’s then ambassador to the Sublime Porte, in what have since become highly contentious circumstances.They were acquired by the British Museum in 1816 after the bankrupt peer was forced to sell them and have been on display there ever since.Explore more on these topicsBulgariaEuropeGreeceArchaeologyParthenon marblesHeritageSculpturenewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘This can’t go on’: tens of thousands protest against housing crisis in Spain | Spain | The Guardian
description: Demonstrators take to the streets of Madrid ⁠and other Spanish cities ⁠after ​new legislation fails to pass
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Demonstrators take to the streets of Madrid ⁠and other Spanish cities ⁠after ​new legislation fails to pass
Content: Demonstrators fill a Madrid city square during a housing protest on Saturday.Photograph: Juan Barbosa/ReutersView image in fullscreenDemonstrators fill a Madrid city square during a housing protest on Saturday.Photograph: Juan Barbosa/ReutersSpain‘This can’t go on’: tens of thousands protest against housing crisis in SpainDemonstrators take to the streets of Madrid ⁠and other Spanish cities ⁠after ​new legislation fails to passStaff and agenciesSat 3 Oct 2026 10.19 EDTLast modified on Sat 3 Oct 2026 17.33 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTens of thousands of people have taken to the streets of Madrid ⁠and other Spanish cities as they step up demands for action to tackle ⁠a mounting housing crisis ⁠after ​government measures were struck down by the opposition.Demonstrators on Saturday waved posters calling for a general strike ⁠after the measures drawn up to address mass anger over the eviction of an 87-year-old woman in ⁠Madrid, and other housing issues,were rejected in parliamenton ​Friday.Authorities said 70,000 people were protesting. Organisers put the figure at 500,000.“It’s a shame,” Nando ‌de Anguulo, 26, ‌who joined the protest in Madrid, told Reuters. “It only proves that it ‌is us, the people, who have to adapt to the political parties, and not the politicians to what the people want, and this can’t go on like that.”Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, may call a snap election for November after the ‌legislation failed to pass, Spanish media reported on Friday, and would be watching the strength of Saturday’s ​protests before making a decision.View image in fullscreenThousands of demonstrators took to the streets of Madrid.Photograph: Alejandro Martinez Velez/ReutersThe demonstrations have dominated the national conversation, breathing new life intoSánchez’s beleaguered governmentand shifting attention away from the lingering impact ofrecent events in Ceuta.Protests on Saturday were peaceful in 50 Spanish cities. In the south-eastern city of Valencia, demonstrators clashed with police who fired rubber bullets and teargas ⁠to break up the protests.About 30 people managed to get inside ​the City ​of Arts and Sciences, a ​landmark cultural building in the city, before they were ​ousted by ‌police.One protester in Madrid, Marcos Sainz, a librarian, 26, said he used to rent a two-bedroom apartment with friends for a monthly rent of 900 euros ($1,000) but that a one-bedroom flat often now cost 1,000 euros – or half the median monthly salary in the capital.He told AFP he would protest rental spikes “until someone dares to regulate it all, as (otherwise) we’ll all have to leave Madrid and that would be a shame as I am from Madrid”.Javier, 31, a solar panel installer, said: “We are demanding a fundamental right: decent housing, stability and conditions allowing us to construct a decent life project.” He added: “I spend half of my salary on a tiny room.”“What we are feeling in the streets is a new energy that we haven’t seen in a long time, an energy that is showing that eight days of people power can achieve more than eight years of progressive government,” Valeria Racu, one of the spokespeople of the Tenants’ Union organising the protest, said in a statement.“Now begins real politics – politics which has always belonged to the people and which will return once and for all to the streets,” she said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenProtesters clash with police during the demonstration in Valencia.Photograph: Kai Forsterling/EPALate on Saturday groups of far-right protesters, some of them performing Nazi salutes, tried to get to the camp in Madrid but were blocked by police.One video posted on the website of Spanish daily El País showed police chasing some members of the group through the streets and the newspaper also reported that officers had made three arrests.On Friday, Sánchez’s Socialist-led coalition put forward two decrees that included a range of measures aimed at improving access to housing, from a ban on evictions until 2030 to the regulation of temporary lettings and lettings by room.Despite the anger of the protesters outside parliament, the conservative People’s party, the far-right Vox and the Catalan pro-independence party Junts voted against both decrees.The People’s party said it had voted in line with its belief that building, rather than regulating, was the best way to address the crisis. “Housing doesn’t become more affordable through decrees; it becomes more affordable by building ​more homes,” said the lawmaker Juan Bravo.View image in fullscreenA demonstrator holds up a sign reading ‘Right to a Roof’ on Plaza de Espana in Madrid.Photograph: Javier Soriano/AFP/Getty ImagesNews of the package’s rejection was met with boos and cries of “shame” outside. “Your profits, our misery,” the protesters chanted.The long-simmering anger at soaring housing costs boiled over late last month, when 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal, who uses a wheelchair, wasevicted from the home she had lived in for 70 years. The octogenarian said she was unable to afford the 230% rent hike demanded by the investment fund that bought her apartment.Reuters and AFP contributed to this report.Explore more on these topicsSpainEuropeRenting propertyHousingProtestnewsShareReuse this content

title: They embraced the Fiat 500, the Vespa, even tuk-tuks. But will Romans draw the line at the golf cart?  | Italy | The Guardian
description: Authorities crack down on trade they says risks spiralling out of control – but operators say they are being targeted unfairly
Author: Angela Giuffrida
Headline: Authorities crack down on trade they says risks spiralling out of control – but operators say they are being targeted unfairly
Content: A tourist golf cart passes in front of the Colosseum.Photograph: Victor Sokolowicz/The GuardianView image in fullscreenA tourist golf cart passes in front of the Colosseum.Photograph: Victor Sokolowicz/The GuardianItalyThey embraced the Fiat 500, the Vespa, even tuk-tuks. But will Romans draw the line at the golf cart?Authorities crack down on trade they says risks spiralling out of control – but operators say they are being targeted unfairlyAngela Giuffridain RomeSat 3 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 3 Oct 2026 09.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOn the edge of Piazza Navona, one of the grandest squares in central Rome, Barry and Linda, visitors from Texas in the US, stepped out of a golf cart. They planned to cross the square on foot, perhaps stopping to admire Lorenzo Bernini’s 17th-century Fountain of the Four Rivers, before being picked up by their driver at the opposite end.The couple had already done a walking tour on day one of their trip, and had been so exasperated by a stifling three-hour shuffle along a corridor towards the Sistine Chapel on day two that by the third day they wanted to give their tired feet a rest.View image in fullscreenAmerican tourists Barry and Linda on foot in Piazza Navona.Photograph: Victor Sokolowicz/The Guardian“When I first heard you could do golf cart tours in Rome, I thought to myself: that sounds a little weird,” said Barry. “But then we decided to try it out.” He said the most enjoyable thing about the experience was “feeling the breeze”.Rome is a difficult city to navigate, noted Linda, especially its ancient narrow streets in the centre. “There are no sidewalks,” she said. “Our feet were hurting and we needed a break.”For visitors, golf cart tours offer respite from the heat, crowds and cobbles. For residents, however, their proliferation in recent years has become another source of frustration in a city already wrestling with traffic and overtourism.View image in fullscreenRome’s leaders are pushing for regionwide measures to properly regulate the carts.Photograph: Victor Sokolowicz/The GuardianTaxi drivers are especially incensed, accusing golf cart operators of stealing their business, while one local newspaper said the city had been “taken hostage” by the vehicles.Now Rome authorities are cracking down on the burgeoning trade. Police intensified checks this week after the news agencyAdnkronosreported that 90% of the roughly 500 golf carts circulating in the city were operating without authorisation.In recent days, police stopped 131 carts around Piazza Navona, the Pantheon, Circo Massimo and the Spanish Steps, issuing €38,000 of fines for offences ranging from unlicensed driving to illegal parking.Rome’s leaders are pushing for regionwide measures to properly regulate an activity that “risks spiralling out of control”, Eugenio Patanè, a councillor for mobility, told the news agency Adnkronos.View image in fullscreenA golf cart in traffic in Rome.Photograph: Victor Sokolowicz/The GuardianPrices vary based on the type of tour and duration, but the cost per person can start at €100 and exceed €400 for a half-day trip. Barry and Linda paid €310 for their three-hour ride. “But it’s worth it,” said Barry.Rome’s traffic problem is hardly new. Julius Caesar tried to tackle the issue more than 2,000 years ago by banning private vehicles and commercial carts from the city’s streets during the day. Today, pedestrians, cars, scooters, delivery vans and the occasional roguehorse-drawn carriageall jostle for space.View image in fullscreenNora and Carlo outside their shop Trevimage near the Pantheon.Photograph: Victor Sokolowicz/The GuardianTourists can also take tours in Fiat 500s, on Vespas with sidecars, and even in tuk-tuks. But the golf carts seem to have drawn a special kind of wrath.“There are too many of them,” said Nora Fahmi, who works at Trevimage, an art photography shop behind the Pantheon. “We’ve had this shop for 13 years and have seen all sorts of things, but the golf cart situation is kind of wild.”Nearby, two teenagers from Israel were taking a rest on a parked cart. “We just want a lift to the Colosseum but you have to book online,” said their mother, Miri. “Rome is too crowded and it’s difficult to walk.”View image in fullscreenTwo young tourists rest in a golf cart parked in the town centre.Photograph: Victor Sokolowicz/The GuardianElisa Isacco, who lives in the Monti area, spares no sympathy for the weary tourists. “What do they actually see or learn about Rome when they are on one of these things?” she said. “I find myself having to dodge them all the time – Rome is chaotic, it’s like a jungle.”Amid the clampdown, several golf cart tour operators have banned staff from speaking to the press. But Leo Pavoncello, a driver for an operator in the Jewish Ghetto area, was happy to publicly defend the trade.“Golf carts are silent and eco-friendly,” he said. “Rome is not an easy city to visit but these vehicles allow people with disabilities and families with children to see the sites in a comfortable way. On top of that, they provide jobs for young people.”View image in fullscreenA golf cart waiting for a group of tourists in Piazza Navona.Photograph: Victor Sokolowicz/The GuardianPavoncello, who was subjected to the police checks and was found to be operating fully legitimately, argued that a few rotten apples were giving the business a bad name.“I don’t understand why they are targeting us,” he said, although he suspects “taxi lobbies” are piling on the pressure. “But Rome is a touristic city that has always been full of traffic, and the golf carts are simply another mode of transport.”Explore more on these topicsItalyOvertourismEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘The enemy is tearing our city apart’: terror in Kyiv as Russia ramps up attacks | Ukraine | The Guardian
description: Mayor Vitali Klitschko says Kyivans can no longer pretend it is ‘peacetime’ amid strikes on school, hospital and bridge
Author: Pjotr Sauer
Headline: Mayor Vitali Klitschko says Kyivans can no longer pretend it is ‘peacetime’ amid strikes on school, hospital and bridge
Content: A woman and child passing the site of a Russian drone strike in Kyiv city centre this week.Photograph: Julia Kochetova/The GuardianView image in fullscreenA woman and child passing the site of a Russian drone strike in Kyiv city centre this week.Photograph: Julia Kochetova/The GuardianUkraine‘The enemy is tearing our city apart’: terror in Kyiv as Russia ramps up attacksMayor Vitali Klitschko says Kyivans can no longer pretend it is ‘peacetime’ amid strikes on school, hospital and bridgePjotr Sauerin KyivSat 3 Oct 2026 04.52 EDTFirst published on Fri 2 Oct 2026 10.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleValeriya Tkachenko was dropping her son off at school in central Kyiv when the air raid alert sounded. Staff hurried the children and parents into the shelter, where the frightened lawyer spent the next two hours with her son.“I’m scared to death all day about what could happen to my son,” she said as she emerged from the shelter, already late for work.A day earlier, a Russian jet-powered drone had struck a school nearby. “And I can’t plan anything any more,” she said. “It’s not sustainable like this.”View image in fullscreenSmoke rises after a Russian drone hit the Academy of Sciences building in Kyiv on Monday.Photograph: Julia Kochetova/The GuardianView image in fullscreenFirefighters tackling a blaze in the city centre.Photograph: Julia Kochetova/The GuardianAcross the city on Friday morning, Artem Marchenko, an IT worker, was forced to abandon his car and walk for 20 minutes across the Pivdennyi, or Southern, Bridge on his way to work after repeated Russian strikes damaged the crossing.He feared Russia would soon target Kyiv’s other bridges, paralysing movement across a city of about 3 million people, the two halves of which are divided by the Dnipro.On Saturday morning, Russia targeted a second major bridge connecting Kyiv, damaging the road surface on the Northern Bridge and temporarily halting traffic.Kyiv is entering its most difficult period since the early days of the invasion, asintensifying Russian attacksreshape everyday life in a capital that Moscow is seeking to plunge into darkness.MapFor weeks, the main worry in the capital had been the coming winter, when Russia is expected once again to try to plungeUkraineinto darkness and cold. But a sharp escalation in Russian attacks has left many residents feeling that some of the hardship they had been bracing for is already here.“The capital is in a very dramatic situation. And it’s no longer possible to pretend that we can live now as we do in peacetime,” the Kyiv mayor,Vitali Klitschko, said on Friday. “The enemy is tearing Kyiv apart.”View image in fullscreenRescue workers running to a shelter during an air threat.Photograph: Julia Kochetova/The GuardianThis week alone, Russian missiles and drones have struck offices, datacentres, a school and hospital and one of Kyiv’s main bridges. Moscow has also started its attacks on Ukraine’s energy, targeting a thermal power plant and other energy facilities, leaving several neighbourhoods without power and water by morning.Volodymyr Zelenskyy underlined the apparent shift in Russian tactics in aninterviewwith the Financial Times this week, saying Vladimir Putin had recently ordered his commanders to abandon the rules of war.“They want Ukrainians to leave the capital … and show that if you don’t have the capital you don’t have the country,” Zelenskyy said in separate comments to reporters.Until recently, Kyiv had retained a deceptively normal rhythm, while cities closer to the front, including Kharkiv and Dnipro, absorbed the brunt of daily missile and drone attacks. Now, residents joke grimly that the balance is beginning to shift, with those cities at times feeling safer than the capital.View image in fullscreenA volunteer medic crew on patrol in Kyiv.Photograph: Julia Kochetova/The GuardianThe city is confronting a particularly dangerous combination of an acute shortage of Patriot interceptors for ballistic missiles and a new generation of faster, jet-powered Russian drones that are harder to shoot down.‘We just have to adapt’: Kyiv residents prepare for a hard winter aheadRead moreKyiv is racing to fast-track a new generation of interceptor drones capable of taking down the jet-powered models. Several are already in use, according to three defence industry sources, though they said it could still take weeks or months to deploy them at a scale sufficient to provide meaningful protection for the capital.At the same time, Russia’s advances on the battlefield remain relatively slow and are coming at enormous cost.Moscow captured about 361 sq km in September, according to the military analyst Konrad Muzyka, an increase on recent months but still far short of the pace needed to seize the rest of the Donbas before winter, when offensive operations typically become more difficult.View image in fullscreenA man with a tattoo reading ‘immortal’ standing near the site of a Russian drone strike in Kyiv.Photograph: Julia Kochetova/The GuardianUkraine, meanwhile, has clawed back about 126 sq km in a series of counteroffensives in the east, being conducted under the codename Vivaldi. That slower-moving battle on the ground is increasingly at odds with what is happening far behind the front. The contrast reflects a broader shift in the war, as Ukraine’s major cities come under growing pressure.“You can be quite successful in the land domain, but if you are vulnerable in the air, especially in the rear, that is the vulnerability your opponent is going to exploit,” said Mykola Bielieskov, a military analyst at Ukraine’s government-run National Institute for Strategic Studies.Ukrainian officials have been warning their European counterparts about the scale of the looming threat. According to the New York Times, Ukraine’s energy minister, Denys Shmyhal, recently briefed European counterparts on an intercepted Russian plan to use as many as 1,000 missiles, drones and bombs against the country’s energy system. The targets included electrical substations, hydroelectric and thermal power plants and boiler houses, in what appeared to be an effort to plunge Ukrainian cities into darkness and cold and create a humanitarian crisis.“Russia plans to freeze Kyiv out, to throw it back into the stone age,” said one senior western diplomat in Kyiv, speaking on condition of anonymity.Western diplomats say publicly that they intend to remain in Kyiv, mindful that leaving would hand Moscow a propaganda victory and risk creating the impression that Ukraine was being abandoned. However, privately two senior diplomats said contingency plans were being drawn up to relocate embassies to Lviv or eastern Poland if Russia began deliberately targeting foreign missions.“The situation is obviously deteriorating fast,” the diplomat said.Explore more on these topicsUkraineRussiaEuropeVitali KlitschkonewsShareReuse this content

title: Flydubai co-pilot used crash axe to attack captain, says UAE | Flydubai plane incident | The Guardian
description: Attorney general says ‘terrorist attack’ was attempted by suspect who is said to have been barred from flying by Oman because of extremist views
Author: Jessie Williams
Headline: Attorney general says ‘terrorist attack’ was attempted by suspect who is said to have been barred from flying by Oman because of extremist views
Content: Indian pilot Smit Machchhar, the captain of flydubai flight FZ 1073, whose quick thinking was praised after the incident.Photograph: Israel's Foreign Ministry/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenIndian pilot Smit Machchhar, the captain of flydubai flight FZ 1073, whose quick thinking was praised after the incident.Photograph: Israel's Foreign Ministry/AFP/Getty ImagesFlydubai plane incidentFlydubai co-pilot used crash axe to attack captain, says UAEAttorney general says ‘terrorist attack’ was attempted by suspect who is said to have been barred from flying by Oman because of extremist viewsJessie Williamsand agenciesSat 3 Oct 2026 07.56 EDTFirst published on Sat 3 Oct 2026 03.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe co-pilot of flydubai flight FZ1073 used an axe to attempt to carry out a “terrorist attack” during the Israel-bound flight, the United ⁠Arab Emirates prosecutor general has said.Disaster was narrowly averted on Wednesday when passengers and crew intervened to stop the co-pilot’s attempt to take control of the plane, which had 182 people onboard and plunged 16,625ft in just over 30 seconds. The descent was so extreme that part of the rudder was ripped off.Investigators have been trying to establish how the alleged attacker, who was seen by witnesses repeatedly stabbing the pilot in the cockpit, managed to smuggle a weapon onboard.But on Saturday, Gen Hamad ‌Saif Al Shamsi, a UAE prosecutor, said the co-pilot had used a crash axe to mount the attack, an implement typically kept inside the cockpit to use in emergencies, such as crashes or fires, and which would not have needed to be brought onboard covertly.“Investigations into the incident involving flydubai flight FZ1073 found that the co-pilot had attempted to ​carry out a terrorist attack,” Al Shamsi was quoted as saying by the state news agency WAM.Media outlets have named the co-pilot as Hammam al-Hammami, an Omani national. Speaking to the Associated Press, a Gulf diplomat said investigations were under way to establish whether he acted as a “lone wolf or had any connection with any extremist groups”.The Wall Street Journal reported that the co-pilot had been barred from flying by Oman over concerns he had adopted extremist views. He was then moved to an administrative job at Oman Air, according to the official, before being hired by the UAE-based budget airline flydubai.3:28How the stabbing incident unfolded on Israel-bound flydubai plane | DeconstructedSuicide by plane or terrorism? Speculation over motive in flight 1073 attackRead moreIt was not immediately clear to what extent he was vetted when he was hired.A British university, Buckinghamshire New University, said a student named Hamam al-Hammami had “previously completed a distance-learning course in aviation management” at the institution. It added: “He did not undertake any pilot training at the university.”A flydubai spokesperson on Saturday said the circumstances surrounding the incident were still ‌under investigation and the airline was not in a position to comment further.The airline’s flights between Dubai and Tel Aviv have been suspended until further notice following the attack.A former flydubai crew member told the Wall Street Journal that all its pilots were subject to security screening before flights, as well as medical checks at least once a year.How the co-pilot managed to be working in the cockpit on Wednesday morning is acentral question for investigators. It also raises serious concerns about background checks in aviation recruitment. Israel says it has agreements with foreign carriers to keep pilots out of its airspace who come from nations with which it does not maintain diplomatic relations. Israel and Oman do not have formal diplomatic relations.Security agencies from four regional countries were working to establish the co-pilot’s motives, aided by the US and other western governments, an official said, speaking on condition of anonymity to discuss details of the investigation.View image in fullscreenOne of the people injured in the incident.Photograph: Amit SegalOn Friday, Anwar Gargash, a senior adviser to the UAE president, called the attack a “dangerous terrorist act”. The incident is a test for the UAE government, which has earned a reputation for effective measures against extremist activities but has also bristled in the past over criticism of security lapses.Little else was immediately known about the co-pilot’s background. His Instagram account was active until the day of the flight and then deleted.The Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, said on Friday that the co-pilot had undergone “Islamist radicalisation” but provided no evidence. He added that Israel was looking into whether the co-pilot had acted under anyone’s direction and warned that anyone involved would pay a “heavy price”.Most of the ​passengers onboard were Israeli nationals.The Indian captain, Smit Machchhar,who had multiple stab wounds, has been praised for his bravery. He said he used his remaining energy while being stabbed to unlock the cockpit door, allowing people who had noticed loud noises to come in, tackle the co-pilot and stabilise the plane.In a video call with the Indian prime minister, Narendra Modi, Machchhar said: “I was lying on the floor injured but I told myself to go for one last push to open the door from inside.“Others came in and also played a role [in controlling the situation]. I was of course fighting for my own life, but at the same time I knew I was not going to let others die.After passengers restrained the attacker, two reserve pilots, who were onboard, safely landed the plane at Tabuk airport in north-western Saudi Arabia at 06.58 local time. The captain and co-pilot were taken to the UAE, as it leads the investigation. Officials have said a number of countries including Israel are participating.Netanyahu on Saturday said he wanted to invite Machchhar and Modi to light a flame at a national ceremony for Israel’s Independence Day next May, saying the role was usually reserved for Israeli citizens.In a video his office released of his telephone conversation with the hospitalised captain, he said: “You are a true hero of the brave peoples of India and Israel and you are a hero of the entire world.”With Associated Press and ReutersExplore more on these topicsFlydubai plane incidentUnited Arab EmiratesAir transportIsraelMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Man shot dead at London memorial service in ‘senseless act of violence’ | London | The Guardian
description: Forty-year-old victim declared dead at the scene in East Acton in a ‘senseless act of violence’
Author: Nadeem Badshah
Headline: Forty-year-old victim declared dead at the scene in East Acton in a ‘senseless act of violence’
Content: Police were called on Friday at 7.47pm after multiple shots were heard by members of the public in East Acton.Photograph: Peter Byrne/PAView image in fullscreenPolice were called on Friday at 7.47pm after multiple shots were heard by members of the public in East Acton.Photograph: Peter Byrne/PALondonMan shot dead at London memorial service in ‘senseless act of violence’Forty-year-old victim declared dead at the scene in East Acton in a ‘senseless act of violence’Nadeem BadshahSat 3 Oct 2026 18.04 EDTLast modified on Sat 3 Oct 2026 18.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA murder investigation has been launched after a 40-year-old man was shot dead in a “senseless act of violence” during a memorial service in westLondon, police have said.Police were called on Friday at 7.47pm after multiple shots were heard in East Acton.Officers attended alongside the London ambulance service. The victim was treated at the scene on the junction of Braybrook Street and Erconwald Street, however, he was pronounced dead.The Metropolitan police said about 40 to 50 people were at the scene, including children. The man’s family have been informed and are being supported by specialist officers.A postmortem examination is scheduled to establish the cause of death, but the victim is believed to have sustained a gunshot wound, the force added.No arrests have been made.DCI Brian Howie, who is leading the investigation, said: “Our thoughts are with the family and friends of a man whose life was taken in a senseless act of violence.“We understand a large number of people had gathered for a memorial service and what should have been a time to come together in remembrance has instead left a family devastated.“We believe between 40 and 50 people, including children, were present when this incident occurred. Someone knows what happened and we need them to come forward.“If you were around Erconwald Street, Braybrook Street, the surrounding roads or Wormwood Scrubs playground between 6pm and 8pm, please think carefully about what you saw. Did you see anyone carrying or concealing weapons, people on bicycles acting suspiciously or vehicles being driven at speed?“We also want to hear from anyone with photographs, video, dashcam, doorbell or mobile phone footage or who has seen anything relevant on social media.”Explore more on these topicsLondonCrimePoliceGun crimenewsShareReuse this content

title: Tories would expand free childcare to high earners, Badenoch says | Conservatives | The Guardian
description: Kemi Badenoch says those earning more than £100,000 should not be discouraged from working more
Author: Peter Walker
Headline: Kemi Badenoch says those earning more than £100,000 should not be discouraged from working more
Content: Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch (right) and Laura Trott, shadow education secretary, meet parents and toddlers ahead of the Conservative party conference on 3 October.Photograph: Ian Forsyth/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenConservative leader Kemi Badenoch (right) and Laura Trott, shadow education secretary, meet parents and toddlers ahead of the Conservative party conference on 3 October.Photograph: Ian Forsyth/Getty ImagesConservativesTories would expand free childcare to high earners, Badenoch saysKemi Badenoch says those earning more than £100,000 should not be discouraged from working morePeter WalkerSenior political correspondentSat 3 Oct 2026 17.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 3 Oct 2026 17.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheConservativeshave unveiled a proposed £700m childcare giveaway for high earners ahead of their annual conference, saying they would end the “cliff edge” where free entitlement ends at salaries above £100,000.The plan, set out the day before the event begins in Birmingham, follows the earlier proposal by Kemi Badenoch’s party toabolish most stamp duty, another change to taxation that would disproportionately benefit wealthier people.Under the current system, put in place under Rishi Sunak’s government, families with young children in England are eligible for 30 hours a week of free childcare, but this cuts off if one parent earns more than £100,000, irrespective of another parent’s salary.Under the Conservative plans, this limit would be abolished, with all parents working 16 or more hours a week able to claim the childcare.The party says it would cost aabout £700m a year, which it says would be paid for by cutting jobs at organisations such as Arts Council England and the Environment Agency.In comments released to promote the idea, Badenoch said the current system was “absurd” and a disincentive to work more.She said: “Conservatives believe that you shouldn’t be punished for working more, but this childcare cliff edge does exactly that.“I’m a mum-of-three and I’ve had to make the same choices many families have had to make on work and childcare. Those choices are difficult already, government should not be making them harder.“No one should be turning down a promotion or a pay rise because they literally cannot afford to earn more.“It is often women who end up carrying more of the childcare responsibility so a system that makes it harder for them to progress in their careers is not helping families, it is not helping women and it is definitely not helping the economy.”A Labour spokesperson said: “It tells you everything you need to know about the Tories that the first of their own tax policies they want to unpick is one helping higher earners. They clearly don’t want to admit that they set the thresholds in the first place.”The idea of abolishing stamp duty on people’s primary residences in England and Northern Ireland was unveiled by Badenoch at last year’s conference, costing an estimated £9bn a year.While some economists have argued that stamp duty can have a drag on the housing market and even the economy, as it disincentivises moving, scrapping it rather than reforming the tax would disproportionately benefit better-off people and those in London and south-east England.The other main policy set out ahead of the conference was a plan to build 50,000 new prison spaces in England and Wales, a 50% expansion in capacity.This would be paid for in part by slashing overseas aid to £1bn a year, a 90% cut on current plans. Under Keir Starmer, Labour said they wouldreduce aidfrom 0.5% of GDP to 0.3% by 2027, but even that lower proportion would still amount to £9bn a year.When Reform UKannounced plansto cut aid to £1bn a year, aid groups warned that this would not cover existing contributions to global bodies such as the UN and World Bank, shredding Britain’s international influence.Explore more on these topicsConservativesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Tories plan to extend cuts beyond £47bn previously pledged, leak reveals | Conservatives | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith told party members last year he had discussed making further savings if they win next election
Author: Kiran Stacey
Headline: Exclusive: Shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith told party members last year he had discussed making further savings if they win next election
