Content: Andrew Griffith’s comments suggest the Conservatives are planning to make cuts similar in scale to those made during the austerity years.Photograph: Leon Neal/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAndrew Griffith’s comments suggest the Conservatives are planning to make cuts similar in scale to those made during the austerity years.Photograph: Leon Neal/Getty ImagesConservativesTories plan to extend cuts beyond £47bn previously pledged, leak revealsExclusive: Shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith told party members last year he had discussed making further savings if they win next electionKiran StaceyPolicy editorSat 3 Oct 2026 11.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Conservatives are planning to make sweeping cuts beyond the£47bn announced last yearif they win the next election, according to leaked comments by the shadow chancellor.Speaking last year when he was shadow business secretary, Andrew Griffith told Conservative members he and fellow shadow cabinet ministers had discussed making further cuts in “every part of government”.The comments, which have emerged on the eve of the Tory party conference in Birmingham, suggested that theConservativesare planning to make cuts similar in scale to those made during the austerity years should they take power.More than a fifth of UK’s ‘austerity children’ scarred by poverty, study saysRead moreLast October, Griffith said: “There are decisions made and signed up to by everybody to deliver that £47bn. Last week at the shadow cabinet, we talked about [how] we will need to go further.“The rate at which the economy is deteriorating, as well as our ambition to cut more taxes, means that we will have to find further savings, and I’m up for that in my department. I know there are areas that we can make savings, and that’s true of every every part of government.”He added: “There is a moral mission to get our economy growing, give people opportunity, as well as let people keep more of what they earn. It’s pretty simple. We’re Conservative, this is what we stand for.”A Tory spokesperson acknowledged the party was seeking to make cuts beyond what it had already announced.“Under Kemi Badenoch’s leadership, the Conservatives have consistently advocated for a smaller state and a government that does fewer things but better,” the spokesperson said.“InBirmingham, we will go further, setting out further savings to Labour’s bloated welfare bill and cracking down on wasteful spending as part of our plans to build a stronger economy and a stronger country.”Kemi Badenoch has previously outlined how the government wouldcut government spendingby £47bn, mainly by cutting welfare spending for all non-British or EU citizens.The plans would also save £8bn by cutting 132,000 civil service jobs, another £1.6bn by scrapping almost all of Labour’s clean energy scheme and more than £7bn by cutting international aid.In August she promoted Griffith, who previously worked as chief operating officer for Sky, from his role as shadow business secretary.In government, Griffith worked in the Treasury under Kwasi Kwarteng and was one of the ministers tasked with defending the mini-budget even as the markets tanked in response.On Friday Badenoch promised another £4bn of spending reductions, including taking another £2.5bn out of the aid budget – leaving it with just £1bn as year – as well as reducing the budget of the Department for Culture, Media and Sport by £1bn.The Tory leader said she would use half of those savings to pay for an additional 50,000 prison places. She has previously promised to use half of any cuts she makes to reduce the deficit.Griffiths’ leaked comments come as the Tories prepare to gather in Birmingham for their annual conference, with Badenoch seeking to make a virtue of the growing distance between Labour’s plans for government and her own.The prime minister, Andy Burnham, has promised a series of potentially expensive interventions, including a new national care service and public control over utility companies, as he seeks to end what he calls “40 years of neoliberalism”.However, Badenoch, who has calledMargaret Thatcherher hero, is attempting to gain an electoral advantage with her vision of lower taxes and a significantly smaller state.“[Thatcher] is somebody who brought a lot of wealth and prosperity to this country,” the Tory leader told ITV Meridian on Friday.“Privatisation was a success … I don’t think that Andy Burnham running the water companies is the answer to those problems.”The Tories remain in third place in the polls, behind Labour and Reform UK, although Badenoch’s personal ratings have rallied over the last 12 months.Explore more on these topicsConservativesConservative conferenceAusterityPublic sector cutsLabourMargaret ThatcherBirminghamnewsShareReuse this content

title: UK-Iran national arrested over alleged bomb plot at RAF Fairford released on bail | UK news | The Guardian
description: The 25-year-old was the sixth man detained as counter-terrorism police investigate ‘possible foreign state involvement’
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The 25-year-old was the sixth man detained as counter-terrorism police investigate ‘possible foreign state involvement’
Content: Police patrol the perimeter of RAF Fairford as a US bomber lands.Photograph: Ben Birchall/PAView image in fullscreenPolice patrol the perimeter of RAF Fairford as a US bomber lands.Photograph: Ben Birchall/PAUK newsUK-Iran national arrested over alleged bomb plot at RAF Fairford released on bailThe 25-year-old was the sixth man detained as counter-terrorism police investigate ‘possible foreign state involvement’PA MediaSat 3 Oct 2026 09.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA sixth man who was arrested in connection with a suspected terrorist plot at RAF Fairford has been released on bail.The 25-year-old, a dual UK-Iranian national, was arrested on suspicion of preparing terrorist acts under section 5 of the Terrorism Act 2006.He was detained on Thursday in the borough of Westminster, London, where searches of two properties have now concluded.The investigation into the incident is still under way, counter-terrorism police said.Last weekend, five British nationals, all in their mid-20s, were arrested on suspicion of explosives offences and terrorism and then bailed.The arrests were made after three suspicious vans were spotted near the military site in Gloucestershire.View image in fullscreenFive men were arrested last weekend after police were alerted to suspicious vans near RAF Fairford.Photograph: BBCVicki Evans, the senior national coordinator for Counter Terrorism Policing, previously said the investigation was “hugely complex”, adding that specialist teams were “interrogating multiple lines of inquiry”.She said: “As we’ve made clear, we’re looking at all possible angles – including possible foreign state involvement.”The prime minister, Andy Burnham, has said there were “strong indications” Iran played a part in the incident near the Gloucestershire military base.RAF Fairford has been used in recent months by US bombers after former prime minister Keir Starmer granted Washington permission to use British bases for “defensive” strikes against Tehran.View image in fullscreenA B‑1B Lancer bomber departs RAF Fairford airbase after police declared a major incident at the base last weekend.Photograph: Toby Shepheard/ReutersCounter-terrorism police have said a quantity of petrol, but no explosive devices, was found in the vans that had sparked the security alert near the airbase.On Thursday, the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, claimed Israel handed Britain intelligence about the suspected terror plot.Netanyahu said his country warned UK authorities about the “Iranian-sponsored attack” shortly before Britain’s announcement of a ban on trade with illegal Israeli settlements in the West Bank.Explore more on these topicsUK newsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Greens would nationalise Thames and SE Water without paying compensation, says deputy leader – as it happened | Politics | The Guardian
description: Rachel Millward tells Brighton conference: ‘Forget compensation for shareholders and creditors, these are insolvent companies’
Author: Frances Mao
Headline: Rachel Millward tells Brighton conference: ‘Forget compensation for shareholders and creditors, these are insolvent companies’
Content: 05.36 EDTMillward calls for immediate takeback of 'failed' water companiesShe calls for national takeover of South East Water and Thames Water, without compensation for shareholders. She tells conference:double quotation markBurnham’s 10 year plan of gentle threats and vague notions of control is not enough. Too many of our water companies have already failed.Right here in Sussex, we too often find ourselves driving to pick up bottled water because nothing is coming out of our taps.Not a single major reservoir has been built in this country since the beginning of privatisation 35 years ago.And so, today, the Green Party is announcing that we would, immediately - not in 10 years, but before Christmas, bring South East Water and Thames Water back into public ownership at no cost to the tax payer.We have all the tools we need to make it happen. Forget compensation for shareholders and creditors, these are insolvent companies.Earlier she had laid out the issue:double quotation markWe see the sewage being pumped into our river by private profit making companies - and we see just how far wrong we’ve gone.Water - the very stuff of life - uniquely found on this planet in the whole wide universe - the stuff we’re made of - it replenishes us, cleans us, connects us… and we — sold it.ShareUpdated at05.57 EDT

title: Trump appears to share personal phone number of US senator in ploy to push permanent daylight savings | Donald Trump | The Guardian
description: US president urges Americans to call Tom Cotton to support bill to make daylight saving time permanent
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: US president urges Americans to call Tom Cotton to support bill to make daylight saving time permanent
Content: Donald Trump and Tom Cotton in Washington DC in 2017.Photograph: REX/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenDonald Trump and Tom Cotton in Washington DC in 2017.Photograph: REX/ShutterstockDonald TrumpTrump appears to share personal phone number of US senator in ploy to push permanent daylight savingsUS president urges Americans to call Tom Cotton to support bill to make daylight saving time permanentAssociated Press and Guardian staffSat 3 Oct 2026 18.07 EDTFirst published on Sat 3 Oct 2026 16.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDonald Trumpon Saturday put pressure on the US senator Tom Cotton ofArkansasto support a bill to make daylight saving time permanent, urging Americans to call what appeared to be the personal cellphone number of his fellow Republican and the chair of the Senate intelligence committee.The Sunshine Protection Actpassedthe House in July, but it faces roadblocks in the Senate, where some Republicans are strongly opposed to it. Proponents, including the president and his administration, argue that the change would provide more daylight during the times that Americans are most active. Detractors said permanent daylight saving time would lead to darker and potentially more hazardous winter mornings when children will be waiting for school buses and parents will be driving to work in darkness.Daylight saving time is that period between spring and fall when clocks in most parts of the US are set one hour ahead of standard time. Not all states observe it – and under the bill, states can opt out of the change if their respective legislatures act to do so before the bill’s enactment.“For some reason, Tom is stopping the Bill,” Trump wrote on social media, noting that passing the proposal would give professional golfers more time on the greens. “So, everyone inArkansas… tell Tom to, GET IT DONE! It will be appreciated by all.”“Call Tom on his cellphone,” Trump added, and included a phone number with an Arkansas area code. The Associated Press called the number, but no one answered – and the voicemail box was full.The Guardian also called and was greeted with a message from the service carrier saying, “The wireless customer you are calling is not available. Please try again later.”Cotton, a member of Republican leadership, reiterated his opposition to permanent daylight saving time in a social media post of his own on Saturday afternoon, though he is not the only Republican who opposes it.“No one likes changing the clock, me included, but Congress has enacted permanent daylight saving time multiple times before and repealed it each time once Americans experienced absurdly late sunrises in the winter,” he wrote. “Arkansans don’t want their kids going to school in the pitch dark, and I’ll always put Arkansas first.”Cotton argued last year on the Senate floor that many Arkansans wouldn’t get sunrise until 8am or 8.30am during the dead of winter if daylight saving time was permanent. In that case, at the height of winter, people in Seattle wouldn’t see sunrise until 9am; and in Williston, North Dakota, the sun wouldn’t rise until nearly 9.45am, Cotton said.“The darkness of permanent daylight savings time would be especially harmful for schoolchildren and working Americans,” Cotton said. “As we saw in 1974, kids would … walk to school in the pitch black.”As he left the White House later on Saturday for a campaign rally in Ohio, Trump was asked why he had posted Cotton’s phone number.“We want to get away from this ridiculous way and custom of every – twice a year, turning your clocks back, turning your clocks forward, being late for dinner, being late for very important meetings,” Trump replied.Pointing to the White House behind him, Trump said that he was speaking from personal experience. “Last time, six months ago, we’re changing clocks, and nobody changed the clocks, and everybody’s late … it discombobulates everybody,” he said.This is not the first time Trump has released a US senator’s phone number.While competing for the 2016 Republican presidential nomination, the US senator Lindsey Graham of South Carolina described Trump as “unfit for office” after Trump denigrated the military service of the US senator John McCain of Arizona. Trump then released Graham’s personal cellphone number. That prompted a viral video in which the senator dramatically destroyed a series of flip phones. Graham later became a close ally of Trump before dying in July. McCain died in 2018.A 2025 poll from the AP-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research shows that if forced to choose, most Americans would prefer to keep that extra hour of daylight in the evening. Only 12% of US adults favor the current system of daylight saving time, which requires people in most states to reset clocks twice a year, while 47% are opposed and 40% are neutral.Members of Congress have long been interested in the potential benefits and costs of daylight saving time since it was first adopted as a wartime measure in 1942 during the second world war. The Senate passed a bill in 2022 to make daylight saving time permanent, but it stalled in the House.Explore more on these topicsDonald TrumpUS SenateUS CongressUS politicsArkansasnewsShareReuse this content

title: Tennessee’s top prison official resigning after botched execution of Christa Pike | Tennessee | The Guardian
description: Frank Strada leaving position as state launches independent investigation into what went wrong
Author: Marina Dunbar
Headline: Frank Strada leaving position as state launches independent investigation into what went wrong
Content: Frank Strada in Nashville, Tennessee, on 11 December 2025.Photograph: George Walker IV/APView image in fullscreenFrank Strada in Nashville, Tennessee, on 11 December 2025.Photograph: George Walker IV/APTennesseeTennessee’s top prison official resigning after botched execution of Christa PikeFrank Strada leaving position as state launches independent investigation into what went wrongMarina Dunbarand agenciesSat 3 Oct 2026 13.09 EDTLast modified on Sat 3 Oct 2026 15.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTennessee’s top prison official is stepping down in the aftermath of the failed execution of death row prisonerChrista Pike, the state’s governor Bill Lee announced Saturday.Frank Strada, the department of correction commissioner, will leave his position later in October as the state launches an independent investigation into what went wrong during Wednesday’s botched execution of Pike, according to Lee.Strada for his part said his resignation would allow that review to move forward in the best interests ofTennessee.“Serving as commissioner of the Tennessee department of correction has been a great honor, and I continue to believe the department carried out its responsibilities in accordance with the established protocol,” Strada said in his resignation statement.“Even so, stepping aside is in the best interest of Tennesseans as the independent review moves forward,” he said. “I believe this review is entirely appropriate and necessary, and I look forward to doing everything I can to help determine exactly what occurred.”Strada handed in his resignation amid intensifying scrutiny of Tennessee’s closely guarded execution procedures after Pike was injected with lethal drugs on Wednesdaybut survived. She became the first death row prisoner in the US to undergo such an execution attempt and live.Pike’s attorney Randy Spivey, who witnessed the procedure from inside the death chamber, described what happened as “cruel and torturous”. He said he personally counted seven needles inserted into Pike’s left arm, “one of which appeared to be bent when it was pulled from her”.Attorneys have alleged that Pike’s failed lethal injection was the fifth “botched” executioncarried out under Strada’s leadershipin two states since 2022, as the Guardian reported on Saturday, hours before his resignation was announced.Pikeremained unconsciousand on a ventilator at a hospital as of Friday, according to a court filing submitted by her attorneys. Her lawyers said hospital personnel were trying to save her life and, as of late Thursday, were working to clear the two doses of the execution drug from her system.Wednesday’s extraordinary breakdown inside Tennessee’s execution chamber has triggered demands for an explanation from people on both sides of the death penalty debate. Besides ordering the independent review into case, Lee has paused the scheduling of executions in Tennessee.Pike’s attorneys said they believe complications involving intravenous lines caused pentobarbital to enter her body rather than her bloodstream.“Frank Strada’s resignation does not change the fact that Tennessee is shrouding its executions in secrecy,” Kit Thomas, a death row attorney in the federal public defender’s office in Nashville, said in a statement. “When Governor Lee hired Strada to fix execution problems in Tennessee his problematic history of executions in Arizona was well known. Strada then oversaw the implementation of a new protocol that ignored the recommendations of the independent investigation and weakened protections leading to a string of problems in Tennessee, including this week’s horrific botched execution attempt and another one in May. Until there is transparency and accountability, botched executions will keep happening.”Laura Porter, the executive director of the US Campaign to End the Death Penalty, said in a statement: “Hopefully this is the beginning of accountability and an end to secrecy that enables these debacles.”“Attorneys and community leaders across Tennessee have been trying for some time to get the Governor and the administration to take seriously the huge problems with the competency of the state’s execution process,” Porter’s statement continued. “They were ignored.”Pike, 50, was sentenced to death for the 1995 killing of teenage classmate Colleen Slemmer. Pike and her then boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, killed Slemmer at a job training camp in Knoxville.A pentagram had been carved into Slemmer’s chest.After the murder, Pike was diagnosed with bipolar and post-traumatic stress disorders, her attorneys said.“It took me numerous years to even realize the gravity of what I’d done,” Pike had said in an earlier petition for clemency. “Even more to accept how many lives I affected. I took the life of someone’s child, sister, friend. It sickens me now to think I had the ability to commit such a crime.”Had her execution that day succeeded, Pike on Wednesday would have been the first woman put to death in Tennessee in more than 200 years.The Associated Press contributed reportingExplore more on these topicsTennesseeCapital punishment (US news)US prisonsUS crimeUS politicsCapital punishment (World news)newsShareReuse this content

title: Florida jury finds ex-sheriff’s deputy not guilty in shooting death of Black air force airman | Florida | The Guardian
description: Roger Fortson was shot by deputy when he opened door with gun in hand after a false domestic disturbance call
Author: Marina Dunbar
Headline: Roger Fortson was shot by deputy when he opened door with gun in hand after a false domestic disturbance call
Content: Chantemekki Fortson, mother of Roger Fortson, holds a photo of her son during a news conference on 9 May 2024 in Fort Walton Beach, Florida.Photograph: Gerald Herbert/APView image in fullscreenChantemekki Fortson, mother of Roger Fortson, holds a photo of her son during a news conference on 9 May 2024 in Fort Walton Beach, Florida.Photograph: Gerald Herbert/APFloridaFlorida jury finds ex-sheriff’s deputy not guilty in shooting death of Black air force airmanRoger Fortson was shot by deputy when he opened door with gun in hand after a false domestic disturbance callMarina DunbarSat 3 Oct 2026 12.44 EDTLast modified on Sat 3 Oct 2026 12.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAFloridajury recently found former sheriff’s deputy Eddie Duran not guilty ofmanslaughterwith a firearm in the fatal shooting of Roger Fortson, a Black US air force airman who was killed inside his apartment after authorities responded to an unfounded report of a domestic disturbance.An Okaloosa county jury acquitted Duran, 38, on Thursday after about two hours of deliberations. He had faced up to 30 years in prison if convicted.Duran, who is Hispanic, was an Okaloosa county sheriff’s deputy in May 2024 when he was sent to Fortson’s apartment in Fort Walton Beach where Fortson – originally fromAtlanta– was stationed.Former Dallas police officer convicted of murdering Black neighbor given early paroleRead moreAuthorities have said Duran was directed to the apartment after a report of a domestic disturbance that turned out to be false.After Duran repeatedly knocked on the door,Fortsonanswered while holding a handgun at his side with the weapon pointed toward the ground. Authorities say Duran fired multiple times before telling Fortson to drop the gun. The encounter was captured on the deputy’s body camera.Thursday’s verdict came after a four-day trial.One day after Duran was acquitted, civil rights attorney Ben Crump said that Fortson’s family would continue its legal fight and vowed to “seek accountability” through the civil court system for the 2024 shooting.While the criminal prosecution has ended with Duran’s acquittal, a federal civil rights lawsuit filed by Fortson’s family remains pending.“Roger’s life and his service will always matter,” Crump said ina statementon Friday. “His family will keep fighting for him, and we will stand with them as they pursue their civil rights case in federal court and seek accountability for the tragic loss of his life.”Duran was fired from the Okaloosa sheriff’s office after killing Fortson. His defense attorney argued that the former deputy was “doing his job” and said Fortson would still be alive if he had not armed himself before answering the door.Fortson’s mother, Chantemekki Fortson, told the Atlanta news outletWXIAshe was unsurprised by the verdict, citing the speed of the jury’s deliberations. “They went to deliberate for just two hours,” she said. “So, again, I wasn’t surprised.”She also said the trial forced her to face details surrounding her son’s death that she had spent the previous two years trying to avoid.“Now I can’t do that,” she told WXIA. “Like he’s really gone.“He’s never coming back. He’s never gonna say, ‘Mom, what you doing? Mom, you wanna go get something to eat? Mom, you need do your hair.’ Like I’m never going to hear my baby’s voice no more.”Explore more on these topicsFloridaUS crimeUS justice systemAtlantaUS policingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Shop clerk and son charged with selling illegal kratom after two Ole Miss students die from suspected overdoses | Mississippi | The Guardian
description: Aidan Hamilton and Robert Strang died after apparently ingesting kratom product last month
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Aidan Hamilton and Robert Strang died after apparently ingesting kratom product last month
Content: Mosleh and his son were arrested after a DEA informant allegedly purchased the kratom product in their store.Photograph: Joe Burbank/APView image in fullscreenMosleh and his son were arrested after a DEA informant allegedly purchased the kratom product in their store.Photograph: Joe Burbank/APMississippiShop clerk and son charged with selling illegal kratom after two Ole Miss students die from suspected overdosesAidan Hamilton and Robert Strang died after apparently ingesting kratom product last monthAssociated PressSat 3 Oct 2026 12.17 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFederal authorities investigating the recent deaths of two University ofMississippistudents have charged a store clerk and his son with selling an illegal kratom product, prosecutors announced on Friday.A drug taskforce inMississippihad previously urged people to avoid kratom, an herbal substance that acts as a stimulant at low doses and a sedative at high doses, after authorities found packages of kratom derivatives while investigating the deaths on 21 September.It is still not clear whether those substances contributed to either death – but federal prosecutors said both appear consistent with drug overdoses. Two state agencies were working to expedite toxicology reports for the students, the Mississippi governor, Tate Reeves,saidin a 23 September statement. The Lafayette county metro narcotics unit said on Thursday that the investigation remained active and additional charges were possible.Kratom poisonings soar in US as experts blame synthetic versions and caution against bansRead moreBank records show one of the students, Aidan Hamilton, made multiple purchases in September from a vape, tobacco and beer store in Oxford, Mississippi, where the university is located, according to a federal court filing.On 24 September, an informant sent to the store by investigators bought kratom-based pills from the clerk, 51-year-old Yahya Mohamed Mosleh, who warned the informant to “be careful taking the pills because people were dying from them”, the US Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) special agent Michael Dassance said in an affidavit.Authorities later detained Mosleh and his son, 18-year-old Islam Yahya Mosleh, who was working behind the counter, and charged them each with one count of possession with the intent to distribute a controlled substance.Attorneys Scott Davis and AE Harlow Jr, who respectively represent the elder Mosleh and Islam Mosleh, said in emails that they had no comment. The defendants appeared on Thursday before a magistrate judge, who ruled there was sufficient evidence to charge them.Kratom, which comes from a tree native to south-east Asia, is legal at the federal level. But some state and local governments have banned it, and federal authorities have issued warnings about its risks.Proponents say that in its pure, ground-leaf form, kratom is a safe, natural herbal supplement that can help manage pain, anxiety and depression, and ease the effects of opioid withdrawal. They say the danger is from kratom derivatives, which are often synthetic and can be highly potent.In August, the DEA banned three kratom-related compounds.The 25 September affidavit from Dassance, the DEA agent, said one of the banned compounds was listed as an ingredient in products seized from the Oxford store and Hamilton’s room.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Around 2-3 times a daySign up toBreaking News USGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHamilton – a freshman from Englewood, Colorado – and the other student who died, Robert Strang, a junior from Atlanta, were found in different locations, one on campus and the other off campus.Investigators found opened packages of kratom or synthetic kratom, labeled “Smax”, in Hamilton’s room with some pills missing, according to the DEA agent’s affidavit. A package of Smax was also found in Strang’s room, though the affidavit says he bought it from a different store.Yahya Mosleh told the informant who went to the store on 24 September to be quiet when other customers came in and pushed the kratom pills out of sight. When the customers left, he completed the sale, according to the affidavit, again telling the informant to be careful.Eleven states have banned kratom. Others, including Mississippi, have regulated it, in part by requiring people to be 21 or older to buy it.The city of Oxford, additionally, has implemented its own kratom ban.Explore more on these topicsMississippiDrugsUS crimenewsShareReuse this content

title: TSA to prohibit airport security officers from sitting down while checking travelers’ IDs | Trump administration | The Guardian
description: TSA says rule change is meant to keep officers ‘alert’, but union says it ignores safety and ‘common decency’
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: TSA says rule change is meant to keep officers ‘alert’, but union says it ignores safety and ‘common decency’
Content: A TSA spokesperson justified the rule change by saying that officers must be ‘capable of performing their vital national security function’.Photograph: Nam Y Huh/APView image in fullscreenA TSA spokesperson justified the rule change by saying that officers must be ‘capable of performing their vital national security function’.Photograph: Nam Y Huh/APTrump administrationTSA to prohibit airport security officers from sitting down while checking travelers’ IDsTSA says rule change is meant to keep officers ‘alert’, but union says it ignores safety and ‘common decency’Keely AougaSat 3 Oct 2026 11.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleUS airport security officers who verify boarding passes and IDs ahead of security checkpoints will no longer be allowed to sit down while working.The Transportation Security Administration (TSA) was moving forward with this change in policy to keep officers “alert”, the agency confirmed recently.“This welcome change reinforces both our security posture and our commitment to hospitality by having these officers on their feet and alert,” a TSA spokesperson said in astatement to ABC News.“All officers must meet fitness for duty requirements to be capable of performing their vital national security function while simultaneously creating a welcoming and professional environment for travelers,” the statement added.The American Federation of Government Employees Council (AFGEC), the union representing TSA officers, pushed back on this decision and said in astatementthat it was not involved in the decision.“These chairs serve as basic ergonomic and safety support for officers that stand and walk on hard surfaces all day,” the union added. “TSA is treating this matter like it is a privilege – it is not; it is basic safety and common decency for the workforce.”Additionally, the union is calling the TSA’s move a “disregard for employee rights and safety”.“This disregard for employee rights and safety is an example of a broad pattern of TSA’s true consideration of the employees who keep our nation safe,” the union’s statement said.The TSA has navigated a tumultuous year after withstanding a 76-day government shutdown from February to April that resulted in officers working without pay.Due to the shutdown, some TSA workers did not report for unpaid duty or quit their jobs – andlines at security checkpoints grewacross the US.TSA workers were finally paid at the end of March after a presidential order from Donald Trump. The government shutdown ended on 30 April after the US House passed a bill funding the Department of Homeland Security.Furthermore, the labor union israising alarmsover a new program that will expand privatizing security checkpoints at three airports.The AFGE has beenreviewinglegal options to fight back against the privatization push from the Trump administration.As TSA workers navigate the growing changes to the agency under theTrump administration, the union is urging congressional and senatorial leaders to join its “collective resistance” against the administration.“This is an opportune time to meet with members and non-members alike to tell and show them the importance of joining this union to form our collective resistance against this regime that is literally attempting to take out our workforce through whichever means possible,” it concluded.Explore more on these topicsTrump administrationAir transportUS unionsUS politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: The American dream remains elusive in the valley that inspired East of Eden | California | The Guardian
description: John Steinbeck’s hometown of Salinas is the least affordable city in the US for the middle class, a recent Brookings Institution analysis found
Author: Gaya Gupta
Headline: John Steinbeck’s hometown of Salinas is the least affordable city in the US for the middle class, a recent Brookings Institution analysis found
Content: ‘This will be a valley of great richness one day,’ Steinbeck wrote in East of Eden. ‘And happy people will live here, thousands and thousands.’Composite: Rita Liu/The Guardian/Getty Images/Monterey countyView image in fullscreen‘This will be a valley of great richness one day,’ Steinbeck wrote in East of Eden. ‘And happy people will live here, thousands and thousands.’Composite: Rita Liu/The Guardian/Getty Images/Monterey countyCaliforniaThe American dream remains elusive in the valley that inspired East of EdenJohn Steinbeck’s hometown of Salinas is the least affordable city in the US for the middle class, a recent Brookings Institution analysis foundGaya Guptain Salinas, CaliforniaSat 3 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 3 Oct 2026 05.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNestled between two mountain ranges at the crook of central California’s coastline sits a valley known as the “salad bowl of the world”.Farm workers stoop over neatly lined rows of crops off Highway 101 to harvest more than half of the nation’s supply of lettuce and nearly a third of its strawberries. The soil here is so rich that authorJohn Steinbeckmade the Salinas valley the promised land in his literary depictions of people chasing the American dream: immigrants, farm workers, westward-moving hopefuls, hungering for a better life.It’s a story that continues to capture the American imagination: Netflix has adapted Steinbeck’s 1952 blockbuster novel, East of Eden, into a limited series starring Florence Pugh, released 1 October.“This will be a valley of great richness one day,” Steinbeck wrote of the farmland in East of Eden. “And happy people will live here, thousands and thousands.”View image in fullscreenThe Salinas valley in California.Photograph: Pgiam/Getty Images/iStockphotoBut Steinbeck also understood just how difficult it can be to achieve that elusive American dream. Even after some his characters found their way to Salinas and other parts of California’s agricultural valley, many remained stuck in low-paying jobs, making barely enough to scrape by, let alone own their own land.That reality persists in the Salinas of today – an area at the sharp edge of a national affordability crisis that is reshaping politics across the US, and much of the rest of the world.A recent Brookings Institution analysis found that Salinas is the least affordable city in the US for the middle class, defined as the middle 60% of income earners. Nearly 60% of the middle class in the Salinas area – which spans households making $38,000 to $193,000 – can’t afford basic necessities, double the national average, according to the analysis. And for Salinas’s Latino middle class, which make up 40% of all middle-class households, three-quarters struggle to afford everyday life.Residents specifically say that homeownership, the modern symbol of the American dream, is out of reach. It’s an issue that is playing out across the country: half of all renter households and about a quarter of homeowner households spend more than 30% of their income on housing, according to the latest data from the US census.“It really calls in question: what is the middle class?” said Andre Perry, a senior fellow at Brookings who oversaw the study. Many towns like Salinas that served as havens for the middle class are now out of reach. “People go to Salinas as a reprieve from San Francisco and some of these high-priced cities, but in actuality, they’re finding it more difficult to live,” he said.Solutions are not easy to come by. The rising cost of living has torn Salinas apart. New housing has grown at a snail’s pace, and a rent-stabilization policy has bitterly divided residents.If life in places like Salinas becomes too expensive for American families, where do they go next?‘Everything’s changed’Steinbeck had a conflicted relationship with his home town, said Gavin Jones, chair of the English department at Stanford University and a Steinbeck scholar, one that he often reflected in his writing. For many of Steinbeck’s characters, California and its farmland ultimately prove to be gutting disappointments after everything they sacrificed to get there.“It’s kind of the promised land. It’s this realm of richness,” said Jones of the role Salinas played in Steinbeck’s magnum opus. “But then of course, it’s also a fallen paradise … it’s not quite Eden, it’s east of Eden.”Steinbeck was born to a solidly middle-class family and was raised in a turreted, Victorian-style house that still stands just a few blocks away from Salinas’s downtown. He was long critical of the hypocrisy and “underbelly” he saw in his social demographic, Jones said, and worked alongside immigrant workers on nearby farms while dropping in and out of Stanford University.View image in fullscreenThe house in Salinas, California, where author John Steinbeck was born, seen on 25 February 1978.Photograph: Chris Pizzello/APSteinbeck was also “very American” in his idealized vision of social mobility, ascendancy and agency, Jones added, and would have likely been outraged at the affordability struggles many still face in the US, accentuated by theincreasingly“K-shaped economy” with the rich getting richer as the poor slide down the other side.“One wonders if the conditions are that much different today in the central valley, especially for agricultural workers … from the conditions that Steinbeck represented in the 1930s,” Jones said.Gaye Freedman, 75, and her husband had been searching for somewhere affordable to live for years before they moved to Salinas in 2017, where their son was raising a baby as a single dad. Though they passed up more affordable cities in northern California, the beautiful, year-round weather – cool, foggy mornings that give way to balmy afternoons – as well as proximate medical care for older adults made their decision easier.But Freedman, who earned a doctorate degree in educational psychology from the University of Southern California, was unable to find much work in Salinas that paid much beyond minimum wage. She currently works part-time at a school.Between part-time jobs and social security, Freedman and her husband make about $75,000 total and pay $1,850 for their one-bedroom apartment, which became a rent-stabilized unit in 2024. After rent and Medicare payments, they don’t have much left to spare on groceries, gas and unexpected maintenance on their 14-year-old car. The balance on their credit card, she said, keeps climbing.“This is the first time in my life I’ve actually had to think about what I’m cooking, because I can’t afford to cook what I usually would,” she said. “We’re eating a lot more stews and spaghetti and chicken. I’m definitely thinking of what lasts more than one day.”View image in fullscreenGaye Freedman in her neighborhood in Salinas, on 22 July.Photograph: Nic Coury/The GuardianFreedman and her husband have considered moving, but many of the affordable cities nearby lack medical care facilities or infrastructure that will be crucial for the couple as they get older.Other residents cited similar concerns of getting pushed out by the cost of living. Salvador Herrera, 52, a former construction worker who grew up in Salinas, said gone are the days of his childhood where a family could raise their children in their own apartment unit or home. In Salinas, it is now common for multiple families to live together: garages are partitioned with curtains; single bedrooms are crammed with young children and parents; and bathrooms are shared among dozens.Herrera supports his family using disability payments after an injury on the job left him unable to work. Rising rent has sometimes meant weeks where he has just $50 to spend on groceries for himself and his two children.“Everything’s changed. Especially the housing, it’s way too expensive. And the pay is cheap nowadays,” he said.Salinas’s close proximity to Silicon valley leaves it vulnerable to the same housing woes faced by the rest of the Bay Area, housing experts say.Its surrounding farmland also makes it difficult to expand and build there, all of which has led to a persistent lack of housing supply that has pushed up prices for years. Meanwhile, the median household income in Salinas is just shy of $90,000, compared with a median of roughly $150,000 in San Jose or San Francisco.“We got caught up early on Bay Area economics,” Salinas mayor Dennis Donohue said at a Starbucks across from the Salinas Sports Complex, where he was attending an agricultural biotechnology conference. “You have all the economic challenges of the Bay Area impacting Salinas and this area without corresponding economic opportunities.”All of this pressure comes even as California is home to some of the most progressive housing policies in the US, with rent caps on most households statewide and further protections at the local level. Still, residents face the highest median monthly housing costs in the country, according to the latest census data.Critics on both sides of the political aisle have in part criticized the state’s governor, Gavin Newsom, for the state’s cost-of-living crisis, including sky-high housing costs. Newsom, who is considering a presidential run, has blamed Trump but may well find voters – and his opponents – put the blame closer to home.View image in fullscreenHomes listed for sale in Salinas, on 26 July.Photograph: Nic Coury/The GuardianMeanwhile, housing is one of the most potent issues at the voting polls:a recent survey from CNBCfound that the high cost of housing was the most pressing concern for voters aged 18 to 34 years old.Trouble in paradiseThe Salinas city council sent Freedman and many more struggling households a lifeline in 2024, when itpassed a rent-stabilization ordinancethat capped annual rent increases on certain multifamily rental properties to either 2.75% or three-quarters of the annual inflation rate, whichever is less. Freedman says she’s saved thousands of dollars already because of the caps her landlord now places on her rent increases each year.But the town has been heavily divided on the policy. When a new city council board took over the next year,it repealed the policy, arguing the ordinance unfairly penalized apartment property owners and would discourage much-needed housing construction.A referendum vote was announced for this November after advocacy groups gathered enough signatures. Rent stabilization will remain until then, but it’s unclear where voters will land.It’s a deeply emotional issue for Salinas, said Tony Barrera, a longtime resident and a city council representative who was among the minority who voted to keep rent stabilization in 2025. His district is overwhelmingly supportive of keeping the measures in place: 70% are renters and 80% are field workers, he said. About a third are undocumented, which means they won’t be able to vote in the fall.But he also raised concerns that landlords in his district would not be able to afford their mortgage or property maintenance with the ordinance. If they sell their homes, he added, that could end up driving rents up further for his constituents.“I’m caught in the middle,” he said.Matt Huerta, an affordable housing expert based in Salinas and an advocate for rent stabilization, said that landlords can apply for exemptions if they need to raise rents higher than the ordinance allows.“We recognize that sometimes costs are higher than inflation. Sometimes tariffs come in, and all of a sudden you can’t get that refrigerator or water heater,” he said. “There’s an application process for that.”Amy Salmina, a property manager in Salinas, said many of the middle-class homeowners she works with have been selling their properties due to rising costs. Most are in their 60s and bought rental properties as investments, but rising property taxes and insurance have ultimately handed them greater losses.View image in fullscreenAgricultural fields bordering a neighborhood in Salinas, on 24 July.Photograph: Nic Coury/The GuardianHousing specifically for the middle class is severely lacking in Salinas, she added, and economic opportunities aren’t keeping up with growth.“We have so much help [for] the low-income, which is great,” she said. “But we’re forgetting about the middle class,” she added, referring to families who make “too much money to get any assistance or to get lower-income housing”.Salmina’s family has lived in Salinas for four generations, but she is doubtful that her children will be able to afford to stay.“My son’s a firefighter. I don’t even know how they’re going to be able to buy a house,” she said. “I told all my kids: ‘Look, unless you have two incomes, you guys won’t be able to stay here.’”Those fighting against rent stabilization say that the law would exacerbate the town’s housing crisis, because it could disincentivize investors or developers looking to build in the area. But advocates argue that the city’s rent-stabilization ordinance only applies to buildings built before 1995, so newly built units can still be listed at market price.For years, the city has struggled with a housing supply that hasn’t kept pace with its population. Even though the Salinas city council approved a plan in 2008 tobuild 11,500 new residential units, the Great Recession made it nearly impossible to finance any new construction, said Donohue, who had been in the middle of his first mayoral term at the time.New construction was also stopped by Covid and has been slow to pick up even six years later. Now, with mortgage rates surpassing 7%, a 20-month high, and the US Federal Reserve poised to raise interest rates further, borrowing costs are exacerbating the crisis.But Donohue has optimism for the future of the town, which he says exports “vegetables and too many of our kids”. He and other local officials are trying to bring more job opportunities to the area, while the city council recently approved a down payment assistance plan for first-time homebuyers.“I’m the mayor of the hometown of John Steinbeck,” Donohue said. “If any city should know how to tell a story, it should be this one. I’m confident the city, the book, will have a happy ending.”He just can’t tell you how long it will take.Explore more on these topicsCaliforniaUS income inequalityHousingJohn SteinbeckInequalityWest CoastUS politicsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Manchester City’s guilty verdict brings football’s great sell-off crashing to earth | Manchester City | The Guardian
description: On the day Andy Burnham spoke of the wrong turn Britain took under Thatcher, football was facing a day of reckoning over its own story of corporate acquisition
Author: David Conn
Headline: On the day Andy Burnham spoke of the wrong turn Britain took under Thatcher, football was facing a day of reckoning over its own story of corporate acquisition
Content: Clubs like City, formed in the Victorian smog of industry, were sold off just when football finally had enough wealth to go round.Composite: Guardian Design/Getty Images/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenClubs like City, formed in the Victorian smog of industry, were sold off just when football finally had enough wealth to go round.Composite: Guardian Design/Getty Images/ShutterstockThe Saturday readManchester CityManchester City’s guilty verdict brings football’s great sell-off crashing to earthOn the day Andy Burnham spoke of the wrong turn Britain took under Thatcher, football was facing a day of reckoning over its own story of corporate acquisitionDavid ConnSat 3 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 3 Oct 2026 01.02 EDTShareIt was somehow fitting that Tuesday’s damning ruling againstManchester Citylanded in the heart of the Labour party conference, in the afterglow of Andy Burnham’s rapturously received prime minister’s speech.I was there, and read the astonishing 40 pages of findings – that City created “sham” contracts toboost income artificially by £900m– on my phone during a long meeting of the Socialist Campaign Group, where people were celebrating Keir Starmer’s ousting and Burnham’s more leftwing direction.At the core of Burnham’s speech was the wrong turn he says Britain took underMargaret Thatcherin the 1980s, selling off and privatising council housing, water, energy, transport and care. “We built the common good,” he said, but “the common wealth … created for the many was seen as an opportunity for the few.”He could have been talking about football, too. Where Manchester City have ended up, having been bought by Sheikh Mansour of the Abu Dhabi ruling family in 2008, is a culmination of decades in which “the people’s game” has been carved up for profits. Clubs like City, formed in the Victorian smog of industry by churches, schools and workplaces, then built by generations of supporters into powerful homes of belonging, were sold off just when football finally had enough wealth to go round.I investigated and reported on that financial carve up in my early years of journalism, and Burnham worked on it too, at the start of his political career, as the administrator of New Labour’s football taskforce.My 1997 book, The Football Business, in which I likened football’s commercialisation to Thatcher’s privatisations, chimed with many supporters’ groups campaigning against rocketing ticket prices, exclusive pay-TV deals, and the drawbridge the newly mega-richPremier Leaguehad pulled up behind it.My moment of clarity had come at Manchester City, reporting on an earlier takeover, in 1994 by a beloved former player, Francis “Franny” Lee. I grew up in Manchester and from as early as I could answer the challenge – “which club do you support?” – it was always City for me. My dad took me, fast-walking, hand-in-hand, to big matches in the 1970s, floodlit glory nights of my boyhood. I have always loved the colour blue, especially sky blue, and have never really worn anything red in my life.View image in fullscreenDennis Tueart of Manchester City scores the winning goal against Newcastle United with an overhead kick, 1976.Photograph: Granger/Historical Picture Archive/AlamyFor supporters of my generation, the only trophy City won was the 1976 League Cup, claimed with a wondrous overhead “bicycle” kick goal by our winger, Dennis Tueart. I like art as much as the next ignoramus, but the photograph of Tueart’s goal must be the picture I have gazed at more than any other: the perfection of it, Tueart’s straight back in mid-air, arcing the ball behind him into the Wembley net, Newcastle’s opposition defenders frozen in time for ever.But unlike Manchester United, Liverpool and Arsenal, City never had a period of sustained success. They compressed a golden age into two years, 1968-70, and soon after that League Cup triumph, they were relegated, in 1983. For years, while City fans became celebrated for their loyalty and sod-it humour – taking bananas and other inflatables to matches – there always remained a mournful yearning for success to return.When Lee finally took City over, acclaimed by all supporters, it seemed like deliverance. As a fan in the old Maine Road stadium, I cheered him on Saturday, then as a journalist on Monday I pestered for an interview. They agreed, and I was escorted behind the scenes, along some threadbare corridors into the chairman’s office, where Franny sat glowing behind the desk.View image in fullscreenAn aeroplane flies over Maine Road during a game v Liverpool with a banner urging for chair Peter Swales to leave and be replaced by Francis Lee, October 1993.Photograph: David Davies/Offside/Getty ImagesEverybody involved was so delighted to have pulled it off that they shared details quite gleefully. And that was when I first understood that Manchester City wasn’t a club at all. It was a company, with “owners”, and this had been a corporate acquisition. Franny was one of many other business people, a consortium, who had bought the shares.Later, one of the lawyers proudly showed me some corporate engineering they had done. They had formed a holding company, Manchester City plc, that would own the old football club company.The new millions fromRupert Murdoch’s Sky TVhad poured into the Premier League,a breakaway in 1992 by the top clubs from sharing TV money withthe clubs in the other three divisions of the Football League. This boosted the value of the top club-companies, and the new consortium planned to float City on the stock exchange, like Manchester United and others, where ultimately their shares could then be sold at a profit.I learned that holding companies were formed to bypass the longstanding rules of the Football Association – the game’s governing body – that restricted shareholders being paid dividends, and directors a salary. The FA imposed those at the dawn of professional football in 1892, allowing clubs to form limited liability companies, but limiting the personal money shareholders could make.This was to retain the collective, service ethos of a club. A century on, the rules were still in the FA’s handbook, at No 34. To the relatively small but formidable core of people who really care about these principles, “rule 34” became totemic of football’s sell-off, surrendered to enable vast personal gains by investors. That was now deemed antiquated, blazers’ bureaucracy that must not restrain football’s new business dynamism. To me, it was all a gut punch.This critique was put forcefully to Labour’s football taskforce, with calls by the Football Supporters’ Association for strong regulation to harness the benefits of the new era. Fans understood that German football’s response to the pay TV transformation was to permit corporate reorganisations, but require clubs to be controlled “50% plus one” by mutual supporters associations.New Labour was never going to introduce a football regulator or major reforms, but Burnham worked hard for concrete improvements.The Premier League agreed to distribute 5% of its TV deal to improving desolate grassroots playing facilities via a new grant-giving body,the Football Foundation, which has been transformative. Burnham also championed mutual fan ownership of clubs, helping to establish an organisation, Supporters Direct, to promote it.But the impossible cost for fans of buying and sustaining their clubs has meant over the years that few are mutually owned. The Premier League roared on, and the sell-offs became more corporate. Some original shareholders made fortunes selling, mostly to US investors: about £90m by Martin Edwards at Manchester United; £90m by the Littlewoods pools heir David Moores for selling his Liverpool shares.View image in fullscreenManchester City fans after watching their team win at Stoke but still get relegated in May 1998.Photograph: Alex Livesey/Allsport/Getty ImagesLee and his consortium never managed it, though, and City were relegated to football’s third tier in 1998. Famously he said City would have won a room full of trophies “if cups were awarded for cock-ups”.Mansour’s acquisition of Manchester City10 years later can be seen as the pure essence of “Manchesterism” – spending public money on cultural assets and infrastructure to attract business investors – long before Burnham became mayor of Greater Manchester in 2017 and coined that word this year. The splendid new stadium was built for the 2002 Commonwealth Games with £127m from Manchester city council and the national lottery, the council spending £22m on removing the athletics track and conversion for City to move in. The plan was part of the regeneration of east Manchester, where industry had cranked and smoked, then died in the 1980s.The council leaders could hardly have imagined that cups-for-cock-ups Manchester City would then attract one of the world’s richest buyers, and the oil wealth of the Gulf. But the Premier League’s global ubiquity, the new stadium and the loyal City crowd all added up for Abu Dhabi.If you set aside the glaring concerns about the ruler of a country taking over a local heritage football club, the human rights and geopolitical complications that introduces, and the central dissonance of clubs being owned by investors at all, Mansour has been a dream for Manchester. He has poured billions into the club, to attract, buy and pay the world’s best players and the best manager, Pep Guardiola.View image in fullscreenBoys dressed in head scarves before the first game after the club was bought by the Abu Dhabi United group.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianHis new corporate regime expanded the stadium – named Etihad under a sponsorship deal with the Abu Dhabi state airline, which has now complained that the Premier League’s communication of the commission’s findingshas created “damaging implications” for it.As Burnham acknowledged this week when he described the Abu Dhabi ownership as “a huge partner in the building of modern Manchester”, and gave thanks for the money put in, they have also invested in property development, converting long-derelict mills into apartments for young professionals Manchester was seeking to attract.The dizzying findings of financial cheating were finally delivered this week from a Premier League investigation process that took eight years, which City repeatedly tried to block. City will appeal, and claim, as they have throughout, that they have“irrefutable evidence”disproving the findings of the three-person commission, which took almost two years.View image in fullscreenManchester City’s Vincent Kompany lifts the Premier League trophy after their victory over West Ham at the Etihad Stadium on 11 May 2014.Photograph: Andrew Yates/AFP/Getty ImagesAt the core of Mansour’s ownership has been a ruthless determination not just to make his Premier League acquisition competitive, but to attain total domination. Before 2008, in 116 years of professional football, City only wonthe old First Division championshiptwice.Mansour’s regime has secured the Premier League eight times so far, four FA Cup victories, and the pinnacle, the Champions League,in 2023. The League Cup, so rare and special to my generation, has been brought back from Wembley seven times.Burnham has boldly broken with accepting Thatcher’s great sell-offs, saying they produced today’s fractures.As he left the stage to applauseand acclaim, football’s great sell-off was crashing to earth.

title: Lamine Yamal stars again as Spain see off Czechia and maintain perfect start | Nations League | The Guardian
description: For the third consecutive game the teenager scored inside six minutes, curling in another outrageous goal as Spain shone on their World Cup homecoming
Author: Sid Lowe
Headline: For the third consecutive game the teenager scored inside six minutes, curling in another outrageous goal as Spain shone on their World Cup homecoming
Content: Lamine Yamal opens the scoring for Spain against Czechia in Oviedo.Photograph: Manu Fernández/APView image in fullscreenLamine Yamal opens the scoring for Spain against Czechia in Oviedo.Photograph: Manu Fernández/APNations LeagueLamine Yamal stars again as Spain see off Czechia and maintain perfect startSid LoweSat 3 Oct 2026 17.13 EDTLast modified on Sat 3 Oct 2026 18.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLamine Yamal says he feels like Superman or Spider-Man sometimes, and Spain’s fans are starting to wonder if he just might be. There is something comic book hero about what the teenager is doing right now, some unexplained super power swelling inside him. For the third consecutive game he scored inside six minutes, curling in another outrageous goal as Spain completed their World Cup homecoming in Oviedo with a 3-1 win over Czechia that leaves them a single point from theNations Leaguequarter finals already. Spain’s manager, Luis de la Fuente, put it simply: “Lamine Yamal is on course to become a legend.”Lamine Yamal: ‘Football is mechanised but players like me have that special spark’Read moreAnd yet in a game which seemed to have been done at half-time, when Spain led 2-0 after Rodrigo Hernandez had added the second and Lamine Yamal was withdrawn, his show seemingly over, the danger returned.Czechia, vastly improved after the break, pulled one back through Jiri Slama on 69 and then were denied a 79th-minute equaliser when Vassilis Fotias, the referee, who rescued Spain, harshly ruled out a Ryan Naderi goal – apparently for a foul on Robin Le Normand as the free-kick that led to it was swung in.Reduced to 10 men soon after, still furious, Czechia finally fell with two minutes left when Mikel Merino madeSpainsafe. Theseleccion’sfirst visit to the Carlos Tartiere in 11 years had ended the way they had hoped. Welcomed back as world and European champions once more, they were applauded off as winners again. A night that had begun with Rodri being presented with the World Cup by Santi Cazorla and Juan Mata, academy products at Real Oviedo and members of the generation to which all others would forever be compared, ended with a jeopardy no one anticipated when it started in a way that has become implausibly, absurdly familiar.Lamine Yamal had scored after 104 seconds at Wembley and 70 in Seville, as Spain defeated England and Croatia. And the silly thing was that here, his goal might have come even sooner. Fifteen seconds in, the first frisson of excitement went round this place as he chased down the goalkeeper and after just fifty-seven Oviedo almost exploded. But, running on to a Dani Olmo pass, Lamine Yamal calmly guided a shot past the goalkeeper Antonin Kinsky … and past the post.He would just have to wait until the sixth minute was up instead. Playing a quick one-two with Dani Olmo, Lamine Yamal took possession on the top right corner of the area and curled another outrageous shot into the far corner, the ridiculous becoming routine. They had been playing five minutes 20 seconds, another stadium letting out a roar that spoke of delight but also a kind of disbelief. 320 seconds he had been out there, taking him to 494 seconds to score three.View image in fullscreenRodri reacts after scoring Spain’s second in OviedoPhotograph: Petr David Josek/APSpain weren’t hurrying but they were controlling, and the chances were accumulating: by half-time they had taken 13 shots to one, and enjoyed 70% of possession. They had also added a second on 32 minutes. Rodri collected near the centre circle and did something he rarely does. The man who sometimes seems to be walking, effortlessly controlling the game with his mind and without fuss, happy enough to drop the ball off to others to do their thing, went off on a run. Advancing through the midfield, he slotted to Pedri whose return, with the help of a defender’s touch, set him up to shoot high into the net.Next Lamine Yamal slipped in Alex Baena, denied by Kinsky. A little dinked pass from Baena then found Lamine whose shot, slightly scuffed, went wide. At the break Baena, who had drawn “oohs” with one glorious touch, was withdrawn and so too was Lamine Yamal, his work here done, another show over. The game, on the other hand, was not. That at least was Czechia’s intention and it should probably have been their reward too, the visitors taking a decisive step forward and a degree of control. They also reduced the deficit with 20 minutes to go.The move began deep: as it progressed up the right and through the middle, Jiri Slama was sprinting to catch up. Adam Hlozek saw him coming and played the ball into his path for him to steer it low and true beyond David Raya.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionA first error from Spain’s keeper almost gave Czechia an equaliser when Raya stepped out to play and his misplaced pass only found Ondrej Lingr, and a second error really should have done soon after. But if there was relief for Spain when Lingr’s shot drifted wide of an unguarded goal, it was even greater when the referee ruled out Ryan Nadel’s effort.For Czechia there was disbelief. Michal Sadilek’s long cross had been headed goalwards by Ladislav Krejci, and Raya, reaching by the bar, could not hold on. The ball dropped on the line, where Nadel nudged it in. The referee, though, had blown. For Santi Denia on the touchline it was hard to take and it was equally difficult not to feel sympathy. All the more when Krejci was soon sent off and then Víctor Muñoz was sent clear, dashed into the area where Kinsky blocked and Merino, forever alive, finished off the festivities.Explore more on these topicsNations LeagueSpainCzechiamatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Qatar and Abu Dhabi grands prix to go ahead despite Middle East conflict, says F1 chief  | Formula One 2026 | The Guardian
description: Formula One chief Stefano Domenicali said the final races of the season in Qatar and Abu Dhabi will go ahead as planned despite conflict in the Middle East
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Formula One chief Stefano Domenicali said the final races of the season in Qatar and Abu Dhabi will go ahead as planned despite conflict in the Middle East
Content: McLaren’s Lando Norris races at last season’s Abu Dhabi Grand Prix at the Yas Marina Circuit, where the final race of this season will be staged.Photograph: David Davies/PAView image in fullscreenMcLaren’s Lando Norris races at last season’s Abu Dhabi Grand Prix at the Yas Marina Circuit, where the final race of this season will be staged.Photograph: David Davies/PAFormula One 2026Qatar and Abu Dhabi grands prix to go ahead despite Middle East conflict, says F1 chiefDomenicali confirms schedule for final racesBahrain and Saudi Arabia races were scrappedAFPSat 3 Oct 2026 11.51 EDTLast modified on Sat 3 Oct 2026 13.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe final races of theFormula Oneseason in Qatar and Abu Dhabi will go ahead as planned despite the conflict in the Middle East, the sport’s chief executive, Stefano Domenicali, said on Saturday.‘I want to go’: Lewis Hamilton hopes F1 is able to end season in Middle EastRead more“Based on the information we have, everything is confirmed for [us to stay in] Qatar and Abu Dhabi,” Domenicali told the French broadcaster Canal+ on the sidelines of the Bahrain Grand Prix, which was relocated to the Sepang circuit in Malaysia.Speaking to Sky Sport Italia, the head of motorsport’s blue riband series “confirmed the schedule for the final two grands prix” of the year in Qatar on 29 November and Abu Dhabi on 6 December.The Bahrain and Saudi Arabia grands prixwere scrapped earlier this season due to the start of the US-led war with Iran.Domenicali insisted “that everything was in order” and that “teams and drivers were being kept informed of the situation”. He added that 99% of tickets had been sold in Abu Dhabi and that the season-ending race was generating “great excitement”.However, not all drivers want to compete in the Gulf. Max Verstappen,who will start from pole position in Malaysia on Sunday, said during the week he would prefer if the season did not finish in Qatar and Abu Dhabi.View image in fullscreen“Everything is confirmed for [us to stay in] Qatar and Abu Dhabi,’ Stefano Domenicali told Canal+.Photograph: Jakub Porzycki/NurPhoto/Shutterstock“Normally I am happy to go to Qatar and Abu Dhabi, but you know, when there is a war nearby, and if some of the countries are in conflict with each other, then I think we shouldn’t go,” he told ViaPlay. “Then, it doesn’t matter if you have a contract or not, I think. But it’s not up to me.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |FortnightlySign up toThe HotspotA new fortnightly newsletter covering the intersection of sport and the climate crisisEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionOne of the options discussed was moving the Emirati race to Imola in Italy.Explore more on these topicsFormula One 2026Formula OneMotor sportnewsShareReuse this content

title: WNBA playoffs: Valkyries rally from 16 down to oust Wings and reach last four | WNBA | The Guardian
description: Gabby Williams scored 19 points as Golden State erased a 16-point deficit to beat Dallas 77-73 and advance to the WNBA semi-finals
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Gabby Williams scored 19 points as Golden State erased a 16-point deficit to beat Dallas 77-73 and advance to the WNBA semi-finals
Content: Gabby Williams celebrates after the Golden State Valkyries’ 77-73 win over the Dallas Wings in Game 3 of their first-round WNBA playoff series on Friday in San Francisco.Photograph: Jeff Chiu/APView image in fullscreenGabby Williams celebrates after the Golden State Valkyries’ 77-73 win over the Dallas Wings in Game 3 of their first-round WNBA playoff series on Friday in San Francisco.Photograph: Jeff Chiu/APWNBAWNBA playoffs: Valkyries rally from 16 down to oust Wings and reach last fourGolden State rally from 16 down for 77-73 victoryWilliams scores 19 and hits go-ahead jumperValkyries advance to face defending champion AcesAgenciesSat 3 Oct 2026 12.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGabby Williams scored 19 points and hit a go-ahead 17-footer with 1:17 remaining, and theGolden State Valkyrieswon a late replay review to complete a rally from 16 points down and beat the Dallas Wings 77-73 on Friday night in a wild deciding Game 3 of their first-round WNBA playoff series.With 13.1 seconds left and Golden State leading by one, Williams jumped back inbounds to corral her own miss on a play that was originally ruled Dallas’ ball, but Valkyries coach Natalie Nakase – who moments earlier had fallen to her knees on the sideline before being helped up – successfully challenged the call. Nakase walked off the court escorted by a member of her staff after the final buzzer, holding her face as the team celebrated at midcourt.The team said afterward that she was fine and expected to coach Sunday in Game 1, but assistant coach Kasib Powell addressed the media in the postgame news conference where Nakase typically speaks.The Valkyries will be back at rocking Ballhalla for the series opener, with the team’s deafening, violet-crazed home crowd at Chase Center.Arike Ogunbowale knocked down an off-balance jumper with 3:13 to play that put Dallas up by five and finished with 30 points, following a 45-point performance in the Wings’ overtime win Wednesday night at home.Williams scored all but two of her points after halftime. Veronica Burton had 16 points, 10 rebounds and six assists. Burton’s layup with 8:19 to play pulled the Valkyries within 61-59, Williams hit two three-pointers late in the third and they both willed Golden State into the best-of-five semi-finals against the defendingWNBAchampions, the Las Vegas Aces.Tiffany Hayes scored 18 points off the bench, Kaila Charles hit a tying three-pointer with 6:51 left and Kiah Stokes pulled down 13 rebounds.The second-seeded Valkyries won a playoff series for the first time. Last year, they became the first expansion team to reach the playoffs in their inaugural season.View image in fullscreenArike Ogunbowale drives against Veronica Burton during the fourth quarter of the Dallas Wings’ 77-73 loss to the Golden State Valkyries in Game 3 of their first-round WNBA playoff series on Friday in San Francisco.Photograph: Stephen Lam/San Francisco Chronicle/APPaige Bueckers had 17 points and six assists but shot only 3-for-14 for Dallas, making all 10 of her free throws.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Weekly for the 2026 WNBA seasonSign up toWNBA 30A limited run women’s basketball newsletter dedicated to the league’s historic 30th season.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe Valkyries missed three straight three-pointers and nine shots in a row overall to start the third quarter as Dallas used a 9-0 run to take their largest lead at 53-37. Golden State pulled within 59-54 heading into the final 10 minutes.Ogunbowale was 11-for-21 after scoring a playoff-record 45 points in the Wings’ 108-100 overtime win Wednesday night.That prompted Nakase to declare before the game: “We made a promise to ourselves we are going to play the best four quarters of our lives.”She said the Valkyries didn’t recognize themselves in that game – even though the team had scored 100 or more points in the first two matchups, including a 104-80 win in the series opener last Sunday.Explore more on these topicsWNBAGolden State ValkyriesDallas WingsShareReuse this content

title: Ireland cut short news conference as mood darkens further before Israel game  | Republic of Ireland | The Guardian
description: The Republic of Ireland’s press conference on the eve of their match against Israel in Serbia was cut short as head coach Heimir Hallgrímsson fielded questions from Israeli journalists
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The Republic of Ireland’s press conference on the eve of their match against Israel in Serbia was cut short as head coach Heimir Hallgrímsson fielded questions from Israeli journalists
Content: Ireland’s press officer Kieran Crowley signals an end to the Republic’s media briefing alongside head coach Heimir Hallgrímsson in Backa Topola, Serbia.Photograph: Stephen McCarthy/Sportsfile/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenIreland’s press officer Kieran Crowley signals an end to the Republic’s media briefing alongside head coach Heimir Hallgrímsson in Backa Topola, Serbia.Photograph: Stephen McCarthy/Sportsfile/Getty ImagesRepublic of IrelandIreland cut short news conference as mood darkens further before Israel gameIreland manager Hallgrímsson calls for ‘cool heads’Says Uefa must consider whether nations meet againAFPSat 3 Oct 2026 18.19 EDTFirst published on Sat 3 Oct 2026 11.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Republic of Ireland’s press conference on the eve of their second Nations League match against Israel in Serbia was cut short as the head coach, Heimir Hallgrímsson, fielded questions from Israeli journalists.Ireland beatIsrael 3-0 in Hungary in their first matchon Tuesday after a turbulent buildup in which the Irish squad voted to fulfil the fixture despite unease among the team over the war in Gaza.‘A lot of lies’: Ireland manager hits out over coverage of Bazunu exit from Israel gameRead moreDuring thatmatch the Irish players wore armbandsand pointedly lowered their headswhile the Israeli national anthem played. There were no handshakes between the captains before kick-off.With the return leg taking place on Sunday in Backa Topola after the Football Association of Ireland (FAI)refused to host the match at home for security reasons, it was the Ireland manager’s pre-match press conference on Saturday that gave rise to new tensions. One reporter questioned Hallgrímsson on his thoughts about the incident on Wednesday during aFlydubai flight from the UAE to Israel.“What do you say about the people that you support? Their ideology is based on murder,” the journalist asked. “Just this week, one of them tried to kill 170 Israeli passengers, including 27 innocent children and thousands of others.” An Irish press officer replied: “We are not doing any questions like this today. We are doing football questions.”Another journalist then addressed the Ireland manager: “Your players call our players monkeys during the match …”, only to be immediately interrupted by an FAI official repeatedly insisting “that is completely untrue”, while the microphone was taken away from the reporter.View image in fullscreenRepublic of Ireland players bow their heads and wear black armbands in recognition of all lives lost in the Gaza conflict before facing Israel.Photograph: Bernadett Szabó/Reuters“Don’t touch me, don’t touch me,” the journalist exclaimed, as the Irish delegation brought the press conference to an abrupt end.Hallgrímsson had earlier been asked if there should be a conversation about whether Ireland and Israel should meet each other again. He responded: “That’s maybe a question that is not for me to answer. But given that we now have the possibility of looking back and seeing all the things that happened, I think Uefa must take that into consideration that they can’t have this happening again just for players’ welfare.“And, yeah, but it raises awareness of the things that are going on. And, if it changes anything, I think that’s worth it. But I think it’s not for me to answer this one. It’s a good question to Uefa.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“Surviving this, coming out of it together as one would be a massive win for me. That is coming from my heart,” Hallgrímsson added. “All the challenges that this team has gone through, all the criticism. Just surviving as a group after this game, that would be a big win for me and for this group, for the association. There’s been a lot of emotions from the people in Ireland about this, and obviously that affects the players as well.“We want to do good, but it’s always going to be a challenge when the environment is as noisy as it is. So we try to focus on the football side, and we’ve done a lot of things to help in that area. One change that we’ve done in the last games is before we go on to the pitch, we do a little prayer and a huddle with the players and all the staff, just to cool our heads before we go on to the pitch.“Conor Coventry has taken that part, so he is now called Brother Coventry in the squad. But it’s really good when you go into a high-intensity and big-pressure game like we’ve been doing, to start the game with cool heads.”Explore more on these topicsRepublic of IrelandIsraelNations LeaguenewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Portugal’s greatest symbol’: Bruno Fernandes backs Cristiano Ronaldo despite walkout | Portugal | The Guardian
