description: Bruno Fernandes has said Cristiano Ronaldo remains ‘the greatest symbol’ of the Portugal team, despite his decision to walk out on the squad
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Bruno Fernandes has said Cristiano Ronaldo remains ‘the greatest symbol’ of the Portugal team, despite his decision to walk out on the squad
Content: Cristiano Ronaldo hands the captain’s armband to Bruno Fernandes after being substituted in Portugal’s Nations League over Wales.Photograph: João Gregório/NurPhoto/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenCristiano Ronaldo hands the captain’s armband to Bruno Fernandes after being substituted in Portugal’s Nations League over Wales.Photograph: João Gregório/NurPhoto/ShutterstockPortugal‘Portugal’s greatest symbol’: Bruno Fernandes backs Cristiano Ronaldo despite walkoutFernandes: ‘There are no divisions in the national team’Ronaldo left team camp this week in selection rowAgence France-PresseSat 3 Oct 2026 15.02 EDTLast modified on Sat 3 Oct 2026 18.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBruno Fernandes has saidCristiano Ronaldoremains “the greatest symbol” of the Portugal team, despite his decision to walk out on the squad this week.Ronaldo said on Wednesday he had left the team camp after the Portugal coach, Jorge Jesus, said he would not start against Denmark. Portugal went on to win theNations Leaguecontest 4-2 without him, and Ronaldo’s international future remains in doubt.North Macedonia v Scotland, Spain v Czechia, and more: Nations League – liveRead moreThe Manchester United midfielder Fernandes called for unity after a tumultuous few days in whichPortugalfans’ opinions have been split over Ronaldo’s decision, and the future for their country’s leading goalscorer and most capped men’s player.“Regarding Cristiano, I had a conversation with him, and what I told him, and what I repeat here, is this – the most important thing is that, regardless of what happens, Cristiano Ronaldo will never cease to be the greatest symbol of our national team, of our football, and of the country, for what he has done not only in Portugal but throughout the world,” Fernandes told reporters on Saturday.“He has a reserved place not only among the best of all time, but also in the hearts of all Portuguese people, and the most important thing is that we stop dividing things,” Fernandes added. “There are no divisions in the national team, it is one and will remain so, despite any noise that may come from outside.“We are outside of this controversy, but what I ask is that the country does not divide itself, does not make choices, that it respects all sides. At the same time, Cris is and will be the biggest icon of our national team, he deserves everyone’s respect, regardless of who likes him more or [who likes him] less.”Portugal beat Norway 2-1 in Oslo last Sunday with Ronaldo an unused substitute, then prevailed 4-2 in Copenhagen after his departure from the squad, with Fernandes wearing the captain’s armband. The Nations League holders face Norway again on Sunday, this time in Porto.Jorge Jesus, who managed Ronaldo at the Saudi side Al-Nassr before taking the national team job, said the 41-year-old was a “symbol of Portugal,” adding that there would be time to speak about him after the Norway game.“I’m going to focus on the team, on the opponent which is Norway, one of the five best teams in Europe. That’s the problem right now,” said the 72-year-old coach.Explore more on these topicsPortugalCristiano RonaldoNations LeaguenewsShareReuse this content

title: Bowie gets Pocognoli off mark with Scotland victory in North Macedonia | Nations League | The Guardian
description: Sébastien Pocognoli secured his first win in charge of Scotland with Kieron Bowie scoring in a 2-0 win in North Macedonia despite a late red card for Scott McKenna
Author: Ewan Murray
Headline: Sébastien Pocognoli secured his first win in charge of Scotland with Kieron Bowie scoring in a 2-0 win in North Macedonia despite a late red card for Scott McKenna
Content: Kieron Bowie celebrates with Andy Robertson after Scotland’s breakthrough goal.Photograph: Andrew Milligan/PAView image in fullscreenKieron Bowie celebrates with Andy Robertson after Scotland’s breakthrough goal.Photograph: Andrew Milligan/PANations LeagueBowie gets Pocognoli off mark with Scotland victory in North MacedoniaEwan MurraySat 3 Oct 2026 17.01 EDTLast modified on Sat 3 Oct 2026 17.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis was an occasion on which Scotland dare not stumble. By the time Kieron Bowie smashed home a seventh minute opener against aNorth Macedoniaside not without its troubles to seek, it was already clear they would not. Bowie afforded Sébastien Pocognoli his first goal as the Scotland manager. Later, the Belgian had his maiden victory confirmed. Anything else, against such a dismal level of opposition, would have been worthy of significant Scottish embarrassment.John McGinn’s 22nd goal for his country, coming from the penalty spot, meant the scoreline at least almost reflected Scotland’s dominance. Only Scott McKenna’s late sending off and a failure to notch three, four or five could have irked Pocognoli. Scotland remain alive and kicking in section B1 of theNations Leaguewhile aware they will face far, far stiffer challenges. Scotland needed to be professional in North Macedonia and met that task appropriately.Lamine Yamal stars again as Spain see off Czechia and maintain perfect startRead moreOn the occasion of Andy Robertson’s 100th cap, it appeared in the early stages that the Tottenham full-back had been stung by criticism of recent performances inScotlandcolours. Robertson marauded forward at will, including inside five minutes where he forced Stole Dimitrievski into a fine save. McGinn, like Robertson, has been the subject of some scathing words. McGinn’s response was as forceful as his teammate.It was Bowie, though, who afforded Scotland crucial early leeway. Jack Hendry’sred card in the early stagesof Tuesday’s loss to Switzerland led to Bowie being withdrawn from the Scotland attack. Pocognoli retained faith in Bowie in Skopje. Bowie had plenty to do when collecting Billy Gilmour’s pass, 25 yards from goal and with two defenders in close proximity. He set himself before firing a terrific left-foot shot beyond the helpless Dimitrievski.McGinn’s outrageous pass from the right-back position to Robertson, who was operating as a left winger, should have ensured a Scotland second. Robertson opted to shoot and dragged his shot wide when a square pass to Oli McBurnie was the more sensible option. As Ben Gannon-Doak and Bowie missed opportunities, North Macedonia opted for two substitutions with just half an hour played.View image in fullscreenKieron Bowie fires Scotland ahead during the first half.Photograph: Andrew Milligan/PAScotland’s lack of ruthlessness was their only concern. Gannon-Doak was clean through on Dimitrievski within five minutes of the restart but shot tamely at the goalkeeper. Gannon-Doak and Scotland soon believed they had won a penalty, only for the video assistant referee to rightly highlight the Bournemouth player had stood on the foot of Matej Gashtarov rather than vice versa. North Macedonia were clinging on as Bowie tested Dimitrievski from close range.Officialdom was soon to smile on Scotland. The match referee had originally given a foul against McKenna as the centre-back nodded the ball down towards Bowie from a Scotland corner. Not only was that decision reversed but Bojan Miovski was penalised for blocking Bowie’s shot with an arm. McGinn finished low and hard to close this game as a contest. Only three players have scored more Scotland goals than the Aston Villa midfielder.Ryan Christie’s arrival at half-time added composure and creativity to the Scotland midfield. He looks the ideal candidate to link play in Pocognoli’s final third. It will be a surprise if Christie does not start when Slovenia visit Glasgow on Tuesday. Angus Gunn, whose position as the Scotland goalkeeper was questioned before this game, had nothing whatsoever of consequence to do.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMcKenna will miss Slovenia’s visit after upending Agon Elezi, six minutes from time. The episode was regarded as the denial of an obvious scoring opportunity. Robertson’s slack pass had landed his teammate in bother.Robertson later admitted he owes McKenna an apology before reflecting on his cap milestone. “It means everything to me and my family,” said the 32-year-old. “It has been an unbelievable journey. It is emotional for me because I love this country and this is a special achievement. I believe I still have a lot to give.”Handily for Pocognoli, Scotland did not need 11 men to win. McGinn was denied his second of the evening in stoppage time. North Macedonia, who have now gone seven games without scoring a goal, are a desperate lot.Explore more on these topicsNations LeagueNorth MacedoniaScotlandmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Verstappen ends pole wait at Bahrain GP in Malaysia but Russell risks losing more ground | Formula One 2026 | The Guardian
description: Max Verstappen claimed pole position for the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia in Sepang, taking the top spot for Red Bull for the first time this season
Author: Giles Richards
Headline: Max Verstappen claimed pole position for the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia in Sepang, taking the top spot for Red Bull for the first time this season
Content: Red Bull's Max Verstappen raises a first in celebration after finishing qualifying 0.298sec faster than Ferrari’s Lewis Hamilton.Photograph: Jakub Porzycki/ReutersView image in fullscreenRed Bull's Max Verstappen raises a first in celebration after finishing qualifying 0.298sec faster than Ferrari’s Lewis Hamilton.Photograph: Jakub Porzycki/ReutersFormula One 2026Verstappen ends pole wait at Bahrain GP in Malaysia but Russell risks losing more groundFerrari’s Lewis Hamilton starts second on the front rowKimi Antonelli in fourth, George Russell down in eighthGiles RichardsSat 3 Oct 2026 05.47 EDTLast modified on Sat 3 Oct 2026 11.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe wait has been long forMax Verstappenbut when the Dutchman finally claimed his first pole position of the year he did it in no little style. Taking the top spot for Red Bull at the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, Verstappen was all but untouchable.However, what was of greatest import for theFormula Oneworld championship was the gulf between the title leader, Kimi Antonelli, and his Mercedes teammate, George Russell. The latter, somewhat floundering in Sepang, is now in danger of losing further points he can ill afford in pursuit of the Italian.Formula One 2026: Max Verstappen takes pole for Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia – liveRead moreVerstappen delivered a commanding performance in taking Red Bull’s first pole of the season, beating the Ferrari ofLewis Hamilton, who also delivered a mighty lap, into second by three-tenths of a second. Antonelli was fourth but crucially his title rival Russell could mange only eighth.Red Bull’s Isack Hadjar qualified third but has a five-place grid penalty for taking a new engine, meaning Antonelli will start third on the grid and Russell seventh. Charles Leclerc was fifth for Ferrari and the defending world champion, Lando Norris, sixth for McLaren.Verstappen, who has been wrestling with a recalcitrant Red Bull all season and is out of the title fight, has yet to take a win and was understandably pleased with pole. Not least in that his team have done so well to develop the car – and that he could take advantage of it with the control and confidence he has demonstratedso far in Malaysia.“It is fantastic,” Verstappen said. “To finally get it from where we started this season, pretty incredible. I am happy with today and I am going to try to win tomorrow. When you start first, that is the target.”Few would bet against him, although a jubilant Hamilton, taking his best qualifying result since the Hungarian GP, will expect to mix it with the Dutchman from the off, setting up a mouthwatering opening to the race. However, it is in their wake where the title is at stake.Afterhis victory at the last round in Baku, Russell had closed the gap to Antonelli to 66 points with eight rounds remaining and was hopeful of increasing the pressure. Yet he could not hook it up in Malaysia, while Mercedes were also left a little perplexed as to why the swathe of upgrades they brought to the race did not deliver.View image in fullscreenLewis Hamilton will start second on the grid for Sunday’s grand prix at Sepang.Photograph: Robbie Hoad/Every Second Media/ShutterstockNonetheless it was Antonelli who still had a marked advantage over his teammate, despite an unforced error going too wide in Q2 that proved costly. The pressure is now on Russell to try to come back at his teammate, who has every opportunity to further extend his lead.Antonelli conceded that pole might have been beyond him but also noted that the high tyre degradation in Malaysia could yet play a part in what is likely to be a two or even three-stop race.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe RecapThe best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“It’s a shame for the mistake, but with a clean qualifying without the track limit, maybe P2, P3 on the road would have been possible,” said Antonelli. “Max did an incredible job and alsoFerrari. We have to be happy because it could have been much worse. It’s going to be interesting but I think Max has the edge on pace. Tomorrow, the tyre deg is going to be huge.”Red Bull had been hoping to continue to bring their car on in the second half of the season and, although Verstappen’s dissatisfaction with energy-management has remained throughout, he will be buoyed by the advances the team are making – and perhaps even more importantly that they are coming to terms with their car, which bodes well for next season. On this form in qualifying, Verstappen has every chance to claim his first win of 2026 on a track where he was the last driver to win a grand prix, in 2017.Antonelli’s crucial error occurred when he had his first time in Q2 deleted for exceeding track limits. He had to go again, using up another set of the soft tyres he could not afford and leaving him with only one set of the new rubber to use in Q3. He was therefore able to make only one attempt at a hot lap and then with care to avoid another deleted time. It was perhaps moot, so good was Verstappen, who improved on both his decisive laps, finishing with an inch-perfect 1min 35.130sec run to put him three-tenths in front of Hamilton.The race, branded as the Bahrain GP, is being held in Malaysia to replace the meeting that was cancelled earlier this year because of the war in the Middle East. Sepang was the venue for the Malaysian GP between 1999 and 2017.Explore more on these topicsFormula One 2026Max VerstappenLewis HamiltonFormula OneRed BullMercedes GPFerrarinewsShareReuse this content

title: Tuchel convinced England have buried World Cup woes with Croatia thrashing | England | The Guardian
description: Thomas Tuchel said England have moved on from their World Cup pain after seeing his side hand Croatia their biggest ever defeat
Author: Jacob Steinberg
Headline: Thomas Tuchel said England have moved on from their World Cup pain after seeing his side hand Croatia their biggest ever defeat
Content: ‘This dominant performance is the way to move on’: Thomas Tuchel with Bukayo Saka after England’s 7-0 rout of Croatia in Rijeka.Photograph: Bradley Collyer/PAView image in fullscreen‘This dominant performance is the way to move on’: Thomas Tuchel with Bukayo Saka after England’s 7-0 rout of Croatia in Rijeka.Photograph: Bradley Collyer/PAEnglandTuchel convinced England have buried World Cup woes with Croatia thrashing‘We’ll always have a scar, but this is how we move forward’Manager praises ‘complete package’ Scott on full debutJacob Steinbergat Stadion HNK RijekaSat 3 Oct 2026 15.50 EDTLast modified on Sat 3 Oct 2026 19.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThomas Tuchel said England have moved on from their World Cup pain after seeing his side deliver a statement performance in Rijeka and hand Croatia their biggest ever defeat.Tuchel was delighted after hisfront four combined to devastating effectat Stadion HNK Rijeka, where 6,200 local schoolchildren were allowed in free of charge even though the game was supposed to take place behind closed doors after Croatia were punished by Uefa for racist and discriminatory fan behaviour last year.Kane and Saka double up as England school Croatia in historic Nations League routRead moreEngland, who have a firm grip on second place in theirNations Leaguegroup and are confident of reaching next year’s finals, saw Harry Kane and Bukayo Saka each score twice and Jude Bellingham become the first midfielder to register four goal involvements in a game since David Platt against San Marino in 1993.Anthony Gordon and Morgan Rogers were also on the scoresheet and Tuchel believes his players have used this extended international break to consign their limp World Cup semi-final defeat to Argentina to the past.“If you feel pain you have to lay with the pain,” the manager said. “The same with disappointment. It was not easy at the beginning of the camp. We had an excellent performance against Spain. The focus in the meetings, the translation of the meetings on the pitch, to bring it within these circumstances inCroatia, to win this dominant performance is the way to move on. We’ll always have a scar, feel pain, but this is the way to move forward. We’ve played in the same manner all three matches.”Tuchel called it a complete performance.Englandpressed hard, offered invention in possession and were rapid on the counterattack. Kane, who will equal Peter Shilton’s record of 125 caps when England host Czechia in their and fourth final game of the camp on Tuesday, felt it had the power and physicality of a Premier League performance.“They just want to play like this, it’s their belief and wish, their conviction,” Tuchel said. “We don’t have to convince them. Harry plays a very intense game at Bayern. We still think we have a certain edge if we play on the front foot. If we push as often as possible in man for man it’s what the team likes. We have to manage these risks.”View image in fullscreenEngland’s Alex Scott (left) said it was a ‘great honour’ to share the field with Croatia’s Luka Modric (right), one of the Bournemouth midfielder’s favourite players as a child.Photograph: Bradley Collyer/PAThere was also an impressive performance from Alex Scott, who made his full debut in midfield. “First start and what a start,” Tuchel said of the 23-year-old. “He is so smooth on the ball, his decision making. He plays with so much confidence. He is so active. The work rate off the ball makes him the complete package. We had a lot of variety in the centre of the pitch.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionScott was buzzing about facing Luka Modric, who struggled for Croatia. “It’s pretty surreal,” the Bournemouth midfielder said. “Probably one of my favourite players growing up because I had seen him as a boy. One of the best players in the world on his day. To be on the pitch with him and competing is a great honour and thankfully we got the win today.”Kane, who is up to 89 international goals, was delighted with England’s attitude. Croatia, 13th in the world, were looking to bounce back after losing 4-1 to Spain on Tuesday.“Every man was at the highest level,” the captain said. “They rested a lot of players on Tuesday. I feel they saw this as their best opportunity to get into those top two spots. During the week it was beautiful weather, an amazing hotel, looking out to the ocean. We could have fallen into that holiday mode.”Explore more on these topicsEnglandNations LeagueThomas TuchelCroatianewsShareReuse this content

title: Let there be blanks instead of Manchester City’s name on trophies: there was no honour | Manchester City | The Guardian
description: The spaces can stand as a memorial to these lost years both as a rebuke to an era of greed but also a tribute to the Premier League’s hunt for justice
Author: Jonathan Wilson
Headline: The spaces can stand as a memorial to these lost years both as a rebuke to an era of greed but also a tribute to the Premier League’s hunt for justice
Content: Manchester City lift the Premier League trophy in 2018 after the club finished 19 points clear at the top.Photograph: Martin Rickett/PAView image in fullscreenManchester City lift the Premier League trophy in 2018 after the club finished 19 points clear at the top.Photograph: Martin Rickett/PAInside footballManchester CityLet there be blanks instead of Manchester City’s name on trophies: there was no honourJonathan WilsonThe spaces can stand both as a rebuke to an era of greed but also a tribute to the Premier League’s hunt for justiceSat 3 Oct 2026 15.00 EDTShareAt half-time in the 2014 League Cup final, Sunderland led Manchester City 1-0. Yaya Touré equalised with a casually brilliant 30-yard clip 10 minutes after the break, and City went on to win 3-1. City, we now know from the independent commission, were at the time involved ina prolonged and calculated act of cheating, while Touré, the leaks in Der Spiegel suggested, was being paid via a dual contract to disguise exactly how much City were spending. Although precise details were left to the appendices, the commission’s report refers to payments “not recorded in an employment contract … but instead recorded in a consultancy agreement”.Had Sunderland won, they would not merely have ended a 41-year wait for a trophy but would have qualified for the following season’s Europa League. It’s possible, of course, that the strain the extra games placed on the squad would have led to relegation in 2015, rather than the familiar trope of sacking a manager, in this case Gus Poyet, midway through the season, and surviving thanks to a bump under his successor, Dick Advocaat.But it’s also possible that the greater exposure brought by European football, the surge of positivity engendered by unfamiliar and unexpected silverware, may have led toPremier Leagueconsolidation, stability and semi-regular European qualification.Manchester City fans are right to feel angry – now they need to direct it at the owners | Will UnwinRead moreShould Sunderland feel cheated? Of course they should, just as those who came second behind Lance Armstrong should feel cheated; just as Liverpool and Arsenal should feel cheated over the League Cup finals of 2016 and 2018; just as Stoke should feel cheated over the 2011 FA Cup final; just as Manchester United should feel cheated over the Premier League titles in 2012 and 2018 and Liverpool should in 2014; just as every club who played in the same competitions as City between 2009 and 2018 should feel cheated. But does that mean the 2014 League Cup should be taken from City and awarded to Sunderland?These are two different questions, and it’s probably best to deal with the latter first – and this, unfortunately, is where subjectivity is unavoidable. I can’t speak for other Sunderland fans but, personally, I wouldn’t want it.Perhaps this comes from never having seen my club win a major trophy. If it happens, I want it to be pure. I want images that will be remembered down the generations, like the highlights of 1973 – Ian Porterfield’s goal, Jim Montgomery’s save and Bob Stokoe’s celebratory skip across the pitch in mac and trilby.I want the surge of adrenaline when a goal is scored, the agonised wait of injury time, the rush of the final whistle. I want tears and hugs and community and togetherness, all the things my dad’s generation banged on about. I want to get drunk and sing on a train. I don’t want to find out via an alert on my phone 12 years after the fact as I unpack the dishwasher.View image in fullscreenManchester City’s Yaya Touré equalises against Sunderland in the 2014 League Cup final.Photograph: Eddie Keogh/ReutersOthers may feel differently but the arithmetic of trophies won seems far less important than the experience of winning and the memories and sense of comradeship it provokes. Glory denied cannot be rectified a generation later by an independent commission, no matter how august.Awarding rivals league titles seems even less satisfactory. In the 2017-18 season, for instance, the league was effectively over by the end of January with City 15 points clear.As City went on to amass 100 points, there was little point in the four sides behind them – Manchester United, Liverpool, Chelsea and Tottenham, who were separated by five points – exerting themselves to try to rein City in.Their priorities changed. United, Chelsea and Spurs all reached the FA Cup semi-finals. Liverpool got to the Champions League final. In those circumstances, why would any of them have prioritised the league? To award United, who finished second, the title, would seem not just empty but arbitrary.That, though, does not mean City should not be stripped of those titles. They won them unfairly; why on earth should they be allowed to keep them? (And yes, something similar could be said of Chelsea, but that’s an argument for why Chelsea should also have been stripped of titles, not for why City should not be).How can those trophies be left in the record books for future generations unquestioningly to see? How can City stand as the fourth-most successful side in league history when so much of that success was achieved by cheating?skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe argument will be made that City’s players strived hard for those trophies. But so did players for those other teams, the ones who weren’t cheating. And how much easier to win in a deep squad full of high-grade players, drawn to City by the money they were offering, money whose source, the independent commission concluded, had been disguised in contravention of Premier League regulations.View image in fullscreenManchester City with the League Cup in 2014, one of seven major trophies won between 2009 and 2018.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianEuphoric memories cannot be expunged, but it is for City fans (and players and coaching staff and directors) to decide what to do with them. If they still want to exult in Sergio Agüero’s 94th-minute winner to claim the 2012 Premier League title, nobody can stop them. But the rest of the world knows what it was based on, that as the rest of the Premier League played to regulations voted in by the clubs themselves, City did not.That would mean that there was no Premier League champion in 2012, 2014 or 2018, no FA Cup winner in 2011 and no League Cup winner in 2014, 2016 or 2018 (and it does not seem unreasonable to wonder, when all this is done, whether there might be more to be investigated after 2018). If there are blanks on the roll of honour, let them be; there was no honour there.Let the spaces stand as testimony to what those seasons were. Let them stand as a memorial to the years when a foreign entity tried to subvert English football, when a foreign entity took this country’s greatest cultural mode, and all the passion and all the feeling, all the sorrow and all the joy, all the love it has entailed, and tried to twist it for its own political ends. Let them stand as a warning of the dangers of laissez-faire capitalism, when everything, no matter how beloved, could be sold off to the highest bidder.And let them stand as a monument to a Premier League that finally – belatedly? – took action, to a process that maintained its independence, to an institution that, at no little risk to its own wellbeing – a risk that has not gone away – in the end preferred justice and fairness and decency over grubby deals with the rich and powerful.Let the years without a champion stand for ever vacant, both as a rebuke and as a tribute. Sometimes, emptiness can be the most eloquent statement of all.Explore more on these topicsManchester CityInside footballPremier LeaguecommentShareReuse this content

title: Celtic fans throw tennis balls at club owner Dermot Desmond during golf tournament | Celtic | The Guardian
description: Celtic’s principal shareholder Dermot Desmond had tennis balls thrown towards him during the Alfred Dunhill Links golf tournament at St Andrews in a protest from fans
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Celtic’s principal shareholder Dermot Desmond had tennis balls thrown towards him during the Alfred Dunhill Links golf tournament at St Andrews in a protest from fans
Content: Dermot Desmond (centre) leaves St Andrews with security after Celtic fans staged a protest.Photograph: Stuart Wallace/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenDermot Desmond (centre) leaves St Andrews with security after Celtic fans staged a protest.Photograph: Stuart Wallace/ShutterstockCelticCeltic fans throw tennis balls at club owner Dermot Desmond during golf tournamentDesmond escorted off St Andrews course by securityCeltic say the protest ‘brought shame upon the club’Press AssociationSat 3 Oct 2026 18.24 EDTFirst published on Sat 3 Oct 2026 14.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCeltic’s principal shareholder Dermot Desmond had tennis balls thrown towards him during his visit to the Alfred Dunhill Links golf tournament at St Andrews in a protest from fans.The 76-year-old – who has been criticised by supporters for an apparent lack of progress on the pitch – was taking part in the pro-am event on Saturday when the disruption happened on the green of the 15th hole.Tennis balls with pictures of Desmond’s face crossed out were thrown on to the green, with Desmond then escorted off the course by security.The Celtic Fans Collective laterreleased a statement on X, which included video and pictures of the protest, calling for change at the top of the club.View image in fullscreenDermot Desmond is driven away from the course after the fans’ protest.Photograph: Stuart Wallace/Shutterstock“Dermot Desmond has essentially been allowed to run Celtic Football Club whilst using his wealth to hide from supporters and accountability,” the statement said. “Fans took the chance today to send a message that this arrangement cannot continue.”On Saturday evening, Celtic issued a lengthy and strongly-worded statement against the “premeditated action” which “brought shame upon” the name of the club.The statement read: “Celtic Football Club has never sought to prevent supporters from expressing criticism of the club, its board or its shareholders. Supporters are entitled to disagree with decisions, to make their views known and to protest peacefully. What occurred at St Andrews represents a significant and unacceptable escalation.“Those responsible have brought shame upon the name of Celtic Football Club and upon a reputation which generations of Celtic supporters have spent more than a century building. The club no longer accepts that the Celtic Fans Collective can credibly claim to represent the wider Celtic support. Those responsible for today’s events certainly do not speak for the many thousands of Celtic supporters who express their views passionately, peacefully and responsibly.”Celtic said the club would not be “intimidated or coerced by organised acts of disruption”, adding “there is a line between protest and deliberate disruption. Today that line was crossed … The club will protect its employees, directors, shareholders and supporters. The reputation of Celtic Football Club is non negotiable.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMartin O’Neill’s side – who claimed the Premiership title ahead of Hearts after a final-day decider last season as part of a domestic double – currently sit top of the table, two points clear of rivals Rangers.Celtic, though, lost the last three games before the international break, including two defeats by Rangers,one at Parkhead, and were also beaten 3-1 at home by Ferencvaros in their opening Europa League fixture.Explore more on these topicsCelticnewsShareReuse this content

title: Zigiotti Olme capitalises on Liverpool mistake to keep Manchester United moving up WSL | Women's Super League | The Guardian
description: Julia Zigiotti Olme  scored the only goal of the game as Manchester United edged to a 1-0 victory over Liverpool at the Unity Stadium
Author: Guardian sport
Headline: Julia Zigiotti Olme scored the only goal of the game as Manchester United edged to a 1-0 victory over Liverpool at the Unity Stadium
Content: Manchester United’s Julia Zigiotti Olme celebrates after scoring the only goal of the game at the Unity Stadium.Photograph: Poppy Townson/MUFC/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenManchester United’s Julia Zigiotti Olme celebrates after scoring the only goal of the game at the Unity Stadium.Photograph: Poppy Townson/MUFC/Getty ImagesWomen's Super LeagueZigiotti Olme capitalises on Liverpool mistake to keep Manchester United moving up WSLGuardian sportand Press AssociationSat 3 Oct 2026 10.52 EDTLast modified on Sat 3 Oct 2026 12.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJulia Zigiotti Olme’s sixth-minute lob proved enough to earn the Manchester United coach, Eva Olid, a second Women’s Super League victory of the season with a 1-0 home win over Liverpool.Zigiotti Olme capitalised on a mistake by Liverpool goalkeeper, Khiara Keating, and, despite some late pressure by Gareth Taylor’s side, United held on to make it back-to-back league wins.Slegers feels support from Arsenal hierarchy despite dismal run but biggest test loomsRead moreAfter a shaky start under the new head coach, Olid, the Spaniard has now masterminded four consecutive victories in all competitions and United are unbeaten in five matches.This was United’s 250th match since the team reformed in 2018 and Olid watched her side mark the occasion with the breakthrough after six minutes.It was a moment to forget for England goalkeeper Keating after her pass out from the back was intercepted by Zigiotti Olme, who composed herself and chipped home in superb fashion.Liverpool pushed for a leveller and drew a double save from the United goalkeeper, Phallon Tullis-Joyce, midway through the first half. Cornelia Kapocs had a low effort saved by Tullis-Joyce, who got up quickly to deny Beata Olsson on the rebound as well.United’s Jess Park hit the crossbar before half-time with a left-foot strike from the edge of the box before Keating saved at her near post from Andrea Medina on the rebound. Liverpool’s best chance of an equaliser came 20 minutes from time when Jenna Clark found herself free at a corner but she could not direct her header on target.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMoving the GoalpostsNo topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe win moves United level with Liverpool in the WSL, with both teams three points off the European places.Explore more on these topicsWomen's Super LeagueManchester United WomenLiverpool FC WomenWomen's footballmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: UAE may halt UK investments after Manchester City guilty verdict | Manchester City | The Guardian
description: Premier League’s actions would ‘have an influence on the bilateral state relationship’, Emirati officials said
Author: Daniel Lavelle
Headline: Premier League’s actions would ‘have an influence on the bilateral state relationship’, Emirati officials said
Content: The Premier League brought 115 charges against City for breaches of financial rules between 2009 and 2018. Of those charges, 114 were upheld by an independent commission.Photograph: Martin Rickett/PAView image in fullscreenThe Premier League brought 115 charges against City for breaches of financial rules between 2009 and 2018. Of those charges, 114 were upheld by an independent commission.Photograph: Martin Rickett/PAManchester CityUAE may halt UK investments after Manchester City guilty verdictPremier League’s actions would ‘have an influence on the bilateral state relationship’, Emirati officials saidDaniel LavelleSat 3 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 3 Oct 2026 11.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe United Arab Emirates has reportedly warned the government it could cancel big investments in the UK after Manchester City werefound guiltyby an independent commission.Emirati officials said “the Premier League’s actions” would “have an influence on the bilateral state relationship”, according to Bloomberg.Elsewhere, the Telegraph said the UAE is threatening to withdraw a multibillion-pound investment in a Silicon Valley-style Oxbridge tech hub.The Premier League brought 115 charges against the club for breaches of financial rules between 2009 and 2018. Of those charges, 114 were upheld by an independent commission in September, which described City’s activities as a “sham” multiple times, adding that its witnesses used at the hearing were “dishonest.”The Telegraph also reports that the City chair, Khaldoon Al Mubarak, met Jonathan Reynolds, the business secretary, in Downing Street two weeks before the Premier League announced its decision.On Thursday, Downing Street said the guilty verdict against City was “serious”, after Andy Burnham was accused of making a “frankly extraordinary” intervention in support of the football club’s owners.A No 10 spokesperson issued the statement after the prime minister said he would be “really concerned” to see the current owners sell up.The Conservative shadow sport minister, Louie French, had accused the prime minister of “publicly backing the owners” amid an investigation into the club’s funding over recent years, describing his comments as “frankly extraordinary”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionManchester City’s guilty verdict brings football’s great sell-off crashing to earthRead moreAsked by the BBC earlier this week if he was worried about the current owners selling the club, Burnham said: “I would be really concerned to lose them.“They’ve been such a huge partner in the building of modern Manchester, obviously, the building ofManchester Cityinto the global force that it is.”Asked also if his dealings with the club would stand up to scrutiny, he said: “I do actually thank the City Football Group and the wider ownership for the money that they didn’t just put into the Etihad [Stadium] and the campus around it but also into the city – but yes, of course.”The Premier League said an independent commission found City arranged “sham” commercial deals with a number of its sponsors during the period, which were part of a disguised funding scheme whereby those companies were required to pay only a portion of the relevant sponsorship fees.The commission found that the remainder was funded by Abu Dhabi United Group Investment & Development Ltd (ADUG), which owned the club.City lodged an appeal along with a short statement, saying the commission’s ruling contained “clear material errors of law, principle and fact, and is unsafe”.Insisting on its innocence, the club reiterated it had filed “a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence [that] exists in support of all of its positions” on Thursday evening.Explore more on these topicsManchester CityManchesterUnited Arab EmiratesnewsShareReuse this content

title: USMNT v Mexico today: how to watch, TV channels & live stream Saturday 3 October | Soccer | The Guardian
description: How will the USA and Mexico fare today? Here is what to know, including kick-off time, TV channels and live stream options
Author: Graham Ruthven
Headline: How will the USA and Mexico fare today? Here is what to know, including kick-off time, TV channels and live stream options
Content: Mauricio Pochettino’s USMNT face Mexico in Arizona on Saturday night.Photograph: Taylor Nickerson/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenMauricio Pochettino’s USMNT face Mexico in Arizona on Saturday night.Photograph: Taylor Nickerson/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockSoccerUSMNT v Mexico today: how to watch, TV channels & live stream Saturday 3 OctoberHow will the USA and Mexico fare today? Here is what to know, including kick-off time, TV channels and live stream optionsGraham RuthvenSat 3 Oct 2026 17.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMauricio Pochettino’s youthful revolution continued witha 4-2 winfor the US men’s national team over Chile in St Louis just a few days after an even more complete4-2 victoryagainst Peru. A high standard has been set by the next generation.A clash withMexico, however, will be something the likes of Cavan Sullivan, Mathis Albert and Julian Hall have never experienced before. There is no such thing as a friendly match when the USA and El Tri meet.Mexico boast their own prodigy in the shape of Gilberto Mora. There is a growing sense that the 17-year-old will be a defining talent for El Tri in theway Sullivan is projected to be a key figure for the USMNT for years to come.Here is your complete guide on how to watch today’s international friendly fixture, including kick-off times, broadcast networks, and online streaming options.USA v MexicoTime:3am BST/10pm ETStadium:State Farm Stadium (Glendale, Arizona)How to watchUnited States:FS2,Stream on FuboCanada:Stream on FuboWhat to watch forPochettino’s experimental roster was always going to make this international window about the future and so it has proved. The outlook is bright.While Pochettino is building on foundations established at the World Cup, Rafa Márquez is aiming to establish a basis of his own as Mexico’s new manager. Mexico have won their last two meetings with theUSA. Three in a row could suggest the pendulum of power in Concacaf has swung back towards El Tri.With so many key figures such as Christian Pulisic and Raúl Jiménez missing, Saturday’s match in Glendale will be played with a caveat. Both teams have much more talent to call on. Nevertheless, this encounter will mark the first episode of a new era of the rivalry between the USA and Mexico.Player to watch:Cavan Sullivan, USA – The most exciting American wonderkid in a generation is justifying the hype. Sullivan looks like he belongs as an important part of the USMNT and will almost certainly get an opportunity to make his mark against Mexico in Glendale.Explore more on these topicsFootballUSAMexicoUS sportsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Michigan state police rule out claim that Larry Nassar was removed from sex offender registry | Michigan | The Guardian
description: Eaton county prosecuting attorney’s office had said court ruling forced removal of Nassar’s name – but he wasn’t on list because he was imprisoned out of state
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Eaton county prosecuting attorney’s office had said court ruling forced removal of Nassar’s name – but he wasn’t on list because he was imprisoned out of state
Content: Larry Nassar in court in Charlotte, Michigan, in February 2018.Photograph: Matthew Dae Smith/APView image in fullscreenLarry Nassar in court in Charlotte, Michigan, in February 2018.Photograph: Matthew Dae Smith/APMichiganMichigan state police rule out claim that Larry Nassar was removed from sex offender registryEaton county prosecuting attorney’s office had said court ruling forced removal of Nassar’s name – but he wasn’t on list because he was imprisoned out of stateGuardian staffSat 3 Oct 2026 10.07 EDTFirst published on Fri 2 Oct 2026 17.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMichigan has removed more than 20,000 entries from its sex offender registry, but convicted serial abuserLarry Nassaris not one of them – the former Michigan State University and USA Gymnastics doctor was not in that system, as a local prosecutor’s office claimed, because he was serving an out-of-state federal prison sentence, according to state police.On 9 September, theMichigansupreme court ruled that the state’s Sex Offender Registration Act (Sora) cannot be applied retroactively to cases involving offenses committed before the law’s relevant date. Michigan’s state police, as a result, removed more than 20,000 people whose offenses occurred before 1 July 2011 from the agency’s online sex offender database.One of the agencies to prosecute Nassar, the Eaton county prosecuting attorney’s office, asserted that he was among those removed from the Michigan state police sex offender registry. The office – helmed by Republican Michigan state attorney general candidate Doug Lloyd – even shared ascreenshotshowing a search for his name returning zero results.The office also published astatementthat read: “The Michigan supreme court’s decision to eliminate Sora requirements for these offenders is deeply concerning.”The statement was widely reported on in the news media, and it added: “Our community, along with the victims of these crimes, expected the registry to provide a measure of protection and awareness – assurances that have now been removed by the court’s ruling.”But on Friday, Michigan state police released their own statement saying: “Information suggesting that convicted sex offender Nassar was removed from the sex offender registry by the Michigan state police because of the Smith decision is incorrect.”US Bureau of Prisons records show Nassar has been imprisoned at Pennsylvania’s Lewisburg federal correctional institute – and “offenders not currently domiciled, temporarily residing, working, incarcerated or going to school in Michigan do not have the duty to register in Michigan under [Sora], and would not be visible on Michigan’s public sex offender registry”, the state police statement said.“Should the offender later domicile (including being incarcerated), temporarily reside, work or go to school in Michigan, they would be expected to register and be placed on Michigan’s public [sex offender registry] if still required under Sora at that time.”The Eaton county prosecuting attorney’s office on Friday issued a statement, too,saying: “We must correct our earlier social media post about removal of convicted sex offenders from the Michigan sex offender registry … We never contemplated that one of the most notorious sex offenders in the history of the state would not have been registered despite the law requiring otherwise.”The office noted that offenses for which Nassar was convicted in Eaton county and neighboring Ingham county had 2009 and 1998 dates associated with them, which “fall within the time frame [of] the recent supreme court order”. At the time he was sentenced for those offenses in 2018, he was incarcerated in Michigan and would have been required to be registered as a sex offender in the state until being transferred into federal custody out of state, according to the Eaton prosecuting attorney’s office’s statement.“We apologize for the confusion,” the office’s statement said. But the statement also said: “As prosecutors, we have a responsibility to provide information to victims and survivors of sexual assault.”Michigan lawmakers do not have the authority to reverse the state supreme court’s decision. However, the legislature could pass new legislation that would place the affected offenders back in the database.Nassar wassentencedin 2018 to as many as 175 years in state and federal prison after being convicted of sexually abusing women and girls for decades while working at Michigan State University and serving as a doctor for Team USA Gymnastics.As of Friday, Nassar’s projected earliest release date for his federal prison sentence was in 2068, when he would be 104.More than 150 women and girlshave accusedNassar of assault. His accusers include Olympic gold medal-winning gymnasts Aly Raisman, Simone Biles, McKayla Maroney and Gabby Douglas.Nassar pleaded guilty in November 2017 to multiple counts of first-degree criminal sexual conduct. He survived beingstabbedmultiple times in July 2023 while imprisoned.During his sentencing hearing, his accusers delivered impact statements describing the shame and trauma they said they experienced because of Nassar.Information and support for anyone affected by rape or sexual abuse issues is available from the following organizations. In the US,Rainnoffers support on 800-656-4673. In the UK,Rape Crisisoffers support on 0808 500 2222. In Australia, support is available at1800Respect(1800 737 732). Other international helplines can be found atibiblio.org/rcip/internl.htmlExplore more on these topicsMichiganUS crimeUS sportsGymnasticsnewsShareReuse this content

title: OpenAI safety leader quits, warning AI company’s culture is ‘broken’ | OpenAI | The Guardian
description: David Robinson joins other insiders in urging industry to take more care over rapidly developing technology
Author: Dan Milmo
Headline: David Robinson joins other insiders in urging industry to take more care over rapidly developing technology
Content: David Robinson said AI firms were not ‘being nearly careful enough’ about developing the technology.Photograph: Dado Ruvić/ReutersView image in fullscreenDavid Robinson said AI firms were not ‘being nearly careful enough’ about developing the technology.Photograph: Dado Ruvić/ReutersOpenAIOpenAI safety leader quits, warning AI company’s culture is ‘broken’David Robinson joins other insiders in urging industry to take more care over rapidly developing technologyDan MilmoSat 3 Oct 2026 15.41 EDTLast modified on Sat 3 Oct 2026 16.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA safety leader atOpenAIhas quit the company, warning that its culture was broken and that AI firms were not “being nearly careful enough” about developing the technology.David Robinson, who led the writing of safety reports that accompanied the ChatGPT developer’s product releases, explained his resignation in an essay headlined, “I quit OpenAI because its culture is broken”.Robinson wrote that a cultural overhaul was needed at cutting-edge AI firms and incidents such as a “swarm” of OpenAI agents – AI programmes operating autonomously without human oversight –attacking the AI startup Hugging Facewere “typical of the industry, given the speed and flexibility with which people operate”.Writing inThe Atlantic magazine, Robinson wrote: “I agree with other recently departed staff that the companies building this technology aren’t being nearly careful enough. But I believe that we need to look deeper than specific rules or new laws. We need to talk about culture.”Referring to OpenAI’s pace of development, he wrote: “As the company sprints from one launch to the next, it is failing to achieve the level of care that I believe is needed.”OpenAI has, however, shown signs of caution in recent weeks following the Hugging Face incident and the revelation that it has notified more than 100 organisations about rogue agent activity. This week it announced it wasscrapping the release of a next-generation ⁠AI modelafter researchers raised safety concerns ⁠during internal testing. OpenAI hasalso paused trainingof its most advanced models.Geoffrey Irving, who worked at OpenAI and DeepMind before becoming chief scientist of Resolution, also joined the warnings on AI on Saturday.Writing in Time, he said: “Recent warnings about the potential destructive power of AI are understating the severity of the situation.“I believe there’s about a 50% chance we all die because of the development of smarter-than-human AI systems, and that our actions over the next two to 10 years will determine the outcome.”Robinson’s essay also follows the resignation of Jacob Coxon, a researcher at OpenAI rival Anthropic, who quit the Claude chatbot developer last month. He warned AI “could kill us all by the end of the decade” – and wasfollowed by Anthropic warningthere was a more than 10% chance AI would wipe out humanity within the next decade. Critics of such warnings have cautioned, however, that they areunscientificbecause they cannot be verified or falsified.Robinson wrote Silicon Valley lacked an awareness of “how to handle dangerous technology” and “what it means to care for people”. Warning that OpenAI had “unimpeded optimism” about solving problems as they arose, he wrote that this internal culture meant safety failures would only grow as systems become more capable.“Imagine ‘rogue’ agents that work like teams of hackers (for example, holding hospital computer systems for ransom) but never need to sleep,” wrote Robinson.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionRobinson called for two safety changes: that AI firms rely on safety expertise in other fields such as nuclear and aviation and develop “new science” that ensures powerful systems in the future are capable of being reined in when they are operating autonomously.“Given today’s risks, frontier labs need to run like nuclear-power plants or busy airports, with layers of redundancy and careful, time-consuming planning, so that the occasional and inevitable human error does not open a door to disaster,” he wrote.An OpenAI spokesperson said the company was continuing to “strengthen our safety and security practices to address the risks we see today”, while working on dealing with the risks that might be created by future AI breakthroughs.“We’re making sure our models don’t become more capable than we can safely manage and secure, and we pause training or hold back models when we need to slow down,” said the spokesperson.Explore more on these topicsOpenAIAI (artificial intelligence)ComputingData and computer securityEthicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: OpenAI says its review into hacks, including on Australian government sites, is costing $500,000 a day | OpenAI | The Guardian
description: Company says it is reviewing 50 petabytes of data after its agents accessed websites including Medicare without authorisation
Author: Josh Taylor
Headline: Company says it is reviewing 50 petabytes of data after its agents accessed websites including Medicare without authorisation
Content: OpenAI has warned that its review may identify more organisations that have had websites accessed by its AI agents without authorisation.Photograph: Dado Ruvić/ReutersView image in fullscreenOpenAI has warned that its review may identify more organisations that have had websites accessed by its AI agents without authorisation.Photograph: Dado Ruvić/ReutersOpenAIOpenAI says its review into hacks, including on Australian government sites, is costing $500,000 a dayCompany says it is reviewing 50 petabytes of data after its agents accessed websites including Medicare without authorisationGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastJosh TaylorTechnology reporterSat 3 Oct 2026 01.39 EDTLast modified on Sat 3 Oct 2026 01.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOpenAI says its review in response to the Medicare and Hugging Face agent attacks is costing the company more than US$500,000 per day, as it deploys AI to examine data that would take a human 66m years to read.The company has warned the review is ongoing, and more organisations may be informed they’ve been targeted in the near future.OpenAI’s Medicare attack has exposed Australia’s ‘tech debt’. Fixing it could bring a big bill for taxpayersRead moreOn Friday evening,OpenAI revealedagents had hacked into a New South Wales government website in June and accessed historical non-public data on bushfires without authorisation.It is thesixth government website in Australiato be notified by the AI giant since last month of agent activity on their services, after the prime minister, Anthony Albanese,announced OpenAI’s agentshad hacked into Services Australia’s Medicare statistics portal.The reason for the delay compared to the revelation of the Medicare attack is due to the sheer volume of data OpenAI needs to review.In a blog postthis weekthe company revealed the large amount of work involved in reviewing its agents’ activity.OpenAI said it has to review 50 petabytes of data – roughly 50m gigabytes.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email“We’re working back through the records month by month, looking for potential unintended activity beyond the cases we’ve already found,” the company said.“To put that in perspective, if that were all plain English text, it would take one person about 66 million years to read it at 240 words a minute, reading nonstop without ever sleeping or taking a break.”The company is searching records for where models accessed and changed websites, or took actions involving passwords, application programming interface (API) access or other sensitive credentials.AI is being used to help sift through the records, and it was costing the company more than half a million US dollars per day to go through. OpenAI said it also plans to increase its computing power as the process is refined.As of late last month, more than 100 organisations had been notified of having being targeted by OpenAI’s agents, but the company said notifying an organisation does not mean private information was accessed or that their system was compromised.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionOpenAI said it expects to find more cases and notify more organisations about events that may have occurred months ago.Australia is run on legacy systems that AI agents can easily exploit, former UN cyber negotiator warnsRead moreOrganisations will be informed privately if they need to investigate and address potential security issues, and OpenAI has said it will publicly report findings about agent behaviour and identified weaknesses in safeguards for the broader AI sector.“We err on the side of notification when our models’ activity exposes a potential security vulnerability, even in cases where it is unclear if the information accessed was intended to be public, so the organization can investigate and take appropriate action,” OpenAI said.OpenAI discovered the latest NSW government website breach on Tuesday, and informed the state government and the Australian Signals Directorate after a 48-hour review.The Medicare breach has prompted the Australian government to require departments and agencies to undertakea stocktake of legacy technologyto reduce the number of ageing systems within government and reduce the cybersecurity risk they may present in the event of an AI agent attack.Executives from OpenAI, Anthropic, Microsoft and Google will front a joint parliamentary committee on artificial intelligence in Sydney on Tuesday.Explore more on these topicsOpenAIAI (artificial intelligence)Australian politicsMedicare AustralianewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Elon is my prophet’: how Musk’s Doge team took a wrecking ball to Washington | Trump administration | The Guardian
description: When the new ‘department of government efficiency’ sent young techies to disrupt federal agencies, not everyone complied. Here’s what happened when one worker fought to protect immigrant data
Author: Michael Lewis
Headline: When the new ‘department of government efficiency’ sent young techies to disrupt federal agencies, not everyone complied. Here’s what happened when one worker fought to protect immigrant data
Content: Illustration: Justin Metz / Guardian DesignTrump administration‘Elon is my prophet’: how Musk’s Doge team took a wrecking ball to WashingtonWhen the new ‘department of government efficiency’ sent young techies to disrupt federal agencies, not everyone complied. Here’s what happened when one worker fought to protect immigrant dataMichael LewisSat 3 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 3 Oct 2026 05.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn the early hours of Saturday 22 February 2025 the following email landed in the inboxes of the entire US federal workforce:From: HR hr@opm.govSent: Saturday, February 22, 2025Subject: What did you do last week?Importance: HighPlease reply to this email with approx. 5 bullets of what you accomplished last week and cc your manager.Please do not send any classified information, links, or attachments.Deadline is this Monday at 11:59 p.m. EST.When she noticed the email that Saturday night, Kathleen Walters already had far too much going on in her life. Number one was figuring out if the lump in her breast that her doctor had just detected was a tumour. Half of her known blood relatives had died of cancer, and she was now 52: the lump needed understanding.Her work life was harder to dramatise with a list.For a start, the specifics of her job at any given moment, as she would have been the first to point out, couldn’t legally be described to others. She was the chief privacy officer at the Internal Revenue Service. She ran a staff of 650 people tasked with preventing any of the 100,000 IRS employees from losing or leaking or even so much as peeking at, unless they had the authority to peek, any of the 266m tax returns they were just then processing from the previous year. “One hundred thousand people is a big-sized town,” said Kathleen. “In any big-sized town, you have some crazy people. I could easily see someone writing, ‘This weekend I audited Beyoncé.’”Whoever had sent this email asking her to list five things she’d done at work was now demanding that all these people inside the IRS share information that, in many cases, should never be shared. She thought it was nuts.She responded quickly, and vaguely, with five things she had done the previous week, all the while feeling sure no one would ever read what she wrote. Her phone was already exploding with questions from her subordinates – a few of whom were saying that their replies were bouncing back with a “mailbox is full” notice. Now she had to sit and think about how to minimise the damage that might be caused by 100,000 IRS employees thinking that they’d lose their jobs if they didn’t supply some detailed answer about what they’d done during their work week. A meaningful percentage risked being tossed in jail if they described what they did in an email. It was a crime for an IRS employee even to acknowledge that some specific person had or had not filed a tax return. “People don’t understand what the IRS does,” said Kathleen.The email came as a surprise, but then the IRS was suddenly full of surprises. Nine days earlier, on 13 February, a Thursday, the first Doge person turned up in the lobby, unannounced, and security called Traci DiMartini, who ran the IRS’s human capital department.There’s a kid down here who said he needs to get into the building,he said. The kid’s name was Gavin Kliger.double quotation markIf I had a kid who behaved the way he does, I’d slap the shit out of him, Traci said – but then Traci was from PhiladelphiaGavin Kliger.Photograph: Courtesy of CDAOTraci called her counterpart at the Treasury department, as the IRS sits inside Treasury, and Treasury always cleared any new political appointees; Treasury had no record of anyone named Gavin Kliger. Traci then called Tim Curry at the Office of Personnel Management – but he had no idea what was going on. Finally, she called security and asked them to escort the young man to her office.Gavin Kliger came with a chip on his shoulder, it seemed to Traci. He offered not even the faintest smile or the most glancing eye contact. Dressed in black from hoodie to sneaker, he was brusque to the point of rudeness. He looked, and was, just a few years out of college. Eyes on the floor, he explained to Traci that he’d come to sort out the problems inside the IRS and to root out the fraud. “That’s a big job!” she said.Anyone who worked at the IRS knew that it had its problems; fraud wasn’t likely one of them. Its technology infrastructure was a case study in government dysfunction, but its ethical infrastructure was sound. Like all federal employees, its staff wasn’t allowed to accept more than a free cup of coffee from anyone who might want something from their agency.Gavin Kliger, in contrast, struck Traci as problematic. He’d somehow laid his hands on badges granting him access to some crazy number of government buildings. His backpack was stuffed with government-issue phones and at least four laptops – and he was now insisting that Traci supply him with an IRS phone and laptop. He also demanded his own IRS email address, access to computer systems with all the taxpayer information, and a meeting with the acting IRS commissioner, Doug O’Donnell. As Gavin sat there, Traci called Treasury again.That guy you said didn’t exist is now here sitting in my office. What do y’all want me to do with him?The Treasury guy went away, then came back and said that Gavin Kliger had been hired three weeks earlier by the Office of Personnel Management and was attached to Doge – whatever that meant.In her nine years running human capital departments at various federal agencies, Traci had never seen a new political appointee just turn up in the lobby and demand access to the computer systems. “None of this is normal,” she said, “but we’re still trying to be nice.” She explained to Gavin the IRS rules: before anyone was allowed to work inside the building, he needed to pass a tax audit.I don’t need to do that, he said.Yes, you do, she replied.No, I don’t, he said.Yes, you do, she replied.View image in fullscreenKathleen Walters, former IRS chief privacy officer, near the IRS headquarters in Washington DC.Photograph: Stephen Voss/The GuardianThey went back and forth like that a bit until finally Gavin relented. Traci then explained that after he passed the audit, he’d need to be given the mandatory presentations about ethics and taxpayer information. Gavin thought that the IRS should just let him in. “He wanted access to our systems immediately,” said Traci.Traci’s next call, at 6.30pm that Thursday evening, was to Kathleen, to arrange for her to brief Gavin on data privacy laws and to warn her that the experience might not be entirely pleasant. If I had a kid who behaved the way he does, I’d slap the shit out of him, Traci said – but then Traci was from Philadelphia. Traci was always telling Kathleen that she should try a bit less hard to see the best in others.By then word of Doge’s arrival at the IRS had spread, and Kathleen had read about them. Anyone who Googled Gavin’s name found a bit more than usually popped up about any given young Doge person. He’d grown up in southern California, where he was into Asian martial arts and the high-school marching band, then had gone on to the University of California at Berkeley. Graduating in 2020 with a degree in electrical engineering and computer science, he’d taken a job as a programmer at Databricks. He’d also been active on X, where he’d retweeted with apparent approval posts from the white nationalists Steve Laws and Nick Fuentes. “One of Musk’s few Doge lieutenants who has embraced the spotlight,”Forbes wroteof him. Most of the other Muskrats scrubbed the internet of their presence. Gavin had written Substack pieces defending two Trump nominees, Matt Gaetz and Pete Hegseth. He’d deleted his X posts, but the Forbes writer John Hyatt had found a research tool, Web.archive,to revive and analyse them. “What emerges is a portrait of an internet edgelord and Musk and Trump superfan who has disdain for government spending, illegal immigrants, and who enjoys the odd racist and ableist joke,” he wrote.View image in fullscreenIllustration: Justin Metz/The GuardianBy the time Traci called her, Kathleen was gone for the weekend and 50 miles away from the IRS building: she needed to find someone else to do Gavin’s briefing. Kathleen was white; the two women immediately below her were Black. “They’d both already read about him and were both already uncomfortable,” said Kathleen. Phyllis Grimes, her deputy, agreed to fall on the hand grenade.Phyllis, who loved working for Kathleen and saw falling on hand grenades as part of her job, never told her how this one had felt. She knew Gavin had expressed enthusiasm for white nationalists, and he likely knew that she knew. She tried to break the ice by walking in with her hand extended; Gavin stared at it and declined to shake it, though he had shaken the hands of the white men who had offered them. “He was kind of cool towards me,” said Phyllis. Before she could even start the briefing, he said,You know,I’ve heard these rules before at other agencies.Yes, she said,but these rules are different,because no other agency is governed by this privacy law,and this law can get you thrown in jail very quickly. As she walked him through the basics – how you can’t use your personal phone for business, how if you happen to so much as glimpse a form 1040 with someone’s name on it you must avert your eyes – Gavin played on his phone. “He’s multitasking right in front of me, typing and texting,” said Phyllis. “It was, here’s a routine that I must endure.”It fell to Kathleen to draft the five-page agreement required by law for Gavin Kliger to be let inside the IRS building on Monday morning, 17 February. The memo that she wrote over the weekend, and that he signed, gave him access to some of the systems but, explicitly, none that contained taxpayer information.Traci set him up in a conference room with an assistant at the beginning of the week. “People started getting these calls,” said Kathleen. “It was like getting the call from the principal’s office. ‘Gavin wants to see you.’ ”Doge had its own private structure in addition to its official one. Officially, President Trump created Doge with an executive order on his first day in office. The president doesn’t have the authority to create or to fund an executive agency, however. Congress does. TheTrump administrationdodged that problem by taking an office inside the White House created during the second Obama term, the US Digital Service, kicking out the people inside and renaming it the Department of Government Efficiency. The US Digital Service had been given the power to hire talent from the tech sector without going through the usual slow federal hiring process. This now ensured that Doge could hire whomever it wanted without any questions being asked, and make it sound official. In effect, all that Doge had done was create a corpse for itself to occupy.The zombie killed off the spirit of the original life form.  Real Doge had nothing to do with Official Doge or the former US Digital Service or any other government body. Real Doge was more like Elon Musk’s pop-up restaurant. “None of us ever signed a piece of paper saying that we were in Doge,” said one Doge insider. The people who joined either worked for one of Musk’s companies, or knew someone who did, or knew someone who knew someone who did. To be truly a member of Doge was to be included in the group Signal chat and granted access to the sleeping quarters on the sixth floor of the General Services Administration (GSA).double quotation markMusk’s plan was: once you’ve terrified the employees, fire them in huge numbers. If it turns out you screwed up and fired the wrong people, hire some of them backView image in fullscreenIllustration: Justin Metz/The GuardianOfficial Doge employed maybe 10 guys in their 40s and 50s who wore suits and could sort of pass as ordinary political appointees, but none had access to the sixth floor at GSA. “The older guys in the suits were not there to take risks or blow things up,” said one Doge insider. It was hard to say what any of the older Doge suits did except to make way for the young guys when they showed up with explosives.Most of Doge’s inner circle just wanted to exist in the presence of Elon Musk. “It was,Elon is my prophet, and I worship the ground he walks on,” said one of the older Doge insiders.As a Doge member, you could get away with saying – or having said – almost anything. What you couldn’t say is that the government actually sort of worked. Or, if it didn’t work, why it didn’t work. This new game rewarded not understanding but speed. The plan was the same plan Musk had executed two years earlier at Twitter: Make sweeping statements about the incompetence and dishonesty of the people working inside the place before you know much about them. Once you’ve terrified the employees, fire them in huge numbers. If it turns out you screwed up and fired the wrong people, hire some of them back.The people who rallied to the cause and felt qualified to execute Elon Musk’s vision for the federal government shared certain qualities. They were mostly young white males. They were mostly from upper-middle-class or rich families. Most knew or pretended to know how to program a computer. Not all of them, but enough of them for there to be a pattern, had been rejected from the most selective colleges and universities and ended up feeling they’d been screwed by the admissions process. They landed at Penn instead of Princeton, or the University of Nebraska instead of Harvard, with a grievance that added to the foundation of their politics. They thought of themselves as the smartest people in the room and couldn’t understand why the rest of the room didn’t simply stand up and cheer. In Washington they borrowed from Elon Musk their status and sense of superiority. They also seemed to share his pleasure in the idea of people being afraid of them.Even among the young men sleeping inside the GSA, Gavin was regarded as a force. “Wherever he went, entropy went through the roof,” said one. Just weeks into their new jobs as destroyers of government institutions, the Muskrats had given Gavin Kliger a nickname: the Chaos Agent.Another surprising email landed in Kathleen’s inbox on 28 February. It was Friday night. “I don’t know why everything always happened on a Friday night,” she said. She’d taken her daughter for pizza and wasn’t meant to be checking her phone when she spotted the emails. The first one that she read had been sent at 6.34pm by a colleague in the IRS legal department. “Melanie requested a data pull,” it read. “It feels not quite kosher.”Exactly 64 minutes earlier, at 5.30pm, Doug O’Donnell, the acting IRS commissioner, had left his post. O’Donnell’s successor was to be Melanie Krause, until then chief operating officer, who had been installed as acting IRS commissioner by Treasury secretary Scott Bessent. Like Kathleen, Melanie was a career civil servant, though 13 years younger. Kathleen had considered her a friend. “She was really smart, and I thought she meant well,” said Kathleen. “She wasn’t a mean person.” They were both working moms, and Melanie liked to share, and share in, the details of the difficulties. Now she’d apparently told the IRS research department to share taxpayer data. With whom, and for what purpose, became clear in the second email, which came from the IRS director of data management:Kathleen,DHS [the Department of Homeland Security] has requested if we could find addresses for 700,000 names of likely undocumented immigrants.1. Do we have legal authority to use the tax return filing data for this purpose?2. If the answer to Question 1 is yes, then my second question is related to a file we receive from the Social Security Administration (SSA) that contains Date of Birth (DOB), Date of Death (DOD), Gender, Citizenship, and Name Control Information for all issued Social Security Numbers (SSN). Would our MOU allow us to use this perhaps in conjunction to tax return data for this purpose?While it is likely that use of SSA data is also needed. The technical feasibility of being able to produce reliable outcome is unknown but likely very low.ThanksKathleen read the first numbered paragraph and stopped reading. The request was plainly illegal. The IRS couldn’t just hand over great gobs of taxpayer information to the Department of Homeland Security or any other agency without a change in federal privacy law. Changing the law was not trivial. She knew that because she’d just done it – to allow the IRS to share taxpayer data with state child support enforcement agencies. The states wanted to know if former spouses who were failing to pay child support in fact did not have the income to do so – and the IRS alone could answer the question. What Kathleen had asked for in that case could not have been less controversial. Basically no one in American politics was willing to come out against child support enforcement, and the change to the federal law had passed Congress in December 2024 with almost no dissent. Yet it had taken 18 months to get it done, with endless meetings on Capitol Hill and the close involvement of the IRS commissioner and the secretary of health and human services. “Doge couldn’t imagine 18 months,” she said. “Doge didn’t have 18 months. Their whole thing was,If you can’t do it legally,we’ll find some way to do it illegally.”This, Kathleen realised, is how they could grab taxpayer data illegally. By doing it on a Friday night. Using a woman, Melanie Krause, about to take over as acting commissioner, after a 10-minute meeting between her and Scott Bessent. Without informing the executive charged with protecting the information. “She went around me because she knew what my answer is,” said Kathleen.The violation ran deeper than the law. The specific dataset sought by DHS was in a silo reserved for the tax returns filed by people without social security numbers. The IRS had created the so-called Individual Taxpayer Identification Number (Itin) back in 1996 as a mechanism for undocumented workers and other non-citizens who lacked social security numbers to file a return and pay taxes.The programme had been a huge success. The IRS had collected hundreds of billions of dollars in taxes through it. Undocumented workers had been able to demonstrate their commitment to the country, and ease their path to citizenship, by paying more than their fair share. (They were still excluded from most federal benefits.) Now DHS wanted their private data, and it wasn’t hard for Kathleen or anyone else at the IRS to see why. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (Ice) had gone hunting undocumented workers but lacked reliable home addresses for many of them. The tax returns told you where roughly 7 million of them might be found.Donald Trump during the signing of an executive order implementing Doge’s ‘workforce optimization initiative’, in February 2025.Photograph: Andrew Harnik/Getty ImagesThe second Trump administration had a gift for creating such moments. It was as if all at once all these characters in a grand masked ball were forced to remove their disguises and reveal their identities. In the Great Unmasking, the nation’s leading law firms, led by Paul, Weiss, would cave to what amounted toTrump’s blackmail demandsto avoid being shut out of federal business.
