His support for trans rights has resulted in years of death threats and “groomer” smears, which he used to brush off. “But the online world is becoming the real world. People have worked out my address, and one person turned up at my house. If you believe a paedophile lives here, it’s not the maddest thing in the world to come and get me. I’ve been saying for years that our rights are paper-thin, and here we are. What scares me is that I can’t see an end to it. Nothing is going to unseat these tech barons – it will require some sort of revolution to stop them. So for the first time in history, hatred is being monetised by an algorithm.”Davies, 63, is the great chronicler of queer British life, having made his name with the groundbreaking (and jaw-dropping) Queer As Folk in 1999. The show followed the lives of three gay men in Manchester, and was a surprise hit, but not without its provocations. The Daily Mail wrote that, “Any nation which allows this … [is] hell-bent on destruction.” Among the controversies was its depiction of a one-night stand between Stuart, 29, and Nathan, 15. In today’s climate, where accusations of grooming are regularly levelled at gay men, would he still write such an inflammatory storyline? “I would,” he says. “Although it’s slightly different these days – because in 1999 Nathan would’ve been in school undersection 28[a law banning the ‘promotion’ of homosexuality], meaning that he had no one to talk to. I was trying to say, ‘This is what’s going to happen.’ Of course, Nathan wants to get fucked, and he’s got no one to talk to about it. People say: ‘Oh my God, he was 15, that’s illegal.’ It’s a drama!”View image in fullscreenAidan Gillen and Craig Kelly in an episode of Queer as Folk, 1999.Photograph: Channel 4View image in fullscreenThe Queer as Folk cast and crew, Canal Street, Manchester,  1998.Photograph: Courtesy of Russell T DaviesWe’re meeting to discuss The Queerest of Folk, a galloping memoir of Davies’s life as Britain’s most celebrated showrunner. He’s previouslycriticised the new generation of TV writersfor prioritising positive representation over good storytelling – his own interest lies in the nuances. His most recent drama,Tip Toe, about a simmering feud between neighbours on opposite ends of the political divide that boils into a horrific act of violence, upset some viewers by including a gender-critical character, Stephanie. What inspired her? “I think it’s important to hear all voices. Years and Years and It’s a Sin both had lead gay characters who were Tory voters – if you watch most dramas you’d think those people don’t exist. I know people who are gender critical. The whole argument is so polarised that to some people the fact that she’s gender critical means she might as well be a murderer, which is just nonsense. There are people with genuine concerns, and they need to be discussed. Where is the debate?”Another character, Melba, delivers a powerful monologue about the state of LGBTQ+ rights, with a fleeting reference to ‘‘women who are furious, and with good reason”. What did he mean? “He’s saying maybe on the issue of women’s sports he agrees [with a gender-critical perspective]. We left it vague, but why’s there an assumption that no camp gay man would ever say that? Why’s it a surprise? I could absolutely go out on Canal Street and find you a rightwing drag queen. It’s important to show that. It’s kind of my job to show those complexities.”Davies is a titan of television – and in real life. His 6ft 6in frame fills the doorway of his Swansea home, where he greets me with literal open arms. Inside, I’m gratified to discover that the TV is on; he famously never turns it off, even when he goes out (“My new one turns itself off automatically. I really resent that.”).It continues humming away in the living room while we chat at his dining room table, which features a ceramic Tardis and is overlooked by an original Peanuts cartoon illustration – a rare splurge that cost him £2,000. His parents, both classics teachers, were the same, leaving the TV on even when they had guests.double quotation markDavies was three when he watched William Hartnell  regenerate as the Doctor. ‘That episode is missing from the BBC archives, but it’s burned into my head’View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Harry Borden/The GuardianDespite their “awe” at television, Davies could never quite bring himself to admit to his father that he wrote for it full-time. “My mum said never to tell him that I didn’t have a normal nine-to-five job, because he would just nag me about it, he’d never understand. So until his death he never knew.” In 1991, when Davies quit his job as a children’s TV producer to pursue writing, he omitted to tell his dad, Vivian. “When I’d have dramas on television that I’d written, he’d ask: ‘When did you do that, then?’ And I’d say: ‘In my spare time.’” Vivian was blind for the last 25 years of his life, which could make him quite “angry and result in moments of nastiness which didn’t become him” (hence the “yesterday’s man” comment). One consequence of his blindness was that Davies’s mum had to narrate the action of Queer As Folk to him. Davies prefers not to dwell on this. “Can you imagine her having to describe rimming? I think I gave it to them on Christmas Eve.”His first memory is at three and a half watching the originalDoctor Who, William Hartnell, regenerate. “Someone told me the other day that you don’t have strong memories before the age of six, but that’s not true. That episode is missing from the BBC archives, but it’s burned into my head.” It was an origin story in more ways than one; his biggest triumph came when he successfully lobbied the BBC to relaunch Doctor Who after a 16-year hiatus (today, I notice that even his shower is home to a toy Dalek). During his initial tenure as showrunner, from 2005 to 2010, it became the No 1 show on British television. In June 2009, he decided to leave on a high, moving to Los Angeles where he was commissioned to write Cucumber (about a middle-aged man confronting his gay shame) for Showtime, but declined roles rewriting Skyfall and working on a George Lucas Star Wars project. He later turned down another role writing on a little show called Succession.Then in 2011, Davies’s partner of 12 years, Andrew Smith, started having “hallucinations of an Edwardian lady smiling at him sarcastically”. These turned out to be symptoms of a stage four brain tumour, and Smith was initially given just 18 months to live. In a2007 interview, Davies had said his focus was on his work adding: “If I’m writing, I would walk over [Andrew’s] body if he had a heart attack.” But when Smith fell ill, the opposite turned out to be true. The pair moved back to the UK, and Davies quit work to become Smith’s carer. “I surprised myself. Before that, I’d have thought I wouldn’t be able to do it; I’d hire nurses and get people in and outsource it. But when it comes to it, you realise you don’t want a stranger looking after him.”View image in fullscreenDavies with his late partner, Andrew Smith.Photograph: Courtesy of Russell T DaviesDespite his initial prognosis, Smith lived until 2018. Davies resumed working from their home in Manchester – relocating Cucumber from Seattle to Canal Street and winning best writer at the Bafta Cymru awards for A Very English Scandal, among other projects – but rarely left Smith’s side. “We were together for 20 years, but when I think of him now, I think of the last eight years,” he says, his Welsh boom softening.“Up until that time, we’d never really lived together. From 2011 onwards, the memories are vivid. I remember every day, almost. It’s weird, because there’s intimacy in a life-or-death situation. There was honesty. He lived much longer than expected, and so every year after that became a joy.” After his death, Davies writes that he spent eight years sitting at home. In practice, this meant completing Years and Years, a surprise return as showrunner on Doctor Who, and writing the RoyalTelevisionSociety award-winning It’s a Sin (about the Aids crisis), the Helena Bonham Carter-starring biographical miniseries Nolly (about another of his early obsessions, the Crossroads star Noele Gordon) and Tip Toe, alongside other ventures. Aside from these professional highs, Davies concedes that, “It was a little bit monastic.” Then, once again, his optimism rallies. “But I’m happy watching the telly. It was quiet, but that was fine.”Last year, this relative quiet was broken when Davies met Oliver Cole, a 27-year-old model on Instagram. “I normally ignore DMs, but I looked at his photos and thought, ‘Oh, hello!’” he hoots. “We DMd each other for about three months. Not sexting. I didn’t think it was anything like that, because of his age. But he was such a nice man that I thought I’d have dinner with him. It turned out it was far more than that. He’s lovely.” Cole has since become Davies’s third ever boyfriend. “Isn’t that mad?”I’m curious to know how Davies’s friends reacted to their 36-year age difference. “They were all very polite. I’m absolutely certain behind my back some of them were saying: ‘What the hell?’ But then they met him. He’s quite extraordinary. He’s Australian, and they tend to be quite tough and ahead of the game and know what they think. I was dreading what [Davies’s long-term producer] Nicola Shindler might think. Then she met him and said: ‘Oh! I get it, he’s lovely.’” Did Smith encourage Davies to meet someone else after his death? “He’d be really happy. His doctor was at another hospital when the final scan results came in saying he was going to die. She phoned me and said: ‘I can come to the hospital tomorrow and tell him, or you can.’ Actually, I was honoured to tell him. I thought it was better coming from me than anyone else. And this describes how lovely he was – when I told him, the first thing he said was: ‘I feel sorry for you.’ I found that extraordinary. Nobody knew me better than Andrew, and I think he’d be sad to think of me on my own.”Davies divides his time between houses in Manchester and Swansea, replicas of each other, with the same crockery and Pantone colour mugs (today’s choice is yellow). He’s “saved like a miser”, since the early 90s, when he was told it was impossible for writers to make money. This nest egg allowed him to care for Smith during the years when he didn’t work, but even today he struggles to spend. “I’m still miserly. If I like a shirt that costs £20, a voice says: ‘Can I afford that?’ I get paid a nice wage, but I’ll see something online I like for £30 and think: ‘That’s too much!’” In the late 90s, he went out on Canal Street every night of the week – he met Smith in Cruz 101 nightclub 10 minutes before closing – but these days he’s happiest writing, or in front of the TV, and has a dread of parties. Kate Bush invited him for dinner during his first stint on Doctor Who, but he’s yet to fix a date.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenDavies with his partner, Oliver Cole.Photograph: Dave Benett/Jed Cullen/Getty Images for The National TheatreIn January, Cole persuaded Davies to take his first holiday in 14 years, to New York. “It was lovely,” he smiles. “Although I’m not a natural traveller, I can’t bear airports, they’re horrible.”Last November, Cole posted a video of himself in the Tardis. Is he a Doctor Who fan? “He is, but that takes about five minutes of conversation; it’s not like we sit there discussing [show antagonist] the Rani. When it became a relationship, I reported it to the bosses at Doctor Who, in case anyone tried to say I was abusing my position by going out with a fan.” At its height, the show was drawing a record 13 million viewers, which I suggest represents quite a wide dating pool of fans. “And there’s not many you’d go out with,” he laughs. “You know that’s true!”View image in fullscreenDavies with the cast of It’s a Sin.Photograph: Courtesy of Russell T DaviesIf Davies is ribbingly dismissive of some of the show’s more rabid fandom, then the feeling has become mutual. Twenty-one years after he rocketed Doctor Who to unprecedented heights, his most recent time as showrunner was polarising, with some fans criticising convoluted story arcs and anti-climactic plot resolutions. In June, his exit left the show at a perilous juncture. A Disney+ partnership with the BBC ended after two seasons of disappointing ratings, and the show is now off air while production of future series is put out to competitive tender.Was he wounded by the reaction? “I’m not personally wounded by that,” he says. “I thought it was a shame. And maybe I wonder if I should have done something different. Except I fucking love what I did!” He erupts into guffaws. “I work really hard on my shows, and I genuinely love them. I think there are waves of hatred, and maybe in a few years it’ll be more appreciated. But it’s appreciated by ME!” What does he think it would take to save the show? “Part of the problem is that there seem to be spasms and ruptures and cuts at the BBC. My worry is that there’s nobody there to champion it. You need a producer saying: ‘What about Doctor Who? What about Doctor Who? What about Doctor Who?’ every single day. That’s gone. In 2005, I made it exactly like a 9pm ITV drama, with a lot of the rhythms of everyday life. That concept has gone now, so maybe it’ll end up as a vertical drama [clip shows designed to be watched on a smartphone] with a cliffhanger every two minutes? When it returns, it should be part of whatever the rest of telly is doing.” He won’t be drawn on who he should be the next Doctor. “I’ve made the mistake of saying so-and-so would be good, and the next thing you know, journalists are at their door.”double quotation markHe spoke to Harvey Weinstein about financing. ‘He could’ve solved all our problems, but I couldn’t even bear a phone call with the man. He gave me the shivers’View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Harry Borden/The GuardianFor now, Davies remains a free agent, and you’d be naive to try to predict his next move. After the success of Queer As Folk he immediately alienated a sub-sector of his gay audience by making a romcom, Bob and Rose, in which a gay man falls in love with a woman; when It’s a Sin broke streaming records, he followed it with the not-exactly-timely miniseries about Noele Gordon’s sacking from Crossroads in 1981. In 2015, when the head of BBC drama commissioning paid him a home visit following the ratings hit of his first four series of Doctor Who, Davies leveraged their interest to make his version of A Midsummer Night’s Dream, starring Elaine Paige. He spoke to Harvey Weinstein about providing extra financing, but got the creeps. “I should have been running after the money, he could’ve solved all our problems, but I couldn’t even bear a phone call with the man. He was just baleful, he gave me the shivers. My producer Faith Penhale, who was on the call, might as well not have been. She had the schedules, the budgets – and he just dismissed her.”While his pedigree now affords him a degree of creative freedom, Christmas 2017 found Davies in a position where the BBC had initially turned down Years and Years, while It’s a Sin had originally been rejected by the BBC, ITV and Channel 4 (one executive asked if Davies knew Elton John and suggested that he might be able to turn it into a musical). He says he’s fond of a Tolstoy quote: “The revolutions have to keep on happening.” Only, “I looked it up the other day and there’s no record of him saying that, so maybe I made it up!” Does he feel that he kicks doors open, only  to watch them close again? “You know those slow pneumatic hinges that close automatically? I think that’s what happens. They ‘hisss’ closed slowly.”His ideas gestate for years – decades even – before they’re committed to the page in a flurry (he first had the idea for It’s a Sin more than 30 years ago; one Doctor Who script was written in the course of a weekend). Unusually, his first draft is often his final draft. Bonham Carter has said of Nolly that: “It’s the only time I’ve ever been involved in something that the script that I read ended up immaculately on the screen. There was not one thing cut, not one thing re-ordered.” Davies recently struck upon a fresh idea, and sent the first script to his producer, only for her to remind him that he’d already pitched it to her back in 2018. After the operatic trauma of Tip Toe, he’s hoping to give this one a happy ending. “I’m very excited. These are strange days for telly, so I  hope it gets made.” And if not? “I’ll write something else.” The revolutions will keep happening.The Queerest of Folk: A Life in Television by Russell T Davies, published on 8 October by Transworld at £25. title: ‘My hips can’t help but move’: readers on the songs that always get them dancing | Music | The Guardian
description: From Northern soul and 90s bangers to disco classics and indie anthems, readers share the floorfillers that never fail to start the party
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: From Northern soul and 90s bangers to disco classics and indie anthems, readers share the floorfillers that never fail to start the party
Content: Wedding crashers … Scissor Sisters on stage at  Wilderness Festival, Oxfordshire, 1 August 2026.Photograph: Jim Dyson/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenWedding crashers … Scissor Sisters on stage at  Wilderness Festival, Oxfordshire, 1 August 2026.Photograph: Jim Dyson/Getty ImagesMusic‘My hips can’t help but move’: readers on the songs that always get them dancingFrom Northern soul and 90s bangers to disco classics and indie anthems, readers share the floorfillers that never fail to start the partySat 3 Oct 2026 00.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleI Don’t Feel Like Dancin’ – Scissor SistersMy now-husband and I attended a wedding. The reception was boring. No one was dancing and people were wondering if it was too early to leave. We sat at our table thinking what song would get everyone up on to the dancefloor. We chose I Don’t Feel Like Dancin’. When I asked the DJ to play it he laughed and said: “That’s appropriate.” We danced by ourselves and people started joining us. The party kicked off and we all had a great time. Years later, we played the song at our own wedding. It makes me happy.Rachael,46,WarringtonCelebrity Skin – HoleI used to go to rock clubs in the early 2000s and this was the only song they’d play with a female vocalist. Me and my friend danced like maniacs, forcing the guys off the dancefloor.Heather, LondonReturn of the Mack – Mark MorrisonIt’s a guilty pleasure for sure, but Return of the Mack always gets me out there. It has been a favourite of mine and my twin brother’s since we first heard it. The melody transcends the cheese and lyrics to make it a booty bopper I can’t resist. The last time my brother and I were back home at a very stodgy bar, this surprisingly came on and we immediately transformed the bar into our dancefloor. Some others actually followed. Music truly does transcend all.Dave, 56, Portland,USI Bet You Look Good on the Dancefloor – Arctic MonkeysIt’s a song that I’ve grown up with and was a staple at the nightclub Welly in Hull that I used to go to when I was in sixth form and university. It was the first song I put down when my wife and I were choosing our wedding evening playlist. It’s timeless.Chris Brough,31,YorkTemptation – New OrderAn extremely danceable classic from an iconic band, which is guaranteed to get everybody up and moving.Calle Jershed, 55,Gothenburg, SwedenRock Lobster – The B-52sView image in fullscreenHere comes a stingray … The B-52s: Fred Schneider, Kate Pierson, Ricky Wilson, Keith Strickland and Cindy Wilson.Photograph: Lynn Goldsmith/Corbis/VCG/Getty ImagesThis is the one that always gets me up, wherever I am. It’s like I was hypnotised way back when I first heard it – I always immediately spring up from my seat when it’s on.Julie Gibson,61,NorthamptonshireI Believe in Miracles – The Jackson SistersIt’s soulful, funky and utterly hypnotic – the song grabs me instantly.Bernd Wagner,Mainz, GermanyGroove Is in the Heart – Deee-LiteIt is still sensational, and so inventive. It pops and crackles along at a rollicking pace, Lady Miss Kier’s vocals give way to insane drum breaks, and it never grows old. It’s funky as hell and just wonderful.Alex,52,SouthamptonLast Dance – Donna SummerWhen I was a college student in the 70s, I loved going to discos. This is such a joyful song. To this day, when I hear it I cannot sit still.Terry Heimbaugh, 70,Illinois,USSex & Drugs & Rock & Roll – Ian DuryOpening with an ambitious drum roll, it moves instantly into a killer riff. This song combines whimsical lyrics with tightly executed funk that’s an absolute joy to dance to.Kate, East CambridgeshireBlinding Lights – The WeekndView image in fullscreenGorgeous … The Weeknd live in Atlanta, 21 August 2025.Photograph: Prince Williams/WireImageMy taste is eclectic, but rarely includes songs that chart. This is a gorgeous exception. The composition is so simple but it’s combined into something so full and rich. Immediately I’m dancing.Jack, 32,BristolMan 2 Man Meets Man Parrish – Male StripperThis song will always get me on the dancefloor. It’s so catchy and the opening few bars are so distinctive that it puts a massive smile on my face.Tim,60,PrestwickButter – BTSButter has a great beat and has also helped me introduce more people to the world of K-pop. It holds great memories for me, of connecting to other people when I was feeling low. This song just has a way of bringing people together, no matter what genre they like.Gwen, Sydney, AustraliaRocks – Primal ScreamYes, it’s a Rolling Stones rip-off but it is pure adrenaline and rock’n’roll euphoria.Dave Ross,GlasgowCalifornia Love – 2Pac ftDr DreView image in fullscreen‘Shake it, shake it, baby’ … Tupac Shakur live in Chicago, March 1994.Photograph: Raymond Boyd/Getty ImagesAs soon as I hear those first few notes, my hips can’t help but move. 2Pac’s “shake it, shake it, baby” is a command I cannot deny. Something about this song reminds me of being 18, hitting the dancefloor and being carefree.Rachael, 39,Sydney, AustraliaDo I Love You (Indeed I Do) – Frank WilsonI have always loved Northern soul and Do I Love You (Indeed I Do) is the song which always gets me dancing. I will often request it at wedding functions. It brings back memories of a bygone age, growing up in a deprived area where music was a way of gathering together at the local youth club.Julie, 68, ShropshireBrimfulof Asha – CornershopWhen I hear it, I absolutely can’t stay still, no matter how knackered I am. And I can listen to it time after time and not get sick of it.Barbara Manighetti, 65,Wellington, New ZealandMoveon Up – Curtis MayfieldIt’s the greatest song ever written in my opinion – it has just four main chords, but it’s so uplifting.Michael, 43, Madrid, SpainJump Around – House of PainThe distinctive horn at the beginning is like a calling, and then the hip-hop beat starts, and you’re already a goner within the first few seconds. There’s something about the track: not only do you jump, but you also want to shout out the chorus on the dancefloor. It’s a 90s banger with attitude.Sofia Ilyas, 45,LondonIce Ice Baby – Vanilla IceI remember my two sisters and I dancing to this song when it played on MTV back in the 90s. We would jump around the living room. I still listen to it now, dancing around the house with my dogs watching curiously. It triggers a happiness switch in my mind.Lara, 39,Bengaluru, IndiaLet Me Be Your Fantasy – Baby DI only have to hear the whisper of “Let me be your fantasy” at the beginning and I’ll be on the floor dragging anyone in my path. This track is such a mood booster.Debbie, 51,LondonMr Brightside – The KillersIt was once played at a friend’s wedding – I maniacally jumped up and down on the dancefloor and the bride audibly guffawed.Neil Vicker, 63, NewburyPeople featured in the article responded to a Communitycallout. You can contributehere.Explore more on these topicsMusicPop and rockPlaylistsDance musicIndiefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Brave from the beginning’: 20 years of Friday Night Lights – the sports drama that dared to be different | Television | The Guardian
description: It launched the careers of Jesse Plemons and Michael B Jordan, and let its stars improvise in a way that was fresh and new. This show about smalltown US football was confident, trailblazing – and wonderful
Author: Michael Hann
Headline: It launched the careers of Jesse Plemons and Michael B Jordan, and let its stars improvise in a way that was fresh and new. This show about smalltown US football was confident, trailblazing – and wonderful
Content: Power couple … Kyle Chandler and Connie Britton in Friday Night Lights (2006).Photograph: Album/AlamyView image in fullscreenPower couple … Kyle Chandler and Connie Britton in Friday Night Lights (2006).Photograph: Album/AlamyTelevision‘Brave from the beginning’: 20 years of Friday Night Lights – the sports drama that dared to be differentIt launched the careers of Jesse Plemons and Michael B Jordan, and let its stars improvise in a way that was fresh and new. This show about smalltown US football was confident, trailblazing – and wonderfulMichael HannSat 3 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 3 Oct 2026 10.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleI’ve been around the south of the US enough to have seen the importance of football: little burgs where the high-school football field has stands that wouldn’t disgrace a League Two soccer club in the UK. Friday Night Lights, which was first broadcast 20 years ago, is set in the most fervent edges of that world, smalltown Texas, where what happens under the floodlights at the end of the working week defines the mood of the place for days to come.Britt Daniel, the frontman of the Texas band Spoon, grew up in one such town, Temple. “Friday Night Lights is based on Odessa, and Odessa and Temple are very, very similar,” he told me in 2017. “The high schools used to play each other at football, and they’re the kind of towns where everything happens on Friday because it’s the football game. I didn’t really think about it until many years later, but you really risked being beaten [up]. Not just harassed, but beaten. Everywhere you went, you really had to look over your shoulder. If you were at the mall, if you were at the parking lot, if you were at a party – people really wanted to fight.”That was the world into which the Pulitzer-winning reporter HG “Buzz” Bissinger inserted himself. In 1988, he moved to Odessa with his family to write a book about smalltown football. He expected something folksier than he ended up with, which was a portrait of young men being simultaneously revved up like boxers and told to be gentle like priests, all the while burdened with the expectations of their whole community and the pressure to win college scholarships.View image in fullscreenField of dreams … the Dillon Panthers in Friday Night Lights.Photograph: Bill Records/Nbc-Tv/Kobal/REX/ShutterstockIt was also a portrait of a town riven with racism, where football sucked precious resources from classroom budgets, and where evidence was everywhere that football was a broken dream, especially in the former golden boys, with their state championship rings, still hanging around Odessa rather than lighting up the NFL.The book came out in 1990 and was acclaimed everywhere except Odessa. In 1993, it inspired a TV series, Against the Grain, that lasted a single series, and propelled the young Ben Affleck nowhere. There was a 2004 movie that stuck more closely to the book, and was pretty good. And then there was the 2006 series – created by the director of the movie, Peter Berg – which used the book as a starting point for something wonderful: Friday Night Lights.double quotation markThey’re the kind of towns where everything happens on Friday night because it’s the football gameOdessa became Dillon, home of the Dillon Panthers. In came characters, some clearly based on their counterparts in the book, others entirely new. Out went some of Bissinger’s more troubling reporting, but the thrust of his discomfort with much of life in Odessa was reflected in Dillon.Friday Night Lights ended up being so good that it transcended difficulties, some of its own making, that might have killed it. Its second season was cut short by a writers’ strike, but was also hampered by melodramatic plotlines. After that second season, with ratings low despite critical acclaim, NBC planned to scrap the show before coming to a co-production deal that saw it air first on cable for the remaining three seasons. It was so good it was possible to forgive its fairytale elements – the show’s de facto hero, coach Eric Taylor (Kyle Chandler), moving to a school across town with no money and no football programme, and making them state champions inside two seasons.View image in fullscreenRising star … Michael B Jordan as Vince Howard, who appeared in the final two series of Friday Night Lights.Photograph: Album/AlamyEric and his wife Tami (Connie Britton, in the role of her lifetime – as was Chandler), a part-time counsellor who somehow becomes principal of Dillon High, are the moral heart of the show, he stern and hard but loyal and trusting, she softer and more empathetic but just as determined. They row, sometimes very badly; they struggle with bringing up their deeply irritating teenage daughter; they live with the insecurity that comes with being a coach at a school with high expectations, and the constant attention and demands it brings.The show was brave from the beginning. The pilot episode introduced us to the square-jawed leader, the quarterback Jason Street, and his sparkly toothed cheerleader girlfriend Lyla Garrity, our leading man and lady, surely. By the end of the episode, his back was broken. No more football, all hopes and dreams and expectations gone.View image in fullscreenYoung love … Jesse Plemons (left) and Adrianne Palicki in season two of Friday Night Lights.Photograph: NBC/Getty ImagesThe breakout star of the show was supposed to be Taylor Kitsch, playing brooding, handsome, drunken, violent, womanising Tim Riggins, in the vein of James Dean at his most sullen, so puppyish you could forgive him anything, even if Coach couldn’t. He’s the one who went straight to starring roles, but the real winner was the potato-ish actor playing an initially incidental character called Landry Clarke, who grew more central as the series progressed: that wasJesse Plemons, perfect as a teenager who’s clever but knows that is rarely an advantage and often a disadvantage in this world, especially when paired with a lack of the only thing that is respected: physical prowess. (Landry’s hapless and hopeless alt-rock band is just the perfect thing for his character.)A more likely star emerged inMichael B Jordan, making the transition from child soap player to dramatic actor as the quarterback Vince Howard in the final two series (his flirtation with Jurnee Smollett’s Jess Merriweather is one of the show’s most touching relationships).Berg encouraged his cast to improvise, had scenes filmed with handheld cameras and did away with “blocking” – the discipline of telling actors exactly where to move throughout a scene. As long as story beats were met, they could adapt dialogue and reactions. It gave the show a naturalism that felt new and fresh in a network drama: when characters paused to think of a reply, they were actually thinking, not just pausing.View image in fullscreenFresh-faced … Ben Affleck (left) in Against the Grain, a 1993 TV adaptation of the book that inspired Friday Night Lights.Photograph: Everett Collection Inc/AlamyThe female characters had lives of their own and weren’t simply adjuncts to the football (Britton had played coach Billy Bob Thornton’s wife in the movie, and had not been willing to return only to reprise looking pretty in the corner). Admittedly, except for quarterback Matt Saracen’s dementia-ridden grandma, they were all stunningly beautiful, but then so were pretty much all the men. Berg’s camera, though, had a covetous eye for its young cast, male and female alike: it’s hard not to look great through a filter against a Texas sunset, as Kitsch was so often shown, often muttering, “Texas f’rever.”Friday Night Lights didn’t overstay its welcome: 76 episodes over five seasons. At times it creaked, but its humanity always tethered it, and its sense of place was constant. If Buffy the Vampire Slayer’s Sunnydale was hilarious because it would just invent locations – here are some docks! Here’s an airport! – Dillon was the opposite. It had nothing. Fast food, a bar, a car dealership, and the open range. All it had was football, and the Friday night lights. Just like Odessa and Temple, towns where anything could go wrong.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionJesse PlemonsMichael B JordanConnie BrittonfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: I craved a mean girl’s approval until My Little Pony broke the spell | Television | The Guardian
description: I didn’t realise my school infatuation was just making fun of me, but then an episode of the cartoon series taught me the attributes of true companionship
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: I didn’t realise my school infatuation was just making fun of me, but then an episode of the cartoon series taught me the attributes of true companionship
Content: ‘I lived for that cartoon. It had all the things I loved’ … My Little Pony: Friendship Is Magic.Illustration: Martin O'Neill/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘I lived for that cartoon. It had all the things I loved’ … My Little Pony: Friendship Is Magic.Illustration: Martin O'Neill/The GuardianMy cultural awakeningTelevisionI craved a mean girl’s approval until My Little Pony broke the spellI didn’t realise my school infatuation was just making fun of me, but then an episode of the cartoon series taught me the attributes of true companionshipFatimah MerchantSat 3 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen I was seven, I was obsessed with one particular classmate. She was the only girl taller than me and she never let me forget it. She was allowed to wear colourful nail polish and had shiny Lelli Kelly shoes, while I had short, plain nails and had to make do with classic black Clarks. I craved her approval.That spring she got an iPhone, and deliberately shunned me for a while afterwards. I cried for hours, but I wasn’t confused. I understood, and even respected it. Why would she grace me with her aura? I was lucky she let me sit at her table at all, even if it was only to taunt me for still bringing in a packed lunch. She was my best friend – I was always holding out hope that one day I would be hers.Growing up neurodivergent, I struggled to recognise when someone was making fun of me. I had sat through the same anti-bullying assemblies as everyone else, but I could not understand what that looked like in practice. So each day I would come home upset from school, kick off my stupid, ugly Clarks shoes, and tumble on to the sofa with my little sister to watch My Little Pony: Friendship Is Magic.I lived for that cartoon. It had all the things I loved: talking creatures, bright colours, catchy songs and a multitude of branded dolls, clothes and stationery that I begged my parents for. But what fascinated me most were the Elements of Harmony. Each of the “Mane Six” ponies represented an “Element” that made her a good friend: honesty, kindness, laughter, generosity, loyalty and magic.double quotation markI tried to assign her elements of a good friend: Honesty? No. Kindness? No. Loyalty? Definitely notI started assigning the Elements to my own friends, a little game I played in my head. One friend was definitely kindness. That one was honesty. My sister was so funny that she could only be laughter. I went through my friends one by one, trying to work out which quality best represented them.Then I got to her. I couldn’t think of one. I went through the list again. Honesty? No. Kindness? No. Generosity? Not really. Loyalty? Definitely not. Laughter? Not when she was the only one laughing.My favourite song was A True, True Friend from the season three finale. In the episode, Twilight Sparkle and her friends have their identities mixed up, and the ponies work together to help one another become themselves again. The song is essentially a celebration of showing up for your friends, unique as they are. They all have their specific traits, their own things they are good at. The true, true friend is someone who helps you find and access your own talents, without overshadowing you or making you feel bad for not having the same things they do.Eurovision made me realise that I was autistic at 34Read moreOne morning, in the car on the way to school, I started singing that song in my head. My inner voice grew louder as I walked towards the corner of the playground where the subject of my devotion was telling a story to her admirers, gesticulating wildly. As I looked at them, the chorus ricocheted around in my head.Then I simply turned around and walked away. I joined a girl I knew slightly who was reading a wildlife book alone on a bench. I asked her if she liked ponies.More than a decade later, I still feel guided by the Elements of Harmony. I love my friends for their quirks, the things that are just them. My best friend from sixth form is so clever she is like Twilight Sparkle in the flesh. My university roomie sends me weird reels and buys me takeaways when I’m skint. When I need brutal honesty, I know my sister will be more than eager to serve it to me.I even think about that girl from primary school. I worry about whether she was hurt when I walked away from her that day. We just weren’t right for each other. And that’s OK. Maybe her elements are different. But I have my people.Share your cultural awakeningsYou can tell us how a cultural moment has prompted you to make a major life change by filling in the form below or emailing us on cultural.awakening@theguardian.com.Please share your story if you are 18 or over, anonymously if you wish. title: ‘Happy Christmas, Ange’: why we have always loved a dramatic TV divorce | Television | The Guardian
description: Untying the knot is having a television moment with the launch of the HBO legal thriller War and BBC’s The Split Up
Author: Michael Hogan
Headline: Untying the knot is having a television moment with the launch of the HBO legal thriller War and BBC’s The Split Up
Content: Leslie Grantham and Anita Dobson as Den and Angie Watts: 30.1m viewers saw him serve her with divorce papers on Christmas Day.Photograph: BBCView image in fullscreenLeslie Grantham and Anita Dobson as Den and Angie Watts: 30.1m viewers saw him serve her with divorce papers on Christmas Day.Photograph: BBCTelevision‘Happy Christmas, Ange’: why we have always loved a dramatic TV divorceUntying the knot is having a television moment with the launch of the HBO legal thriller War and BBC’s The Split UpMichael HoganSat 3 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 3 Oct 2026 07.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere were105,002 divorcesin England and Wales last year, according to the Office for National Statistics (ONS). Right now, it feels like there are almost as many on TV.The new HBOlegal thriller War, which launched on Sky Atlantic on Friday night, chronicles what it calls “the highest-profile divorce case in UK history”. This enjoyably juicy eight-parter is joined in the weekend schedules by the BBC ​dramaThe Split Up– a Manchester-based spin-off from Abi Morgan’s The Split – following a British Asian family law firm specialising in elite divorces.In broadcasting terms, untying the knot is definitely having a moment. With about four in 10 real-life marriages ending in divorce, it’s no wonder viewers can’t look away.War traces the cataclysmic break-up between a narcissistic Hollywood star, Carla Duval (played by Sienna Miller), and her philandering tech billionaire husband Morgan Henderson (Dominic West). Their split sparks a ruthless battle between two rival law firms as they fight for the considerable spoils.“If they play dirty,” says one bloodthirsty brief, “we will be totally and utterly filthy.” Cue honey traps and underhand tactics. The bitter fallout is all played out in the public eye as the celebrity couple come under intense media scrutiny. With its illicit office affairs and drug-fuelled toilet cubicle romps, TV lawyers haven’t been this sexy since This Life.The series is created by George Kay, whose previous credits include Lupin, Hijack and The Long Shadow. When Kay hit upon the premise of a high-stakes divorce, he realised this was a world ripe with dramatic potential. The prenups and property disputes reminded Kay of the glossy legal procedurals he grew up watching, such as Ally McBeal and LA Law. More recent reference points include Suits and The Good Wife.It might have the aspirational sheen and starry cast of a US prestige drama but War is set in London, widely acknowledged as the divorce capital of the world. English courts have a reputation for fairness, expertise and generosity to the financially weaker party. Foreign wives fight to have their claims heard in London. In turn, this has spawned an entire industry of specialist ​practices, forensic accountants and private investigators.Leading man West did his research by listening to theBBCpodcast Good Bad Billionaire and by picking the brains of rich divorcees. “I asked one wealthy guy how brutal it gets,” West told this week’s Radio Times. “He said, ‘It gets absolutely awful.’ I suppose the richer they are, the more appalling the divorce is.”His co-star Miller agrees that marriage becomes a “a commodity to be bartered with – and the more acrimonious, the more money for the lawyers”. Top divorce solicitors have a £1,200 hourly rate. Barristers can charge £10,000 a hearing. Costs soon add up. With an increasing number of long marriages ending in divorce, contested cases can become even more tangled.ONS data shows that couples who divorced in 2025 had been married for an average of 13 years, the longest since records began in 1963. Jess Knauf, the director of client strategy at the mediation service Mediate UK, said: “A 13-year marriage usually means a shared home, pensions and children. When couples separate later in life, there is simply more to sort out.”Writer Kay had plenty of real-life cases to go to for inspiration, from multibillion-pound claims against Russian oligarchs to tech moguls Bill Gates and Jeff Bezos’s record-breaking settlements. He lifted one memorable scene – in the opening episode, Carla is served with divorce papers on the red carpet at her movie premiere – directly from the headlines. In 2022, Olivia Wilde was served child custody papers from her ex-fiance the Ted Lasso star Jason Sudeikis while speaking on stage at a cinema convention, introducing her film Don’t Worry Darling.Full of double-crossing and delicious plot twists, War makes for addictive viewing. In fact, fictional divorces have long kept audiences entertained and enthralled. Here are just a few all-time favourites.Den and Angie Watts (EastEnders)“Happy Christmas, Ange!” On Christmas Day 1986, the Queen Vic landlord Dirty Den exacted revenge for his wife, Angie, faking terminal cancer by gifting her divorce papers. A mind-boggling 30.1 million tuned in, making it the most viewed British TV programme ever.Don and Betty Draper(Mad Men)They looked picture perfect but the marriage between adulterous ad exec Don (Jon Hamm) and icy blonde Betty (January Jones) was a messy one. They split during the third season, with Don angrily insisting that Betty “won’t get a nickel”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe GuideGet our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every FridayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBlake and Alexis Carrington (Dynasty)Much action in the 80s supersoap was driven by the feud between the oil magnate Blake (John Forsythe) and his scheming ex Alexis (Joan Collins in her shoulderpadded pomp). Her rivalry with his new wife, Krystle (Linda Evans), descended into camp catfights.Walter and Skyler White (Breaking Bad)When the terminally ill chemistry teacher Walt (Bryan Cranston) became a drug lord, his wife, Skyler (Anna Gunn), widely reviled for putting a damper on his activities, demanded a divorce in exchange for her silence.View image in fullscreenFrasier and Lilith Crane in Cheers.Photograph: Maximum Film/AlamyFrasier and Lilith Crane (Cheers/Frasier)The mismatched psychiatrists married, then split, on Cheers. It wasn’t until Kelsey Grammer’s spinoff that their divorce was confirmed. Even Eddie the dog was scared of formidable Lilith. Frasier’s brother, Niles, had his own nemesis ex, the much-feared but never seen Maris.Ken and Deirdre Barlow(Coronation Street)“Don’t make me walk out that door, Ken!” Somehow the cobbles stalwarts rode out the nation-gripping scandal of Deirdre’s steamy affair with Mike Baldwin. The final straw came when Ken slept with his secretary, Wendy Crozier. Ken and Deirdre remarried 15 years later.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionDivorceHBOBBCOffice for National StatisticsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: TV tonight: Strictly shakes up movie week! | Television & radio | The Guardian
description: All celebrities will dance to a classic film track for the first time in the show’s history. Plus: Lesley Manville’s fun murder mystery. Here’s what to watch this evening
Author: Hollie Richardson
Headline: All celebrities will dance to a classic film track for the first time in the show’s history. Plus: Lesley Manville’s fun murder mystery. Here’s what to watch this evening
Content: It takes three … Strictly Come Dancing on BBC One.Photograph: Guy Levy/BBC/PAView image in fullscreenIt takes three … Strictly Come Dancing on BBC One.Photograph: Guy Levy/BBC/PATV tonightTelevision & radioTV tonight: Strictly shakes up movie week!All celebrities will dance to a classic film track for the first time in the show’s history. Plus: Lesley Manville’s fun murder mystery. Here’s what to watch this eveningHollie Richardson,Alexi Duggins,Jack Seale,Graeme VirtueandSimon WardellSat 3 Oct 2026 01.15 EDTLast modified on Sat 3 Oct 2026 01.17 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleStrictly Come Dancing6.15pm, BBC OneCamera, action! For the first time in Strictly history, all the contestants will get their closeup in movie week. It’s also the first elimination of the series, with the result being announced on Sunday at 7.10pm. Before then, the dancers take us into the worlds of Beauty and the Beast, A Star Is Born, Pretty Woman and … Baywatch! Will John and Katya remain at the top of the scoreboard? Or is it another couple’s time to shine?Hollie RichardsonWisdom of the Crowd8.50pm, BBC OneIt’s audience v contestant in another round of John Bishop’s upbeat new quizshow. “How many times is YMCA sung in the Village People’s hit song?” is just one question everybody needs to answer – but will someone steal the prize pot from the “crowd” by answering correctly?HRBuckingham Palace: A Year in the Life8.50pm, Channel 5This profile of our monarchical overlords’ tastefully modest abode through the seasons reaches spring. Brace yourselves for looks at rare daffodils, VE day preparations and an experience that will surely be familiar to all as British summer time looms – having to reset your 500 historic clocks.Alexi DugginsParis Police 19109.10pm, BBC FourAs it concludes, this stylish French period drama becomes a courtroom saga, with dastardly manoeuvres in dark rooms replaced by the public joust that is the trial of the damned, elusive Marguerite Steinheil (Evelyne Brochu). At this point, the Paris press become more important than the police: who cares what the verdict is, when public opinion matters more?Jack SealeMarble Hall Murders9.35pm, BBC OneView image in fullscreenDetective work … Lesley Manville in Marble Hall Murders on BBC One.Photograph: BBC/Eleventh Hour Films/Sony Pictures Television/Jonathan HessionMark Bonnar and Patricia Hodge guest-star in the final series of this enjoyably meta murder mystery trilogy. Book editor Susan (Lesley Manville) is mentoring a troubled writer who is taking over the Atticus Pünd (Tim McMullan) detective novels, and this week she warns him of the danger of mixing real life – or rather, people – too much with fiction.HRThe Golden Cobra11pm, BBC ThreeNamed for a sub-par Indian takeaway in a small Gwent town, this lo-fi animated comedy is like a surreal Welsh take on Bob’s Burgers. This marathon of six episodes includes some sly digs at the coal-mining heritage industry and a bombastic car chase featuring a TV detector van.Graeme VirtueFilm choiceKill, 10.50pm, BBC FourView image in fullscreenRelentlessly bloody … Lakshya in Kill on BBC Four.Photograph: undefined Film PR handoutA non-stop train is a terrific vehicle for an action thriller. The good guys and the bad guys are trapped together and there’s minimal space to swing a sickle, so you have to come up with original ways to disable your foe. In Nikhil Nagesh Bhat’s relentlessly bloody, often exhilarating Indian film, top commando Amrit (Lakshya) boards the New Delhi service to be with his secret lover, who is engaged to another, but this coincides with a heist by a family of bandits, led by the psychotic Fani (Raghav Juyal). It’s the one against the many, but no prizes for guessing the result.Simon WardellLive sportWomen’s Super League Football: Man United v Liverpool, 1.15pm, BBC OneAt Progress With Unity Stadium.Prem Rugby Union: Bristol v Northampton, 2.30pm, TNT Sports 1Followed by Gloucester v Harlequins at 5.15pm, and Newcastle v Leicester at 7.30pm.Uefa Nations League Football: Croatia v England, 4.15pm, ITV1At Stadion HNK Rijeka. title: Deepfake review – ingenious interview with a PM who dances around every issue | Dance | The Guardian
description: An interrogater tries to get to the bottom of a surreal scandal while green screen actors meddle with the story in Jess and Morgs’ inventive production
Author: Sanjoy Roy
Headline: An interrogater tries to get to the bottom of a surreal scandal while green screen actors meddle with the story in Jess and Morgs’ inventive production
Content: Unravelling … Kennedy Muntanga as the prime minister with dancers Cathy Grealish, Dylan Springer and Tommi Sutton in Deepfake at Sadler’s Wells East, London.Photograph: Foteini ChristofilopoulouView image in fullscreenUnravelling … Kennedy Muntanga as the prime minister with dancers Cathy Grealish, Dylan Springer and Tommi Sutton in Deepfake at Sadler’s Wells East, London.Photograph: Foteini ChristofilopoulouDanceReviewDeepfake review – ingenious interview with a PM who dances around every issueSadler’s Wells East, LondonAn interrogater tries to get to the bottom of a surreal scandal while green screen actors meddle with the story in Jess and Morgs’ inventive productionSanjoy RoySat 3 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhat audiences remember most from a political interview, a voiceover tells the prime minister (Kennedy Muntanga) as he prepares to face his TV interrogator (Rebecca Bassett-Graham, coiffed à la Emily Maitlis), is less the words themselves than the tone of voice and the tenor of the body. Muntanga is on point, then: his arms sweep, his fingers beetle and his hands spread out, as if he were wordlessly fielding fly-by questions and offering open statements. It’s the moves and the staging that count.This setup lands right in the zone for creative duoJess and Morgs(Jessica Wright and Morgann Runacre-Temple), whose turf is a congenial mix of choreography, film and theatre. In Deepfake, along with writerJeff James, they explore the various unravellings of an encounter in which the interviewer tries to find the truth behind a surreal – but maybe real? – story in which the PM was seen variously spattered with yellow paint, with his flies undone, and partaking in a ritual involving a deer’s head.View image in fullscreenEmily Maitlis-alike … Rebecca Bassett-Graham in Deepfake.Photograph: Foteini ChristofilopoulouThe content of these scenarios perhaps matters less than the ingenious manner of their staging (props to the design team too), which deploys green screen, live relay and other film and stage effects to storify the interview with simulated settings, duplicates of the figure of the PM, selective perspectives and closeups of the central encounter. Spidering about the main characters and manipulating the sets are a team of seven dancers in green body stockings, anonymously blending into the background but integral to the whole media matrix.‘This gap opens up of doubt and scepticism about everything’: Jess and Morgs confront the politics of deepfakesRead moreInitially the tone is paranoid and conspiratorial, the dancers syncing to voiceovers that then start to glitch (a signature device ofworks by Crystal Pite and Jonathon Young). There are ambiguous, unvoiced duets which intimate, intriguingly, that interviewer and interviewee may not only be playing the same game of moves and countermoves, but might sometimes even be on the same side. Later, the piece starts shifting gears, swerving through farce, parody (there’s some delightful and very unexpected play with 19th-century ballet), absurdism, and ultimately a kind of comic bathos, equally unexpected.It’s inventive, clever, exactly executed and quite a lot of fun, but the tone is also scattershot, and the piece ends up feeling more lightweight than its deepfake premise had promised – as if it wasn’t quite convinced by its own story.AtSadler’s Wells East, London, until 3 OctoberExplore more on these topicsDanceTheatreSadler's WellsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Henry Harris’s recipe for vegetarian endive au gratin | Food | The Guardian
description: A worthy, meat-free version of the best comfort dish ever, this French classic is best served with a chilled red and a crisp salad
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: A worthy, meat-free version of the best comfort dish ever, this French classic is best served with a chilled red and a crisp salad
Content: Henry Harris’ vegetarian endive au gratin.Photograph: Louise Hagger/The Guardian. Food styling: Emily Kydd. Prop styling: Jennifer Kay. Food styling assistant: Laura Lawrence.View image in fullscreenHenry Harris’ vegetarian endive au gratin.Photograph: Louise Hagger/The Guardian. Food styling: Emily Kydd. Prop styling: Jennifer Kay. Food styling assistant: Laura Lawrence.FoodHenry Harris’s recipe for vegetarian endive au gratinA worthy, meat-free version of the best comfort dish ever, this French classic is best served with a chilled red and a crisp saladHenry HarrisSat 3 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis is the best comfort dish on planet Earth. Cauliflower cheese held that title when I was a child, but I still remember the first time I ate this gratin, made bySimon Hopkinsonat his restaurant Hilaire in London, and wanting to take it away and eat it in a quiet corner. Endive when braised well retains a gentle bitterness that contrasts beautifully with a cheese-heavy bechamel. This dish is traditionally made with comté and with each endive wrapped in a slice of cooked ham, but some dark, crisp-fried mushrooms and emmental serve very well as good, savoury vegetarian alternatives.Endive au gratinA chilled beaujolais and a salad are good friends to serve alongside.Prep10 minInfuse1 hrCook1 hr, plus coolingServes4600ml milk1 bay leaf6 black peppercorns1 small onion, peeled and sliced2 parsley stalks(if you have them)2 large flat mushrooms120g unsalted butterSalt and black pepper4 heads endiveNutmeg50g plain flour1 pinch cayenne pepper, to taste200gemmental(suitable for vegetarians), gratedHeat the oven to 180C (160C fan)/350F/gas 4. Put the milk in a saucepan with the bay, peppercorns, sliced onion and parsley stalks, if using. Bring to a boil, then take off the heat and leave to infuse for an hour.Finely slice the mushrooms. Melt a third of the butter in a shallow pan on a gentle heat, then add the mushrooms, season and cook until they release their juices. Turn up the heat just enough so the liquid simmers and evaporates, leaving you with just the mushrooms and melted butter. (Don’t be tempted to tip out those juices, because they are full of flavour and need returning to the mushrooms.) Keep cooking the mushrooms, stirring from time to time, until they brown and turn a little leathery, then transfer to a plate lined with kitchen towel to absorb the excess butter.Melt another third of the butter in a heavy, ovenproof pan and, when it’s just starting to foam, add the endives and season with salt, pepper and a good rasping of freshly grated nutmeg. Turn down the heat and cook gently, turning frequently, until nicely coloured all over. Cover loosely with foil and transfer to the oven for 40 minutes to an hour, until completely tender. Remove from the oven and leave to cool a little. (The outer leaves will probably need pulling off, because they’ll be quite brown and crisp by now.)While the endive is roasting, make the bechamel. Reheat the infused milk. Melt the remaining third of the butter in a saucepan, add the flour and cook, stirring, for two minutes. Strain the hot milk into a jug, then whisk it into the flour mixture and keep whisking over a gentle heat for a good five minutes, until you have a thick, glossy sauce. Season with a pinch of cayenne, then stir in two-thirds of the cheese, until it melts. Taste and adjust the seasoning as needed.Heat the grill. Scatter the fried mushrooms over the base of four individual gratin dishes (or one large one), and top with the braised endives. Spoon over the hot bechamel, scatter over the remaining grated cheese and grill until bubbling and golden. Serve immediately.Henry Harris is chef/co-owner ofBouchon Racine, London EC1. His book, The Racine Effect, is published by Quadrille at £40.
